general_review.topic: instruction: Does L2 pronunciation instruction work for adults, what should it target, and which outcome measures show real progress?
general_review.summary:
Method note: WebFetch was blocked by the network proxy for every publisher and index domain, and the web-search budget ran out near the end. Each citation below was therefore checked through search-engine extracts of its abstract or index page (Wiley, OUP, Cambridge, ASHA, ERIC, Benjamins, SAGE). No full texts were read. The numbers come from those abstracts. Where a number could not be confirmed (for example the exact controlled-vs-spontaneous effect sizes in Saito & Plonsky 2019), it is left out.

The bottom line is clear and consistent across meta-analyses. Pronunciation instruction for adults works: d = 0.80 between groups across 86 reports (Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015), and d = 0.76 across 65 studies and 2,793 learners (Yao et al. 2025). But the gains are largest, and best documented, on exactly what v1 measures: specific features in controlled read-aloud speech, scored against a native model. The evidence that such gains carry over to spontaneous speech, and to how well listeners understand it, is much weaker (Saito & Plonsky 2019; Thomson & Derwing 2015; ReCALL CAPT review 2024).

Being understood and sounding native are only partly related. Across 49 reports, intelligibility correlates with accentedness at only r = .32, while fluency correlates with comprehensibility at r = .82 (Chau & Huensch 2025). The field's consensus (Levis 2005/2020; Crowther 2026) is the "intelligibility principle": aim for speech that is easy to understand, not native-like.

What helps understanding most:
- **Sounds that carry many word distinctions** (high "functional load"), rather than every phoneme.
- **Word stress.**
- **Fluency**, meaning pausing and articulation rate.
- **Prosody and connected speech**, meaning rhythm, prominence and phrasing. Studies that trained these produced better comprehensibility in spontaneous speech than studies that trained only vowels and consonants (Derwing, Munro & Wiebe 1998; Gordon & Darcy 2016, 2022; Saito 2021).

How to teach it:
- Give explicit explanations plus corrective feedback. Instruction without feedback did not help (Saito & Lyster 2012), and explicit feedback raised the effect of speech-recognition-based training to g = 0.86 (Ngo et al. 2024).
- Plan for weeks, not days. The successful programs ran 10–16 weeks, and short speech-recognition interventions showed no advantage over controls.
- Spread practice out. In one perception-training study, spaced sessions roughly doubled both the gains and their retention compared with massed practice (Saito & Chen 2025).
- Few studies test whether gains last, so the app must check retention itself.
- Adults can improve even after decades. Derwing et al. (2014) trained speakers who had lived in an English-speaking country for about 19 years and found gains in comprehensibility and intelligibility. But exposure alone does not guarantee progress: in Derwing & Munro (2013), the Mandarin-speaking group showed no change over 7 years. The learner's first language shapes the path, so the app needs to diagnose it.
- The French evidence is thin. Semester-long L2 French courses reduced segmental errors and pauses, but did not reliably change listener ratings (Inceoglu 2019).

Recommended outcome measures, kept separate from practice scores:
1. **Primary: intelligibility and comprehensibility of unscripted speech.** Use a picture description or a monologue on a prompt the learner has not seen. Estimate intelligibility with a speech-recognition transcript, used only as a proxy. Periodically export clips so a human listener can transcribe them and rate ease of understanding on a 9-point scale.
2. **Fluency timing measures:** articulation rate, frequency and position of silent pauses, and mean length of run.
3. **Accuracy of trained features on words never practised**, in both read and spontaneous speech.
4. **Delayed retention tests** 2–4 weeks after a feature's training block ends.
5. **Azure accuracy and prosody scores** only as a secondary, clearly labelled indicator of how native-like the speech sounds.

findings.claim: Pronunciation instruction reliably improves adult L2 pronunciation, with medium-to-large average effects, including computer-assisted and ASR-based formats.
findings.population: Adult and adolescent L2 learners, mostly university/adult ESL/EFL; CAPT meta-analyses include some younger learners
findings.effect_notes: Lee et al. 2015: 86 reports; d = 0.80 between groups, 0.89 within groups (N-weighted); larger effects for longer treatments, treatments with feedback, and controlled outcome measures. Yao et al. 2025 (JSLHR): 65 studies, 2,793 learners, 223 effect sizes, d = 0.762. Thomson & Derwing 2015: 82% of 75 studies reported improvement. CAPT: Mahdi & Al Khateeb 2019 d = 0.68 (20 studies, n = 1,014; more effective for beginner/intermediate than advanced learners); Almusharraf 2024 medium overall effect (31 studies, 42 effect sizes); Ngo et al. 2024 ASR g = 0.69 (15 studies, 38 effect sizes).
findings.design_implication: A self-directed, computer-assisted app is a legitimate way to deliver training. But headline effect sizes are upper bounds, because most come from controlled, feature-specific tests (see instruction-2). The app should promise feature-level improvement, not a global accent change, and should aim for the conditions linked to larger effects: longer programs, feedback, and explicit teaching.

findings.claim: Instruction effects are largest when outcomes are specific features in controlled (read-aloud, monitored) speech. Effects on global listener judgments such as comprehensibility in spontaneous speech are much smaller or unclear. Most studies, CAPT studies in particular, never measure spontaneous or global outcomes.
findings.population: Adult L2 learners across 77 (Saito & Plonsky) and 86 (Lee et al.) studies; the CAPT review covers 30 studies, mostly adult English learners
findings.effect_notes: Saito & Plonsky 2019: 77 studies (1982-2017), coded global vs specific, human vs acoustic, and controlled vs spontaneous. Instruction was most effective for monitored production of specific features; its efficacy on global, human-rated, spontaneous measures was 'relatively unclear' (exact d values not verified). Lee et al. 2015: controlled outcomes gave larger effects. Thomson & Derwing 2015: most studies measured discrete features, and only a small minority showed gains in comprehensibility or intelligibility. ReCALL CAPT review 2024 (30 studies, 1999-2022): practice was mainly listen-and-repeat and read-aloud drilling, outcomes were mainly controlled discrete accuracy, and few studies used intelligibility or comprehensibility.
findings.design_implication: Read-aloud accuracy on scripted sentences is the easiest score to move and the least evidence of real-world change. Every training block should end in a spontaneous speaking task on unseen prompts (picture narration, retell, 60-second opinion). The progress dashboard should report spontaneous-speech outcomes as the headline and controlled-task scores as secondary. Repeated scripted sentences must not count as progress evidence, because rehearsing an item inflates its score.

findings.claim: Accentedness, comprehensibility (ease of understanding) and intelligibility (actual understanding) are related but partly independent dimensions: heavily accented speech can be highly intelligible. Intelligibility is only weakly related to accentedness. Fluency is strongly related to comprehensibility. The field's consensus goal is intelligibility and comprehensibility, not native-likeness (the Intelligibility Principle).
findings.population: Adult L2 speakers rated by L1 and L2 listeners (49 reports, 1995-2023); the original Munro & Derwing study used 10 Mandarin L1 speakers and 18 listeners
findings.effect_notes: Chau & Huensch 2025 (SSLA), 3-level meta-analysis of 49 reports and 141 correlations: fluency-comprehensibility r = .82, comprehensibility-accentedness .75, fluency-accentedness .62, intelligibility-comprehensibility .57, intelligibility-accentedness .32. Controlled tasks inflated some correlations. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition 2025: 50 speakers, 570 listeners; intelligibility-comprehensibility r = .81, nonlinear, breakpoint at 64% transcription accuracy.
findings.design_implication: Make intelligibility and comprehensibility the app's goal and headline metric. Do not treat similarity to the native TTS/Azure acoustic model (effectively an accent score) as the goal. Feedback should never flag an accent feature as an 'error' unless it plausibly harms understanding. Intelligibility has a threshold effect (breakpoint about 64% of words understood), so a learner below it should first fix the understanding-breaking errors, and one above it should shift to fluency and prosody for ease of understanding.

findings.claim: Different features drive comprehensibility and accentedness. Accentedness is tied mainly to segmental (consonant/vowel) accuracy and rhythm. Comprehensibility is tied to a broader set: segmental errors, word stress, fluency (speech rate, pauses), and also vocabulary and grammar in spontaneous speech. Stress misplacement can harm intelligibility for both native and non-native listeners.
findings.population: French L1 adult speakers of English (Trofimovich & Isaacs 2012, n = 40; Saito, Trofimovich & Isaacs 2017, n = 40); Spanish L1 adult learners of French (Bergeron & Trofimovich 2017, n = 40); 37 ESL listener studies (Saito 2021)
findings.effect_notes: Trofimovich & Isaacs 2012: 19 speech measures, 60 novice raters plus 3 teachers; accent linked to rhythm and segmental/syllable-structure accuracy, comprehensibility to grammar and lexis. Saito et al. 2017: comprehensibility linked to vowel/consonant errors, word stress, fluency, lexis and grammar; accentedness mainly to vowel/consonant errors and word stress. Saito 2021 meta (37 listener studies): comprehensibility related to segmental, prosodic and temporal features; accentedness strongly tied to consonant and vowel accuracy. Bergeron & Trofimovich 2017: in the more complex interview task, accentedness and comprehensibility shared the same linguistic profile.
findings.design_implication: The priority model should weight word stress and temporal fluency heavily, not only phoneme accuracy. Spontaneous tasks should be scored for pause frequency and location and for articulation rate. For French L1 speakers of English, English lexical stress should be a first-class track, since Field 2005 found rightward stress shifts especially damaging. Because comprehensibility in complex spontaneous tasks also reflects vocabulary and grammar (Bergeron & Trofimovich 2017, L2 French), spontaneous prompts should be level-appropriate, and the app should not blame pronunciation for lexical breakdowns.

findings.claim: Not all segmental errors matter equally. Errors on high-functional-load contrasts (sound pairs that distinguish many words) and structural errors (sound insertion or deletion, consonant-cluster simplification, inappropriate syllable reduction) harm comprehensibility and intelligibility. Low-functional-load substitutions mostly affect accent.
findings.population: Adult ESL/EFL speakers: Cantonese L1 (Munro & Derwing 2006), Japanese EFL (Suzukida & Saito 2021, n = 40 in Exp. 1), speakers of six English varieties rated by 60 listeners (Kang et al.)
findings.effect_notes: Suzukida & Saito 2021: only high-functional-load consonant substitutions (e.g., /l/-/r/, /v/-/b/) negatively affected native listeners' comprehensibility judgments. Munro & Derwing 2006: comprehensibility related to high-functional-load errors, and less to low-functional-load ones. Kang, Thomson & Moran 2018/2020: the number of specific features (C/V insertion/deletion, syllable reduction, cluster divergence) predicted intelligibility and listening comprehension. All evidence is correlational and English-only.
findings.design_implication: Choose drill targets by communicative impact × error frequency, not by 'lowest rolling average score'. Add a functional-load weight to each phoneme contrast, plus separate detectors for insertions, deletions and cluster simplification, which Azure reports as omission and insertion errors. For French, no validated functional-load hierarchy was found. Use minimal-pair lexical frequency as a provisional weight and flag it as unvalidated.

findings.claim: In a small number of short classroom quasi-experiments with small samples, prosody- and global-focused instruction produced comprehensibility and fluency gains in spontaneous speech where segment-focused instruction did not. Those studies are Derwing, Munro & Wiebe 1998 (12 weeks), Gordon & Darcy 2016 and 2022, and Darcy & Rocca 2022. In Derwing et al. 1998, both segmental and global instruction improved controlled sentence reading. This supports giving prosody substantial weight. It does not show a fixed ratio or that segment-focused instruction cannot transfer. Segmental instruction with feedback on a high-impact sound has reached spontaneous production of that sound (Saito & Lyster 2012). One ASR meta-analysis (Ngo et al. 2024) reports larger effects for segmental than suprasegmental targets. That comparison rests on few suprasegmental studies and may reflect what current tools are built to target.
findings.population: Adult ESL learners in Canada (Derwing et al. 1998, 12 weeks); Costa Rican university EFL learners (Gordon & Darcy 2022, 10 weeks); US ESL (Darcy & Rocca 2022); 17 ESL training studies (Saito 2021); 15 ASR studies (Ngo et al. 2024)
findings.effect_notes: Derwing, Munro & Wiebe 1998: 48 listeners rated sentences, 6 teachers rated narratives; the global/prosody group improved comprehensibility and fluency in narratives, while both instructed groups improved only on sentence reading. Gordon & Darcy 2016 and 2022: only the suprasegmental group improved comprehensibility and fluency in spontaneous speech; the segmental and mixed groups did not; no group improved in accentedness. Saito 2021: instruction produced larger gains in comprehensibility than in native-likeness, clearest when it targeted prosody. Ngo et al. 2024: ASR effects g = 0.82 for segmentals vs g = 0.37 for suprasegmentals. Samples are small, so the evidence is not definitive.
findings.design_implication: Give prosody and fluency training at least equal weight to phoneme drills, not a single 'prosody track' among three. English: lexical stress, vowel reduction, prominence and thought groups. French: phrase-final prominence, enchaînement and liaison, syllable timing. Each prosody lesson should end in a communicative, contextualized use of the feature (the 'integrated' model in Darcy & Rocca 2022). Because Azure-style ASR scoring is weaker on suprasegmentals, prosody feedback needs dedicated measures such as stress placement, pause location and F0 contour comparison, not a single prosody number.

citations.ref: Derwing, Munro & Wiebe (1998). Evidence in favor of a broad framework for pronunciation instruction. Language Learning 48(3), 393-410. doi:10.1111/0023-8333.00047

findings.claim: Corrective feedback is consistently linked to larger instructional effects: it is a significant moderator in Lee et al. 2015. In one classroom study on a single English sound (Saito & Lyster 2012, 65 Japanese learners, 4 hours), feedback was needed for gains that reached spontaneous speech, and form-focused instruction without feedback showed no significant change. Evidence that explicit articulatory or phonetic explanation adds value beyond practice with good input is mixed. Saito 2013 (SSLA) and an SSLA explicit-vs-implicit study (likely Zhang & Yuan 2020) found advantages. Kissling 2013 (Modern Language Journal, Spanish FL) found explicit phonetics instruction no better than the same practice without explicit explanation.
findings.population: Japanese EFL adults (Saito & Lyster 2012, n = 65, 4 h of form-focused instruction); an SSLA explicit-vs-implicit study on word-final devoicing; ASR studies with explicit feedback (8 studies in Ngo et al. 2024); adult ESL learners in Hirschi et al. 2025
findings.effect_notes: Lee et al. 2015: feedback was a significant moderator (larger effects). Saito & Lyster 2012: form-focused instruction plus recasts improved /ɹ/ (F3) in both controlled and spontaneous speech; the same instruction without feedback and the control group showed no significant change; generalization to novel words was unclear. Ngo et al. 2024: explicit corrective feedback g = 0.86 vs overall ASR g = 0.69. The SSLA explicit-instruction study found explicit > implicit on all four acoustic measures. Crowther & Loewen 2025 review the instructed-SLA evidence on which instruction types work best.
findings.design_implication: Every targeted drill should include: (1) a short explicit explanation of how to make the sound or pattern and how to hear it (diagram, slowed contrast audio); (2) specific, actionable corrective feedback, such as which segment went wrong and what to change ('tongue further back', 'lengthen the stressed vowel'), not only a traffic-light colour; (3) a feedback-enabled practice phase in meaningful sentences and short free speech. LLM-generated narrative feedback on high-functional-load segments, prominence, thought groups and pauses has early support (Hirschi et al. 2025), but is exploratory.

findings.claim: Across studies, longer treatments are associated with larger effects in meta-analytic moderator analyses (Lee et al. 2015). This is a between-study correlation, confounded with design and outcome type. Short ASR interventions may show little advantage over non-ASR comparison conditions (one meta-analytic moderator, not re-checked). Programs that improved spontaneous comprehensibility have ranged from a few weeks to about 16 weeks. A 4-hour form-focused intervention with feedback improved one sound in spontaneous speech (Saito & Lyster 2012), so 10-16 weeks is a typical study length, not an established threshold. Evidence that spaced schedules beat massed schedules for phonetic learning comes mainly from a few recent perception-training studies. It is untested for production, and in other L2 domains shorter spacing has sometimes beaten longer spacing.
findings.population: Adult L2 learners (meta-analytic moderators); Mandarin-speaking learners of English /ɛ/-/æ/ perception (Saito & Chen 2025); English [i]-[ɪ] training (Li, MLJ)
findings.effect_notes: Lee et al. 2015: longer interventions gave larger effects. Ngo et al. 2024: medium-to-long ASR training gave higher outcomes, and short training had no advantage over non-ASR conditions. Uchihara, Karas & Thomson 2025: total training time moderated perceptual training effects. Program lengths in successful studies: Derwing et al. 1998, 12 weeks; Gordon & Darcy 2022, 10 weeks; Kennedy et al. 2014, 15 weeks; Inceoglu 2019, 16 weeks. Saito & Chen 2025: spaced groups' effect sizes roughly double the massed group's for immediate gains and retention; equal vs expanding spacing did not differ. Spacing evidence is from perception training and needs replication for production.
findings.design_implication: Design the product as a multi-week program: 8-16-week cycles of short daily or near-daily sessions (about 15-20 minutes). Rotate each target feature on an expanding or equal spacing schedule rather than drilling it to mastery in one sitting. Set expectations in the UI: feature accuracy can move within days, but spontaneous comprehensibility and fluency change over weeks to months. A session planner should schedule revisits of mastered features at growing intervals.

findings.claim: Whether gains last and generalize is under-tested for production. Perceptual training gains are retained and partly generalize. Production gains from perception-only training are small, generalize weakly to untrained words, and are not clearly retained.
findings.population: Adult L2 learners in perceptual/HVPT training studies (79 studies; 31 production studies; 25 years of perception-training research)
findings.effect_notes: Uchihara, Karas & Thomson 2025: HVPT perception gains g = 0.92 pre-post (k = 96) and g = 0.67 vs control (k = 32); long-term retention confirmed, some generalization to novel stimuli. Applied Psycholinguistics 2024 (31 studies): small-to-medium production gains, +10.5% on trained items and +4.5% on untrained items; no strong support for retention or generalization; perception-production gain correlation negligible at participant level. Sakai & Moorman 2018: perception training d = 0.92 on perception, d = 0.54 on production. Thomson & Derwing 2015 flagged the lack of delayed posttests.
findings.design_implication: Only count progress that survives delay and transfers. (1) Hold out untrained words and sentences for each target feature and test only on those. (2) Schedule a delayed retention probe 2-4 weeks after a feature's training block. (3) Mark a feature 'learned' only when accuracy holds on untrained items at the delayed probe, in both read and spontaneous speech. Include short perception (listen-and-identify) exercises for difficult contrasts, since they give reliable perceptual gains, but always pair them with production practice and feedback.

findings.claim: Saito & Plonsky (2019) proposed a framework that separates construct (global vs specific), scoring method (human vs automatic) and elicitation (controlled vs spontaneous). This is a measurement proposal, not an empirical finding. One training, validation and generalization study (Saito et al., SSLA) showed that phonological, prosodic and temporal features can predict listener comprehensibility at group level. Evidence on how closely ASR intelligibility tracks human listeners for an individual speaker is very limited. One small study (Inceoglu, Chen & Lim 2023, 4 speakers) found agreement on average but divergence for most individuals. Older research found ASR far worse than human listeners on L2 speech (Derwing, Munro & Carbonaro 2000). Agreement is likely to depend on the ASR system and the speaker, so per-user validation is prudent, but its size is not established.
findings.population: 190 L1 and L2 English speakers (automated comprehensibility study); 4 Taiwanese intermediate EFL speakers × 12 L1 listeners (Inceoglu et al. 2023)
findings.effect_notes: Saito & Plonsky 2019 proposed the three-parameter measurement framework. The SSLA 2022 automated comprehensibility study: a regression on phonological, prosodic and temporal measures (articulation rate, pause frequency) significantly predicted naive listeners' comprehensibility levels in picture descriptions. Inceoglu, Chen & Lim 2023: word task ASR 40.8% vs listeners 38.6%; sentence task ASR 75.5% vs listeners 83.9%; similar error types, but ASR mirrored listener judgments for only 1 of 4 speakers. Chau & Huensch 2025: fluency-comprehensibility r = .82 supports temporal measures as a good proxy.
findings.design_implication: Build a separate 'Progress Check' (every 2-4 weeks) distinct from practice, with a fixed battery. (A) Spontaneous intelligibility proxy: the learner speaks on an unseen picture or prompt, the ASR transcript is compared with the learner's own corrected intended transcript, and word-level recognition is logged. (B) Temporal fluency from word timestamps: articulation rate, pause frequency and whether pauses fall inside or between clauses, mean length of run. (C) Feature accuracy on held-out items. (D) Optional human gold standard: export 3-4 clips for a native or proficient listener to transcribe (intelligibility) and rate ease of understanding on a 9-point scale (comprehensibility). Use it to check that the automated proxies track real listeners for this particular user. (E) Azure accuracy/prosody shown only as a secondary 'native-model similarity' indicator.

findings.claim: For L2 French, explicit pronunciation courses reduce segmental errors and pausing, but the evidence base is much thinner than for English, and listener-rated comprehensibility and accentedness did not reliably improve. Connected-speech features (liaison, enchaînement) are slow to change.
findings.population: Adult/university learners of French (Kennedy et al. 2014, n = 30, 15 weeks; Inceoglu 2019, 16-week online course; System 2013 explicit phonetics study); Spanish L1 learners of French (Bergeron & Trofimovich 2017)
findings.effect_notes: Inceoglu 2019: significant decrease in segmental errors and unfilled pause frequency across all tasks (including conversation) and fluency gains in reading and conversation; liaison and enchaînement showed a positive but non-significant trend; no significant change in listener ratings of accentedness, comprehensibility or fluency (5 native raters). Kennedy, Blanchet & Trofimovich 2014: 30 adults, 15-week course on segmentals, suprasegmentals, liaison, enchaînement, intonation and fluency. The System 2013 study found a significant between-group advantage for explicit phonetics instruction in L2 French.
findings.design_implication: Do not assume English-derived targets and effect sizes carry over to French. For fr-FR, focus on segmental accuracy for high-impact contrasts and on fluency, both of which responded to instruction. Treat liaison and enchaînement as long-horizon goals with spaced practice. Measure French progress with listener-based spontaneous tasks, since read-aloud gains did not show up in listener ratings. Add awareness and self-reflection prompts ('what did you notice about your /y/?'), because Kennedy et al. describe awareness and instruction as mutually reinforcing.

citations.ref: Inceoglu (2019). Exploring the effects of instruction on L2 French learner pronunciation, accentedness, comprehensibility, and fluency: An online classroom study. Journal of Second Language Pronunciation 5(2), 223-246.

findings.claim: One small workplace training study (Derwing et al. 2014) reported gains in perception and comprehensibility, with some intelligibility gains, in long-resident adult immigrants (mean of about 19 years in Canada) after targeted training. This suggests that improvement remains possible after long residence, but it is a single small study without a randomized control. In a 7-year longitudinal study of small groups (Derwing & Munro 2013), a Slavic-L1 group improved in comprehensibility and fluency while a Mandarin-L1 group did not. The authors linked this to differences in communicative experience and willingness to communicate, which were confounded with L1 group. Other longitudinal work suggests that accent-related change is concentrated early in residence.
findings.population: Adult immigrants to Canada: 7-year longitudinal study of Mandarin L1 vs Slavic L1 speakers (Derwing & Munro 2013); workplace trainees averaging 19 years of residence (Derwing et al. 2014)
findings.effect_notes: Derwing & Munro 2013: Mandarin L1 group showed no change on any dimension over 7 years; the Slavic L1 group improved in comprehensibility and fluency; accent improvement was limited to the first 2 years. Derwing et al. 2014: significant improvement in perception, comprehensibility and intelligibility after workplace training; no change in fluency; accent rated stronger at one posttest.
findings.design_implication: The app needs an onboarding diagnostic: first language(s), which language is native vs L2, and a baseline spontaneous sample in each target language. That drives an L1-specific priority list rather than one generic phoneme inventory. Frame the goal as understandable speech, which is achievable at any age, rather than accent removal, which is unlikely to change much. Because gains depend on real communicative use (conversation depth and willingness to communicate in Derwing & Munro 2013), include transfer prompts: a short real-life speaking mission each week, logged by the learner.

citations.ref: Derwing & Munro (2013). The development of L2 oral language skills in two L1 groups: A 7-year study. Language Learning 63, 163-185. doi:10.1111/lang.12000
Derwing, Munro, Foote, Waugh & Fleming (2014). Opening the window on comprehensible pronunciation after 19 years: A workplace training study. Language Learning 64, 526-548. doi:10.1111/lang.12053

does_not_work_verified.claim: Aiming for native-likeness or accent reduction
does_not_work_verified.notes: The core recommendation (target intelligibility and comprehensibility) is well supported: Munro & Derwing 1995; Derwing & Munro 1997; the Levis intelligibility principle. One supporting reason is overstated. 'Accent rarely changed in instruction studies' is not accurate: in Derwing et al. 1998, both instructed groups improved accentedness in sentence reading, and Saito 2021 reports gains in native-likeness, smaller than the gains in comprehensibility. Accent can move a little in controlled speech. It moves little in spontaneous speech and is not needed for being understood. The r = .32 figure (Chau & Huensch 2025) was not verified.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Assuming read-aloud or listen-and-repeat drilling transfers on its own to spontaneous speech
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by Derwing et al. 1998 (segmental group: sentence gains only), Saito & Plonsky 2019, Lee et al. 2015 (controlled > free outcomes) and Thomson & Derwing 2015. The ReCALL CAPT review is Amrate & Tsai (ReCALL 37(1), 2025). Note: transfer is not impossible. It seems to need feedback, explicit information and meaningful practice (Saito & Lyster 2012; Saito 2013).

does_not_work_verified.claim: Practice or form-focused instruction without corrective feedback
does_not_work_verified.notes: The feedback part is supported: Saito & Lyster 2012 (FFI-only showed no significant change; FFI+CF improved in controlled and spontaneous speech; one sound, intact classes), plus the feedback moderator in Lee et al. 2015. The add-on 'implicit-only instruction was outperformed by explicit' is mixed evidence, not settled. Kissling (2013, Modern Language Journal) found explicit phonetics instruction no better than equivalent practice without explanation. The SSLA study is cited without authors.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Perception-only training as the main route to better pronunciation
does_not_work_verified.notes: Broadly supported: production transfer from perception training is smaller and less consistent than perception gains (Sakai & Moorman 2018; the 2024 Applied Psycholinguistics meta-analysis, figures not re-checked). d = 0.54 is 'small to medium' by L2 benchmarks, not simply 'small'. Some studies do show production gains that are retained (Bradlow et al. 1999; Thomson 2011, CALICO). Perception training is a useful component, not a sufficient route.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Relying on exposure or immersion alone
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by Derwing & Munro 2013: the Mandarin-L1 group showed no change over 7 years. The groups were small and the design observational, and the authors attribute differences to communicative experience and willingness to communicate, not to exposure per se. Consistent with other longitudinal work showing early plateaus.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Treating every phoneme error as equally important
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by correlational listener studies: Munro & Derwing 2006 (exploratory, Cantonese L1) and Suzukida & Saito 2021 (Japanese L1). Kang et al. 2018 and 2020 add syllable-structure errors as intelligibility predictors. All English-only and rating-based. Functional-load rankings are themselves approximate.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using an automated score as the sole measure of an individual's intelligibility
does_not_work_verified.notes: The recommendation is prudent, but the evidence cited is very thin: 4 speakers in Inceoglu et al. 2023, figures not re-checked. Older evidence that ASR performs much worse than human listeners on L2 speech (Derwing, Munro & Carbonaro 2000, TESOL Quarterly 34(3)) also supports validating against human listeners. Modern ASR is better, and the size of any individual-level divergence is unknown.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Lack of evidence for tongue-twister speed ladders, speaking faster, or over-articulation drills
does_not_work_verified.notes: I know of no controlled L2 study showing that tongue-twister speed drills improve comprehensibility, so as an absence-of-evidence claim it stands. Nuances: (1) Munro & Derwing's speaking-rate studies (1998 Language Learning; 2001 SSLA) found listeners judged L2 speech slightly faster than the speaker's habitual rate as optimal, so a slow rate is not automatically clearer. (2) Clear-speech research shows that deliberately clear articulation raises intelligibility for listeners, including when L2 talkers produce it (Smiljanic & Bradlow 2011, JASA). That is evidence about speaking style, not about the training value of over-articulation drills, but it means 'over-articulation' should not be lumped with speed drills.

critique_of_v1: Wrong goal: v1 optimizes Azure accuracy, which measures closeness to a native acoustic model and so works as an accentedness score. The evidence says accentedness is only weakly related to intelligibility (r = .32) and is the dimension least responsive to instruction. The headline goal should be intelligibility and comprehensibility (Levis 2005/2020; Munro & Derwing 1995; Chau & Huensch 2025).

All practice and all measurement use scripted read-aloud sentences, the controlled condition where effects are largest and least transferable. There is no spontaneous speaking task anywhere, so v1 cannot show real-world progress and may show illusory progress (Saito & Plonsky 2019; Lee et al. 2015; Derwing et al. 1998).

Progress charts plot practice-session scores on repeated items. Without held-out items, delayed retention probes, or a separate test battery, rehearsal effects are indistinguishable from learning (Thomson & Derwing 2015; perceptual HVPT production meta-analysis 2024).

Selecting 'weak phonemes' by lowest rolling average ignores functional load and communicative impact. It will chase accent-only, low-impact sounds and is sensitive to ASR scoring noise. It should rank by functional load × frequency × listener impact (Munro & Derwing 2006; Suzukida & Saito 2021; Kang et al. 2018/2020).

Green/amber/red colour feedback is knowledge of result, not explicit instruction or corrective feedback. The evidence favours brief articulatory and auditory explanation plus specific corrective feedback (Saito & Lyster 2012; Ngo et al. 2024, explicit feedback g = 0.86).

Speed ladders (tongue twisters at slow/normal/fast TTS tempo, advancing at 85 accuracy) have no support in the pronunciation-instruction literature reviewed. Speed on memorized twisters is not the fluency construct linked to comprehensibility, which is pausing and articulation rate in unscripted speech. The 85 threshold is arbitrary and measured on rehearsed material.

Prosody is one of three tracks, and v1's single Azure prosody score is the kind of measure ASR tools handle least well (ASR effect on suprasegmentals g = 0.37 vs segmentals g = 0.82). Yet prosody- and fluency-focused instruction is what transferred to spontaneous comprehensibility (Derwing et al. 1998; Gordon & Darcy 2016/2022; Saito 2021). Prosody and fluency should get at least equal weight, with dedicated, interpretable measures.

No program structure: v1 has no multi-week plan, dose, or spacing. Evidence favours longer interventions (10-16 weeks in successful studies) and spaced rather than massed practice (Lee et al. 2015; Ngo et al. 2024; Saito & Chen 2025).

No first-language diagnosis or baseline: the learner's L1 is unknown, yet L1 strongly conditions both priorities and trajectories (Derwing & Munro 2013). v1 applies one generic content set to both languages.

It treats English and French symmetrically, although the French evidence base is thin and French learners' listener-rated gains did not follow read-aloud gains (Inceoglu 2019). Features like liaison and enchaînement need long-horizon, spaced practice rather than tier-advancement ladders.

There is no human-listener anchor. Automated scores are unvalidated for this one speaker, and ASR-listener agreement for individuals can be poor (Inceoglu, Chen & Lim 2023). A periodic export for a human listener to transcribe and rate would provide the gold standard.
open_questions: What is the learner's L1, and is one of English or French their native language? The L2-pronunciation evidence applies only to a non-native language. 'Articulation' goals in a native language (clarity, public speaking) belong to a different evidence base that this topic did not cover.

How well do Azure Pronunciation Assessment accuracy, fluency and prosody scores track human intelligibility and comprehensibility judgments for an individual speaker, especially for fr-FR? Is Azure's prosody assessment actually available for fr-FR? Check the current Azure documentation, since it has historically been more complete for en-US.
No empirically validated functional-load hierarchy for French segmental contrasts was found. What should weight French drill targets?
What dose and schedule suit a self-directed single adult? The evidence mostly comes from 10-16-week classroom courses and from perception-only spacing studies.

How can the app get periodic human-listener ratings in a local, single-user setup (e.g., exported clips rated by a friend or tutor on a 9-point scale, plus transcription), and how often is that needed to calibrate the automated proxies?
Do shadowing, tongue twisters or speed-graded practice improve spontaneous fluency and comprehensibility? These were not covered by the instruction meta-analyses reviewed and need a dedicated search.

Could not verify: the exact controlled-vs-spontaneous and global-vs-specific effect sizes in Saito & Plonsky (2019), the moderator details of Yao et al. (2025), and the exact direction of 'Study 2' in Hu, Kuo & Dixon (2025, LTR: intelligibility interventions g = 0.62 from 18 studies; a comprehensibility-related effect of 0.24 from 10 studies). general_review.topic: perception: Perception training (HVPT) and the perception-production link for L2 English and French
general_review.summary: Listening training is one of the best-supported parts of L2 pronunciation research, and v1 has none of it. The standard method is high variability phonetic training (HVPT). The learner hears minimal-pair words from several talkers, picks which word they heard, and gets feedback on every trial. Two meta-analyses report large gains in perception: Uchihara, Karas & Thomson 2025 (79 studies, pre-post g = 0.92, treatment vs control g = 0.67) and Sakai & Moorman 2018 (d = 0.92). The perception gains last. They also carry over to new words and new talkers, though only in part. Gains in production are real but about half as large: d = 0.54 in Sakai & Moorman 2018, and g = 0.49-0.66 in Uchihara et al. 2024 (31 studies). Production improves by about 10.5% on trained words but only 4.5% on untrained words, and there is little evidence that production gains are retained. So perception training boosts production; it is not a strict prerequisite. Production training with feedback also improves production, and sometimes perception too. Across individual learners, perception gains and production gains are barely correlated. The design factors that matter most are: identification tasks with feedback and explicit attention to the target sound; enough sessions (about 8-15 short sessions for each contrast); and spacing sessions out, since 7-day gaps and spaced schedules gave more durable gains than massed practice. The number of talkers matters less than claimed: a moderate number (2-6) is as good as more, and several large or registered replications found no reliable benefit of many talkers over one or two. Evidence for synthetic/TTS voices is thin. Training on a single-speaker synthetic continuum failed to transfer to natural speech. Two small studies suggest that HVPT with multiple TTS voices can work. Producing a token on every perception trial disrupted perceptual learning in lab studies, so listening and speaking should be practised in separate blocks. For contrasts, evidence is moderate for English /r/-/l/ (Japanese learners), /iː/-/ɪ/, /æ/-/ʌ/, /ð/ and vowels in general. It is limited for French nasal vowels (Inceoglu 2016: perception training improved perception and production, and audiovisual training helped production more). I found no controlled HVPT outcome studies for French /y/-/u/, /e/-/ɛ/, /ø/-/œ/ or /ʁ/, or for English word-final consonants with these learners. Limitation: fetching web pages was blocked in this session, so all details come from abstracts and search-engine summaries of the cited pages, not full texts.

findings.claim: Perceptual phonetic training (identification of minimal pairs with feedback, usually multi-talker) reliably improves adult L2 perception of the trained contrasts: g about 0.92 pre-post, about 0.67 vs controls, about 0.71 after bias correction. Gains are retained for at least 2-3 months and partly generalize to new items and talkers. The evidence is mostly lab studies of university learners of English. The ranking of perception-mode vs production-mode training rests on one unverified 2025 meta-analysis and does not show that perception training beats production training for production outcomes.
findings.population: Adult and adolescent L2 learners, mostly of English. Many first languages (Japanese, Mandarin, Spanish/Catalan, French, Greek, etc.).
findings.effect_notes: Uchihara, Karas & Thomson 2025 (SSLA 47(3)), 79 studies: pre-post g = 0.92 (k = 96); treatment vs control g = 0.67 (k = 32). Retention confirmed; partial generalization to novel stimuli. Moderators: length of L2 learning, response labels, training task, testing task, total training time, target phones, number of talkers. Yao et al. 2025 (JSLHR), 65 studies, 2,793 learners: overall d = 0.762. Perceptual training > production or combined training. Effects on perception > effects on production. Identification outcomes show the largest effects and acoustic measures the smallest. Thomson 2018: critical synthesis of 32 HVPT studies; effective and long-lasting.
findings.design_implication: Make a perception module (listen and identify) a core pillar of the app with its own daily slot, not an optional extra. Default item: the learner hears one word or short phrase, taps one of 2-4 minimal-pair word buttons, then gets immediate right/wrong feedback and replays the correct and chosen items. Track perceptual accuracy for each contrast separately from Azure production scores.

citations.ref: Uchihara, Karas & Thomson (2025). HVPT: A meta-analysis of L2 perceptual training studies. Studies in Second Language Acquisition 47(3), 794-827
Yao et al. (2025). A meta-analysis of second language phonetic training: Exploring overall effect and moderating factors. JSLHR
Thomson (2018). High Variability [Pronunciation] Training (HVPT). Journal of Second Language Pronunciation 4(2), 208-231, doi:10.1075/jslp.17038.tho

findings.claim: Perception-only training transfers to production with smaller effects than on perception (production roughly 55-70% of the perception effect). Gains are larger on trained than on untrained items (about 10.5% vs 4.5%). Individual perception gains predict individual production gains poorly. Retention and generalization of production gains are under-tested rather than shown to be poor; one /r/-/l/ study found production gains retained at 3 months.
findings.population: Adult L2 learners in controlled perception-training studies, mostly learners of English
findings.effect_notes: Sakai & Moorman 2018 (Applied Psycholinguistics 39(1), 187-224): perception d = 0.92, production d = 0.54. Perception and production gains were not significantly correlated. Moderators: target phone, learning context, explicit instruction, proficiency. Uchihara, Karas & Thomson 2024 (Applied Psycholinguistics 45(4), 591-623), 31 studies (43 within-participant and 17 between-participant designs): production g = 0.49 and 0.66. Production gains were +10.5% on trained items vs +4.5% on untrained items. No strong support for production retention or generalization. The perception-production gain link was negligible at the participant level and moderate at the study level. Moderators of production gains: age, learning context, provision of phonetic information, training duration, time per session, elicitation task, prompt modality, outcome measure.
findings.design_implication: Never assume perception drills alone will fix production. Pair each perception block with a production block on the same contrast. Add a short articulatory explanation for each contrast (phonetic information moderates production gains). Measure production on held-out untrained words and in free speech, not only on the drilled items, so progress is not overstated.

citations.ref: Sakai & Moorman (2018). Can perception training improve the production of second language phonemes? Applied Psycholinguistics 39(1)
Uchihara, Karas & Thomson (2024). Does perceptual HVPT improve L2 speech production? Applied Psycholinguistics 45(4)

findings.claim: Multi-talker training gives small and inconsistent advantages over low-variability training. Single-talker training also produces learning (Brekelmans 2022; Giannakopoulou 2017). The benefit of more talkers (up to about 6) seems limited to higher-proficiency or higher-aptitude learners, and high variability can hinder low-aptitude beginners. No study has directly shown that session count or spacing matters more than talker count.
findings.population: Adult L2 learners and naive adult listeners. Children in one comparison. L2 Spanish university learners in the largest RCT.
findings.effect_notes: Zhang, Cheng & Zhang 2021 (JSLHR 64(12)), 18 studies, 549 participants: multi- vs single-talker g = 0.46 [0.08, 0.84] immediately after training, but g = -0.04 at later tests. Zhang et al. 2025 Bayesian network meta-analysis, 32 studies, 998 participants: 6 talkers ranked best (SMD = 2.09 vs no training, SUCRA 94%). Moderate variability plus presentation format was optimal. Brekelmans et al. 2022 (JML, registered report, N = 166 replicating Logan/Lively): evidence for a high-variability benefit was ambiguous. Giannakopoulou et al. 2017 (PeerJ): no multi-talker benefit in adults; children did better with one talker. Nagle, Bruun & Zarate-Sandez 2025 (Applied Psycholinguistics), N = 458: 2-talker = 6-talker, both > control, and the number of sessions completed moderated gains.
findings.design_implication: Use a pool of about 4-6 training voices per language (for example several Azure en-US and fr-FR neural voices, varying sex and age), rather than chasing maximum variety. Spend the effort on number of trials, number of sessions, and word or context variety. Keep 1-2 extra voices out of training and use them only in generalization tests.

Zhang et al. (2025). Determining optimal talker variability for nonnative speech training: Bayesian network meta-analysis. JSLHR
Brekelmans, Lavan, Saito, Clayards & Wonnacott (2022). Does high variability training improve the learning of non-native phoneme contrasts over low variability training? A replication. JML 126
Giannakopoulou, Brown, Clayards & Wonnacott (2017). High or low? PeerJ 5:e3209
Nagle, Bruun & Zarate-Sandez (2025). Comparing lower and higher variability multi-talker perceptual training. Applied Psycholinguistics

findings.claim: Synthetic speech from one talker can fail to transfer to natural speech. HVPT built on several TTS voices is feasible, but the evidence for it is sparse and comes from small studies.
findings.population: Japanese adults (synthetic /r/-/l/ continuum); Chinese learners of English (TTS HVPT); 16 Mandarin/Cantonese adults (mixed synthetic and natural); 30 Arabic-speaking ESL learners (multi- vs single-voice TTS)
findings.effect_notes: Strange & Dittmann 1984 (Perception & Psychophysics 36, 131-145, as described in Giannakopoulou et al. 2017): discrimination training on a single synthetic rock-lock continuum improved synthetic items but did not transfer to natural minimal pairs. Qian, Chukharev-Hudilainen & Levis 2018 (LLT 22(1), 69-96): adaptive HVPT generated automatically from corpus word lists and TTS (two artificial talkers); the paper reports effectiveness and transfer. Wang & Munro 2004 (System 32): graded synthetic-to-natural stimuli, 2 months, /i-ɪ/, /u-ʊ/, /ɛ-æ/: beat controls, transferred to new contexts, retained at 3 months. Al-Shami & Cardoso 2025 (CJAL 28(3)), n = 30, 4 weeks: multi-voice TTS and single-voice TTS both improved; the multi-voice group had better comprehensibility and accentedness ratings.
findings.design_implication: The app can generate HVPT items from many Azure neural voices, including regional variants such as en-GB, en-AU, fr-CA, fr-BE and fr-CH. Also vary speaking rate and pitch slightly and embed words in carrier phrases. Build in a validity check: include some natural human recordings (for example licensed corpus or open-source minimal-pair recordings) in the generalization test set. If accuracy on TTS items rises while accuracy on natural items stays flat, flag that TTS-only training is not transferring. Acoustically check that each TTS voice actually realizes the contrast (for example /e/-/ɛ/ or /ø/-/œ/ in the target position) before using its tokens.

citations.ref: Giannakopoulou et al. (2017), PeerJ, reviewing Strange & Dittmann (1984) synthetic-continuum training
Qian, Chukharev-Hudilainen & Levis (2018). A system for adaptive high-variability segmental perceptual training. Language Learning & Technology 22(1)
Wang & Munro (2004). Computer-based training for learning English vowel contrasts. System 32, 539-552
Al-Shami & Cardoso (2025). Exploring text-to-speech technology as a tool for HVPT. Canadian Journal of Applied Linguistics 28(3)

findings.claim: Identification training with orthographic labels and feedback gives larger perceptual gains than discrimination training (meta-analytic, moderate). Training attention on the specific target feature helps (one small study). Occasional no-feedback trials may be enough once learning is under way, but that rests on one unverified lab study with naive listeners.
findings.population: Advanced Catalan-Spanish learners of English; Mandarin learners of Korean (n = 45); naive adult listeners (feedback-density study)
findings.effect_notes: Carlet & Cebrian 2022 (Applied Psycholinguistics 43(2), 271-299), English /iː/-/ɪ/, /æ/-/ʌ/, /v/-/b/, /d/-/ð/: identification training gave larger gains than discrimination training for vowel identification; the two were comparable for stops. Discrimination training also improved non-target sounds present in the stimuli. Ryu & Kang 2019 (ICPhS), n = 45, identical audio for both groups: coda-focused training > vowel-focused training > no training, so attention to the target matters. Semi-supervised learning study (Attention, Perception & Psychophysics 2019): 60 feedback trials per day alone gave no learning; 60 feedback plus 240 no-feedback trials did; 30 feedback trials abolished learning. Uchihara et al. 2025 and Yao et al. 2025 also found training task and response labels to be significant moderators.
findings.design_implication: Default perception item: 2-alternative forced-choice identification with the two words shown as text (orthographic labels), followed by 3-4-way sets for vowel systems such as English /iː ɪ eɪ ɛ/ or French /e ɛ ø œ/. Use AX or oddity discrimination only as a warm-up for contrasts the learner cannot yet hear. Always name the target contrast on screen. Give feedback on most trials and allow some no-feedback trials in later sessions.

citations.ref: Carlet & Cebrian (2022). The roles of task, segment type, and attention in L2 perceptual training. Applied Psycholinguistics 43(2)
Ryu & Kang (2019). Web-based high variability phonetic training on L2 coda identification. ICPhS 2019
Semi-supervised learning of a nonnative phonetic contrast: How much feedback is enough? (2019)

findings.claim: Spacing perceptual training across days is better than massing it: supported by general L2 spacing research and one or two phonetic-training studies. Longer inter-session gaps may help retention, but that rests on a single study, and other L2 domains show conflicting results. Roughly 1-7 hours in 3-15 short sessions gave lasting gains, mostly for whole vowel sets rather than single contrasts. Learners with smaller L1 vowel inventories may need about 3x more sessions (one study).
findings.population: Adult L2 learners: Mandarin speakers learning English /ɛ/-/æ/ and /i/-/ɪ/; Malaysian multilinguals; Spanish and German L1 learners of English vowels; French L1 learners of English
findings.effect_notes: SSLA 'Optimizing L2 phonetic learning': equal and expanding spacing both beat massed practice; spaced-group effect sizes were about double, both immediately and at retention. Li 2026 (Modern Language Journal): 1-day vs 7-day gaps gave similar immediate gains, but only the 7-day group retained them; the longer gap offset weaker auditory acuity. PLOS ONE 2018 (e0204888): three 20-min sessions (1 h total) of HVPT in adaptive noise gave gains that generalized and lasted 6 months; adaptive noise beat fixed noise. Iverson & Evans 2009 (JASA 126(2)): 5 sessions were enough for German L1 learners; Spanish L1 learners needed 10 more to catch up, and both groups retained the gains. Iverson, Pinet & Evans 2012: 8 sessions improved English vowels for French L1 learners with or without immersion. Melnik & Peperkamp 2021: 8 online sessions improved identification of English /h/ and lexical decision, retained at 4 months.
findings.design_implication: Schedule perception training per contrast: about 8-15 sessions of 10-20 min (about 100-200 trials each), spread over days and weeks rather than crammed. Use a spaced-repetition scheduler that brings back mastered contrasts after growing gaps (1 → 3 → 7+ days). Add adaptive difficulty, for example lowering the signal-to-noise ratio or using harder talkers and contexts as accuracy rises. Run delayed retention probes 2-4 weeks after a contrast is mastered.

citations.ref: Optimizing L2 phonetic learning (Studies in Second Language Acquisition): massed vs equal vs expanding spacing
Li (2026). Lag effects in L2 phonetic training: Longer intersession intervals compensate for auditory individual differences. Modern Language Journal
High variability phonetic training in adaptive adverse conditions is rapid, effective, and sustained. PLOS ONE 13(10): e0204888 (2018)
Iverson & Evans (2009). Learning English vowels with different first-language vowel systems II. JASA 126(2), 866-877
Iverson, Pinet & Evans (2012). Auditory training for experienced and inexperienced second-language learners: Native French speakers learning English vowels. Applied Psycholinguistics 33(1)
Melnik & Peperkamp (2021). HVPT enhances second language lexical processing: online training of French learners of English. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition

findings.claim: Perception and production training each help the other modality somewhat and asymmetrically. In single-session lab studies with naive listeners, producing a token on every perceptual-training trial disrupted perceptual learning, less so for listeners with prior experience. Production training with feedback improved production, and sometimes perception, without the two changing in step. How best to sequence or block perception and production in multi-session L2 training has not been tested.
findings.population: Spanish speakers learning a Basque contrast (lab); naive French speakers learning Danish vowels (n = 27); 115 Japanese EFL university students; small groups of adult learners of English (articulography study; Speakometer app n = 20, no untrained control)
findings.effect_notes: Baese-Berk & Samuel 2016 (JML 89, 23-36): alternating perception and production on each trial disrupted perceptual learning; the disruption was larger when learners produced the token itself and smaller for experienced listeners. Baese-Berk 2019 (APP 81(4)): learning is strongest in the trained modality, and cross-modal transfer is complex. Kartushina et al. 2015 (JASA 138(2)): about 1 h of production training per vowel with visual acoustic feedback improved Danish vowel production by 17% on average; discrimination changed, but not in sync with production. Lee, Plonsky & Saito 2020 (System 88), N = 115, 2 weeks: all groups improved, and perception-based instruction looked more effective for both segmentals and suprasegmentals. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 2026: articulatory-target training (articulography) improved production of /æ/ and perception of related contrasts. Georgiou 2026: a production-focused ASR app improved /iː/-/ɪ/ discrimination and production (weak design).
findings.design_implication: For each contrast use blocks: (1) a perception diagnostic; (2) if the contrast is not yet heard reliably (for example below about 80% identification), perception-first HVPT blocks with no speaking; (3) production blocks with feedback on the same contrast; (4) mixed review only once perception is stable. Do not build the core loop as 'hear model → repeat' on every trial for brand-new contrasts. Production practice should not wait until perception reaches ceiling, because production training independently helps.

citations.ref: Baese-Berk & Samuel (2016). Listeners beware: Speech production may be bad for learning speech sounds. Journal of Memory and Language 89
Baese-Berk (2019). Interactions between speech perception and production during learning of novel phonemic categories. Attention, Perception & Psychophysics 81(4)
Kartushina, Hervais-Adelman, Frauenfelder & Golestani (2015). The effect of phonetic production training with visual feedback on the perception and production of foreign speech sounds. JASA 138(2)
Lee, Plonsky & Saito (2020). The effects of perception- vs. production-based pronunciation instruction. System 88
Improvement of speech perception following articulatory-target based production training for second language acquisition. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience (2026)
Georgiou (2026). Improving nonnative speech perception and production through an AI-powered application. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications 13, 891

findings.claim: Moderate evidence (small samples) that multi-talker perceptual training improves perception and native-listener-judged production of English /r/-/l/ (Japanese learners; production gains retained at 3 months) and of several vowel contrasts (Mandarin and Greek learners), with some transfer to spontaneous speech in one study. For /æ/-/ʌ/ and /d/-/ð/ only perceptual gains are documented. There is no direct training evidence for English word-final consonant contrasts.
findings.population: Japanese adults (/r/-/l/, small samples); Mandarin speakers (22 in Thomson 2011); Greek speakers (Lengeris 2018); Catalan-Spanish learners; Mandarin learners of Korean (codas)
findings.effect_notes: Logan, Lively & Pisoni 1991 and Bradlow et al. 1997 (JASA 101(4), 2299-2310): multi-talker /r/-/l/ identification training generalized to new words and talkers and improved production as judged by native listeners. Individual perception and production vectors were not tightly coupled. Bradlow et al. 1999 (Perception & Psychophysics 61(5)): gains in both perception and production retained at 3 months. Iverson, Hazan & Bannister 2005: learners improved but mostly by applying their L1 flap category more systematically, not by forming a new category. Thomson 2011 (CALICO 28(3)): 20 talkers, 10 Canadian English vowels, picture labels; vowel intelligibility improved in trained and untrained contexts. Lengeris 2018 (JASA EL 144(3)): auditory training improved vowel production in read sentences and spontaneous speech, with larger gains in read sentences. Carlet & Cebrian 2022: /iː/-/ɪ/, /æ/-/ʌ/, /d/-/ð/ trainable. Ryu & Kang 2019: HVPT on codas worked (Korean).
findings.design_implication: The English pack should ship perception sets for /iː/-/ɪ/, /æ/-/ʌ/-/ɑ/, /ɛ/-/æ/, /u/-/ʊ/, /θ/-/s/-/t/-/f/ and /ð/-/d/-/z/, /r/-/l/ (initial, cluster and intervocalic), /h/-zero, and word-final voicing and deletion sets (for example cap/cab, bet/bed, seat/seed, row/rope). Words should be in several positions and carrier phrases. The final-consonant sets are experimental and should be monitored with the in-app generalization probes. Measure transfer to connected and spontaneous speech (for example a picture-description or free-talk task scored by Azure on the target phoneme).

citations.ref: Logan, Lively & Pisoni (1991). Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/: A first report. JASA 89, 874-886

Bradlow, Pisoni, Akahane-Yamada & Tohkura (1997). Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/ IV: Some effects of perceptual learning on speech production. JASA 101(4), doi:10.1121/1.418276
Bradlow, Akahane-Yamada, Pisoni & Tohkura (1999). Long-term retention of learning in perception and production. Perception & Psychophysics 61(5)
Iverson, Hazan & Bannister (2005). Phonetic training with acoustic cue manipulations. JASA 118(5)
Thomson (2011). Computer assisted pronunciation training: Targeting second language vowel perception improves pronunciation. CALICO Journal 28(3)
Lengeris (2018). Computer-based auditory training improves second-language vowel production in spontaneous speech. JASA 144(3) EL165, doi:10.1121/1.5052201

findings.claim: For French contrasts evidence is limited. Perceptual training on the three French nasal vowels improved both perception and production for English-speaking learners, and audiovisual training (seeing the face) improved production more than audio alone. Online homework-style training works about as well as classroom training. I found no controlled outcome studies for /y/-/u/, /e/-/ɛ/, /ø/-/œ/ or /ʁ/.
findings.population: American English learners of French (60 intermediate learners in Inceoglu 2016); university L2 French learners (Becker 2024)
findings.effect_notes: Inceoglu 2016 (Applied Psycholinguistics 37(5), 1175-1199): 6 sessions of audiovisual or audio-only perceptual training on /ɑ̃ ɛ̃ ɔ̃/; both improved perception and production, and the audiovisual group improved production significantly more. Becker 2024: homework-based online nasal-vowel training beat controls on some perception measures and on comprehensibility of word productions; homework was about as good as in-class training; perception-production gain correlation small to medium and not significant. Inceoglu 2022: the Ouïe web HVPT tool covers 10 oral and 3 nasal French vowels, with a familiarisation mode (IPA and articulatory explanation); I found no outcome data. Kartushina et al. 2015 is the reverse direction (French L1 speakers learning Danish /e ɛ y ø/ through production feedback).
findings.design_implication: The French pack should include perception sets for /ɑ̃/-/ɔ̃/-/ɛ̃/ (and nasal vs oral plus nasal consonant, for example beau/bon/bonne), /y/-/u/ (rue/roue, dessus/dessous), /y/-/i/, /e/-/ɛ/ (in positions where the contrast is stable in Standard French), /ø/-/œ/, and /ʁ/-/w/-/l/ onsets. Add a visual articulatory cue (lip rounding, mouth opening) shown next to the audio. Candidates are short video clips or an avatar driven by Azure viseme events, but a synthetic face is unvalidated. Treat all French perception modules as provisional: log per-contrast learning curves and generalization to held-out voices to check efficacy for this learner.

citations.ref: Inceoglu (2016). Effects of perceptual training on second language vowel perception and production. Applied Psycholinguistics 37(5)
Becker (2024). Teaching and researching French nasal vowels: The pros and cons of online training modalities for improving perception and production
Inceoglu (2022). A web-based high variability phonetic training application for French vowels. PSLLT Proceedings

findings.claim: How much a learner gains depends on their L1 and on individual auditory ability. The same training can take about 3x longer for learners from some L1 backgrounds, and proficiency and length of L2 learning change the effects. The app should therefore diagnose perception directly rather than infer targets from production scores or assumed L1 transfer.
findings.population: Adult L2 learners (Spanish vs German L1 learners of English; mixed-L1 samples in the meta-analyses; Mandarin learners of English in the spacing study)
findings.effect_notes: Iverson & Evans 2009: Spanish L1 learners (5-vowel system) needed 15 sessions to match German L1 learners (5 sessions). Sakai & Moorman 2018: proficiency and learning context moderate production transfer. Uchihara et al. 2025: length of L2 learning moderates perception gains. Li 2026: auditory acuity predicted short-term gains, and 7-day spacing reduced its effect on retention.
findings.design_implication: Because the learner's L1 is unknown, onboarding should include a roughly 10-minute perception screener for each language. It should cover about 15-20 candidate contrasts, 2 voices per item and 8-12 trials per contrast, including held-out voices. Rank contrasts by identification accuracy and combine this with Azure production scores to pick 3-5 active targets. Re-run the screener monthly as the progress metric for perception.

citations.ref: Iverson & Evans (2009). JASA 126(2)
Sakai & Moorman (2018). Applied Psycholinguistics 39(1)
Li (2026). Modern Language Journal

findings.claim: In lab studies of naive English listeners learning a Hindi contrast, sleep after training supported generalization to a new talker. Unsupervised exposure to an untrained vowel context at pretest and posttests went with poorer learning and no overnight gain. Blocked contexts beat interleaved contexts during training. It is untested whether generalization probes are harmful only right after a session.
findings.population: Native English-speaking adults learning a Hindi dental-retroflex contrast in the lab (naive listeners, not L2 learners)
findings.effect_notes: Earle & Myers 2015 (JASA): overnight consolidation promoted generalization across talkers, and evening training benefited from sleep. Fuhrmeister & Myers 2017 (JASA EL 142(5), EL448-EL454): testing on an untrained vowel context lowered accuracy on trained items and eliminated overnight improvement.
findings.design_implication: This is low-priority tuning. End each perception session on trained material. Run generalization probes at the start of a later session rather than straight after training. Optionally suggest evening sessions.

citations.ref: Earle & Myers (2015). Overnight consolidation promotes generalization across talkers in the identification of nonnative speech sounds. JASA
Fuhrmeister & Myers (2017). Non-native phonetic learning is destabilized by exposure to phonological variability before and after training. JASA EL 142(5)

does_not_work_verified.claim: 'More talkers is always better' is wrong: benefits are small, fade at delay, did not replicate in a large registered report; 2 talkers matched 6 in a 458-learner RCT.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported in spirit, but the wording overstates. Brekelmans 2022 is coded as a 'mixed' or inconclusive replication, not a failed one. I could not verify the Zhang 2021 fading figures or the Nagle 2025 RCT (N = 458). Uchihara 2025 found talker number a significant moderator for higher-proficiency learners (up to 6 talkers). Better wording: 'more talkers is not reliably better, especially for beginners and low-aptitude learners'.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Interleaving 'listen then say it' on every trial while learning a new contrast disrupts perceptual learning.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by Baese-Berk & Samuel 2016 (JML; abstract confirmed), with limits: single-session lab studies with naive listeners, and the disruption was smaller with prior experience. Persistence across multi-day training in L2 learners is not established. Baese-Berk & Samuel 2023 is a lead to check.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Massed practice is worse: spaced schedules gave about double the effect and better retention, and 7-day gaps beat 1-day gaps.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Spaced beating massed is supported (general L2 spacing meta-analysis, Kim & Webb 2022, plus phonetic-training studies). I could not verify 'about double' (uncited SSLA paper) or '7-day beats 1-day' (Li 2026, single study). The lag result conflicts with Suzuki 2017 (3.3-day beat 7-day, L2 morphology). Kim & Webb found equal and expanding schedules roughly equivalent.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Expecting perception training alone to fix production in untrained words or spontaneous speech, or using individual perception gains to predict production gains: transfer is about half, weak on untrained items (+4.5%), poorly retained, uncorrelated individually.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Mostly supported by Uchihara 2024 and Sakai & Moorman 2018. 'Poorly retained' should read 'retention under-tested'. Bradlow 1999 found /r/-/l/ production gains retained at 3 months.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Judging progress only on trained items overstates learning; acoustic outcome measures show the smallest effects.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The trained vs untrained gap is supported by Uchihara 2024. Saito & Plonsky 2019 (Language Learning 69(3)) found larger effects on controlled than on spontaneous speech measures. The 'acoustic measures smallest' part rests on Yao et al. 2025, which I could not verify.

does_not_work_verified.claim: A production-feedback app without an untrained control group cannot show it caused the gains; single-group pre/post studies (e.g., Speakometer n = 20) are weak evidence.
does_not_work_verified.notes: A methodological point that holds regardless of source. I could not verify the details of the cited Georgiou 2026 paper (Speakometer, n = 20). Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015 found that studies without control groups inflate pronunciation-instruction effects.

critique_of_v1: No perception training at all. Minimal pairs (ship/sheep, vin/vent, rue/roue) are used only as items to read aloud. The learner never does forced-choice identification with feedback, which is the best-supported technique (perception g ≈ 0.9; production g ≈ 0.5-0.66).

One TTS voice per language (fr-FR-DeniseNeural, en-US-JennyNeural, per docs/technical-design.md and docs/api-reference.md) is a low-variability synthetic model, the condition linked to failed transfer to natural speech. There are no held-out voices, so generalization to other talkers is never measured.

The core loop (play reference → record → score) alternates perception and production on every trial. For contrasts the learner cannot yet hear, this matches the design that disrupted perceptual learning (Baese-Berk & Samuel 2016). Perception and production need separate blocks.

Weak phonemes are chosen only from rolling averages of Azure production scores (5 lowest, at least 3 attempts). With the learner's L1 unknown, v1 cannot tell a perceptual problem (cannot hear /y/ vs /u/) from a motor problem (hears it but cannot make it). It needs a perception screener and per-contrast perception tracking.

Moving up a level at ≥85 on the same items rewards memorizing specific items. Production gains roughly halve on untrained items and are poorly retained, so v1 progress charts will overstate learning. It needs held-out word lists, held-out voices, delayed retention probes and spontaneous-speech checks.

There is no spacing or retention schedule. Drills come back immediately based on rolling averages. Spaced schedules (equal or expanding intervals, 7-day gaps) roughly double gains and improve retention.

Speed ladders slow down or speed up the TTS reference (0.75x/1.25x). No perception-training evidence supports tempo-scaled synthetic models. Time-scaling also changes durational cues that are part of some contrasts (for example English tense-lax vowel duration), which may teach the wrong cue. This concern is my inference and is untested.

There is no articulatory explanation or visual (face or lip) information. Providing phonetic information moderates production gains in the HVPT meta-analysis, and audiovisual training improved French nasal-vowel production more than audio alone.

Progress uses only Azure production scores. The app has no perception metric, so it cannot show whether a failing sound is a listening problem, and it cannot show the perception-to-production link the user cares about.
open_questions: Are Azure neural TTS voices as effective as natural human talkers for HVPT, and does TTS-trained perception transfer to real speakers? Only Qian et al. 2018 (two TTS talkers) and Al-Shami & Cardoso 2025 (n = 30) bear on this. A within-learner A/B test (TTS-trained contrasts vs contrasts trained with natural recordings, both tested on natural held-out voices) could answer it for this user.

Do Azure fr-FR voices reliably realize /e/-/ɛ/ and /ø/-/œ/ in every position used? Many native French speakers neutralize these in some positions, and /ɛ̃/-/œ̃/ is widely merged, so tokens need acoustic or native-listener checks before use.

No controlled HVPT outcome studies were found for French /y/-/u/, /ø/-/œ/, /e/-/ɛ/ or /ʁ/, or for English word-final consonant contrasts with French or unknown-L1 learners. Recommendations for these are extrapolated.

The exact moderator estimates in Uchihara et al. 2025 were not accessible: identification vs discrimination effect sizes, best response-label type (orthographic, picture or IPA), and the total-training-time curve. Nor was the direction of the presentation-format effect (talkers blocked vs mixed) in Zhang et al. 2025. Full texts should be checked.

It is unclear whether acoustic cue enhancement or perceptual fading (exaggerated tokens that are gradually normalized) adds value beyond natural-variability HVPT. Iverson, Hazan & Bannister 2005 compared methods, but the summary I had did not show a clear winner.

Does segmental perception training transfer to articulation goals such as clarity, speaking rate and rhythm? Lee, Plonsky & Saito 2020 suggest perception-based suprasegmental instruction works, but evidence linking perception training to fluency or rate gains was not found.

Is incidental or gamified HVPT (Saito et al. 2022, a clay-target shooting game) as effective as explicit identification for a motivated single adult user? Reported benchmarks for explicit HVPT are about 5-15% gains for /r/-/l/ and 15-20% for vowels.

Method limitation: web-page fetching was blocked in this session. All effect sizes and details come from search-engine renderings of abstracts and landing pages at the cited URLs, not from full texts. The findings should be verified against the papers before being written into docs/prd.md.
missed_evidence_flagged: Perrachione, Lee, Ha & Wong (2011). Learning a novel phonological contrast depends on interactions between individual differences and training paradigm design. JASA 130(1), 461-472. High-variability training hurt low-aptitude learners. Relevant to perception-3 and perception-10. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Perrachione+2011+Learning+a+novel+phonological+contrast

Sadakata & McQueen (2014). Individual aptitude in Mandarin lexical tone perception predicts effectiveness of high-variability training. Frontiers in Psychology 5:1318. Interaction between aptitude and variability. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01318/full

Fuhrmeister & Myers (2020). Desirable and undesirable difficulties: Influences of variability, training schedule, and aptitude on nonnative phonetic learning. Attention, Perception & Psychophysics 82. Blocked beat interleaved phonological variability for learning and retention; aptitude predicted overnight gains. Full text cached locally; publisher page not opened. https://link.springer.com/search?query=Desirable+and+undesirable+difficulties+Fuhrmeister+Myers

Saito & Plonsky (2019). Effects of second language pronunciation teaching revisited: A proposed measurement framework and meta-analysis. Language Learning 69(3). Effects are larger on controlled than on spontaneous speech, which supports testing transfer to free speech. https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10068780

Lee, Jang & Plonsky (2015). The effectiveness of second language pronunciation instruction: A meta-analysis. Applied Linguistics 36(3), 345-366. Production-focused instruction yields sizeable production gains; studies without control groups inflate effects. https://doi.org/10.1093/applin/amu040

Kim & Webb (2022). The effects of spaced practice on second language learning: A meta-analysis. Language Learning 72(1). Spaced beat massed; longer spacing better on delayed tests; equal and expanding schedules roughly equivalent. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12479

Suzuki (2017). The optimal distribution of practice for the acquisition of L2 morphology. Language Learning 67(3), 512-545. A 3.3-day lag beat a 7-day lag at 7- and 28-day delayed tests, contrary to 'longer is better' (morphology, not phonetics). https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12236

McCandliss, Fiez, Protopapas, Conway & McClelland (2002). Success and failure in teaching the [r]-[l] contrast to Japanese adults. Cognitive, Affective & Behavioral Neuroscience 2(2), 89-108. Adaptive easy-to-hard training worked without feedback; fixed hard stimuli without feedback failed. Relevant to feedback density and adaptive difficulty. https://doi.org/10.3758/CABN.2.2.89

Lively, Logan & Pisoni (1993). Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/ II: The role of phonetic environment and talker variability in learning new perceptual categories. JASA 94(3), 1242-1255. The original evidence that multi-talker training generalizes to new talkers. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Lively+Logan+Pisoni+1993

Hazan, Sennema, Iba & Faulkner (2005). Effect of audiovisual perceptual training on the perception and production of consonants by Japanese learners of English. Speech Communication 47(3). The audiovisual benefit depends on the contrast (visible labial contrasts gain most). Relevant to perception-8 and perception-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.specom.2005.04.007

Dong, Clayards, Brown & Wonnacott (2019). The effects of high versus low talker variability and individual aptitude on phonetic training of Mandarin lexical tones. PeerJ 7:e7191. Another null result for high variability (moderate confidence in details). https://peerj.com/articles/7191/

Thomson & Derwing (2015). The effectiveness of L2 pronunciation instruction: A narrative review. Applied Linguistics 36(3), 326-344. Most studies measure controlled speech only. https://doi.org/10.1093/applin/amu076

Saito et al. (2022). Incidental and multimodal high variability phonetic training: Potential, limits, and future directions. Language Learning. On the limits of HVPT and incidental variants. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/lang.12503

Earle & Myers (2015b). Sleep and native language interference affect nonnative speech sound learning. JEP:HPP 41(6), 1680. Native-language exposure after training weakens consolidation. Relevant to perception-11. Citation confirmed from a cached reference list. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Earle+Myers+2015+Sleep+and+native+language+interference
