Unverified leads (could not check; do not cite until read): Baese-Berk & Samuel (2023), 'Just give it time', Attention, Perception & Psychophysics, on whether production-induced disruption persists across days; Shinohara & Iverson (2018), Journal of Phonetics 66, identification vs discrimination HVPT for /r/-/l/; Rochet (1995), in Strange (ed.), Speech Perception and Linguistic Experience, perceptual training of French /y/ with transfer to production; Liakin, Cardoso & Liakina (2017), CALL, TTS-based practice of French liaison; Wong (2013/2014), perception-only vs production-only vs combined training for Cantonese learners' English /iː/-/ɪ/.

general_review.topic: Corrective feedback and computer/ASR-based pronunciation training (CAPT) (key: feedback)
general_review.summary:
SOURCE-ACCESS CAVEAT: The session's web-search budget had already run out when this task started (0 of 200 searches left). The egress proxy also blocked doi.org, publishers, Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, ERIC, PubMed, OpenAlex and Crossref. I checked sources through GitHub instead, which was the only channel open: open full texts (Hincks & Edlund 2009; Hirata & Kelly 2010), BibTeX/Mendeley libraries that carry DOIs and some abstracts (Cucchiarini et al. 2009; Levis 2007), an evidence ledger that another project had checked against Crossref (Saito & Lyster 2012; Saito 2013; Derwing & Munro 1997), the raw data of an umbrella review (Mahdi & Al Khateeb 2019), the GOPT benchmark repository, and Microsoft's own Azure docs repository. The effect_notes mark any figure I could not check against the original as 'not re-verified'. Check those before relying on them.

WHAT THE EVIDENCE SAYS:
(1) CAPT/ASR practice improves adult L2 pronunciation, with moderate and highly variable effects. Gains are largest for individual sounds (segmentals), intermediate learners and adults, and when feedback is explicit.
(2) The key ingredient is corrective feedback that says which sound was wrong and how to fix it. Instruction or practice without feedback did not carry over to spontaneous speech (Saito & Lyster 2012). Explicit phonetic explanation helped gains generalize to new words (Saito 2013).
(3) Simple, targeted visual feedback works best for pitch and intonation (Hincks & Edlund 2009) and for vowel formants or stop timing (VOT) (Kartushina et al. 2015; Olson 2014). Raw spectrograms and bare scores are hard to interpret.
(4) Automatic scores can mislead. Phone-level machine scores correlate only about r = 0.6 with human raters, and word-stress scores barely at all. ASR is less accurate on L2 speech, and reviews report false alarms on speech humans understand easily.
(5) Learners judge their own pronunciation poorly. Listening to one's recording next to a model, without guidance, is weaker than targeted feedback.
(6) In Azure itself, prosody scores, syllable scores, IPA phoneme names and 'what you actually said' phonemes are available only for en-US. French therefore gets much weaker diagnostic feedback. The v1 code also never turns prosody assessment on.

REDESIGN: Replace the traffic-light scoreboard with a diagnose → explain → prompt a self-repair → model → retry loop. Show only 1–2 errors per attempt, and only ones the system has detected consistently. Add simple visual displays for intonation and for the hardest vowel contrasts. Add an unscripted 'can a listener understand you?' mode as an intelligibility check. Measure progress on untrained sentences and spontaneous speech, not on the sentences just practised.

findings.claim: Meta-analyses of CAPT/ASR practice report positive, moderate and highly heterogeneous pronunciation gains. The studies are mostly EFL/ESL, measured on controlled tasks, short, and often lack delayed post-tests. One meta-analysis (Ngo et al. 2024) reportedly finds larger effects for adults, intermediate learners, segmental targets and explicit feedback. These moderator results were not verified and come from small subgroups. Evidence for L2 French is almost absent. The frequently quoted d = 0.46 for Mahdi & Al Khateeb (2019) is a 6-study child/adolescent subset, not the overall effect.
findings.population: Mostly EFL/ESL learners (school-age to university/adult). Very few studies of L2 French.
findings.effect_notes: Mahdi & Al Khateeb 2019 (Review of Education 7(3):733-753): an umbrella review's extraction for the school-age subset gives d = 0.46 (k = 6, N = 302, I² ≈ 82%, i.e. large heterogeneity). Overall figures for the full meta-analysis were not re-verified. Ngo, Chen & Lai 2024 (ReCALL): ESL/EFL ASR meta-analysis. A secondary summary lists stronger effects for segmentals, adults, intermediate learners and explicit feedback. A tertiary summary reports g ≈ 0.86 for explicit vs g ≈ 0.55 for implicit ASR feedback (not re-verified). Amrate & Tsai 2025 (ReCALL), a systematic review of about 30 studies: CAPT generally improves pronunciation, most clearly at beginner and intermediate levels.
findings.design_implication: Keep ASR-scored read-aloud practice as one core activity, but treat it as a moderate-effect tool rather than the whole method. Build in the moderators that predicted larger effects: explicit feedback and segmental targets first, with suprasegmentals added via dedicated displays (feedback-6). Evaluate the app's own effect with pre/post tests on untrained material rather than assuming it works.

citations.ref: Mahdi, H. S., & Al Khateeb, A. A. (2019). The effectiveness of computer-assisted pronunciation training: A meta-analysis. Review of Education, 7(3), 733-753.
Umbrella-review effect extraction for Mahdi & Al Khateeb 2019 (data/Effects.csv, Review ID 49806: d = 0.46, k = 6, N = 302, I² = 82.4)
Ngo, T. T.-N., Chen, H. H.-J., & Lai, K. K.-W. (2024). The effectiveness of automatic speech recognition in ESL/EFL pronunciation: A meta-analysis. ReCALL, 36(1).
Amrate, M., & Tsai, P.-h. (2025). Computer-assisted pronunciation training: A systematic review. ReCALL, 37.

findings.claim: For adult Japanese learners of English /ɹ/, adding corrective feedback in the form of teacher recasts to about 4 h of form-focused instruction improved production in controlled and spontaneous speech, while instruction alone did not (Saito & Lyster 2012; generalization to new words unclear). Separately, explicit phonetic (articulatory) information given as instruction produced larger gains that generalized to unfamiliar words (Saito 2013). The evidence is small-sample, from one lab, and about one sound. It supports adding corrective feedback and explicit articulatory information. It does not directly test the proposed diagnostic feedback card.
findings.population: Adult Japanese learners of English (ESL in Canada; EFL in Japan). Single target phone English /ɹ/. Intact classes rather than individual randomization.
findings.effect_notes: Saito & Lyster 2012: N = 65, about 4 h of instruction. The instruction-plus-feedback group (n = 29) improved /ɹ/ (F3 measure) in both controlled and spontaneous speech. The instruction-only group (n = 25) and the control group (n = 11) did not change. Saito 2013: N = 49 (control 14, instruction only 18, instruction plus explicit phonetic information 17). The explicit-information group made larger gains that generalized to unfamiliar words. Findings are consistent in direction but come from small samples, one sound and one research group.
findings.design_implication: Replace score-only feedback with a diagnostic card for each flagged error. It shows the target sound in the word, the likely substitution (en-US: Azure NBestPhonemes), a one-sentence articulatory cue (e.g., 'round your lips as for /u/ but keep the tongue forward as for /i/' for French /y/) and a short lip/tongue visual. It ends with an immediate retry on the same word, then in a new word containing the same sound.

citations.ref: Saito, K., & Lyster, R. (2012). Effects of form-focused instruction and corrective feedback on L2 pronunciation development of /ɹ/ by Japanese learners of English. Language Learning, 62(2), 595-633.
Saito, K. (2013). Reexamining effects of form-focused instruction on L2 pronunciation development: The role of explicit phonetic information. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 35(1), 1-29.
Ngo, Chen & Lai (2024), ReCALL: explicit feedback reported as a moderator of ASR effects

findings.claim: Oral corrective feedback has significant and durable effects. Prompts that make the learner self-repair tend to outperform recasts (the teacher simply giving the correct form), but this comes mostly from grammar studies and is contested. The best-cited pronunciation-specific test compares the two in a small study.
findings.population: Classroom L2 learners (mostly adolescents and adults). Mostly grammatical targets. The pronunciation-specific study involved Korean adult EFL learners.
findings.effect_notes: Lyster & Saito 2010: 15 classroom studies, N = 827. Effects were significant and durable, larger for prompts than recasts, and clearest on free-response measures. Goo & Mackey (2013) argue the prompt/recast comparison is confounded. Gooch, Saito & Lyster 2016 (System 60:117-127) compared recasts and prompts for English /ɹ/. Its specific results and DOI were not re-verified in this session.
findings.design_implication: Use a two-step correction loop. Step 1 is a prompt: 'Try again, focus on the vowel in "tu"', with no audio model, and the retry is rescored. If step 1 fails, step 2 is a recast: play the model, isolated and then in context, and allow a final attempt. Log successful self-repair as a stronger mastery signal than success after hearing the model. Let the user switch to model-first for brand-new sounds.

citations.ref: Lyster, R., & Saito, K. (2010). Oral feedback in classroom SLA: A meta-analysis. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 32(2), 265-302.

Gooch, R., Saito, K., & Lyster, R. (2016). Effects of recasts and prompts on L2 pronunciation development: Teaching English /ɹ/ to Korean adult EFL learners. System, 60, 117-127. (DOI not re-verified)

findings.claim: Automatic pronunciation scores are noisy at the phoneme and word level and can mislead learners. Phone-level machine scores correlate only moderately with human raters, and word-stress scores barely at all. ASR is less accurate on L2 than on L1 speech. Reviews report false error flags on comprehensible speech. Feedback remained useful when restricted to errors the system detected reliably.
findings.population: Automatic scoring benchmarks on non-native English (speechocean762: Mandarin-L1 children and adults reading English). ASR benchmarks over 191 L1 backgrounds. Adult immigrant learners of Dutch (Dutch-CAPT).
findings.effect_notes: GOPT (ICASSP 2022) on speechocean762, correlation with human ratings: phone r ≈ 0.61-0.68, word accuracy ≈ 0.54-0.60, word stress ≈ 0.15-0.33, utterance ≈ 0.72-0.74. Hollands et al. 2022: mean word error rate 10-15 percentage points worse on L2 than L1 English across 191 L1s. Cucchiarini, Neri & Strik 2009 (abstract): error detection was not 100% accurate, yet feedback improved targeted errors after a few hours of use over one month. Neri, Cucchiarini & Strik 2008 is the companion controlled study on segmental quality.
findings.design_implication: Do not flag an error from a single attempt. Flag a sound only when its low score recurs across at least 2-3 attempts and different words. Favour precision over recall: a missed error costs less than a false correction. Show uncertainty wording ('probably', 'the system isn't sure'). Never show word-stress scores. Add an 'I think that was right' button that logs disputes, and periodically calibrate the thresholds against a human rating of 20-30 of the learner's own recordings.

citations.ref: Gong, Y., Chen, Z., Chu, I.-H., Chang, P., & Glass, J. (2022). Transformer-based multi-aspect multi-granularity non-native English speaker pronunciation assessment. ICASSP 2022. Results table in the official repo.

Hollands, S., Blackburn, D., & Christensen, H. (2022). Evaluating the performance of state-of-the-art ASR systems on non-native English using corpora with extensive language background variation. Interspeech 2022, 3958-3962.
Cucchiarini, C., Neri, A., & Strik, H. (2009). Oral proficiency training in Dutch L2: The contribution of ASR-based corrective feedback. Speech Communication, 51(10), 853-863.
Neri, A., Cucchiarini, C., & Strik, H. (2008). The effectiveness of computer-based speech corrective feedback for improving segmental quality in L2 Dutch. ReCALL, 20(2), 225-243.
Amrate & Tsai (2025), ReCALL: CAPT systems still produce erroneous feedback on comprehensible L2 speech

findings.claim: In Azure Pronunciation Assessment, prosody scores, syllable-level results, IPA phoneme names and 'spoken phoneme' alternatives (what the learner actually said) are available only for en-US. A word is tagged 'Mispronunciation' when its accuracy is below 60. Accuracy is defined as closeness to a native speaker's phonemes. French learners therefore get much weaker diagnostic feedback from Azure than English learners.
findings.population: Not applicable (vendor documentation)
findings.effect_notes: From Microsoft's azure-ai-docs repository (how-to-pronunciation-assessment.md): 'Prosody assessment is only available in the en-US locale'. The feature table lists phoneme name (IPA), syllable groups and spoken phonemes as en-US only (SAPI phoneme names also for zh-CN). Monotone and break error types come with the prosody assessment.
findings.design_implication: en-US: enable prosody assessment (v1 never calls it) and request the top 5 alternative phonemes (NBestPhonemeCount = 5), so feedback can say 'you said [ə], target [ɛ]'. fr-FR: do not claim phoneme-specific diagnosis until it is validated. Compute French prosody and timing feedback locally: F0 contour, syllable durations, pause placement, and phrase-final lengthening or rise in the accentual phrase. Consider an open phone recognizer or forced aligner for French segment diagnosis, validated against human judgments.

citations.ref: Microsoft. Use pronunciation assessment (Azure AI Speech), source in MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs
Microsoft Learn, published version of the same page

findings.claim: In one very small randomized study (n = 14 Chinese EFL students), a transient visual meter of pitch variation increased speakers' pitch range more than audio-only self-review, and the increase held in a new presentation given without feedback 48 h later. Effects on intelligibility or rated intonation were not established. Earlier work (Hardison 2004, L2 French) reports benefits of pitch-contour displays with generalization. Overall the evidence is promising but sparse, and it favours simple one-dimension meters over matching a model's contour.
findings.population: Adult Chinese EFL engineering students (n = 14, pair-matched random assignment). Hardison 2004: adult English-speaking learners of French.
findings.effect_notes: Hincks & Edlund 2009: about 3 h of training in half-hour sessions over 4 weeks. The feedback was lights driven by the variation of the learner's pitch (standard deviation in semitones). The visual-feedback group increased pitch variation significantly more than the control, which could only listen to its own recordings (group × time effect, F = 8.36, p < .0005). The between-group difference exceeded 2.5 semitones and held in a new presentation given without feedback. Details of Hardison 2004 (LLT 8(1):34-52) were not re-verified here.
findings.design_implication: For the prosody track, show the learner's pitch contour (semitones, time-aligned) over the model's for the same phrase, or one simple meter (pitch range, or prominence on the target syllable), rather than a spectrogram. English targets: nuclear stress and focus. French targets: phrase-final prominence and continuation rises in accentual phrases. Fade the display over sessions so the skill carries over.

citations.ref: Hincks, R., & Edlund, J. (2009). Promoting increased pitch variation in oral presentations with transient visual feedback. Language Learning & Technology, 13(3), 32-50.

Hardison, D. M. (2004). Generalization of computer-assisted prosody training: Quantitative and qualitative findings. Language Learning & Technology, 8(1), 34-52. (bibliographic details confirmed; URL pattern not verified)

findings.claim: Visual acoustic feedback on segments (real-time vowel formant plots; waveform/spectrogram timing for voice onset time, VOT) can improve adult L2 sound production. Evidence is small-sample, lab or classroom based, and training one vowel can shift the learner's native vowels.
findings.population: Adults in lab settings (Kartushina et al.: native French-speaking adults, as I recall; not re-verified). Olson 2014: English-speaking classroom learners of Spanish (stop VOT).
findings.effect_notes: Kartushina et al. 2015 (JASA 138(2):817-832): production training with visual feedback improved production of foreign vowels. Kartushina et al. 2016 (J. Phonetics 57:21-39): short visual articulatory feedback training also shifted native vowels. Olson 2014 (LLT 18(3):173-192): classroom visual feedback improved VOT. Sample sizes and effect sizes were not re-verified in this session.
findings.design_implication: Offer an optional 'sound lab' for a few hard contrasts only. Vowels use an F1/F2 chart normalized to the learner's own vowel space, with the target region from multiple native talkers (French /y/-/u/, /ø/-/œ/, oral vs nasal vowels; English /i/-/ɪ/, /æ/-/ɛ/). Stops use a VOT meter (English aspirated vs French unaspirated /p t k/). Always pair the display with an articulatory cue, and check that trained sounds do not degrade the other language.

citations.ref: Kartushina, N., Hervais-Adelman, A., Frauenfelder, U. H., & Golestani, N. (2015). The effect of phonetic production training with visual feedback on the perception and production of foreign speech sounds. JASA, 138(2), 817-832.

Kartushina, N., Hervais-Adelman, A., Frauenfelder, U. H., & Golestani, N. (2016). Mutual influences between native and non-native vowels in production: Evidence from short-term visual articulatory feedback training. Journal of Phonetics, 57, 21-39.
Olson, D. J. (2014). Benefits of visual feedback on segmental production in the L2 classroom. Language Learning & Technology, 18(3), 173-192. (URL pattern not verified)

findings.claim: In one randomized lab study of perception (N = 60 naive adults, Japanese vowel length), audio plus mouth video produced a larger pre-post gain than audio only, with marginal posttest differences. Observed beat gestures added nothing in that study. Other studies show that observing or producing durational, pitch or beat gestures can help L2 pronunciation, so gesture evidence is mixed rather than negative. Richer articulatory visualizations (talking heads, ultrasound) have promising small-sample results.
findings.population: Hirata & Kelly 2010: 60 native English-speaking adults learning Japanese vowel-length contrasts (perception). Ultrasound/EMA studies are mostly small-n lab or clinical groups.
findings.effect_notes: Hirata & Kelly 2010: 4 training conditions, N = 60. All groups improved, but audio plus mouth video improved more than audio only. Conditions with hand gestures did not. Outcome was perception, not production.
findings.design_implication: Pair the model audio with video of a real native talker's face (lips visible) instead of voice-only TTS, plus a short lip/tongue animation as explicit phonetic information. Do not build ultrasound or other hardware-based feedback for a home app. Do not use gesture-only cues.

citations.ref: Hirata, Y., & Kelly, S. D. (2010). Effects of lips and hands on auditory learning of second-language speech sounds. JSLHR, 53(2), 298-310.

findings.claim: Adult L2 speakers' self-ratings of their pronunciation and comprehensibility are poorly aligned with listener ratings, so self-perception alone is an unreliable guide. In one small study, learners who only replayed their own recordings (with models) improved less than learners given a targeted visual display. Evidence that unguided replay is generally inferior to explicit feedback is limited.
findings.population: Adult L2 English speakers rated by native listeners (Trofimovich et al. 2016; I recall Francophone learners in Montreal, not re-verified). Adult learners of German (Dlaska & Krekeler). Chinese EFL adults (Hincks & Edlund control group).
findings.effect_notes: Trofimovich et al. 2016 (Bilingualism: Language and Cognition 19(1):122-140): self-ratings of accent, comprehensibility and fluency were poorly aligned with listener ratings (details not re-verified). Hincks & Edlund 2009: the control group, which only listened to its own recordings, improved significantly less than the visual-feedback group. Dlaska & Krekeler 2013 (System 41:25-37) examined short-term effects of individual corrective feedback on pronunciation; magnitudes not re-verified.
findings.design_implication: Replace free 'play TTS, then play mine' with a structured comparison. Loop the same word or syllable model/learner/model/learner, time-aligned, with the specific difference highlighted. Train self-monitoring: before showing a score, ask 'Did you get the /y/? yes/no', track how accurate these predictions are, and gradually withdraw automated feedback as they improve.

citations.ref: Trofimovich, P., Isaacs, T., Kennedy, S., Saito, K., & Crowther, D. (2016). Flawed self-assessment: Investigating self- and other-perception of second language speech. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, 19(1), 122-140. (DOI not re-verified)
Dlaska, A., & Krekeler, C. (2013). The short-term effects of individual corrective feedback on L2 pronunciation. System, 41(1), 25-37.
Hincks & Edlund (2009): control condition with own-recording playback only

findings.claim: Unscripted dictation-style ASR gives learners a listener's-eye view of their intelligibility ('seeing how people hear you'), including learners of French, and supports autonomous practice. The evidence is small-sample and partly qualitative. ASR accuracy on L2 speech differs from human intelligibility.
findings.population: University learners of French (Mroz 2018). Adult ESL/EFL learners (McCrocklin 2016; Inceoglu et al. 2020). ASR accuracy tests on L2 English speech (McCrocklin & Edalatishams 2020).
findings.effect_notes: No pooled effect size. The Mroz 2018 and McCrocklin studies are small and exploratory; outcome details were not re-verified in this session.
findings.design_implication: Add a 'Would a listener understand you?' mode. The learner speaks a sentence or describes a picture without a script, a general speech-to-text model transcribes it, and words recognized differently from the intended text are highlighted. Use it as the main intelligibility check for both languages, especially French, where Azure's phoneme diagnosis is limited. Warn that the recognizer's language model can guess words from context and so mask some errors.

citations.ref: Mroz, A. (2018). Seeing how people hear you: French learners experiencing intelligibility through automatic speech recognition. Foreign Language Annals, 51(3), 617-637.
McCrocklin, S. (2016). Pronunciation learner autonomy: The potential of automatic speech recognition. System, 57, 25-42.
McCrocklin, S., & Edalatishams, I. (2020). Revisiting popular speech recognition software for ESL speech. TESOL Quarterly, 54(4), 1086-1097.
Inceoglu, S., Lim, H., & Chen, W.-H. (2020). ASR for EFL pronunciation practice: Segmental development and learners' beliefs. Journal of AsiaTEFL, 17(3), 824-840.

findings.claim: Pronunciation instruction and feedback effects are largest on controlled tasks (reading practiced words and sentences) and shrink on spontaneous speech and global listener ratings. How gains are measured largely determines how large they look.
findings.population: L2 learners across 77 (Saito & Plonsky 2019) and 86 (Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015) pronunciation-instruction studies, mostly adult L2 English
findings.effect_notes: Saito & Plonsky 2019 (Language Learning 69(3):652-708): 77 studies; they propose a framework distinguishing controlled vs spontaneous tasks and acoustic vs listener-based measures. Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015 (Applied Linguistics 36(3):345-366): an overall large effect with moderators including feedback, treatment length and outcome type. Exact values not re-verified here.
findings.design_implication: Progress charts should track a fixed set of untrained transfer sentences each week and a short spontaneous-speech sample each month (picture description), plus delayed retention checks 1-2 weeks after a sound is marked 'mastered'. Do not treat ≥85 on a just-practised item as mastery.

citations.ref: Saito, K., & Plonsky, L. (2019). Effects of second language pronunciation teaching revisited: A proposed measurement framework and meta-analysis. Language Learning, 69(3), 652-708.
Lee, J., Jang, J., & Plonsky, L. (2015). The effectiveness of second language pronunciation instruction: A meta-analysis. Applied Linguistics, 36(3), 345-366.

findings.claim: Feedback should target a few errors that matter for intelligibility, not every deviation from a native norm. Accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility are partly independent. CAPT researchers have long argued that feedback must be interpretable, focused on intelligibility-relevant errors, and limited to errors the system detects reliably.
findings.population: 48 intermediate adult ESL speakers from four L1s, rated by 26 native listeners (Derwing & Munro 1997). CAPT design reviews.
findings.effect_notes: Derwing & Munro 1997: heavily accented speech could still be fully intelligible, and different linguistic factors drove each dimension. Evidence that focused feedback beats unfocused feedback comes mainly from grammar and writing research; it is weak for pronunciation specifically.
findings.design_implication: Show at most 1-2 corrections per attempt. Rank them by detection confidence, intelligibility impact (the functional load of the contrast) and how often the error recurs. Keep a full per-word view one tap away rather than as the default screen. Frame the goals and dashboard around comprehensibility, not a 'native-likeness' percentage.

citations.ref: Derwing, T. M., & Munro, M. J. (1997). Accent, intelligibility, and comprehensibility: Evidence from four L1s. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 19(1), 1-16.
Neri, A., Cucchiarini, C., & Strik, H. (2002). Feedback in computer assisted pronunciation training: Technology push or demand pull? ICSLP 2002.
Levis, J. (2007). Computer technology in teaching and researching pronunciation. Annual Review of Applied Linguistics, 27, 184-202.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Unguided 'listen to model, then yourself' comparison should not be the main feedback.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Reasonable, but the evidence is weak. The own-recording control in Hincks & Edlund (n = 7 per group) improved, though less than the visual-feedback group, and only pitch variation was measured. The unreliability of self-perception is supported by Trofimovich et al. 2016 and Dlaska & Krekeler 2008 (details not re-verified). Treat this as 'insufficient on its own', not 'harmful'.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Do not trust single-attempt phoneme scores or automatic word-stress scores as ground truth.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The GOPT figures were verified: phone PCC 0.62-0.68, word stress 0.15-0.33. So was the 10-15% L1 vs L2 WER gap in Hollands et al. Caveats: these benchmarks are not of Azure; speechocean762 stress labels are binary and imbalanced; and Azure returns no word-stress score. The recommendation to aggregate across attempts is well founded.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Native-likeness should not be the scoring target; Azure AccuracyScore measures closeness to native phonemes.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The Azure doc text is verified: 'how closely the phonemes match a native speaker's pronunciation'. Derwing & Munro 1997 show that accent is partly independent of intelligibility and comprehensibility. The accuracy score is still useful as a segmental signal. The problem is presenting it as the goal.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Azure provides no French prosody, syllable or 'what you actually said' feedback.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Verified in the Microsoft doc: prosody, syllable groups, IPA phoneme names and spoken phonemes are en-US only. fr-FR still returns accuracy, fluency, completeness and word-level error types. So 'no signal' holds for prosody and for what the learner actually said, not for scoring in general.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Hardware articulatory feedback (ultrasound, EMA) is unsuitable for a home self-study app.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The practical conclusion (needs equipment and expertise) is sound. However, controlled or pre-post adult L2 studies do exist. From memory, not verified in this session: Kocjančič Antolík, Pillot-Loiseau & Kamiyama 2019, JSLP 5(1):72-97, ultrasound feedback for French /y/-/u/ with Japanese learners; and the review by Bliss, Abel & Gick 2018, JSLP 4(1):129-153. The absence of evidence stated in the claim reflects gaps in the search, not in the literature.

critique_of_v1: Feedback is essentially a scoreboard. Every word is coloured green ≥85 / amber 60-84 / red <60, with per-phoneme scores and the expected IPA symbol, but the app never says what the learner produced instead or how to change it, and never asks for an immediate self-repair. The evidence favours explicit, diagnostic feedback followed by a retry (Saito & Lyster 2012; Saito 2013; Lyster & Saito 2010).

Unfocused feedback: colouring every word invites attention to many low-confidence deviations at once. Evidence and CAPT design guidance favour 1-2 reliable, intelligibility-relevant corrections per attempt.

In server/src/services/assess.ts, prosody assessment is never enabled (no enableProsodyAssessment call), so ProsodyScore will be undefined even for en-US. The progress charts and prosody track therefore have no real prosody signal.

Azure prosody, syllable results, IPA phoneme names and spoken-phoneme alternatives exist only for en-US. v1 sets phonemeAlphabet = 'IPA' for every language and builds French 'weak phoneme' drills on per-phoneme scores that may lack reliable labels. French learners get far weaker diagnostics, and the French prosody track (liaison, rhythm, shadowing) cannot be scored by Azure.
v1 never requests NBestPhonemeCount, so even in English it discards the one Azure output that could tell the learner 'you said [ə] instead of [ɛ]'.

'Weak phoneme' selection uses a rolling average of single-attempt phoneme scores. Phone-level machine scores agree with humans only moderately (r ≈ 0.6), and the average mixes different word contexts with no confidence threshold. Drill selection can chase noise and generate false corrections.

The fixed 85/60 thresholds and the ≥85 tier and level gates are not calibrated to intelligibility or to the learner's baseline. Azure itself tags 'Mispronunciation' at word accuracy <60, which is also a nativeness-based cut-off.

Mastery and ladder advancement are judged on the items just practised (controlled reading), where instruction effects are largest. The app has no untrained transfer items, no spontaneous-speech measure and no delayed retention test, so progress will look larger than real gains (Saito & Plonsky 2019).

The model is voice-only TTS, used for side-by-side listening. Unguided listen-and-compare is weaker than targeted feedback, and learners' self-perception is unreliable. There is no talking face (lip video helps: Hirata & Kelly 2010), and no aligned segment-level A/B comparison.

There is no visual feedback of the kinds that have evidence behind them: no pitch contour or pitch-range meter for intonation (Hincks & Edlund 2009), and no vowel-space or VOT display for hard contrasts (Kartushina et al. 2015; Olson 2014).

Speed ladders raise tempo using the same nativeness-based accuracy score. I found no feedback-related evidence that TTS tempo ladders gated on accuracy ≥85 improve articulation, and the fast-TTS model may encourage imitating synthetic timing.

There is no intelligibility check (e.g., unscripted dictation), no learner self-assessment or calibration step, and no way to dispute or flag a wrong score. That leaves no guard against scoring errors and no support for building self-monitoring.
open_questions: The learner's L1 is unknown. It determines which errors are likely and intelligibility-critical, and how biased ASR scoring will be for their accent. Should the app start with a diagnostic recording session rated by a human (tutor or native speaker) to calibrate thresholds?
How reliable is Azure fr-FR phoneme-level accuracy for L2 French? No validation was found, so the app should collect a small human-rated sample before trusting French phoneme diagnosis.

Which French segment diagnosis back-end should replace or supplement Azure (open phone recognizers, forced alignment with goodness-of-pronunciation scoring, wav2vec2-style models)? How accurate are they on L2 French?
Are LLM- or template-generated articulatory explanations accurate enough to serve as the 'explicit phonetic information' that helped in Saito 2013? This needs expert review of the explanation bank.
For self-study apps, is immediate feedback after each attempt better than delayed feedback after a set? Evidence on corrective-feedback timing in pronunciation is unresolved.
How large are the effects of visual formant/VOT feedback for adult learners of French specifically, and do they persist or transfer to spontaneous speech?

The effect sizes marked 'not re-verified' should be checked against the original articles once web access is restored: Ngo et al. 2024 overall and moderator values; the full Mahdi & Al Khateeb 2019 estimate; Lee et al. 2015; Trofimovich et al. 2016; Hardison 2004; Olson 2014; Gooch et al. 2016.
missed_evidence_flagged: Uchihara, T., Karas, M., & Thomson, R. I. (2024). Does perceptual high variability phonetic training improve L2 speech production? A meta-analysis of perception-production connection. Applied Psycholinguistics, 45, 591-623. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716424000195. Perception training without production feedback transfers to production. This contradicts the claim that practice without feedback does not work, and it argues for a perception/HVPT module for both languages.

Uchihara, T., Karas, M., & Thomson, R. I. (2025). High variability phonetic training (HVPT): A meta-analysis of L2 perceptual training studies. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 47, 794-827. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263125100879

Saito, K. (2013). The acquisitional value of recasts in instructed second language speech learning: Teaching the perception and production of English /ɹ/ to adult Japanese learners. Language Learning, 63(3), 499-529. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12015. N = 45, randomized. FFI-only improved on trained words; FFI plus recasts produced gains that generalized to untrained words. Relevant to feedback-2 and feedback-3.

Lambacher, S. G., Martens, W. L., Kakehi, K., Marasinghe, C. A., & Molholt, G. (2005). The effects of identification training on the identification and production of American English vowels by native speakers of Japanese. Applied Psycholinguistics, 26, 227-247. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716405050150. Identification training improved production of the trained vowels.

Li, P., Baills, F., & Prieto, P. (2020). Observing and producing durational hand gestures facilitates the pronunciation of novel vowel-length contrasts. Studies in Second Language Acquisition. Also Baills, F., Suárez-González, N., González-Fuente, S., & Prieto, P. (2019), SSLA 41, 33-58 (pitch gestures, Mandarin tones), and Gluhareva, D., & Prieto, P. (2017), Language Teaching Research 21(5), 609-631 (beat gestures). Bibliographic details come from Scopus reference lists; results are from memory and should be re-checked. These contradict the does-not-work claim about gestures.

Motohashi-Saigo, M., & Hardison, D. M. (2009). Acquisition of L2 Japanese geminates: Training with waveform displays. Language Learning & Technology, 13(2), 29-47. Also Okuno, T., & Hardison, D. M. (2016). Perception-production link in L2 Japanese vowel duration: Training with technology. LLT, 20(2), 61-80. Both show waveform displays working after brief training.

Thomson, R. I., & Derwing, T. M. (2015). The effectiveness of L2 pronunciation instruction: A narrative review. Applied Linguistics, 36(3), 326-344. It adds to feedback-11: few studies test spontaneous speech, and most target nativeness.

Munro, M. J., & Derwing, T. M. (2006). The functional load principle in ESL pronunciation instruction: An exploratory study. System, 34(4), 520-531. Direct but exploratory support for ranking errors by functional load (feedback-12).

McCrocklin, S. (2019). ASR-based dictation practice for second language pronunciation improvement. Journal of Second Language Pronunciation, 5(1), 98-118. A controlled study of dictation-style ASR practice, relevant to feedback-10.
Dlaska, A., & Krekeler, C. (2008). Self-assessment of pronunciation. System, 36(4), 506-516. Direct evidence on how well learners assess their own pronunciation (feedback-9).

Hincks & Edlund (2009), full text, pp. 34-35: the authors argue that making learners match a model's pitch contour is 'probably frustrating and counter-productive' and that contours need training to interpret. This bears on the pitch-overlay design in feedback-6. Copy used for verification: https://github.com/timo-b-roettger/ErrorsLing/blob/c8958ca65f08bd2dadd963bdf9a09d6787b88c81/data/subsample/2009-09-LLT-13_03_hincksedlund.txt

speechocean762 dataset README: half the speakers are children; phone scores are 0-2; word-stress scores are binary {5, 10}. The low stress correlations partly reflect label coarseness, not only model weakness. https://github.com/jimbozhang/speechocean762

Azure language support page: pronunciation assessment covers 33 locales, including fr-FR for accuracy, fluency and completeness. French feedback is reduced, not absent. https://github.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/blob/main/articles/ai-services/speech-service/language-support.md

Randomized study of a 3-D talking head with an airflow model: 'Learning challenging L2 sounds via computer-assisted training: Audiovisual training with an airflow model'. The airflow cue improved Japanese learners' production of Mandarin aspirated stops and generalized to new syllables. Authors and venue not identified (the abstract format suggests Journal of Computer Assisted Learning). This is small-sample support for richer articulatory visualizations (feedback-8).

Liakin, D., Cardoso, W., & Liakina, N. (2015). Learning L2 pronunciation with a mobile speech recognizer: French /y/. CALICO Journal, 32(1), 1-25. One of the few controlled ASR studies for L2 French. From memory; not verified in this session.

Kocjančič Antolík, T., Pillot-Loiseau, C., & Kamiyama, T. (2019). The effectiveness of real-time ultrasound visual feedback on tongue movements in L2 pronunciation training. Journal of Second Language Pronunciation, 5(1), 72-97 (French /y/-/u/). Also Bliss, H., Abel, J., & Gick, B. (2018). Computer-assisted visual articulation feedback in L2 pronunciation instruction: A review. JSLP, 4(1), 129-153. Adult L2 hardware-feedback evidence exists. From memory; not verified in this session.

general_review.topic: motor: Motor learning principles and speech-therapy evidence for articulation
general_review.summary:
VERIFICATION WARNING: No source could be opened in this session. The workflow had already used the whole WebSearch quota (200 of 200 calls). WebFetch and shell access were blocked by the egress proxy for every scholarly host I tried: PubMed/NCBI, PMC, doi.org, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, ASHA Journals, Cochrane, Google Scholar, ERIC, Frontiers, ResearchGate and Wikipedia. Every citation below is recalled from training knowledge. Each DOI is my best recollection and must be checked before it goes into project docs. I gave effect sizes only where I am fairly confident, marked them "verify", and rated strength cautiously. Treat this as a well-informed draft, not a checked review.

SUBSTANCE: The motor-learning evidence points to a different practice engine than v1 has. (1) Judge learning by delayed retention and transfer probes, not by accuracy during practice. v1 advances a level on one immediate score of 85 or more. (2) Adjust practice conditions to the learner's current accuracy, following the challenge-point idea. When a sound is new, use blocked practice with rich feedback on how to move the mouth (knowledge of performance, KP). As accuracy rises, move to mixed, variable practice with faded summary scores (knowledge of results, KR). (3) Get many short productions per session and spread practice across days. (4) Train each target in many phonetic contexts, because speech motor learning is very specific to the utterance practised. (5) Drop non-speech oral motor exercises (NSOMEs), which have no supporting evidence. (6) Aim for intelligibility through 'clear speech' cues and a moderate speaking rate, not maximum speed. Slowing down alone does not produce the clear-speech benefit. Speaking rate relates to L2 comprehensibility in a curve: too slow and too fast both hurt. No controlled evidence shows that fast tongue twisters train L2 articulation.

CAVEATS ON WHO WAS STUDIED: Most speech-specific motor-learning evidence comes from small single-case studies. The groups are adults with acquired apraxia of speech (AOS), children with childhood apraxia of speech (CAS), and children with speech sound disorders (SSD). The rest comes from limb-motor labs or healthy adults learning new speech movements. I know of almost no direct studies with adult L2 learners. Limb meta-analyses also suggest several classic principles (reduced feedback frequency, mixed practice in applied settings, learner self-control) shrink or disappear after correcting for publication bias. So use them as adjustable defaults, not dogma. Finally, adult L2 accent errors are often rooted in perception and sound categories, not only motor execution. Motor practice must therefore be paired with perception and contrast training, which other topics cover.

findings.claim: The learning-performance distinction is well established: how accurate someone is during practice does not reliably predict retention after a delay or transfer to new items, so learning should be measured with delayed retention and transfer probes. The claim that specific practice conditions (blocked order, feedback on every trial, a model before each attempt) lower retention is much weaker. Later meta-analyses find small, absent or bias-inflated effects for blocked vs random practice and for feedback frequency. Complex skills may benefit from more support (Wulf & Shea 2002). No speech or L2 study directly shows that hearing a model before each attempt harms retention.
findings.population: Mainly healthy adults in limb-motor and verbal-learning research. The principle was applied to speech in adults with acquired AOS and children with CAS. There is little direct evidence from adult L2 learners.
findings.effect_notes: Conceptual and integrative reviews, so no pooled effect size. Maas et al. (2008) note that most supporting data are non-speech. None of these sources could be opened this session.
findings.design_implication: Separate PROBE trials from PRACTICE trials. Each session starts with 5-10 probe items on the current targets. Probes have no TTS model, no feedback, and about half are untrained words or sentences. Only probe scores decide level advancement and feed the main progress chart. For example, a target advances when probe accuracy clears the threshold on two different days. Show practice scores separately as 'practice', not 'progress'.

citations.ref: Maas, Robin, Austermann Hula, Freedman, Wulf, Ballard & Schmidt (2008). Principles of motor learning in treatment of motor speech disorders. AJSLP 17(3), 277-298. [not opened this session - verify]
Soderstrom & Bjork (2015). Learning versus performance: An integrative review. Perspectives on Psychological Science 10(2), 176-199. [not opened - verify]
Kantak & Winstein (2012). Learning-performance distinction and memory processes for motor skills. Behavioural Brain Research 228(1), 219-231. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: In limb and sport research, random practice has a retention advantage in lab tasks but a small or unreliable one in applied settings. Brady 2004 reported roughly d = .57 in lab studies vs .19 in applied studies (from a secondary source). Ammar et al. 2023 and 2024 found no reliable long-term benefit. Czyż et al. 2024 (Sci Rep) reported a medium retention benefit, so the meta-analyses disagree. Speech studies (AOS n = 2, CAS n = 4, small AOS review) are mixed. The L2 evidence splits by outcome: interleaving helped grammar accuracy in speaking (Suzuki, Yokosawa & Aline 2020), while blocked task repetition gave better fluency transfer (Suzuki 2021). The challenge-point framework is a plausible heuristic for adapting difficulty, but it has very few direct tests and none in L2 speech. 'Easier conditions for low-skill learners' is its prediction, not an established finding.
findings.population: Meta-analyses: healthy people learning limb or sport skills. Speech: 2 adults with AOS (Knock et al. 2000; random practice gave better retention), 4 children with CAS (Maas & Farinella 2012; no consistent advantage), and a systematic review of AOS studies (Bislick et al. 2012; small, mostly single-case). Challenge point applied to speech: a case study of a child with residual /r/ errors (Hitchcock & McAllister Byun 2015).
findings.effect_notes: Brady (2004) found larger mixed-practice effects in lab tasks than in applied tasks. Ammar et al. (2023) found no reliable mixed-practice benefit in applied sport practice. Speech studies had n = 1-4 per study. Exact effect sizes not recalled reliably; verify.
findings.design_implication: Replace the single 85-or-higher gate with an adaptive controller for each target. Practice runs in blocks of about 10 trials. If a block reaches 80% or more, raise ONE difficulty dimension: word, then phrase, then sentence; more targets interleaved; TTS model removed; feedback reduced; rate varied. If a block falls below 50%, lower one dimension; otherwise hold. A brand-new sound starts with a short blocked run with a model and KP, then moves to interleaving. Limit immediate retries of the same item to 2-3 so 'Retry until green' does not become the default loop.

citations.ref: Guadagnoli & Lee (2004). Challenge point: a framework for conceptualizing the effects of various practice conditions in motor learning. Journal of Motor Behavior 36(2), 212-224. [not opened - verify]

Bislick, Weir, Spencer, Kendall & Yorkston (2012). Do principles of motor learning enhance retention and transfer of speech skills? A systematic review. Aphasiology 26(5), 709-728. [not opened - verify]

Knock, Ballard, Robin & Schmidt (2000). Influence of order of stimulus presentation on speech motor learning: a principles of motor learning perspective. Aphasiology 14(5-6), 653-668. [not opened - verify]
Maas & Farinella (2012). Random versus blocked practice in treatment for childhood apraxia of speech. JSLHR 55(2), 561-578. [not opened - verify]
Ammar et al. (2023). The myth of contextual interference learning benefit in sports practice: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Educational Research Review 39, 100537. [not opened - verify]
Brady (2004). Contextual interference: a meta-analytic study. Perceptual and Motor Skills 99(1), 116-126. [not opened - verify]

Hitchcock & McAllister Byun (2015). Enhancing generalisation in biofeedback intervention using the challenge point framework: a case study. Clinical Linguistics & Phonetics 29(1), 59-75. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: In one somatosensory force-field paradigm, healthy adults' adaptation to a jaw force field was specific to the utterance they trained on (Tremblay, Houle & Ostry 2008). Other paradigms show partial generalization. Auditory (formant) perturbation adaptation carried over to other words with the same vowel and to other vowels (Houde & Jordan 1998). Transfer across utterances is partial and uneven, not absent (Rochet-Capellan, Richer & Ostry 2012). These are short-term adaptation studies in native speakers, not studies of learning new L2 articulatory categories. Practising a target across varied contexts is a reasonable default, supported mainly by limb-motor work and a few small AOS studies. It is untested for L2 articulation.
findings.population: Healthy adult native speakers in a speech lab: jaw force-field adaptation (Tremblay et al. 2008). Support for varied practice comes from adults with AOS (Bislick et al. 2012) and limb-motor work (Maas et al. 2008).
findings.effect_notes: Tremblay et al. used a small lab sample; exact n not recalled. Evidence on varied practice in AOS was limited to a few small studies.
findings.design_implication: For each target sound, generate or author items along several dimensions: position (word start, middle, end, clusters), neighbouring vowels, stressed or unstressed syllable, many different words, carrier phrases, rate, and style (read, repeated, spontaneous prompt). Keep a held-out set of items that are used only for transfer probes. Never serve the same fixed sentence list on every drill; v1 sorts the same pack items word, then sentence, then passage every time.

citations.ref: Tremblay, Houle & Ostry (2008). Specificity of speech motor learning. Journal of Neuroscience 28(10), 2426-2434. [not opened - verify]
Maas et al. (2008). Principles of motor learning in treatment of motor speech disorders. AJSLP 17(3), 277-298. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: More practice is a broadly accepted motor-learning principle, but direct speech evidence on production dose is thin. One alternating-treatments study of 2 children with CAS found faster gains and better generalisation with 100+ productions per session. A systematic review of treatment intensity (Kaipa & Peterson 2016) was inconclusive. In Lee, Jang & Plonsky's L2 pronunciation meta-analysis (86 reports, d = 0.89 within-group, 0.80 between-group), longer interventions had larger effects. That is a between-study moderator and may be confounded, not a dose manipulation. Spacing helps L2 learning in general, mostly vocabulary (Kim & Webb 2022). That meta-analysis also found expanding and equal spacing equivalent. For L2 speaking, schedule effects on delayed tests were limited (Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022).
findings.population: Children with CAS: Edeal & Gildersleeve-Neumann (2011), n = 2. Mixed clinical groups: Kaipa & Peterson (2016). Adult and adolescent L2 learners: Lee, Jang & Plonsky (2015). Spacing claims come mostly from limb and verbal learning.
findings.effect_notes: Lee, Jang & Plonsky (2015): large overall effect, recalled as d of about 0.89 (verify), with longer treatments giving larger effects. Kaipa & Peterson (2016): heterogeneous and inconclusive, no single optimal dose. Edeal & Gildersleeve-Neumann (2011): 2 children only.
findings.design_implication: Make the number of target productions the main dose metric and show it. Favour short items (words, phrases, recordings of 2-4 seconds) so a 10-minute session gives 60-100 target productions. A single minute-long passage gives only a few. Schedule short daily sessions and bring mastered targets back at growing intervals (for example 1, 3, 7 and 14 days). Use long passages mainly as transfer probes.

citations.ref: Kaipa & Peterson (2016). A systematic review of treatment intensity in speech disorders. International Journal of Speech-Language Pathology 18(6), 507-520. [not opened - verify]
Edeal & Gildersleeve-Neumann (2011). The importance of production frequency in therapy for childhood apraxia of speech. AJSLP 20(2), 95-110. [not opened - verify]
Lee, Jang & Plonsky (2015). The effectiveness of second language pronunciation instruction: a meta-analysis. Applied Linguistics 36(3), 345-366. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: The classic 'guidance hypothesis' holds that feedback on every trial creates dependence, so feedback should be reduced or faded. This is not reliably supported. A meta-analysis of motor-learning studies found no dependable retention benefit from reduced feedback frequency. Speech studies are single-case and mixed: reduced or delayed feedback helped retention in some adults with AOS, results were mixed in children with CAS, and a lab study of healthy adults learning non-native consonant clusters did not show the predicted advantage (recalled; verify).
findings.population: Meta-analysis: healthy people in limb and motor tasks. Speech: 4 adults with AOS (Austermann Hula et al. 2008), 4 children with CAS (Maas, Butalla & Farinella 2012), healthy adult English speakers learning non-native clusters (Lowe & Buchwald 2017).
findings.effect_notes: McKay et al. (2022) found no reliable benefit of reduced relative frequency on retention; exact pooled estimate not recalled, verify. The speech studies had n = 4 each, with results differing across participants.
findings.design_implication: Do not hard-code either '100% detailed feedback' or 'always fade'. Default: feedback on every trial while a target is new or at a low challenge level. At higher challenge levels, switch to summary feedback after each block of about 5 trials. Use 'bandwidth' feedback: only flag phonemes or words below a tolerance and stay quiet otherwise. Always let the learner open the details on demand. Log which mode was active so the app can later compare retention for this one learner.

citations.ref: McKay, Hussien, Vinh, Mir-Orefice, Brooks & Ste-Marie (2022). Meta-analysis of the reduced relative feedback frequency effect on motor learning and performance. Psychology of Sport and Exercise 61, 102165. [not opened - verify]

Austermann Hula, Robin, Maas, Ballard & Schmidt (2008). Effects of feedback frequency and timing on acquisition and retention of speech skills in acquired apraxia of speech. JSLHR 51(5), 1088-1113. [not opened - verify]
Maas, Butalla & Farinella (2012). Feedback frequency in treatment for childhood apraxia of speech. AJSLP 21(3), 239-257. [not opened - verify]
Lowe & Buchwald (2017). The impact of feedback frequency on performance in a novel speech motor learning task. JSLHR 60(6S), 1712-1725. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: Feedback given instantly after an attempt can hurt learning compared with feedback delayed by a few seconds. Having learners estimate their own error before seeing the result improves learning, because it builds the internal error detection they need when no feedback is available. In adults with AOS, delayed feedback (about 5 seconds) helped retention for some participants.
findings.population: Healthy adults on lab limb tasks (Swinnen et al. 1990; Guadagnoli & Kohl 2001). Adults with AOS (Austermann Hula et al. 2008, n = 4). No adult L2 studies known.
findings.effect_notes: Group lab experiments with small samples; effect sizes not recalled.
findings.design_implication: After each recording, ask for a one-tap self-rating before showing Azure scores. Options: 'sounded right' / 'not sure' / 'off', or tap the word that felt wrong. Then show the scores. Track how often the learner's self-rating agrees with the scores as a 'self-monitoring' metric. Rising agreement means the learner can catch their own errors outside the app.

citations.ref: Swinnen, Schmidt, Nicholson & Shapiro (1990). Information feedback for skill acquisition: instantaneous knowledge of results degrades learning. JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 16(4), 706-716. [not opened - verify]

Guadagnoli & Kohl (2001). Knowledge of results for motor learning: relationship between error estimation and knowledge of results frequency. Journal of Motor Behavior 33(2), 217-224. [not opened - verify]
Austermann Hula et al. (2008). JSLHR 51(5), 1088-1113. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: Feedback comes in two kinds. Knowledge of results (KR) reports the outcome, such as a score or right/wrong. Knowledge of performance (KP) tells the learner how they moved and how to change it. KP is thought to matter most early on, when a new movement pattern has to be set up; KR suits later refinement. Visual articulatory biofeedback such as ultrasound is a form of KP. A systematic review of ultrasound biofeedback for SSD found mostly positive results, but from low-level designs. Azure scores are KR only.
findings.population: KP vs KR principle: limb motor learning, applied to motor speech disorders (Maas et al. 2008). Ultrasound biofeedback: mostly children and adolescents with SSD, case series and single-case designs (Sugden et al. 2019).
findings.effect_notes: Sugden et al. (2019): many small, low-quality studies; no pooled effect size recalled.
findings.design_implication: Write KP content for every target phoneme in both languages: place, manner, voicing, lip rounding, tongue height and position, a sagittal diagram or short animation, and a 'bridge' from a sound the learner already has. Examples: French /y/ = say /i/ then round the lips; English /θ/ = tongue tip lightly between the teeth, then blow air. Use the substituted phoneme when Azure provides it (e.g., 'you said /s/ for /θ/') to tailor the cue. Show KP automatically when a target is new or accuracy has stalled for 2 or more sessions, then step back to KR only.

citations.ref: Maas et al. (2008). AJSLP 17(3), 277-298. [not opened - verify]

Sugden, Lloyd, Lam & Cleland (2019). Systematic review of ultrasound visual biofeedback in intervention for speech sound disorders. International Journal of Language & Communication Disorders 54(5), 705-728. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: Several meta-analyses reported an external-focus advantage in limb and sport tasks; Chua et al. 2021 found g = 0.58 for learning and g = 0.26 for performance. A 2024 robust Bayesian reanalysis of Chua's data found moderate to strong evidence of publication bias. After correction the effects were negligible: g = 0.15 for retention, 0.09 for transfer and 0.01 for performance, and Bayes factors favoured the null (McKay et al. 2024, Psychological Bulletin). Whether external focus helps is therefore contested and possibly near zero on average. In speech it is essentially untested beyond one non-speech oral-motor study.
findings.population: Healthy adults and athletes in limb and sport tasks (Wulf 2013; Chua et al. 2021). Healthy adults on an oral-motor task (Freedman et al. 2007). No L2 speech studies known.
findings.effect_notes: Chua et al. (2021) reported an external-focus advantage across multiple meta-analyses; pooled values not recalled reliably, and later commentators raised bias concerns (verify). The effect in speech is essentially untested.
findings.design_implication: Frame cues around the sound and the listener. Examples: 'make it clearly SHIP, not SHEEP'; 'let the listener hear the final /t/'; 'make the French /u/ sound darker than /y/'. Use short articulatory (internal) cues only while first establishing a new sound (motor-7), then switch to outcome-focused cues. Do not show long lists of body-part instructions on every trial.

citations.ref: Wulf (2013). Attentional focus and motor learning: a review of 15 years. International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology 6(1), 77-104. [not opened - verify]

Chua, Jimenez-Diaz, Lewthwaite, Kim & Wulf (2021). Superiority of external attentional focus for motor performance and learning: systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Psychological Bulletin 147(6), 618-645. [not opened - verify]
Freedman, Maas, Caligiuri, Wulf & Robin (2007). Internal versus external: oral-motor performance as a function of attentional focus. JSLHR 50(1), 131-136. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: Among treatments for speech sound disorders, minimal-pair contrast therapy has the largest evidence base. The complexity approach proposes that training more complex, later-acquired targets (for example clusters) spreads improvement more widely through the sound system. However, an RCT found more progress with early-developing, stimulable targets. None of this has been tested in adult L2 learners.
findings.population: Children with phonological or speech sound disorders only. Rvachew & Nowak (2001): RCT, n = 48 preschoolers. Complexity studies: mostly small single-case designs.
findings.effect_notes: Baker & McLeod (2011) reviewed over 100 intervention studies, with minimal pairs the most studied approach (verify count). Rvachew & Nowak (2001), n = 48, contradicted the complexity prediction.
findings.design_implication: Organise content around contrasts: the target sound against the learner's actual substitution (from Azure errors or the learner's L1 profile once known). Train each contrast in both perception (identify which word you heard) and production. Choose targets by how much they affect intelligibility (functional load, error consistency), not only by the lowest rolling Azure average. Treat complexity-based generalisation as a hypothesis to test for this learner: after training a harder target (e.g., clusters, /θ/), probe related untrained targets (singletons, /ð/) and keep whichever order works.

citations.ref: Baker & McLeod (2011). Evidence-based practice for children with speech sound disorders: Part 1 narrative review. LSHSS 42(2), 102-139. [not opened - verify]
Gierut (2007). Phonological complexity and language learnability. AJSLP 16(1), 6-17. [not opened - verify]
Rvachew & Nowak (2001). The effect of target-selection strategy on phonological learning. JSLHR 44(3), 610-623. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: Non-speech oral motor exercises (tongue push-ups, lip exercises, blowing, oral 'warm-ups') have no supporting evidence for improving speech sound production. The Cochrane review found too few, too small RCTs to support them, and an earlier ASHA evidence review reached the same conclusion. Clinicians still use them widely. The underlying principle is task specificity: you improve speech by practising speech.
findings.population: Children with developmental SSD (Cochrane review; McCauley et al. 2009). A survey of US speech-language pathologists (Lof & Watson 2008). No adult L2 data.
findings.effect_notes: Lee & Gibbon (2015): very few small RCTs, recalled as roughly 2-3 trials with a few dozen children in total (verify); no evidence that NSOMEs work. The strength rating reflects a consistent absence of positive evidence, not proof of harm.
findings.design_implication: Include no non-speech mouth exercises or 'articulator workouts'. Any warm-up should be speech: syllable sequences on the day's targets (e.g., 'pa-ta-ka', CV syllables with the target) and target words.

citations.ref: Lee & Gibbon (2015). Non-speech oral motor treatment for children with developmental speech sound disorders. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD009383. [not opened - verify]
McCauley, Strand, Lof, Schooling & Frymark (2009). Evidence-based systematic review: effects of nonspeech oral motor exercises on speech. AJSLP 18(4), 343-360. [not opened - verify]
Lof & Watson (2008). A nationwide survey of nonspeech oral motor exercise use: implications for evidence-based practice. LSHSS 39(3), 392-407. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: Deliberate 'clear speech' makes speech more intelligible to both native and non-native listeners. The benefit is not just a matter of speaking slowly. Time-stretching ordinary conversational speech did not make it more intelligible, and trained talkers kept a clear-speech benefit at normal speaking rates. In people with Parkinson's disease or multiple sclerosis, 'clear' instructions beat 'slow' ones, and the wording of the instruction changes how big the benefit is. For non-native talkers: high-proficiency L2 speakers gained intelligibility with clear speech, but late bilinguals gained less, and some of their vowels became LESS intelligible.
findings.population: Listener-side intelligibility studies of mostly native English talkers (Smiljanic & Bradlow 2009). Non-native listeners (Bradlow & Bent 2002). Talkers with Parkinson's disease or MS plus healthy controls (Tjaden et al. 2014). Healthy adults given different instructions (Lam & Tjaden 2013). High-proficiency L2 talkers (Smiljanic & Bradlow 2011). Early vs late Spanish-English bilinguals (Rogers et al. 2010).
findings.effect_notes: Speaking clearly reliably improves intelligibility at the moment of speaking. Whether it carries over into habitual L2 speech after training is not established. Lam & Tjaden (2013): intelligibility was highest with an 'overenunciate' instruction and lowest with habitual speech (recalled; verify). Specific effect sizes not recalled reliably.
findings.design_implication: Add a 'clear vs conversational' articulation track. The learner records the same sentence in habitual style, then with a clear-speech instruction ('over-enunciate each word', 'speak as if to someone hard of hearing'). The app shows the differences it can measure: accuracy and completeness, rate in syllables per second, pauses, and final consonants that were released vs dropped. Open this track only once a target is reasonably accurate, because clear speech amplifies whatever sound category the learner already has, including a wrong one. Do not treat the slow TTS tier as a 'clear' model; slow is not the same as clear.

citations.ref: Smiljanic & Bradlow (2009). Speaking and hearing clearly: talker and listener factors in speaking style changes. Language and Linguistics Compass 3(1), 236-264. [not opened - verify]
Bradlow & Bent (2002). The clear speech effect for non-native listeners. JASA 112(1), 272-284. [not opened - verify]

Picheny, Durlach & Braida (1989). Speaking clearly for the hard of hearing III: an attempt to determine the contribution of speaking rate to differences in intelligibility between clear and conversational speech. JSHR 32(3), 600-603. [not opened - verify]
Krause & Braida (2002). Investigating alternative forms of clear speech: the effects of speaking rate and speaking mode on intelligibility. JASA 112(5), 2165-2172. [not opened - verify]

Tjaden, Sussman & Wilding (2014). Impact of clear, loud, and slow speech on scaled intelligibility and speech severity in Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis. JSLHR 57(3), 779-792. [not opened - verify]
Lam & Tjaden (2013). Intelligibility of clear speech: effect of instruction. JSLHR 56(5), 1429-1440. [not opened - verify]

Smiljanic & Bradlow (2011). Bidirectional clear speech perception benefit for native and high-proficiency non-native talkers and listeners: intelligibility and accentedness. JASA 130(6), 4020-4031. [not opened - verify]
Rogers, DeMasi & Krause (2010). Conversational and clear speech intelligibility of /bVd/ syllables produced by native and non-native English speakers. JASA 128(1), 410-423. [not opened - verify]

findings.claim: For L2 speech, speaking rate relates to listener judgments in a curve: rates that are too slow or too fast both hurt, and the best rate is moderately faster than typical L2 rates but not maximal. Slowing L2 speech down did not improve listener ratings. Tongue twisters are an experimental method for provoking speech errors through competition between similar sounds; I know of no controlled evidence that they train L2 articulation. In contrast, healthy adults practising unfamiliar non-native consonant clusters do become more accurate and fluent with practice.
findings.population: Adult L2 English speakers (Mandarin L1 in Munro & Derwing studies, recalled), judged by native listeners on rate-manipulated recordings. Healthy adult native speakers in tongue-twister and cluster-learning lab studies. No L2 tongue-twister training studies known.
findings.effect_notes: Rate findings come from listener-rating experiments with manipulated recordings, not from training studies. The absence of tongue-twister evidence reflects my knowledge only; it needs a verified search.
findings.design_implication: Replace the 'speed ladder to fast' with rate-control training aimed at a target band near normal conversational rate in syllables per second, with accuracy held steady. Reward stability, meaning a small accuracy drop across slow, normal and slightly-fast, not reaching the fastest tier. Keep consonant-cluster drills, varied across contexts. Keep tongue twisters as optional fun or challenge items, not as the scored core of the articulation track.

citations.ref: Munro & Derwing (2001). Modeling perceptions of the accentedness and comprehensibility of L2 speech: the role of speaking rate. SSLA 23(4), 451-468. [not opened - verify]
Munro & Derwing (1998). The effects of speaking rate on listener evaluations of native and foreign-accented speech. Language Learning 48(2), 159-182. [not opened - verify]

Acheson & MacDonald (2009). Twisting tongues and memories: explorations of the relationship between language production and verbal working memory. Journal of Memory and Language 60(3), 329-350. [not opened - verify]
Segawa, Tourville, Beal & Guenther (2015). The neural correlates of speech motor sequence learning. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience 27(4), 819-831. [not opened - verify]

does_not_work_verified.claim: Non-speech oral motor exercises for improving speech sounds: no supporting evidence; task specificity argues against them.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The Cochrane review (Lee & Gibbon 2015) and the ASHA evidence review (McCauley et al. 2009) both found insufficient evidence of benefit. The evidence is from children with developmental SSD; applying it to adult L2 learners is by analogy. Phrase it as 'no evidence of benefit', not 'proven ineffective'.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Advancing levels or tiers on accuracy during practice or on a single attempt measures performance, not learning, and overestimates mastery without delayed retention or transfer probes.
does_not_work_verified.notes: This is the core learning-performance distinction (Soderstrom & Bjork 2015; Kantak & Winstein 2012), and it is well supported. Direct tests of 'practice-accuracy gating overestimates mastery' in L2 pronunciation apps were not found, but the logic follows from the retention and transfer literature.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Treating maximum speed as the articulation goal (fast-tempo tongue-twister ladders).
does_not_work_verified.notes: Munro & Derwing 1998/2001 support a moderate, not maximal, L2 rate; those are listener-rating studies, not training studies. The tongue-twister statement is correctly framed as absence of evidence. The Acheson & MacDonald DOI should be 10.1016/j.jml.2008.12.002. I could not run a literature search for tongue-twister training studies this session.

does_not_work_verified.claim: 'Slow equals clear': uniformly slowing speech does not produce the clear-speech benefit; a slow TTS reference is not a clear-speech model.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by Picheny et al. 1989 and Uchanski et al. 1996 (time-scaling did not help), Krause & Braida 2002 (clear speech at normal rate kept its benefit) and Tjaden et al. 2014 (slow was least effective). Caveat: rate reduction is still a legitimate strategy for some dysarthric speakers, and slow TTS may help perception or segmentation even though it is not a clear-speech model.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Applying popular motor-learning rules as universal laws (always mix practice, always reduce feedback, always let the learner control feedback).
does_not_work_verified.notes: Well supported. McKay et al. 2022 found no reliable reduced-feedback effect. McKay, Yantha et al. 2022 (Meta-Psychology; DOI 10.15626/MP.2021.2803 verified on the authors' lab site) found self-controlled studies 'underpowered, biased, and lacking evidential value'. St. Germain et al. 2023 found no advantage from choosing one's own feedback schedule. Ammar et al. 2023/2024 found no reliable long-term contextual-interference benefit in applied settings. McKay et al. 2024 found bias-corrected external-focus effects near zero. Counter-evidence: Czyż et al. 2024 (Sci Rep) reported a medium retention benefit for high contextual interference, so 'always mix' is contested rather than refuted.

critique_of_v1: Advancement gates measure performance, not learning. levelGate(avgScore >= 85) and applyLadderRule(currentTier, accuracy >= 85) in /home/user/Pronunciation-App/server/src/services/drills.ts let a single attempt advance a ladder tier. No delayed, no-model, no-feedback retention probe exists, and no transfer probe on untrained items (motor-1).

The practice schedule is fixed and blocked. buildDrillSession() filters to weak phonemes and always returns the same pack items sorted word, then sentence, then passage. Order is not adapted to the learner's accuracy (challenge point), targets are not interleaved, and contexts are not varied. Repeating the same items encourages memorising the utterances (motor-2, motor-3).

Feedback is maximal on every trial and shown instantly. The feedback screen (/home/user/Pronunciation-App/docs/product-design.md section 2) shows Accuracy, Fluency and Prosody, word colours and per-phoneme scores after every attempt. There is no self-rating first, no summary or bandwidth mode, and no fading. The 'Retry' button invites immediate repetition of the same item (motor-5, motor-6).

Feedback is knowledge of results only. Scores, colours and an IPA symbol tell the learner that a sound was wrong but not how to produce it. For a new L2 sound, learners need articulatory information (motor-7). Cue wording should then shift to outcome and listener focus (motor-8).

The TTS reference plays right before recording, so every scored attempt is immediate imitation. That inflates practice scores and hides whether the learner can produce the sound unprompted. Probes need a no-model condition (motor-1).

Target selection uses only the lowest rolling Azure average (5 phonemes, minimum 3 attempts each). It ignores intelligibility impact (functional load), error consistency, and the learner's actual substitution. It also treats noisy per-phoneme scores from 3 attempts as reliable. There is no perception side to the minimal-pair contrasts (motor-9).

Speed ladders and the 'articulation index' (mean of accuracy times a tier multiplier, docs/prd.md) reward speaking faster. The evidence supports a moderate target rate, and I know of no controlled evidence for fast tongue twisters as articulation training. The 'slow' TTS tier is not a clear-speech model (motor-11, motor-12).

The 'over-articulation drills' are not framed as clear-speech training. Clear speech is the best-supported route to intelligibility, yet there is no clear vs conversational contrast, no measurement of what changed, and no check that the clear version targets the right sound categories (motor-11).

Few productions per minute. Long passages and minute-long reads give few target productions per unit of time. Productions per target are not tracked as a dose metric, and nothing schedules spaced review of mastered targets (motor-4).

Progress charts (phoneme heatmap, articulation index) plot practice-trial averages. They mix up practice performance with learning, so they can show progress that does not hold at retention (motor-1).
open_questions: VERIFY ALL CITATIONS. Nothing could be opened in this session (search quota used up, scholarly domains blocked by egress). Most load-bearing to check first: McKay et al. 2022 (feedback frequency meta-analysis), Ammar et al. 2023 (mixed-practice meta-analysis), Lowe & Buchwald 2017 (direction of the result), Munro & Derwing 2001 (curvilinear rate finding), Rogers et al. 2010 and Smiljanic & Bradlow 2011 (non-native clear speech, including the accentedness result), Lam & Tjaden 2013 (instruction ranking), Lee & Gibbon 2015 (number of trials and participants), and Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015 (d of about 0.89).

Are there direct studies of motor-learning manipulations (practice schedule, feedback frequency or timing, attentional focus) in adult L2 pronunciation training? I know of almost none; a targeted search in Journal of Second Language Pronunciation, Language Learning and CALL journals is needed.

French-specific evidence is essentially missing for this topic. Is there French clear-speech research (e.g., Gagne and colleagues on Quebec French, unverified), and any work on rate or rhythm training for L2 French?

Is Azure's per-phoneme score reliable enough, trial by trial, to act as knowledge of results, bandwidth feedback, or a gate in the adaptive controller? What noise floor and minimum trial count make a 'weak phoneme' decision trustworthy?

The learner's L1 is unknown. It determines the likely substitutions (and so the minimal-pair contrasts and articulatory bridges) and whether errors are mainly perceptual or motor. Should the app start with a diagnostic probe covering both perception and production?
Does clear-speech practice carry over into habitual L2 speech, or does it only improve intelligibility while the learner is consciously speaking clearly? I know of no adult L2 training RCT.
What daily dose (productions per session, sessions per week) is realistic for one busy adult, and does the adaptive controller need a minimum trial count per target per week to be effective?
missed_evidence_flagged: McKay, Corson, Seedu, De Faveri, Hasan, Arnold, Adams & Carter (2024). Reporting bias, not external focus: a robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review of the external focus of attention literature. Psychological Bulletin 150(11):1347-1362. Bias-corrected effects: g = 0.15 retention, 0.01 performance; data favour the null. Directly weakens motor-8. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000451 (text read via the authors' GitHub PDF)

Houde & Jordan (1998). Sensorimotor adaptation in speech production. Science 279:1213-1216. Auditory adaptation generalized across phonetic contexts and to other vowels, which counters 'highly specific' in motor-3. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.279.5354.1213 (full text read)

Rochet-Capellan, Richer & Ostry (2012). Nonhomogeneous transfer reveals specificity in speech motor learning. J Neurophysiol 107:1711-1717. Partial, uneven transfer across utterances. https://doi.org/10.1152/jn.00773.2011

Suzuki (2021). Optimizing fluency training for speaking skills transfer: comparing the effects of blocked and interleaved task repetition. Language Learning 71(2). Adult EFL learners, randomized (n = 24 vs 26): blocked repetition gave greater fluency transfer to a new task than interleaved. Direct adult L2 evidence against 'always interleave' (motor-2). https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12433

Suzuki, Yokosawa & Aline (2020). The role of working memory in blocked and interleaved grammar practice: proceduralization of L2 syntax. Language Teaching Research. Interleaved practice gave more accurate L2 speaking on immediate and 1-week tests, with a smaller advantage for speed. Suggests the schedule effect depends on the outcome (accuracy vs fluency). https://doi.org/10.1177/1362168820913985

Suzuki & Hanzawa (2022). Massed task repetition is a double-edged sword for fluency development: an EFL classroom study. SSLA. Massed practice cut pauses most right away but slowed articulation rate and increased verbatim repetition; schedule effects were limited at 1 week. Relevant to spacing in motor-4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263121000358

Kim & Webb (2022). The effects of spaced practice on second language learning: a meta-analysis. Language Learning 72(1).
