Medium-to-large spacing benefit, mostly vocabulary; expanding and equal spacing were statistically equivalent, which bears on motor-4's 1-3-7-14 schedule. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12479

Li & DeKeyser (2019). Distribution of practice effects in the acquisition and retention of L2 Mandarin tonal word production. Modern Language Journal 103(3). A direct test of spacing on L2 pronunciation production; results not checked this session. https://doi.org/10.1111/modl.12580

Saito & Plonsky (2019). Effects of second language pronunciation teaching revisited: a proposed measurement framework and meta-analysis. Language Learning 69(3). An updated 77-study meta-analysis, with effects depending on outcome type; should sit beside Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015 in motor-4. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12345

Ammar et al. (2024). The effects of contextual interference learning on the acquisition and relatively permanent gains in skilled performance: a critical systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. 36 studies; no overall long-term gain for high CI (ES = -0.13, p = 0.18). Authorship inferred, not confirmed; abstract read from a cached index. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z

Czyż et al. (2024). High contextual interference improves retention in motor learning: systematic review and meta-analysis. Scientific Reports. Contrary to Ammar et al.: the meta-analyses disagree. Title confirmed via secondary sources only. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-65753-3

Wulf & Shea (2002). Principles derived from the study of simple skills do not generalize to complex skill learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 9:185-211. Complex skills may benefit from more feedback and guidance, so lab-task principles (motor-1, motor-2, motor-5) may not transfer to articulation. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03196276

Barros, Yantha, Carter, Hussien & Ste-Marie (2019). Examining the impact of error estimation on the effects of self-controlled feedback. Human Movement Science. Error-estimation benefit significant in Experiment 1, not in Experiment 2 (abstract read). Tempers motor-6. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.humov.2018.12.002

McCabe, Preston, Evans & Heard (2023). A pilot randomized control trial of motor-based treatments for childhood apraxia of speech: Rapid Syllable Transition Treatment and ultrasound biofeedback. AJSLP 32. n = 14 children; ultrasound no better than ReST; both groups improved and kept gains at 1 month (abstract read). Relevant to motor-7. https://doi.org/10.1044/2022_AJSLP-22-00144

Lee, Plonsky & Saito (2020). The effects of perception- vs. production-based pronunciation instruction. System 88:102185. Randomized, n = 115 Japanese EFL learners; perception-based training may be more effective for both segmental and suprasegmental features. Adult L2 support for the perception component in motor-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2019.102185

Sakai & Moorman (2018). Can perception training improve the production of second language phonemes? A meta-analytic review of 79 years of research. Applied Psycholinguistics 39(1):187-224. Adult L2 evidence that perception training carries over to production. Not opened this session. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716417000418

Bliss, Abel & Gick (2018). Computer-assisted visual articulation feedback in L2 pronunciation instruction: a review. Journal of Second Language Pronunciation 4(1):129-153. Also Antolík, Pillot-Loiseau & Kamiyama (2019), JSLP 5(1):72-97: ultrasound feedback for Japanese learners of French /y/-/u/. Adult L2 KP evidence missing from motor-7. Neither was opened, and the bibliographic details are from memory and need checking. https://doi.org/10.1075/jslp.00006.bli

Namasivayam et al. (2015). Treatment intensity and childhood apraxia of speech. IJLCD. n = 37; 2 sessions/week beat 1/week. Stronger intensity evidence than the n = 2 study in motor-4, though still in children (secondary summary). https://doi.org/10.1111/1460-6984.12154

Uchanski, Choi, Braida, Reed & Durlach (1996). Speaking clearly for the hard of hearing IV: further studies of the role of speaking rate. JSHR 39(3):494-509. Non-uniform time-scaling also failed to reproduce the clear-speech benefit, which strengthens motor-11 and the 'slow is not clear' claim. Bibliographic details verified in a BibTeX file; no DOI link found.

general_review.summary:
ACCESS LIMITATION: the web-search budget for this session was already used up (200/200), and the egress proxy blocked every scholarly host I tried: doi.org, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, ERIC, PubMed, Wiley, arXiv, HAL, LLT and learn.microsoft.com. So I could not open publisher pages. I read every source cited below first-hand from copies hosted on GitHub. These are: (a) full texts, such as Hincks & Edlund 2009 (LLT), Hirata & Kelly 2010 (JSLHR), two 2022 SSLA articles and Korzekwa et al. 2021 (arXiv); (b) abstract records in Zotero, Mendeley or Scopus exports and journal-abstract corpora, for example Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015, Thomson & Derwing 2015, Kang 2010, Hahn 2004, Arvaniti 2012, Tremblay et al. 2018 and Lee, Plonsky & Saito 2020; (c) peer-reviewed open-access books from Language Science Press (Sbranna 2025; Pešková 2023; Walton 2023); (d) the Azure pronunciation-assessment docs (copy dated Nov 2025 / Sep 2026). Each citation gives both the canonical DOI or URL and the GitHub copy I actually read. I could NOT open several landmark studies the brief names: Derwing, Munro & Wiebe 1998; Field 2005; Hardison 2004; Levis & Pickering 2004; Gordon & Darcy 2016/2022; Munro & Derwing 2001; Gluhareva & Prieto 2017; Saito & Plonsky 2019; Saito 2021; Suzuki, Kormos & Uchihara 2021. I found no L2 study at all on French liaison or enchaînement. Where these appear below, they are either absent or reported only as described by another peer-reviewed source I did read, and I flag that.

MAIN CONCLUSIONS: (1) Pronunciation instruction works, with a large average effect in a meta-analysis (d = 0.80–0.89). Effects are larger with longer training and with feedback. But most studies measure read-aloud speech, so gains in spontaneous speech are less certain. (2) Suprasegmentals carry a large share of comprehensibility and accentedness: speaking rate, pausing, pitch range, word stress, and nuclear (sentence) stress or focus. So the app should build prosody training around specific, measurable features, not one holistic prosody score. (3) The features worth targeting differ by language direction. English: word stress, contrastive/nuclear stress, and phrasing and pausing. French: grouping speech into accentual phrases, with the last syllable of each phrase lengthened and, in non-final phrases, rising in pitch. First-language transfer is strong in both directions. French-L1 listeners have trouble hearing stress contrasts ("stress deafness"). English-L1 learners carry falling pitch accents and word-initial prominence into French. Since the learner's L1 is unknown, the app needs a short L1 and prosody diagnostic. (4) Training that starts with perception (identifying stress, focus and phrase boundaries), plus visual pitch feedback that is normalized to the speaker and focuses on the shape of the contour, has the most support among tools an app can deliver. Embodied rhythm training (clapping or tapping) and shadowing have mixed or weak support. (5) The v1 design has several parts with no evidence behind them or that the evidence contradicts: tongue-twister speed ladders, 'stress-timing' and 'even-syllable rhythm' as scored targets, a holistic Azure ProsodyScore (en-US only, so the French prosody track gets no prosody scoring), read-aloud-only assessment, and no perception training.

findings.claim: Explicit pronunciation instruction produces large average gains. Gains are larger with longer interventions and with feedback. But most studies test read-aloud or controlled speech (which inflates effects), few measure spontaneous speech, and suprasegmentals are studied less often than segmentals.
findings.population: Adult and adolescent L2 learners, mostly of English; 86 reports in the meta-analysis and 75 studies in the narrative review
findings.effect_notes: Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015: 86 unique reports; N-weighted d = 0.89 within-group and 0.80 between-group. Moderators with larger effects: longer interventions, treatments that gave feedback, and more controlled outcome measures. Thomson & Derwing 2015: 75 studies; read-aloud was the most common assessment; very few measured spontaneous speech; some lacked control groups; most promoted native-like targets despite claiming intelligibility goals.
findings.design_implication: Plan a multi-week programme with explicit, specific feedback on every attempt. Treat read-aloud scores as practice signals only. Make the headline progress measure a spontaneous-speech transfer task done periodically (picture description or 60-second retell), recorded, analysed for prosodic features, and optionally rated for comprehensibility (ease of understanding) by a listener. Do not report read-aloud gains as proof of improvement.

citations.ref: Lee, J., Jang, J., & Plonsky, L. (2015). The effectiveness of second language pronunciation instruction: A meta-analysis. Applied Linguistics, 36(3). Abstract read from Red Hen journal-abstract corpus.
GitHub copy of the Lee et al. 2015 abstract (read)
Thomson, R. I., & Derwing, T. M. (2015). The effectiveness of L2 pronunciation instruction: A narrative review. Applied Linguistics 36(3).
GitHub copy of the Thomson & Derwing 2015 abstract (read)

findings.claim: In Kang (2010) (11 ITAs, 58 US undergraduate raters), temporal and prosodic measures contributed independently: comprehensibility was mostly associated with speaking rate, and accentedness was best predicted by pitch range and word stress. Warren, Elgort & Crabbe (2009) found prosodic information important for comprehensibility and no significant differences between naive and experienced raters. Their segment-filtered stimuli were rated for NATIVENESS, not comprehensibility, so they do not show that 'prosody alone drives comprehensibility'. Other work finds comprehensibility also depends strongly on lexicogrammar, fluency and high-functional-load segmental errors, so prosody is one of several drivers.
findings.population: Adult L2 English speakers (international teaching assistants; Mandarin-L1 learners) rated by native-English listeners
findings.effect_notes: Kang 2010: 5-minute lecture excerpts from 11 ITAs; 58 US undergraduate raters; Praat measures of speech rate, pauses, stress and pitch range. Comprehensibility was mostly associated with speaking rate; accent was best predicted by pitch range and word-stress measures. Warren, Elgort & Crabbe 2009 (LLT 13(3):87-102): prosody important for comprehensibility; no difference between naive and experienced raters. Sbranna (2025, peer-reviewed book) summarizes that prosodic deviations affect accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility more than segmental deviations, citing Derwing, Munro & Wiebe 1998, Munro 1995 and Gordon & Darcy 2022 — secondary report; I could not open those originals. Small speaker samples; correlation, not causation.
findings.design_implication: Extract a small set of interpretable prosodic measures per attempt: articulation or speech rate, number and location of pauses, pitch range in semitones, and whether stressed and focused syllables are prominent. Show them as separate, explained indicators rather than one score. Since naive listeners are valid raters, allow an optional human comprehensibility rating (1–9) of the monthly spontaneous sample.

citations.ref: Kang, O. (2010). Relative salience of suprasegmental features on judgments of L2 comprehensibility and accentedness. System, 38(2), 301–315.
GitHub copy of the Kang 2010 RIS record with abstract (read)

Warren, P., Elgort, I., & Crabbe, D. (2009). Comprehensibility and prosody ratings for pronunciation software development. Language Learning & Technology 13(3), 87–102. Abstract read in Vakila thesis bibliography.
Sbranna, S. (2025). Prosody and interactional fluency of Italian learners of German (Language Science Press; book DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15726570), ch. 1 literature review (read)

findings.claim: Hahn (2004): in one experiment with three versions of an ITA lecture, correct primary (nuclear) stress gave significantly better content recall and more favourable speaker evaluations than misplaced or missing stress; the processing-ease difference was not significant. Monotone (no-focus) delivery was rated least favourably, but by Hincks & Edlund's account, misplaced focus was slightly HARDER to comprehend than monotone, though listeners still preferred it. Lee & Fraundorf (2022): even higher-proficiency Korean-L1 learners did not reach native-like use of contrastive accents in comprehension, even with self-paced listening. That points to a form–meaning mapping difficulty, but no instruction was tested. An OUP ELT position paper (Walker, Low & Setter 2021) lists nuclear stress and word stress as priorities for international intelligibility.
findings.population: Native English undergraduate listeners hearing manipulated versions of an ITA lecture (Hahn); L1 Korean learners of English (Lee & Fraundorf); expert panel
findings.effect_notes: Hahn 2004 (TESOL Quarterly 38(2):201–223): three versions of the same lecture (primary stress correct, misplaced, missing); correct stress gave significantly better recall and evaluations; processing-ease difference not significant. Hincks & Edlund (2009) describe Hahn's result: monotone and misplaced focus reduced recall, and listeners preferred misplaced to no focus. Lee & Fraundorf 2022 (SSLA 44:942–966): even with self-paced listening, higher-proficiency Korean learners did not reach native-like use of contrastive accents. Walker, Low & Setter 2021 (OUP expert panel) list nuclear stress and word stress as priorities for international intelligibility. They also warn that learners working alone with apps over-focus on individual sounds.
findings.design_implication: Add a nuclear/contrastive stress module for English. Use question–answer and correction contexts ('Did you rent a HOUSE?' → 'No, I rented a FLAT'), so the correct focus word follows from the meaning. Score whether the pitch peak and lengthening fall on the intended word, using word-level F0 and duration taken from Azure word and phoneme offsets. Give specific feedback: 'your main emphasis landed on X, not Y'. Include a listening version: pick which word the speaker emphasized and what it implies.

citations.ref: Hahn, L. D. (2004). Primary stress and intelligibility: Research to motivate the teaching of suprasegmentals. TESOL Quarterly, 38(2), 201–223.
Hahn 2004 abstract in Vakila thesis bibliography (read)
Lee, E.-K., & Fraundorf, S. (2022). Do L1–L2 differences in discourse processing reflect processing demands or difficulty of form-function mapping? SSLA 44, 942–966 (full text read)
GitHub full-text copy of Lee & Fraundorf 2022
Walker, R., Low, E., & Setter, J. (2021). English pronunciation for a global world. Oxford University Press ELT position paper (www.oup.com/elt/expert); copy read

findings.claim: Native French listeners show a replicated difficulty encoding lexical-stress contrasts in short-term-memory tasks (ABX and sequence recall with Spanish-type stimuli), and it persisted even in advanced French learners of Spanish (Dupoux et al. 1997, 2008). The deficit depends on the task: French listeners can respond to acoustic stress cues, and in one lab study they learned to store and retrieve trained stress contrasts. The authors of that study (Schwab & Llisterri 2011) state their results 'do not seem to support' stress deafness. None of the cited studies test French learners of ENGLISH. English-L1 learners of Spanish recall stress contrasts worse than segmental contrasts, which improves modestly with proficiency. One lexical-stress error detector for Slavic/Baltic L2 English reached 94.8% precision at an operating point deliberately fixed near 50% recall; recall can be traded against precision.
findings.population: Native French and Spanish listeners (Dupoux 1997, non-learners); French learners of Spanish (Dupoux 2008); French speakers learning pseudowords (Schwab & Llisterri 2011, lab); L1-English learners of Spanish (Ortin & Simonet 2022); Slavic/Baltic L2 English speech (Korzekwa)
findings.effect_notes: Dupoux et al. 1997 (JML 36:406–421): in an ABX task French listeners had significantly more difficulty than Spanish listeners with accent contrasts; they can respond to the acoustic correlates, so the deficit sits in short-term memory encoding. Dupoux et al. 2008 (Cognition 106:682–706; metadata and a secondary description in the Vakila 2015 thesis): the deficit persists in French learners of Spanish. Schwab & Llisterri 2011 (ICPhS): French speakers could store and retrieve trained stress contrasts. Ortin & Simonet 2022 (SSLA): L1-English learners recalled stress contrasts worse than segmental contrasts; this improved modestly with proficiency. Bonneau 2011 pilot (secondary, via Vakila): visual+audio feedback on English stress helped French beginners; advanced learners gained as much just from hearing a reference. Korzekwa et al. 2021: best detector reached 94.8% precision but only 49.2% recall for incorrectly stressed words. I could not open Field 2005 (TESOL Q 39(3)); Walker et al. 2021 cite it for 'misplaced word stress blocks word recognition' examples.
findings.design_implication: Branch on the L1 diagnostic. For a French-L1 learner of English, start with perception tasks in which stress changes the word or its meaning: 'which syllable is strongest?', REcord vs reCORD, odd-one-out with several voices. Then move to production of multisyllabic, high-frequency words, with feedback on the stressed syllable (duration, F0 and intensity relative to its neighbours) and on reduced vowels in unstressed syllables. Scaffold the feedback: rich visual and auditory contrast for beginners, a plain reference model for advanced users. Because detectors miss about half of stress errors, flag an error only when highly confident, and never present 'no error flagged' as 'correct'.

citations.ref: Dupoux, E., Pallier, C., Sebastián, N., & Mehler, J. (1997). A destressing 'deafness' in French? Journal of Memory and Language, 36(3), 406–421.
Vakila thesis bibliography with abstracts for Dupoux 1997, Schwab & Llisterri 2011 and Dupoux et al. 2008 metadata (read)
Dupoux, E., Sebastián-Gallés, N., Navarrete, E., & Peperkamp, S. (2008). Persistent stress 'deafness': The case of French learners of Spanish. Cognition 106, 682–706 (metadata only)
Vakila, A. (2015) MSc thesis background chapter: French stress, expected errors, Bonneau 2011 and Bissiri resynthesis findings (read)
Ortin, R., & Simonet, M. (2022). Phonological processing of stress by native English speakers learning Spanish as a second language. SSLA 44, 460–482 (full text read)
Korzekwa, D., et al. (2021). Detection of lexical stress errors in non-native (L2) English with data augmentation and attention (arXiv 2012.14788; full text read)

findings.claim: In a small pilot (n = 14 Chinese learners of English; 7 visual versus 7 audio-feedback), about 3 hours of practice with TRANSIENT visual feedback (flashing lights showing the amount of pitch variation, not a pitch-contour display) increased pitch variation more than audio-only feedback. The difference (over 2.5 semitones) persisted into a new presentation. Two raters with only moderate agreement perceived little change in pronunciation or intelligibility. Earlier work (de Bot 1983; Hardison 2004, which to my knowledge studied English-speaking learners of FRENCH) reported benefits of real-time pitch displays. Hincks & Edlund ARGUE, without testing it, that requiring exact contour matching is probably frustrating. They also note octave errors in pitch tracking and normalise pitch per speaker in semitones.
findings.population: Adult Chinese learners of English at intermediate–advanced level (Hincks & Edlund); adult L2 English learners (Hardison 2004, and Levis & Pickering 2004, as described by others)
findings.effect_notes: Hincks & Edlund 2009 (LLT 13(3):32–50): n = 14 (7 visual-feedback, 7 audio-feedback); pitch variation = SD of F0 in semitones over 10-second windows. Between-group effect F = 6.74, p = .027, effect size reported as 0.40 (the symbol was lost in extraction; likely partial eta²). The between-group difference exceeded 2.5 semitones and persisted into a new presentation. Two expert raters saw little change in intelligibility. Hardison 2004 and Levis & Pickering 2004 are known to me only via descriptions in Hincks & Edlund 2009 and Pešková 2023 (peer-reviewed book); I could not open them. Pešková adds that imitation plus pitch visualization has 'yielded positive results' (Chun 1998; Niebuhr et al. 2017). Evidence is mostly from English learners; little from L2 French.
findings.design_implication: Show a smoothed pitch contour in semitones, normalized to the learner's own range (calibrate floor and ceiling from a warm-up), overlaid on one or more model contours from human voices. Highlight only target events: the English nuclear accent and the final fall or rise; the rise at the end of each French accentual phrase. Score contour shape at those points, not point-by-point closeness to the model. For longer speech, add a live 'monotone ↔ varied' meter like Hincks & Edlund's. Discard unvoiced and octave-jump frames, and let the user replay audio in sync with the contour.

findings.claim: One randomised study (N = 115 Japanese university EFL learners; two 30-minute sessions; individual randomisation) gave explicit instruction on either segmental or 'syllabic' targets (syllable structure, word stress, lax syllables; not intonation). All four instruction groups gained on word-level pronunciation of 10 target words, and perception-based instruction 'may be the more effective' method for both target types. A separate randomised classroom study (N = 64 EAP learners) found that 100 minutes of paratone and prosodic-phrasing instruction improved LISTENING comprehension more than product-oriented listening practice. In a 5-month immersion study (N = 46 Chinese learners), overall L2 speech gains, segmental and prosodic together, were associated with explicit auditory processing ability; this was correlational and involved no training.
findings.population: Adult learners: Japanese EFL university students (N = 115); post-secondary EAP learners of English (N = 64, randomly assigned); Chinese learners of English in immersion (N = 46)
findings.effect_notes: Lee, Plonsky & Saito 2020 (System, 10.1016/j.system.2019.102185): N = 115; two weeks; segmental or suprasegmental targets × perception- or production-based training; pre/post/delayed tests. All groups gained; perception-based training looked more effective for both feature types (no pooled effect size in the abstract). EAP prosody study (title 'The effects of prosody instruction on listening comprehension in an EAP classroom context'; authors and journal not verified — Scopus-derived record): 64 learners randomly assigned; 100 minutes of instruction on paratone and prosodic phrasing beat equal time of product-oriented listening practice, on both target-feature comprehension and general listening tests. Sun, Saito & Tierney 2021 (SSLA): 46 learners over 5 months; prosody gains were linked to explicit auditory processing (remembering and reproducing music sequences).
findings.design_implication: Pair each prosody target with listening tasks that give immediate feedback: 'Which word was stressed?', 'Statement or question?', 'Where is the phrase boundary?', 'Which meaning did the speaker intend?' Use several human voices. Sequence each unit as hear/identify, then imitate, then produce in context. Add a quick optional auditory-processing screen (pitch and duration discrimination, rhythm reproduction) to predict who needs more perceptual scaffolding. Report listening-comprehension gains as a side benefit.

findings.claim: In 28 Catalan children aged 7–8, clapping to the rhythmic structure of French cognate words while repeating them improved rated accentedness more than repetition alone, and only the clapping group lengthened word-final vowels. For adults, Baills, Alazard-Guiu & Prieto (2022, Applied Linguistics 43(4)) report in their title that embodied prosodic training improves accentedness and suprasegmental accuracy (abstract not verified here). One 2025 monograph (Sbranna; a single sentence in a discussion section, not a systematic review) lists it among studies 'showing no robust' effects. Watching hand gestures did not improve adults' PERCEPTION of Japanese vowel length, whereas seeing lip movements did (Hirata & Kelly 2010).
findings.population: Catalan children aged 7–8 learning French words (N = 28); learners of French in Baills et al. 2022 (details not verified); native English adults learning Japanese vowel length (N = 60)
findings.effect_notes: Baills & Prieto 2023 (Language Teaching Research 27; DOI 10.1177/1362168820986716): 28 children; clapping group improved accentedness significantly more than non-clapping; only the clapping group lengthened word-final vowels. Baills, Alazard-Guiu & Prieto 2022 (Applied Linguistics 43(4):776–804): I read only the title and metadata; Sbranna 2025 lists it among prosodic-training studies 'showing no robust' effects — conflicting signals, unresolved. Hirata & Kelly 2010 (JSLHR 53:298–310): 60 adults in 4 conditions; audio-mouth training beat audio-only; the two hand-gesture conditions did not.
findings.design_implication: Offer an optional 'tap the beat' mode rather than making it core. The learner taps (space bar or touchscreen) on stressed syllables in English, or on the lengthened final syllable of each French accentual phrase, while speaking. The app compares tap times with syllable nuclei from Azure phoneme offsets. Because the evidence is mixed and comes mostly from children, test it within the one user (alternate weeks with and without tapping; compare prosody measures) before building more on it.

findings.claim: French prominence sits at the phrase level, not the word level. The basic unit is the accentual phrase (typically 3–4 syllables). Its final syllable is lengthened, and in non-final phrases it carries a pitch rise; the utterance ends in a fall. English-L1 learners transfer word-initial and falling accents, have trouble producing target-like phrase-final rises and phrases of the right size, and use the phrase-final F0 rise as a word-boundary cue less than Dutch-L1 learners do. Recent French exposure predicted use of that cue better than native language did.
findings.population: English-L1 (Anglophone Canadian and US) and Dutch-L1 adult learners of French; native French listeners
findings.effect_notes: Walton 2023 (peer-reviewed LSRL proceedings chapter) reviews the AP structure (Jun & Fougeron 2000/2002) and transfer findings (Lepetit 1989; Colantoni 2014). Its own sample (2 × 6 learners) was too small to show group differences. Tremblay, Broersma & Coughlin 2018 (Bilingualism: L&C 21(3):640–652): visual-world eye-tracking; Dutch listeners used the F0 rise earlier and more than English listeners (matched proficiency). Namjoshi et al. 2012: in artificial-language segmentation, recent exposure predicted use of the F0-rise cue better than L1 did. None of these are training studies. I found NO accessible L2 intervention study on liaison or enchaînement.
findings.design_implication: Build the French prosody track around accentual-phrase chunking instead of 'even syllables'. (a) Show texts with AP brackets. (b) Measure per phrase the final-syllable to mean-syllable duration ratio and the F0 rise on the final syllable, from Azure phoneme offsets plus an in-app pitch tracker. (c) Flag English-style patterns: lengthening or pitch peaks on word-initial syllables, falls at non-final phrase ends. (d) Add listening segmentation exercises where the rise marks the word end. (e) Teach liaison and enchaînement inside these phrase chunks, so resyllabification across words happens within the phrase. This last point comes from descriptive phonology, not intervention evidence. Encourage large amounts of French listening, since recent exposure matters.

findings.claim: Rhythm metrics such as %V, ΔC, PVIs and Varcos do not reliably separate 'stress-timed' from 'syllable-timed' languages. Scores vary widely between speakers and with elicitation method and syllable complexity, often by as much as between languages. Acoustic support for strict isochrony (equal intervals between stresses or syllables) has not been found. Expert guidance for international intelligibility rates stress-timed rhythm and native pitch-movement patterns as 'not important', and says weak forms and vowel reduction should be taught for listening, not required in production.
findings.population: Native speakers of English, German, Greek, Italian, Korean and Spanish (8 per language; Arvaniti); expert consensus for ELF learners
findings.effect_notes: Arvaniti 2012 (Journal of Phonetics 40(3):351–373): three elicitation methods; classifications 'inconsistent across metrics'; differences often non-significant even for English vs Spanish; comparisons 'unsafe at best'. A 2023 Language Science Press grammar chapter (book 472, ch. 1) likewise notes no acoustic support for the dichotomy. Walker, Low & Setter 2021 Table 2: stress-timed rhythm 'Not important' for EIL; vowel reduction and weak forms 'only taught for receptive purposes'. The expert consensus concerns international (ELF) intelligibility; a learner aiming at native listeners may still benefit from weak forms.
findings.design_implication: Do not compute or display a 'stress-timing' or 'syllable-timing' score, nPVI or similar metric as a learner target. Replace them with concrete, word-anchored targets: English stressed-syllable prominence and reduced function words in context (listening first, then optional production), and French phrase-final lengthening and rise (prosody-8). If the app ever computes rhythm metrics, compare them only against the learner's own earlier recordings of the same text.

findings.claim: Speaking rate was the feature most associated with comprehensibility in Kang (2010) (11 ITAs). In one small randomised study (N = 36 university students; three 20-minute sessions), the 4/3/2 activity combined with metalinguistic correction improved fluency and past-tense accuracy across topics; within-clause pausing and regular past tense did not change. The abstract does not report the 4/3/2-only result. Other task-repetition studies found that mid-clause pausing CAN decrease and that this transfers to new tasks, depending on the repetition schedule (Suzuki 2021; Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022). Azure's word-level UnexpectedBreak and MissingBreak confidences (suggested threshold 0.75) are available only when prosody assessment is enabled, and prosody assessment is en-US only.
findings.population: University-level L2 English learners (N = 36, randomly assigned to 3 groups); ITAs (Kang); Azure documentation
findings.effect_notes: 4/3/2 study (title 'Effects of the 4/3/2 activity revisited: Extending Boers (2014) and Thai & Boers (2016)'; authors and journal not verified): N = 36, three 20-minute sessions; groups Control, 4/3/2, 4/3/2 + accuracy enhancement. The combined condition improved fluency and accuracy across topics; within-clause pause reduction and regular past tense did not change. Kang 2010: comprehensibility mainly associated with speaking rate. Azure docs: word-level UnexpectedBreak and MissingBreak confidences with a suggested 0.75 threshold; en-US only. I could not open the Suzuki, Kormos & Uchihara 2021 meta-analysis on utterance vs perceived fluency (MLJ 105(2)) or Munro & Derwing 2001 on optimal speaking rate.
findings.design_implication: Replace tongue-twister speed ladders with a 4/3/2-style ladder on meaningful content: retell the same story or answer the same question in about 90, then 60, then 45 seconds, with corrective feedback between rounds. Measure articulation rate, mean length of run, and pause location: at phrase or clause boundaries is fine, mid-phrase is flagged. Use Azure word offsets (all locales) for pause locations and Azure Break flags for en-US. In reading passages, pre-mark chunk boundaries and reward pausing at them rather than raw speed.

findings.claim: Over two weeks of choral repetition (shadowing) training, 47 Chinese EFL students' speech became significantly more comprehensible. No control group is described in the abstract, so the improvement cannot be attributed to shadowing itself. The size of improvement in nativelikeness was associated with audio-motor integration (ability to remember and reproduce sound sequences), a correlational link.
findings.population: Chinese EFL students (N = 47); adult learners
findings.effect_notes: Shao, Saito & Tierney 2023 (TESOL Quarterly, 10.1002/tesq.3120): N = 47; two weeks of shadowing; comprehensibility improved significantly over time. The abstract does not describe a control group, so the gains cannot be attributed to shadowing alone. Foote & McDonough 2017 (JSLP 3(1):34–56; DOI 10.1075/jslp.3.1.02foo) is known to me only from metadata.
findings.design_implication: Keep shadowing as a mode, but use human recordings of natural connected speech (with an optional slowed version that preserves pitch) rather than only TTS. Measure how closely the learner's timing and pitch contour follow the model, on the prosodic targets only. Present shadowing as a fluency and prosody tool, not accent erasure. Pair it with the auditory screen from prosody-6 and give more perceptual scaffolding to learners with weaker audio-motor integration.

findings.claim: Azure's prosody assessment is available only for en-US. For fr-FR (and every other locale) no ProsodyScore is returned, and the overall PronScore is computed without it. Where available, ProsodyScore is one utterance-level number covering 'stress, intonation, speaking speed, and rhythm'. The only word-level prosody feedback is Break (unexpected or missing break) and Monotone. Monotone is detected over the whole utterance and copied to every word. Syllable groups are also en-US only. PronScore weights the lowest sub-score most heavily (0.4 or 0.6).
findings.population: N/A (vendor documentation)
findings.effect_notes: From the Azure docs: 'Prosody assessment is only available in the en-US locale'; the Feedback field includes Break and Intonation; the Intonation error type currently supports only Monotone; the suggested break-confidence threshold is 0.75. With prosody: PronScore = 0.4·s0 + 0.2·s1 + 0.2·s2 + 0.2·s3 (reading), with scores sorted from lowest (s0) to highest. fr-FR and fr-CA are supported for pronunciation assessment in general, but not for prosody. As far as I found, Microsoft publishes no validation of ProsodyScore against human L2 comprehensibility ratings.
findings.design_implication: For French, do not show a prosody score. Compute app-side prosody features instead: an in-browser or server pitch tracker (e.g., autocorrelation or YIN on the 16 kHz WAV) plus syllable and phone timing from Azure phoneme offsets, which are available in fr-FR. For English, surface the Break and Monotone details at word level instead of only the holistic number, and treat ProsodyScore as secondary until it has been checked against the learner's own human-rated samples.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Scoring 'stress-timing' or 'syllable-timing' (including 'even-syllable rhythm') with rhythm metrics or isochrony targets.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Arvaniti 2012 and the OUP Table 2 are verified. Caveat: metrics can still track within-learner L2 change on the same text (White & Mattys 2007). The 'not important' rating is an EIL/Lingua Franca Core position, not a consensus for native-listener goals.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Tongue-twister speed ladders as articulation or fluency training.
does_not_work_verified.notes: This is an honest absence-of-evidence claim; none of the cited sources test tongue twisters. The sub-claim that 'within-clause pausing did not improve even then' holds only for the one 4/3/2 study. Suzuki 2021 (Language Learning) and Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022 (SSLA) found mid-clause pauses decreased with task repetition, depending on schedule.

does_not_work_verified.claim: A single holistic prosody score without saying what to change.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The Azure facts are verified: one utterance-level ProsodyScore, en-US only, with word-level feedback limited to Break and Monotone. The Lee et al. moderator is 'treatments providing feedback' in general; no study compares holistic with specific scores. This is a reasonable inference, not a tested finding.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Requiring learners to match a model pitch contour point by point.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Hincks & Edlund state this ('probably frustrating and counter-productive'), mention attitude and dialect in contours, and note octave errors. It is an argument, not an experimental result. Only a transient pitch-VARIATION meter was tested; 'shape-based' feedback was not.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Judging progress only on read-aloud or controlled tasks.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Verified in both 2015 abstracts. Saito & Plonsky 2019 (Language Learning 69(3)) reinforces it: effects are smaller on spontaneous and global measures.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Relying on implicit exposure alone for prosodic form–meaning mappings such as focus/contrastive accent and information status.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Lee & Fraundorf 2022 shows non-native PROCESSING (comprehension) of contrastive accents in proficient Korean-L1 learners. Sbranna 2025 (Italian learners of German) shows non-target PRODUCTION by information status and argues implicit learning is insufficient. Neither source tests whether explicit instruction fixes the problem.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Merely watching hand gestures to learn a durational contrast.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Hirata & Kelly 2010 is verified, but it concerns perception of vowel length after observing gestures. Studies of gesture PRODUCTION (Li, Baills & Prieto 2020; Zhang, Baills & Prieto 2020) report benefits, so this should not be generalised to 'gestures don't help'.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Novel intonation gadgets without controlled evidence (kazoo example).
does_not_work_verified.notes: The kazoo abstract is verified: 'a group-specific analysis did not yield clear results'. However, the authors also say it 'has potential', and individual improvement was more common in the kazoo group. This is 'no clear evidence', not evidence that it fails.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Trusting an automatic lexical-stress error detector's silence.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The advice is sound, but the figure is misread. Korzekwa et al. fixed recall near 50% by design, to compare precision with Ferrer et al., so 49.2% recall is a chosen operating point, not a ceiling. The detector was for Slavic/Baltic speakers. Azure offers no lexical-stress error detection at all.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Aiming at native-like accent.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Thomson & Derwing 2015: 'most research surveyed promoted native-like pronunciation as the target.' The OUP paper treats accent features that do not affect intelligibility as optional, but explicitly lets learners choose a native-accent goal. The app should make this a user choice rather than forbid it.

critique_of_v1: The French prosody track has no scoring. v1 relies on Azure ProsodyScore (server/src/services/assess.ts stores detail.ProsodyScore), which Azure returns only for en-US. The whole French prosody track (liaison, enchaînement, 'even-syllable rhythm', shadowing) therefore gets no automated prosody feedback, and French PronScore uses a different weighting than English, so the two languages' scores are not comparable.

'Even-syllable rhythm' is the wrong target for French. French prominence is organized by accentual phrases with final lengthening and a rise on non-final phrases. English-L1 learners characteristically get these phrase-final rises and phrase sizes wrong. Drilling 'evenness' could even reinforce a flat, unphrased delivery.

'Stress-timing' is not a valid measurable target for English, since rhythm metrics are unreliable (Arvaniti 2012). The English prosody track should target word stress, nuclear or contrastive stress, and phrasing and pausing, which the evidence ties to comprehensibility and recall (Kang 2010; Hahn 2004).

Speed ladders are untested. Treating accuracy at faster TTS tempos as 'articulation quality' and advancing at ≥85 has no validation that I could find. Tongue twisters are not meaningful speech, and the comprehensibility literature relates speed to spontaneous speaking rate and pause location, not to fast reading of tongue twisters. Slowing or speeding TTS through SSML rate also changes prosody in ways that are not natural slow or fast speech (untested).

The weak-sound engine targets only segments. It picks phonemes by lowest rolling Azure score and ignores prosodic targets and how much each error matters to intelligibility. Expert guidance specifically warns that self-study apps over-focus on individual sounds while nuclear stress is 'just as important'.

Assessment is read-aloud only. There is no spontaneous-speech task, so v1 cannot tell whether practice transfers, which is exactly the gap reviews identify. Progress charts built on read-aloud Azure scores will likely overstate real gains.

There is no perception training. Every exercise is production (hear model, then speak). Evidence favours perception-based training, especially for a French-L1 learner of English, whose main obstacle is encoding stress contrasts. Listening identification tasks for stress, focus and phrase boundaries are missing.

The feedback is holistic and not actionable. Green, amber and red on words and phonemes plus one prosody number do not tell the learner where the pitch peak or pause should go. v1 ignores Azure's word-level Break and Monotone data and offers no pitch-contour visualization, the prosody feedback tool with the most direct evidence.

There is no L1 diagnostic. Transfer patterns run in opposite directions: French-L1 learners have stress deafness and put stress on final syllables in English; English-L1 learners carry falling, word-initial accents into French. With the L1 unknown, v1 cannot prioritize, so a short onboarding diagnostic is needed.

TTS is the only model voice. Evidence for shadowing and visual feedback comes mostly from human model recordings. Single synthetic voices give learners no variability, while perception training works better with several voices.

The 85-point thresholds and the 'articulation index' are arbitrary. As far as I found, nothing validates Azure accuracy or fluency, especially for fr-FR, against human comprehensibility judgments of L2 speech. The app should check its metrics against occasional human ratings of the learner's own spontaneous speech.
open_questions: What is the learner's L1? The priorities differ sharply. If French-L1: English word stress perception and production, nuclear stress, and vowel reduction for listening. If English-L1: French accentual-phrase final rise and lengthening, and suppressing word-initial stress. If another L1: a diagnostic for both.

Evidence gap: I found and opened no L2 intervention study on French liaison or enchaînement (e.g., Racine & Detey; Howard; Tremblay 2011 on liaison-initial words). This needs a proper search before designing that module around more than descriptive phonology.

Several landmark sources could not be opened because of network restrictions and should be verified before being quoted in product docs: Derwing, Munro & Wiebe 1998; Field 2005; Hardison 2004; Levis & Pickering 2004; Gordon & Darcy 2016 and 2022; Munro & Derwing 2001 (optimal speaking rate); Gluhareva & Prieto 2017; Saito & Plonsky 2019; Saito 2021 (TESOL Q meta-analysis); Suzuki, Kormos & Uchihara 2021 (fluency meta-analysis); Baills, Alazard-Guiu & Prieto 2022 (full abstract; its title and Sbranna's 2025 summary conflict).

Does Azure's fr-FR accuracy or fluency, or any app-computed French prosody measure, correlate with native-listener comprehensibility of this learner's speech? A small N-of-1 check (monthly spontaneous samples rated by 2–3 native listeners) is needed.

Can reliable F0 and syllable-duration extraction run in the browser or on the local Node server for accentual-phrase and nuclear-stress scoring? How robust is it to the learner's microphone and noise?
How long should the training run? The meta-analysis shows longer interventions do better; what minimum weekly dose and duration should the app plan and track?
Does embodied tapping or clapping help an adult self-studying alone? It should be tested within the one user before being made core.

Should English vowel reduction and weak forms be production targets or listening-only? That depends on whether the learner's goal is native-listener comprehensibility or international (ELF) intelligibility.
