Sakai, M., & Moorman, C. (2018). Can perception training improve the production of second language phonemes? A meta-analytic review. Applied Psycholinguistics 39(1), 187–224. Perception training transfers to production, but the production gains are smaller; relevant to prosody-6. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716417000418 (not opened here)

White, L., & Mattys, S. L. (2007). Calibrating rhythm: First language and second language studies. Journal of Phonetics 35(4), 501–522. Rhythm metrics (e.g., VarcoV, %V) differ between L1 and L2 speech and can track L2 development; supports using them only as within-learner comparisons. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wocn.2007.02.003 (not opened here)

Tremblay, A., Namjoshi, J., Spinelli, E., et al. (2017). Experience with a second language affects the use of fundamental frequency in speech segmentation. PLoS ONE 12(7): e0181709. Supports the 'exposure matters' point for the French phrase-final F0 rise. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0181709 (metadata verified via bibliography)

Azure implementation constraint the review missed: phoneme names are returned only for en-US (IPA) and en-US/zh-CN (SAPI); 'For other locales, you can only get the phoneme score.' Syllable groups are en-US only. French syllable-level prosody features therefore cannot rely on labelled Azure phones. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/speech-service/how-to-pronunciation-assessment.md

general_review.topic: fluency: Shadowing, imitation, read-aloud, and fluency/automatization (including the speed-accuracy trade-off behind the v1 speed ladder)

findings.claim: A 2025 narrative systematic review of 44 shadowing studies has no pooled effect sizes, and most of its studies are low-quality pre/post designs. By its reported vote counts, fluency (mostly speech rate) and comprehensibility outcomes were usually positive and prosody was mixed-to-positive. Segmental and accentedness outcomes were inconclusive, and only 1 of the 44 studies had a delayed post-test. Shadowing is a plausible fluency and prosody trainer, not a proven one. Its effect on segments and accent is unknown, and there is no evidence it is ineffective there.
findings.population: Mostly adult and university L2 learners; target languages in the reviewed studies: English 27, Japanese 5, French 1
findings.effect_notes:
Whitworth & Rose (2025, Research Synthesis in Applied Linguistics 1(2):239–269): 44 studies, PRISMA-guided narrative synthesis, no pooled effect sizes.
- Fluency: positive in 8/8 studies, mostly speech-rate measures.
- Comprehensibility: positive in 7/9, including both high-quality studies.
- Prosody: generally positive but mixed.
- Segmental accuracy: inconclusive (4 studies; the 2 positive ones were low quality).
- Accentedness: the best study (Foote & McDonough 2017, 8 weeks of mobile shadowing) found no gain.
- Durability: only 1 of 44 studies had a delayed post-test.

Typical dosage in the primary studies: 10–15 min sessions, 3–4×/week for 4–8 weeks, about 5 passes per passage before a plateau (Shiki et al. 2010).

Caveat: I could not reach the publisher page. These figures come from an independent verification against the open-access Oxford thesis behind the review.
findings.design_implication:
Keep shadowing, but take it out of the phoneme-accuracy pipeline.
- Score shadowing on timing alignment with the model (lag, speech-rate ratio, pause placement), on stress/F0-contour similarity, and on a comprehensibility proxy (the share of words ASR recovers). Never score it per phoneme.
- Default dosage: one 1–2 min passage, about 5 passes, 10–15 min per session, 3–4 sessions a week; rotate passages weekly.
- Durability is unknown, so after each shadowing block schedule a delayed re-test (7 days or more) plus an unscripted retell. Show those results, not in-session scores.

citations.ref: Whitworth & Rose (2025). A systematic review of research on shadowing for second language pronunciation teaching. Research Synthesis in Applied Linguistics 1(2)
Oxford thesis underlying Whitworth & Rose (open access)
Foote & McDonough (2017). Using shadowing with mobile technology to improve L2 pronunciation. Journal of Second Language Pronunciation 3(1), 34–56
Independent verification of the review's outcome table (Hikaya/arabic-buddy research review, Sept 2026)

findings.claim: One small L2 French study (30 female Mandarin-L1 students, split by method and level) found post-test gains in perception and production of /ɥi/. Shadowing improved production (F3-F2 separation) only for intermediate learners, and improved perception for beginners and intermediates. The authors suggest shadowing is an alternative to imitation when proficiency allows the learner to succeed at the task. No study shows delayed imitation is better than shadowing for beginners' production. One small study (Guyot-Talbot et al. 2016) found that repetition with a visual F0 display moved French learners' English question contours closer to the model. Starting beginners on delayed imitation is a reasonable default, not an evidence-based rule.
findings.population: 30 Mandarin-L1 (female) university learners of French; Japanese EFL learners (Hamada); French-L1 university students of English
findings.effect_notes:
Fu, Adda-Decker & Kühnert (2024, JEP), L2 French:
- 30 learners; 4 weeks of autonomous training with delayed imitation vs shadowing on French /ɥi/.
- Both methods improved perception and production.
- Shadowing improved perception for beginners and intermediates, but improved production (a larger F3–F2 separation of /i/ in /ɥi/, distinguishing it from /y/) only for intermediates.
- The authors conclude shadowing is a valid alternative only when proficiency allows the learner to succeed at the task.

Hamada (2016, Language Teaching Research): shadowing benefits lower-proficiency EFL learners most, mainly in phoneme perception and word recognition. This comes from secondary summaries; I did not open the abstract.

Guyot-Talbot, Heidlmayr & Ferragne (2016, JEP):
- French-L1 students of English did 3 sessions of repeating English questions, with their F0 contour on the nuclear syllable shown next to the model's.
- The distance to the model's contour fell significantly from pre-test to post-test.
- The abstract gives no sample size.
findings.design_implication:
Replace the speed ladder with an imitation-mode ladder:
1. Delayed imitation of a short chunk with text visible, plus an F0 and timing overlay against the model.
2. The same with text hidden.
3. Text-visible shadowing.
4. Blind shadowing.
5. Retelling the passage without text.

Promote the learner on task success, for example ASR recovers 90% or more of the words and the learner stays within about 1 s of the model. Speaking faster is not the criterion. A beginner in either language starts at mode 1.

citations.ref: Fu, Adda-Decker & Kühnert (2024). Effets du shadowing et de l'imitation en tant que méthodes d'entraînement à la prononciation du /ɥi/ en français. JEP 2024, 332–341
Hamada (2016). Shadowing: Who benefits and how? Language Teaching Research
Hamada (2019). Shadowing: What is it? How to use it. Where will it go? RELC Journal 50(3)
Guyot-Talbot, Heidlmayr & Ferragne (2016). Entraînements à la prosodie des questions ouvertes et fermées de l'anglais chez des apprenants francophones. JEP 2016

findings.claim: Listeners judge fluency mainly from pauses and speed. Repairs matter little. Listeners weigh these cues the same way in native and non-native speech, and perceived fluency is only weakly related to perceived accent.
findings.population: Native Dutch raters judging adult L2 Dutch speech (Turkish-L1 and English-L1 learners); the pause/speed manipulations used native and non-native speech
findings.effect_notes:
- Bosker et al. (2013, Language Testing 30(2)): 4 experiments with untrained raters. Pause and speed measures best predicted fluency ratings; repair measures contributed very little.
- Bosker et al. (2014, Language Learning 64(3)): phonetically manipulating pauses and speed changed ratings of native and non-native speech in the same way.
- Pinget et al. (2014, Language Testing 31(3)): 90 speech fragments, 20 fluency raters and 20 accent raters. Acoustic fluency measures predicted fluency ratings well; perceived fluency and accent were only weakly related.
- Suzuki, Kormos & Uchihara (2021, Modern Language Journal 105(2), 435–463) meta-analysed utterance–perceived fluency correlations. I could verify only its bibliographic record, not its effect sizes.
findings.design_implication:
Show Fluency as its own dimension, built from speed and pausing, never mixed into pronunciation accuracy or accent.
- Give self-corrections and repetitions little weight.
- Phrase feedback in listener terms, for example "6 pauses inside phrases per 100 syllables; listeners notice these most", not as closeness to a native speaker.
- Keep the accent/segment score on a separate panel so the learner does not conflate the two.

citations.ref: Bosker, Pinget, Quené, Sanders & de Jong (2013). What makes speech sound fluent? The contributions of pauses, speed and repairs. Language Testing 30(2), 159–175 (author-hosted abstract)
Bosker et al. (2014). The perception of fluency in native and nonnative speech. Language Learning 64(3), 579–614
Pinget, Bosker, Quené & de Jong (2014). Native speakers' perceptions of fluency and accent in L2 speech. Language Testing 31(3), 349–365
Suzuki, Kormos & Uchihara (2021). The relationship between utterance and perceived fluency: A meta-analysis of correlational studies. Modern Language Journal 105(2)
Author publication pages with abstracts (H. R. Bosker)

findings.claim: In one SEM study of 128 Japanese EFL learners (mostly B1-B2), articulation rate was the strongest indicator of the speed-fluency factor (β=.88-.91). Mid-clause pause ratio was the strongest indicator of breakdown fluency (β=.92-.96), well above mean pause duration, end-clause pauses and filled pauses. This matches meta-analytic evidence that speed and pause frequency track perceived fluency. Evidence that mean pause length and filled pauses mainly reflect L1 speaking style is limited to small samples. Kahng 2020 (N=44) found they were best predicted by the matching L1 measures. De Jong et al. 2015 (N=51) found silent-pause duration did not predict proficiency, while most other uncorrected measures did. L1 correction improved only syllable duration.
findings.population: 128 Japanese EFL university learners (mostly CEFR B1–B2); 44 Chinese EFL learners; 51 Turkish-L1 and English-L1 learners of Dutch; British Council Aptis test takers
findings.effect_notes:
Suzuki & Kormos (2023, SSLA 45): 128 learners, 4 tasks, structural equation modelling, 250 ms silent-pause threshold.
- Articulation rate loaded β=.88–.91 on speed fluency.
- Mid-clause pause ratio loaded β=.92–.96 on breakdown fluency, well above end-clause pause ratio (.37–.52), filled-pause ratio (.55–.63) and mean pause duration (.53–.69).
- Self-repetition was the main repair indicator but reflects speaking style.
- The processing-speed factor predicted speed fluency in all four tasks (β=.43–.61).

Kahng (2020), as reported in Suzuki & Kormos: 44 learners.
- Mid-clause pause ratio and self-corrections were not predicted by the speaker's L1 fluency, so they are L2-specific.
- Mean pause duration and filled-pause ratio were best predicted by the matching L1 measures.

De Jong et al. (2015, Applied Psycholinguistics 36): 51 learners.
- Syllable duration corrected for L1 behaviour predicted L2 proficiency better than the raw measure.
- Silent-pause duration did not predict proficiency.

Tavakoli, Nakatsuhara & Hunter (2020): speed measures separate adjacent CEFR levels, and mid-clause pausing is the L2 signature. This comes via an independent verification document.

citations.ref: Suzuki & Kormos (2023). The multidimensionality of second language oral fluency: Interfacing cognitive fluency and utterance fluency. SSLA 45
Full text (GROBID TEI) of Suzuki & Kormos (2023), used for the coefficients
Kahng (2020). Explaining second language utterance fluency: Contribution of cognitive fluency and first language utterance fluency. Applied Psycholinguistics 41
De Jong, Groenhout, Schoonen & Hulstijn (2015). Second language fluency: Speaking style or proficiency? Applied Psycholinguistics 36
Tavakoli, Nakatsuhara & Hunter (2020). Aspects of fluency across assessed levels of speaking proficiency. Modern Language Journal 104(1), 169–191
Tavakoli (2011). Pausing patterns: Differences between L2 learners and native speakers. ELT Journal 65

findings.claim: One conference study used about 12,000 recordings from 215 young low-intermediate learners of French. Syllable counts from Google ASR transcripts matched manual counts far better (R²=.874, MAE 1.23) than a signal-only Praat script (R²=.585, MAE 4.25). ASR-based speech rate and run length correlated about r=.59 with a vocabulary-size test, and about r=.61-.63 after manual correction and pruning, against .46-.48 for signal-based versions. For L2 English, an ML annotator of disfluencies and pause location has been validated (Matsuura et al. 2025). Its released tool is English-trained and licensed CC BY-NC. Azure documents FluencyScore only as similarity to native silent-break use, and ProsodyScore as en-US only. I found no public validation of either against human fluency ratings. Automatic, ASR-based fluency metrics look feasible and better than signal-only ones. For French they rest on one non-peer-reviewed study with adolescents.
findings.population: 215 low-intermediate teenage learners of French (about 12,000 recordings); validation corpora for Matsuura et al.; vendor documentation
findings.effect_notes:
Bibauw, Escouflaire, François & Desmet (AILA 2021 conference talk, author-hosted):
- Syllable counts from ASR transcripts agreed with manual counts far better (R²=.874, MAE 1.23) than a signal-only Praat syllable-nuclei script (R²=.585, MAE 4.25).
- Correlations with vocabulary-size proficiency (semi-automatic, pruned): length of runs r=.628, speech rate r=.609, articulation rate r=.524.
- Fully ASR-based speech rate reached r=.585, against .461 for the signal-based version.
- Pruning fillers, repetitions and L1 words raised validity (speech-rate r went from .579 to .609).

Matsuura et al. (2025, Research Methods in Applied Linguistics 4(1)) validated machine-learning annotation of disfluencies and of mid- vs end-clause pause location; the tool is open source.

Microsoft documentation: FluencyScore only indicates "how closely the speech matches a native speaker's use of silent breaks between words", and prosody assessment is available only for en-US.

Caveats: the French data are adolescents and come from a conference talk, not a journal paper.
findings.design_implication:
Build one local fluency engine that behaves the same in en-US and fr-FR:
1. Take Azure word offsets from scripted or unscripted mode.
2. Prune fillers, repetitions and non-target-language words.
3. Count syllables from the recognised text, not from the waveform.
4. Compute the fluency-4 metrics.

Do not show Azure's ProsodyScore for French, because it does not exist, and do not label Azure's FluencyScore as "fluency". Before trusting automatic pause-location labels, check them against 20–30 hand-annotated recordings of the user.

citations.ref: Bibauw, Escouflaire, François & Desmet (2021). Automatizing L2 fluency measurement: validity and developmental sensitivity of temporal fluency metrics variations. AILA 2021 (author-hosted abstract and results)

Matsuura, Suzuki, Takizawa, Saeki & Matsuyama (2025). Gauging the validity of machine learning-based temporal feature annotation to measure fluency in speech automatically. Research Methods in Applied Linguistics 4(1)
FluencyFeatureAnnotator (open-source implementation of Matsuura et al.)
Microsoft Learn: Use pronunciation assessment (FluencyScore definition; prosody en-US only; scripted vs unscripted)
De Jong & Bosker (2013). Choosing a threshold for silent pauses to measure second language fluency. DiSS 2013

findings.claim: Repeating the same oral task reliably raises fluency on that task: speech rate goes up and filled pauses go down, with patterns that vary by proficiency and task (Lambert et al. 2017, N=32). One small classroom study (de Jong & Perfetti 2011, N=24) found fluency gains carried over to new topics only when the same topic was repeated. That group reused non-topic-specific phrases. Whether accuracy and complexity gains are smaller than fluency gains is contested. The one verified meta-analysis with those figures is on written task repetition, and secondary accounts disagree about what the 2025 oral meta-analysis found.
findings.population: Mostly adult and university ESL/EFL learners (24 ESL students; 32 Japanese EFL learners at 3 levels; meta-analytic samples)
findings.effect_notes:
De Jong & Perfetti (2011, Language Learning 61(2)): 24 ESL students, 3 sessions of 4/3/2 timed speeches.
- Both groups improved during training.
- Only the group that repeated the same topic kept its fluency gains on a post-test with new topics.
- That group reused non-topic-specific phrases across repetitions, which the authors read as proceduralization.

Lambert, Kormos & Minn (2017, SSLA): 32 learners, 3 task types × 6 repetitions. Speech rate rose and mid-clause and clause-final filled pauses fell; patterns varied by proficiency and task.

Meta-analyses:
- An oral task-repetition meta-analysis (Abdi Tabari, Zhuang & Farahanynia 2025, System 135) reports fluency as the most robust benefit. I could not verify its effect sizes.
- Liu & Tang (2025, Language Teaching Research), on written repetition: 17 studies, 442 learners; fluency g=0.51, accuracy g=0.24, lexical g=0.24, syntactic complexity g=0.06 (not significant). This comes via a secondary verification.
findings.design_implication:
Make "say it again" the core fluency loop, in EN or FR:
1. The learner gives a 60–120 s unscripted monologue (retell, describe or give an opinion).
2. They hear their recording and the model's key chunks.
3. They deliver the same message twice more, with the time limits shrinking gently.
4. They answer a new prompt on a related topic.

Progress is scored on the new-topic answer, not on the repeated one.

citations.ref: de Jong & Perfetti (2011). Fluency training in the ESL classroom: An experimental study of fluency development and proceduralization. Language Learning 61(2), 533–568
Lambert, Kormos & Minn (2017). Task repetition and second language speech processing. SSLA
Abdi Tabari, Zhuang & Farahanynia (2025). Task repetition and L2 oral performance: A meta-analysis. System 135, 103868
Secondary verification of the conflicting task-repetition meta-analyses (Liu & Tang 2025 figures)
Crossref-verified study summaries (LinguaChat primary-source database)

findings.claim: In one quasi-experimental EFL classroom study (N=79 in intact classes), massed repetition cut pausing the most at the immediate post-test. It also slowed articulation and increased verbatim repetition. At a 1-week delayed post-test with a new story, the schedules differed little. Massed practice gave no lasting advantage, but spacing was not shown to be better either. A 116-learner study reportedly found similar delayed fluency gains for 1-day and 7-day spacing. In a small randomized study (N=36, 12 per group), adding delayed metalinguistic correction to 4/3/2 improved both fluency and accuracy across topics. Mid-clause pausing and regular past tense did not change. A 10-learner study suggests time pressure may undercut accuracy and encourage verbatim recycling.
findings.population: 79 Japanese EFL university students; 36 university EFL students; 10 adults (Boers)
findings.effect_notes:
Suzuki & Hanzawa (2022, SSLA): 79 students; a narrative task repeated 6 times, either massed, short-spaced or long-spaced; tested on new transfer stories.
- Massed practice cut pausing most at the immediate post-test, but brought slower articulation rate and more verbatim repetition.
- At the 1-week delayed post-test the schedules did not differ on most measures.

Tran & Saito (2021, Language Teaching Research): 36 students, three 20-minute sessions, randomly assigned to control, 4/3/2, or 4/3/2 plus delayed metalinguistic correction.
- Only 4/3/2 plus correction improved both fluency and accuracy across topics.
- Mid-clause pauses and regular past-tense accuracy did not change.

Boers (2014, RELC Journal 45), 10 adults, reported via the Tran & Saito record and a secondary summary: shrinking time "undermined potential gains in accuracy" and produced a "strikingly high amount of verbatim duplication".
findings.design_implication:
Do not gate progress on climbing within a single session.
- Spread the repetitions of a task over 2–3 days.
- Between repetitions, give one or two targeted corrections, for example a mispronounced high-frequency word or a missing chunk.
- Detect verbatim recycling (high n-gram overlap with the previous attempt) and prompt the learner to rephrase.
- Count a result only on a delayed (7 days or more) transfer attempt.

citations.ref: Suzuki & Hanzawa (2022). Massed task repetition is a double-edged sword for fluency development: An EFL classroom study. SSLA
Tran & Saito (2021). Effects of the 4/3/2 activity revisited: Extending Boers (2014) and Thai & Boers (2016). Language Teaching Research (author PDF)
Scopus abstract record of Tran & Saito (2021), with the Boers (2014) reference

findings.claim: In native-speaker lab studies, speaking rate is not what makes clear speech intelligible. Trained talkers kept a clear-speech intelligibility advantage at normal rates (Krause & Braida 2002), and Bradlow et al. (1996) found no correlation between sentence duration and intelligibility. Faster tempo is therefore not a valid proxy for articulation quality. For L2 learners, one SEM study found the processing-speed factor, best indexed by sentence-construction speed, predicted speed fluency. Articulatory speed loaded only slightly lower on that factor, with overlapping confidence intervals. Vocabulary contributed to speed fluency only in reading-based retell tasks.
findings.population: Native English talkers (clear-speech studies); 128 Japanese EFL learners (cognitive-fluency modelling); L2 Dutch learners (Pinget et al.)
findings.effect_notes:
Krause & Braida (2002, JASA 112(5)), as reviewed in McCloy's dissertation:
- Trained native talkers produced clear speech at a normal rate (about 187 wpm, against about 218 wpm for fast speech).
- That speech kept its intelligibility advantage, so the clear-speech benefit was independent of rate.
- Bradlow et al. (1996) found no correlation between mean sentence duration and intelligibility.

Suzuki & Kormos (2023), processing-speed factor:
- Sentence-construction speed (Maze RT) was the strongest component (β=.79–.82).
- Articulatory speed in controlled production was weaker (β=.64–.66).
- Vocabulary size was the main linguistic resource (β=.85–.88).

Caveat: the rate-vs-clarity evidence is from native speakers. I found no L2 study showing that tongue-twister or tempo training transfers to conversational articulation.
findings.design_implication:
Drop the 0.75×/1×/1.25× tempo ladder and the accuracy × tempo-multiplier articulation index.
- Train clarity at the learner's comfortable rate: full vowels in stressed syllables, released consonants in clusters, and pauses at phrase boundaries rather than inside phrases.
- Build speed only indirectly, through task repetition and chunks.
- If tongue twisters stay, keep them as optional warm-ups that do not count toward progress.

citations.ref: Krause & Braida (2002). Investigating alternative forms of clear speech: The effects of speaking rate and speaking mode on intelligibility. JASA 112(5), 2165–2172
McCloy dissertation, literature review on intelligibility and speech rate (discusses Krause & Braida 2002; Bradlow et al. 1996)
Suzuki & Kormos (2023). SSLA 45
Pinget et al. (2014). Language Testing 31(3)

findings.claim: Practice transfers mostly to the kind of speaking that was practised. Read-aloud and pronunciation-drill gains do not reliably show up in spontaneous speech.
findings.population: 61 university students learning an artificial language (DeKeyser); 77 pronunciation-instruction studies of L2 learners (Saito & Plonsky); 128 Japanese EFL learners (Suzuki & Kormos)
findings.effect_notes:
- DeKeyser (1997, SSLA): 61 students, 8 weeks of computer practice in a miniature artificial language. Learning followed a power function. Transfer was skill-specific: comprehension practice improved comprehension, production practice improved production, with little cross-skill transfer.
- Saito & Plonsky (2019, Language Learning; 77 studies): instruction works best on specific features measured under controlled conditions; effects on globally rated spontaneous speech are much less clear. This comes via a secondary summary.
- Suzuki & Kormos (2023): the link between cognitive and utterance fluency differed between reading-based and open speaking tasks.
- Cucchiarini, Strik & Boves (2002) compared automatic fluency assessment of read vs spontaneous speech; I verified only the bibliographic record.
- Azure offers an unscripted speaking mode.
findings.design_implication:
End every session with at least one unscripted turn in the target language, for example answering a question or retelling the shadowed passage without text. Assess it in Azure's unscripted mode plus the local fluency engine.

Progress charts should show spontaneous-speech metrics as the main line. Read-aloud and shadowing scores appear only as secondary practice metrics.

citations.ref: DeKeyser (1997). Beyond explicit rule learning: Automatizing second language morphosyntax. SSLA
Saito & Plonsky (2019). Effects of second language pronunciation teaching revisited. Language Learning 69(3)
Cucchiarini, Strik & Boves (2002). Quantitative assessment of second language learners' fluency: Comparisons between read and spontaneous speech. JASA 111(6), 2862–2873
Microsoft Learn: scripted vs unscripted pronunciation assessment

findings.claim: Correlational studies of L2 English learners link multiword-sequence and lexical-bundle use to oral fluency across proficiency levels (Tavakoli & Uchihara 2020; Hougham et al. 2024). I did not verify which fluency dimensions (speed or pausing) are involved. In one small study (N=24), the repetition group whose fluency gains transferred reused generic phrases. Causal evidence that teaching chunks raises fluency is thin: Boers et al. 2006 (n=32) measured judges' perceived proficiency, not temporal fluency. There is no French-specific evidence.
findings.population: L2 English learners across proficiency levels (Tavakoli & Uchihara; Hougham et al.); 24 ESL students (de Jong & Perfetti)
findings.effect_notes:
- Tavakoli & Uchihara (2020, Language Learning 70(2), 506–547): multiword sequences are associated with oral fluency across proficiency levels. This is correlational and comes via a 2026 conference abstract that summarizes it.
- Hougham, Clenton & Uchihara (2024, System 121) separate the contributions of shorter and longer lexical bundles to fluency.
- De Jong & Perfetti (2011): the group whose gains transferred had reused non-topic phrases.
- The causal chunk-teaching evidence is small (for example Boers et al. 2006, n=32, with a formal replication call, per a secondary verification).
- No French-specific evidence was found.
findings.design_implication:
Keep a bank of 200–300 high-frequency spoken frames and discourse markers for each language.
- EN examples: "the thing is…", "what I mean is…".
- FR examples: "en fait…", "je pense que…", "c'est-à-dire…", with liaison and enchaînement modelled inside each chunk.

Use the chunks as imitation and shadowing material and as scaffolds in monologue prompts, and track how often they are reused in spontaneous speech. Present this as a well-grounded bet, not a proven lever.

citations.ref: Tavakoli & Uchihara (2020). To what extent are multiword sequences associated with oral fluency? Language Learning 70(2), 506–547
Hougham, Clenton & Uchihara (2024). Disentangling the contributions of shorter vs. longer lexical bundles to L2 oral fluency. System 121, 103243
Hollis et al. (2026). Beyond Monologues: Predicting L2 Fluency in Academic Multilogues (H-LRF abstract summarizing the chunk–fluency literature)
de Jong & Perfetti (2011). Language Learning 61(2)

findings.claim: In lab rating experiments, long 'reluctant' turn gaps lowered perceived fluency of non-native speech (Van Os et al. 2020). In one semester-long quasi-experiment (N=167 in 4 intact classes), peer interaction alone improved fluency. Adding corrective feedback added accuracy gains, and both CF groups improved in accuracy and fluency. Evidence that fluency grows with the amount of real speaking comes from self-selected or correlational comparisons: intensive domestic immersion vs classroom for 28 US learners of French, and 32 immigrants grouped by L1 with differing out-of-class exposure.
findings.population: Native Dutch raters of manipulated dialogues; 167 Japanese university EFL students; 28 US university learners of French; 32 adult immigrant ESL learners in Canada
findings.effect_notes:
- Van Os et al. (2020, Language Learning 70(4)): in manipulated dialogues, "reluctant" answers (long turn gaps) lowered the perceived fluency of non-native speech; overly "eager" answers did not.
- Sato & Lyster (2012, SSLA): 167 students in 4 intact classes over 1 semester. Peer interaction alone improved fluency; interaction plus corrective feedback improved both accuracy and fluency.
- Freed, Segalowitz & Dewey (2004, SSLA), L2 French: 28 learners. Intensive domestic immersion produced gains in total words, longest turn, speech rate and fluidity; at-home classroom learners made no significant fluency gains. Groups were self-selected.
- Derwing, Munro & Thomson (2007, Applied Linguistics): 32 learners over 22 months. Only the group with more out-of-class English use improved, and only slightly, in fluency and comprehensibility.
findings.design_implication:
Add an interaction mode:
- The app asks short spoken questions (TTS voice, optionally generated by an LLM) and the learner answers unscripted.
- For each answer, measure time to first word, mid-clause pauses and speech rate.
- Give feedback after the turn, not during it.

Use this mode as the main transfer probe, and show a weekly counter of unscripted speaking minutes, since the volume of genuine speaking predicts growth.

citations.ref: Van Os et al. (2020). Fluency in dialogue: Turn-taking behavior shapes perceived fluency in native and nonnative speech. Language Learning 70(4), 1183–1217
Sato & Lyster (2012). Peer interaction and corrective feedback for accuracy and fluency development. SSLA
Freed, Segalowitz & Dewey (2004). Context of learning and second language fluency in French. SSLA
Derwing, Munro & Thomson (2007). A longitudinal study of ESL learners' fluency and comprehensibility development. Applied Linguistics

findings.claim: Sentence repetition (elicited imitation) is a quick and valid probe of overall proficiency. That makes it useful for placing the learner in each language when their L1 and level are unknown.
findings.population: 21 studies, 1,089 L2 learners across several target languages
findings.effect_notes:
Yan, Maeda, Lv & Ginther (2016, Language Testing), 24 effect sizes:
- Elicited imitation discriminated between proficiency levels with Hedges' g=1.34.
- Sentence length and scoring method moderate the result.

This is reported via two independent secondary summaries; I did not open the abstract. It is evidence for a diagnostic, not a training effect.

citations.ref: Yan, Maeda, Lv & Ginther (2016). Elicited imitation as a measure of second language proficiency: A narrative review and meta-analysis. Language Testing
Secondary summary with effect size (Enigma-Solved research notes)

does_not_work_verified.claim: Speed ladder (0.75x to 1.25x TTS tempo, advance at 85 or more accuracy) as a proxy for articulation
does_not_work_verified.notes: I found no evidence for tempo ladders either, and native clear-speech work says rate is not what drives intelligibility. Two sub-claims are misstated. First, Suzuki & Hanzawa show the schedule differences shrank at 1 week; they do not show massed gains 'disappear'. Second, the L2 rate literature (Munro & Derwing 1998, 2001) shows rate does affect comprehensibility ratings, and L2 speakers are often too slow. Rate is relevant to listeners, but that is no argument for tempo-ladder training. Clinical rate work mostly slows speakers down to aid intelligibility (dysarthria), the opposite direction, and it is not an L2 population.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Shadowing as accent-reduction or segment training
does_not_work_verified.notes: This matches the review's reported segmental and accentedness outcomes. I could access those only through a secondary AI-written doc; the publisher was blocked. Frame it as 'unproven', not 'ineffective'. Other secondary summaries report accuracy gains in some studies (Mori 2011; Hsu 2025, n=42), which I could not verify.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using Azure's single FluencyScore and ProsodyScore as the fluency or articulation measure
does_not_work_verified.notes: Confirmed verbatim from the MicrosoftDocs GitHub source. FluencyScore is 'how closely the speech matches a native speaker's use of silent breaks between words' and is reported only at the full-text level. 'Prosody assessment is only available in the en-US locale', and syllable-level scores are en-US only. That it cannot separate mid-clause from boundary pauses is an inference from those definitions. I found no published validation of either score against human ratings.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Scoring raw pause length, filled pauses or self-repetitions as disfluency without an L1 baseline
does_not_work_verified.notes: This holds only partly. De Jong et al. 2015 (N=51) found silent-pause duration did not predict proficiency. Most other uncorrected measures did predict it, and L1 correction improved only syllable duration. Kahng 2020 (N=44) found pause duration and filled pauses tracked the matching L1 measures. The self-repetition-as-style point is weaker and rests on citations. Down-weight these measures rather than treating an L1 baseline as essential.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Heavy penalties for self-repairs
does_not_work_verified.notes: The Bosker et al. 2013 abstract says 'repair measures contributed only very little' to perceived fluency. This is consistent with the 2021 meta-analysis (effect sizes not verified).

does_not_work_verified.claim: Treating improvement on the item just repeated as learning
does_not_work_verified.notes: The principle, that in-task gains are not transfer, is sound. The stated evidence is misreported: Suzuki & Hanzawa found schedule effects 'limited' at 1 week on a novel story, not that the gains vanished. The 'only same-message repetition transferred' result comes from one study of 24.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Assuming read-aloud or drill accuracy transfers to spontaneous conversation
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by the pronunciation meta-analyses (Saito & Plonsky 2019; Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015), which find larger effects on controlled outcomes. Derwing et al. 1998 found segmental-only instruction did not carry over to narratives. DeKeyser 1997 is only an analogy, since it compared comprehension with production.

does_not_work_verified.claim: A globally slowed model voice as a clearer target
does_not_work_verified.notes: The preprint was confirmed via the GitHub mirror: Tuttösí et al., arXiv 2603.30032, 'Covertly improving intelligibility with data-driven adaptations of speech timing'. Its abstract says listeners judged global slowing clearer 'even though it actually increased comprehension errors', and that targeted slowing helped L2 listeners with vowel contrasts. It cites Aoki & Zellou (2024, J. Phonetics 104:101328), where non-native-directed speech gave no intelligibility advantage to Mandarin-L1 listeners. The evidence is weak, as the finding says: a preprint about listening to synthesized vowel contrasts.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Mirroring and tongue-twister speed drills as fluency or articulation builders for L2 adults
does_not_work_verified.notes: This is an absence-of-evidence claim; I found no controlled L2 studies either. With search blocked, I cannot rule them out. De Jong & Mora (2019, SSLA 41(1):227-239) directly tests whether articulatory skill relates to L1/L2 fluency and should be checked before making claims either way.

critique_of_v1: The core articulation construct is misdefined. docs/prd.md defines articulation as 'accuracy under speed' and technical-design.md calls accuracy-under-tempo 'the standard speech-therapy proxy'. The evidence says perceived fluency depends on pause location and speed in spontaneous speech, and that clarity can be improved without changing rate. The speed ladder makes rate the progression variable, which is the wrong target.

The articulation index, mean(accuracy × tier multiplier 0.9/1.0/1.15), mixes accuracy and tempo into one number with no construct validity. It should be split into speed (articulation rate), breakdown (mid-clause pauses per 100 syllables), repair, and accuracy, each reported separately.

The ≥85 tier gate on tongue twisters rewards memorised, verbatim performance of one repeated string within a session. Research shows massed-practice gains vanish at one week and time pressure produces verbatim recycling and accuracy loss (Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022; Boers 2014). There are no spaced or delayed checks.

All three tracks are scripted read-aloud of reference text. There is no unscripted or interactive speaking and no transfer probe on unseen prompts, so progress charts measure practised items. Transfer is skill-specific and read-aloud gains shrink in spontaneous speech.

The main Fluency number comes from Azure's FluencyScore, an opaque 'silent breaks vs native' score. The articulation panel's 'unexpected pause list' does not separate mid-clause from clause-boundary pauses, and raw pause durations penalise personal or L1 style. Azure ProsodyScore is en-US only, so the French prosody track (liaison, enchaînement, rhythm) has no prosody measurement at all.

Shadowing is confined to the prosody track, uses TTS 'at matched pace', and runs through the same accuracy scoring. It should be scored on timing and prosody alignment and comprehensibility, gated by proficiency (imitation first for beginners), given a dosage structure (about 5 passes, 10–15 min, 3–4×/week), and followed by delayed re-tests.

Tongue-twister and cluster content ('les chaussettes de l'archiduchesse', 'je ne le lui redemanderai pas') is low-frequency, non-communicative material. The fluency bottleneck is formulation, meaning vocabulary, sentence construction and chunks, and v1 has no chunk or formulaic content or monologue tasks that train it.

There is no L1 baseline and no placement probe even though the learner's L1 and level are unknown. Fluency norms cannot be personalised, and the app cannot tell which language is the L2 or where to start.
Slowed 0.75× TTS is used as the entry tier. Slowing a model uniformly is not evidence-based as a clarity aid, and imitating an artificially slowed or sped-up voice trains an unnatural timing pattern.
open_questions: Do shadowing gains last? Only 1 of 44 studies in the 2025 review had a delayed post-test. The app should test this on its own user by logging 7- and 30-day re-tests.

Does any rate or tongue-twister training transfer to conversational articulation in adult L2 learners? No L2 study was found. De Jong & Mora (2019, SSLA 41(1)), 'Does having good articulatory skills lead to more fluent speech in first and second languages?', is directly relevant but I could not open it.

Which fluency norms and clause-boundary rules apply to L2 French? Relevant work (Préfontaine & Kormos 2015, MLJ, https://doi.org/10.1111/modl.12186; Segalowitz, French & Guay 2017, https://doi.org/10.7202/1050813ar; Detey et al. 2020, Speech Communication, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.specom.2020.10.001) could only be verified bibliographically.
What are the exact pooled effect sizes in Suzuki, Kormos & Uchihara (2021) and in the 2025 oral task-repetition meta-analysis (Abdi Tabari et al.)? They were not verifiable from this environment.

How accurate are Azure's word timings, and its unscripted recognition, on accented spontaneous French and English? Automatic pause-location labels need validating against hand annotation of the user's own speech.

If the user's L1 is French or English, work in that language is refinement of an L1 (public-speaking clarity) rather than L2 acquisition, and the SLA evidence above applies mainly to the other language. Which case applies must be settled before choosing targets.

What is the best mix of shadowing, imitation, 4/3/2 monologues and interaction for one self-directed adult? No randomised comparison of app-based fluency programmes for adults exists in either language.
missed_evidence_flagged: Kakitani, J., & Kormos, J. (2024). The effects of distributed practice on second language fluency development. SSLA 46, 770-794. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263124000251. According to a secondary summary, 116 learners showed similar delayed fluency gains with 1-day and 7-day spacing. This undercuts 'spacing works better' in fluency-7 and argues against hard-coding one spacing interval.

Kostromitina, M., & Plonsky, L. (2022). Elicited imitation tasks as a measure of L2 proficiency: A meta-analysis. SSLA 44(3), 886-911. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263121000395. A newer, independent meta-analysis that supports fluency-12.

Lee, J., Jang, J., & Plonsky, L. (2015). The effectiveness of second language pronunciation instruction: A meta-analysis. Applied Linguistics 36(3), 345-366. https://academic.oup.com/applij/article/36/3/345/2422438. 86 reports, with larger effects for controlled outcome measures. Supports fluency-9.

Derwing, T. M., Munro, M. J., & Wiebe, G. (1998). Evidence in favor of a broad framework for pronunciation instruction. Language Learning 48(3), 393-410. The segmental-instruction group improved on read sentences only; the global/prosody group also improved in extemporaneous narratives. Directly relevant to fluency-9 and to what the app trains.

Munro, M. J., & Derwing, T. M. (1998). The effects of speaking rate on listener evaluations of native and foreign-accented speech. Language Learning 48(2), 159-182; and Munro & Derwing (2001). Modeling perceptions of the accentedness and comprehensibility of L2 speech: The role of speaking rate. SSLA 23(4), 451-468. L2 speakers are often slower than optimal, and modest speeding improved ratings. This qualifies fluency-8.

Hardison, D. M. (2004). Generalization of computer-assisted prosody training: Quantitative and qualitative findings. Language Learning & Technology 8(1), 34-52 (open access). English-L1 learners of L2 French trained with visual F0 displays improved prosody, and the gains generalized to novel sentences. This is the strongest French-specific support for the pitch-overlay feedback in fluency-2.

TESOL Quarterly 50(2), 447-471. https://doi.org/10.1002/tesq.244. An explicit fluency-strategy intervention study (content from memory, not verified here). The evidence base on teaching fluency directly is missing from the findings.

Detey, S., Fontan, L., Le Coz, M., & Jmel, S. (2020). Computer-assisted assessment of phonetic fluency in a second language: A longitudinal study of Japanese learners of French. Speech Communication 125, 69-79. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.specom.2020.10.001. A peer-reviewed French-specific automatic fluency study that fluency-5 lacks.

Uchihara, T., Karas, M., & Thomson, R. I. (2024). Does perceptual HVPT improve L2 speech production? A meta-analysis of perception-production connection. Applied Psycholinguistics 45, 591-623. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716424000195. Perception gains carry over to production only partly. Relevant to 'shadowing helps perception first' in fluency-2.

De Jong, N. H., & Mora, J. C. (2019). Does having good articulatory skills lead to more fluent speech in first and second languages? SSLA 41(1), 227-239. Directly tests the articulatory-speed question behind fluency-8 and the tongue-twister claim.

Aoki, N. B., & Zellou, G. (2024). Being clear about clear speech: Intelligibility of hard-of-hearing-directed, non-native-directed, and casual speech for L1- and L2-English listeners. Journal of Phonetics 104, 101328. Peer-reviewed support for the global-slowdown does-not-work claim, stronger than the preprint.
