Canadian Journal of Applied Linguistics 20(2), 90-116. https://doi.org/10.7202/1050813ar. Evidence on which utterance-fluency measures pick up short-term gains in adults.

Hsu (2025), Journal of Computers in Education, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40692-025-00374-x. Shadowing plus ASR, n=42, 10 weeks. A secondary summary reports pronunciation accuracy and fluency gains, especially for lower-performing students. This is possible contrary evidence to fluency-1 and fluency-2; unverified.

Verification limits for this whole report: publisher sites, doi.org, Crossref, OpenAlex, ACL Anthology web and Microsoft Learn were blocked by the egress proxy, and the WebSearch budget was exhausted. Checks used GitHub-hosted mirrors instead: ACL Anthology XML, author sites, a GROBID full text, Scopus/OpenAlex records and the MicrosoftDocs source. Where only AI-written secondary docs were available, the verdicts are cautious.

general_review.topic: Learning science for pronunciation and articulation training: scheduling (spacing, retrieval, interleaving vs blocking, desirable difficulties, deliberate practice), self-assessment and self-monitoring, goals and self-efficacy, adherence and dropout, session length and frequency
general_review.summary:
The v1 practice loop is: hear the TTS model, imitate it, retry until the score is green, then advance at 85 or more. The learning-science evidence points the other way on almost every step.

(1) Spacing is the best-supported lever. Practice on a target should be spread over days, and mastery should only count after a delayed check. The meta-analyses cover mostly L2 vocabulary and grammar; pronunciation-specific spacing data is thin.
(2) For speaking skills, gaps of a few days worked better than weekly gaps. Repeating the same item many times in a row gave mixed results: fewer pauses, but slower articulation and more verbatim repetition.
(3) Interleaving is not always better. For new, hard sound contrasts and for fluency, blocked practice won in several studies. The design should start blocked and switch to mixed practice as the learner stabilises.
(4) Scores during a session, especially right after hearing a model, mislead both the learner and the app. Progress should be measured with 'cold', delayed checks and transfer checks on new material.
(5) Self-assessment is biased, usually towards overestimation, and gets more accurate with feedback. A light calibration loop is worth adding, but self-ratings should never drive scheduling.
(6) Adherence needs structure, not gimmicks. The best-supported tools are:
- specific goals and if-then plans (d = .65)
- short, frequent sessions
- no punishment for a missed day
- a way back after a break
- visible evidence of mastery to build self-efficacy.

Evidence strength: strong for spacing and implementation intentions in general. Moderate or mixed for interleaving, task repetition and self-assessment in speech. Weak for exact session length. Almost no study includes French learners.

How sources were checked: WebSearch was exhausted and publisher, DOI and index sites were blocked in this environment. Sources were opened through GitHub-hosted copies instead: an author PDF (Fuhrmeister & Myers), Scopus abstract exports, RIS exports, and curated evidence records with Crossref-checked metadata. Figures that come only from secondary records are flagged in effect_notes and should be re-checked against the originals before they are published.

findings.claim: Spacing practice of the same L2 targets across sessions beats massing it for retention (medium-to-large effect; mostly vocabulary and grammar studies). Longer gaps match shorter gaps on immediate tests but beat them on delayed tests, and the best gap grows with how long the material must be retained. Equal and expanding schedules are about equivalent overall; expanding may help when there are many retrievals. There is no pronunciation-specific synthesis, and only isolated pronunciation studies exist (e.g., Li & DeKeyser 2019 on Mandarin tones).
findings.population: Mostly adolescent and adult L2 learners studying vocabulary and grammar (Kim & Webb). Cepeda: verbal recall, mostly native-speaker adults. Bird: 38 adult L1-Malay learners of English grammar. Nakata: 128 Japanese EFL university students. No pronunciation-specific spacing meta-analysis was found.
findings.effect_notes: Kim & Webb 2022 (Language Learning): 48 experiments, 98 effect sizes, N = 3,411. Spaced practice had a medium-to-large effect over massed practice. Shorter spacing matched longer spacing on immediate posttests but lost on delayed posttests. Equal and expanding schedules were statistically equivalent. These figures agree across several independent verification records; the publisher abstract could not be opened here. Cepeda et al. 2006: 839 assessments from 317 experiments; the best gap between study sessions grows with how long the material must be retained. Bird 2010: 3-day vs 14-day gaps did not differ at 7 days, but the 14-day group was better at 60 days. Nakata 2015: spaced beat massed; expanding spacing was no better than equal spacing. Pronunciation-specific evidence is weak.
findings.design_implication: Build the core scheduler as a spaced queue of targets: sound contrasts, words, phrases and prosodic patterns. Each target comes back on later days, for example next day, about 3 days, about 1 week, then longer. A simple equal-or-expanding rule is enough; no complex algorithm is needed. A target counts as learned only after a successful check on a later day, never after a good score in the session where it was trained. Spread a fixed number of repetitions per target over several sessions instead of spending them in one sitting.

citations.ref: Kim, S. K., & Webb, S. (2022). The effects of spaced practice on second language learning: A meta-analysis. Language Learning, 72, 269-319.
Verification ledger with Kim & Webb figures (48 experiments, 98 effect sizes, N = 3,411)
Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380.
Bird, S. (2010). Effects of distributed practice on the acquisition of second language English syntax. Applied Psycholinguistics.
Nakata, T. (2015). Effects of expanding and equal spacing on second language vocabulary learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition.

findings.claim: In one lab study (n = 60, miniature language), 3.3-day spacing produced more accurate oral production of morphology than 7-day spacing, which lasted to 28 days, with no speed difference. In one quasi-experimental classroom study (n = 79, intact classes), six massed repetitions of a narrative reduced pauses but slowed articulation and increased verbatim repetition; schedule effects were limited after 1 week. The best spacing gap for speaking skills is not settled, and L2 meta-analytic data favour longer gaps for long-delayed retention.
findings.population: Adults learning to produce the morphology of a miniature language aloud (Suzuki 2017), and Japanese EFL university students at A2-B1 in intact classes (Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022). Neither study targets segmental pronunciation.
findings.effect_notes: Suzuki 2017 (Language Learning 67(3), 512-545): n = 60, four training sessions, 3.3-day vs 7-day intervals. The 3.3-day group was more accurate from session 3 onward and kept that advantage on 7-day and 28-day delayed posttests (small-to-medium effect sizes). Speed did not differ. Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022 (SSLA): quasi-experimental, massed n = 20, short-spaced n = 23, long-spaced n = 21, control n = 15; learners narrated the same cartoon 6 times. On the immediate posttest with a new cartoon, massed practice reduced pauses the most but slowed articulation rate and increased verbatim repetition. Schedule effects were limited at 1 week.
findings.design_implication: Schedule each active speaking target 2-4 times a week in short blocks, not once a week in a long block. Within a session, cap consecutive repeats of the same item (for example 3), then move on and bring it back later that session or on another day. Track articulation rate, pause location and length, and repetitions alongside accuracy, so the app can spot trade-offs such as 'fewer pauses but slower' or 'faster but less clear'.

citations.ref: Suzuki, Y. (2017). The optimal distribution of practice for the acquisition of L2 morphology: A conceptual replication and extension. Language Learning, 67(3), 512-545 (abstract read in RIS export)
RIS export containing the Suzuki (2017) abstract
Suzuki, Y., & Hanzawa, K. (2022). Massed task repetition is a double-edged sword for fluency development: An EFL classroom study. Studies in Second Language Acquisition.
ERCT record with the Suzuki & Hanzawa abstract and group sizes

findings.claim: Interleaving (mixing categories) helps category discrimination on average. But for new, hard speech-sound contrasts and for speaking fluency, blocked practice did better in several studies, while interleaving helped L2 grammar accuracy. The benefit depends on the learning stage, how similar the categories are, and the learner's aptitude.
findings.population: Brunmair & Richter: mostly non-language category learning in students. Fuhrmeister & Myers: 136 monolingual US-English undergraduates learning to hear a Hindi dental-retroflex contrast (perception only). Suzuki 2021: Japanese EFL university students. Suzuki, Yokosawa & Aline 2020: 60 EFL learners.
findings.effect_notes: Brunmair & Richter 2019: 59 studies, 238 effect sizes, 158 samples. Overall interleaving effect g = 0.42 (paintings g = 0.67, maths g = 0.34). For words, blocking was better (g = -0.39). Interleaving helps more when categories resemble each other. Fuhrmeister & Myers 2020: 600 training trials in one evening session, retested the next morning. Blocked beat interleaved for both learning and retention; only higher-aptitude listeners handled interleaving. The authors note the contrast with multi-week HVPT studies, where learners were not naive to the sounds. Suzuki 2021 (RCT): blocked n = 24, interleaved n = 26, control n = 18, over 3 days. Blocked task repetition produced faster articulation and shorter mid-clause pauses on new cartoons. Suzuki, Yokosawa & Aline 2020: interleaved beat blocked for relative-clause accuracy at immediate and 1-week tests, with a smaller advantage for speed.
findings.design_implication: Apply a 'blocked first, then mixed' rule to each contrast. Introduce a new contrast in a short blocked set with one voice and one phonetic context, for example French /y/-/u/ or /ɑ̃/-/ɔ̃/, or English /ɪ/-/iː/ or /θ/-/s/. Once performance is stable across two sessions, switch to interleaved sets that mix the confusable pair with each other and with other targets, using several voices and contexts. For fluency tasks, keep repetition blocked within a session and spaced across days. Base the switch on the learner's own performance, since aptitude changes the effect.

citations.ref: Fuhrmeister, P., & Myers, E. B. (2020). Desirable and undesirable difficulties: Influences of variability, training schedule, and aptitude on nonnative phonetic learning. Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 82(4), 2049-2065 (full text read)
Author-hosted PDF of Fuhrmeister & Myers (2020)
Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029-1052.
Suzuki, Y. (2021). Optimizing fluency training for speaking skills transfer: Comparing the effects of blocked and interleaved task repetition. Language Learning.
ERCT record with the Suzuki (2021) abstract and group sizes

Suzuki, Y., Yokosawa, S., & Aline, D. (2020). The role of working memory in blocked and interleaved grammar practice: Proceduralization of L2 syntax. Language Teaching Research (abstract in Scopus export)

findings.claim: Retrieval practice (producing an answer from memory, with feedback) reliably improves retention compared with restudying. For pronunciation, the closest equivalent is saying a target before hearing the model, rather than imitating a model just heard. That pronunciation equivalent has not been tested directly.
findings.population: School and university students, mostly verbal and academic content. No L2 pronunciation study compared 'say first, then hear' with 'hear, then imitate'.
findings.effect_notes: Yang et al. 2021 (Psychological Bulletin): 222 independent studies, 48,478 students, overall g = 0.499. The effect was moderated by feedback, number of test repetitions and format match. A recent study (three preregistered online experiments, 5 sessions 2 days apart) found retrieval beat restudy, except when learners had to rate their memory on every trial, which reversed the effect. That is a caution against self-ratings on every trial. Applying retrieval to pronunciation is an extrapolation.
findings.design_implication: Default drill: show the text and a phonetic cue, and the learner says it first (a 'cold' attempt). The attempt is scored, then the learner hears the model and tries again. Only cold attempts count toward mastery and progress charts. Keep 'listen first' TTS for introducing new targets and for perception work, not for every trial. Give specific feedback after every retrieval attempt.

citations.ref: Yang, C., Luo, L., Vadillo, M. A., Yu, R., & Shanks, D. R. (2021). Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: A systematic and meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 147(4), 399-435 (abstract quoted in verification record)
Verification record quoting the Yang et al., Cepeda et al., and Brunmair & Richter abstracts
'Spaced Retrieval Practice: Can Restudying Trump Retrieval?' (Scopus abstract export, D3124)

findings.verified_url: https://github.com/eternity4719/HowToLiveBetter/blob/main/docs/核实记录/追加-戒烟戒酒学习与拖延的具体办法.md

findings.claim: Repeating the same monologue or narrative several times raises speech rate and reduces filled pauses on that task (n = 32). Small classroom studies found that fluency gains carried over to new topics after same-topic repetition (n = 24), and after 4/3/2 combined with delayed metalinguistic correction (n = 36, randomised), which also improved irregular past-tense accuracy but not mid-clause pausing or regular past tense. There is no evidence yet on pronunciation accuracy or intelligibility, and none on French.
findings.population: Adult ESL/EFL learners: Japanese EFL learners and mixed-L1 ESL classes. Small samples, English only; no French studies were found.
findings.effect_notes: de Jong & Perfetti 2011 (Language Learning): n = 24, three sessions of 4/3/2 speeches. Only the group that repeated the same topic kept fluency gains on new topics. Lambert, Kormos & Minn 2017 (SSLA): n = 32 Japanese EFL learners, six repetitions of three task types. Speech rate rose and filled pauses fell across repetitions. '4/3/2 activity revisited' (Language Teaching Research, 2021): n = 36, randomised into three groups, three 20-minute sessions. 4/3/2 plus metalinguistic correction improved fluency and accuracy across topics, but mid-clause pauses and some forms did not change. The de Jong and Lambert details come from Crossref/ERIC-checked evidence records.
findings.design_implication: Replace tongue-twister speed ladders with 'retell ladders'. The learner speaks on a prompt, or retells a short passage, 3 times with shrinking time limits (for example 90 -> 60 -> 45 seconds). Between rounds they get 1-2 targeted feedback points. Rounds are scored on speech rate, pauses (especially mid-clause), repetitions, and intelligibility of the target words. Use spontaneous or semi-spontaneous speech in both languages, not only read-aloud text.

citations.ref: de Jong, N., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Fluency training in the ESL classroom: An experimental study of fluency development and proceduralization. Language Learning.
Lambert, C., Kormos, J., & Minn, D. (2017). Task repetition and second language speech processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition.
'Effects of the 4/3/2 activity revisited: Extending Boers (2014) and Thai & Boers (2016)', Language Teaching Research 2021 (Scopus abstract export, D1522)
Crossref/ERIC-checked evidence records (de Jong & Perfetti; Lambert et al.)

findings.claim: Performance during practice can diverge from later retention and transfer, so in-session scores are not proof of learning (Soderstrom & Bjork 2015). In lab category learning, learners tend to choose blocking for confusable categories; explaining that telling categories apart means finding their differences, and why that matters, increases interleaving. Learners give lower learning judgments when effort feels high; a meta-analysis found those judgments still predicted outcomes, so the evidence that learners misread effort comes from other lab studies (e.g., Kirk-Johnson et al. 2019), not from this meta-analysis.
findings.population: University students in lab and online category-learning and memory tasks (Abel & de Bruin; David et al.). Japanese EFL learners (Suzuki 2021).
findings.effect_notes: Abel & de Bruin 2024: Exp. 1 N = 190, Exp. 2 N = 134. Learners chose blocking. Explaining that telling categories apart means spotting their differences, and stressing why that matters, increased their choice of interleaving. David et al. 2024: meta-analytic SEM. Higher perceived effort went with lower judgments of learning (β = -.19); judgments went with outcomes (β = .29); the indirect path from effort to outcome was β = -.05. Suzuki 2021: blocked practice showed clear advantages during training (longer runs, higher phonation-time ratio) that did not appear as pretest-posttest gains. Theoretical frame: the desirable-difficulty framework for L2 practice (Suzuki, Nakata & DeKeyser 2019, Modern Language Journal 103, 713-720).
findings.design_implication: The app, not the learner, should decide what to practise, when, and whether it is blocked or mixed. Add short explanations of why mixed, harder practice is used and that the effort is expected. Keep 'practice scores' separate from 'progress'. Progress comes only from cold, delayed checks on items not practised that day, plus regular transfer checks on unseen sentences and free speech. Show retries as practice, not as proof of learning.

citations.ref: Abel, R., & de Bruin, A. (2024). Why do learners (under)utilize interleaving in learning confusable categories? Educational Psychology Review (abstract in Scopus export D3158)

David, L., Biwer, F., Baars, M., Wijnia, L., Paas, F., & de Bruin, A. (2024). The relation between perceived mental effort, monitoring judgments, and learning outcomes: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 66 (abstract in Scopus export D3156)
Scopus abstract export D3156 (David et al. 2024)
Suzuki, Y. (2021). Optimizing fluency training for speaking skills transfer. Language Learning.

findings.claim: Learners' self-assessments are only moderately related to expert judgments and are biased, usually towards overestimation. L2 speech research specifically reports flawed self-assessment of one's own speech. Accuracy improves with feedback and with experience of self-assessing.
findings.population: Mostly university students across many fields (160 studies, 29,352 participants). The included studies cover L2 speech (Trofimovich et al. 2016) and a French pronunciation course (Lappin-Fortin & Rye 2014). Dlaska & Krekeler 2008 studied self-assessment of L2 pronunciation.
findings.effect_notes: León, Panadero & García-Martínez 2023: overall overestimation g = 0.206; mean relationship with expert scores z = 0.472. Overestimation was smaller with feedback, more self-assessment experience and more content knowledge. Heterogeneity was high. For Trofimovich et al. 2016 and Dlaska & Krekeler 2008, only titles and bibliographic data could be checked here (via reference lists and bibliography files), so no figures are claimed from them.
findings.design_implication: Add a light calibration loop. On a sample of attempts, not every trial, the learner marks the word they think was weakest and rates clarity (1-5) before the score appears. The app then shows its score next to the self-rating and tracks calibration over time as a skill in its own right, since self-monitoring is what the learner has off-app. When learner and machine disagree, route to listening and discrimination work. Offer listen-back of the learner's recording next to the model with the specific error highlighted, because feedback is what improves self-assessment. Never use self-ratings to drive scheduling or mastery.

citations.ref: León, S. P., Panadero, E., & García-Martínez, I. (2023). How accurate are our students? A meta-analytic systematic review on self-assessment scoring accuracy. Educational Psychology Review, 35, 106.

Scopus abstract and reference export of León et al. (2023), including Trofimovich et al. (2016) 'Flawed self-assessment: Investigating self- and other-perception of second language speech' (Bilingualism: Language and Cognition 19(1), 122-140) and Lappin-Fortin & Rye (2014) French pronunciation course
Dlaska, A., & Krekeler, C. (2008). Self-assessment of pronunciation. System, 36(4), 506-516 (bibliographic record only)

findings.claim: Accumulated deliberate practice explains a modest share of skill differences. After the 2018 corrigendum the figures are about 24% for games, 23% music, 20% sports, 5% education and 1% professions (overall r of about .38, about 14%). The meta-analysis does not measure practice quality, so focusing on specific targets, informative feedback and suitable difficulty is a reasonable design hypothesis, not an established finding.
findings.population: Mixed fields (games, music, sports, education, professions), with few L2 speech studies. Bu et al. 2021: 8 adult Korean learners of English.
findings.effect_notes: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald 2014 (Psychological Science 25(8), 1608-1618): deliberate practice explained 26% of variance for games, 21% for music, 18% for sports, 4% for education and under 1% for professions (overall r = .35, about 12%). These figures come from a verification dossier quoting p. 1612. The definition of deliberate practice is disputed. Bu et al. 2021: high-variability production practice on English /r/ gave short-term acoustic change, but only 1 of 8 participants kept a functionally relevant gain at follow-up (d from -1.26 to 0.29).
findings.design_implication: Build each session around 1-2 high-value targets at a difficulty that is challenging but achievable. Give immediate, specific feedback that names the sound and what to change, and vary the contexts. Measure 'effective attempts on target' rather than minutes. Do not promise outcomes based on hours spent.

citations.ref: Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z., & Oswald, F. L. (2014). Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: A meta-analysis. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1608-1618 (bibliographic record)
Verification dossier quoting the Macnamara et al. (2014) variance figures (p. 1612)
Bu, L., Nagano, M., Harel, D., & McAllister, T. (2021). Effects of practice variability on second-language speech production training. Folia Phoniatrica et Logopaedica.

findings.claim: If-then plans reliably but modestly increase goal attainment. The 2006 estimate (d = .65, 94 tests) has been revised down by a 642-test meta-analysis (pooled d of about .36; about .15 after bias correction; smaller in field settings and at follow-ups of several months). There are no tests in language apps.
findings.population: Adults and students pursuing health, academic and other goals; not tested in L2 pronunciation apps.
findings.effect_notes: Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006: 94 independent tests; d = .65 on goal attainment. The quoted abstract says the plans helped with starting, with shielding from distraction, and with disengaging from failing actions. Secondary records report N of about 8,461 and d = .58 for self-set goals; one randomised field trial on gym plans found a null result, so effects vary by setting.
findings.design_implication: At onboarding, ask for three things. First, a concrete goal tied to real use, such as 'be understood on phone calls in French' or 'present in English without being asked to repeat'. Second, a weekly target, such as 4 sessions. Third, 1-2 if-then plans with a specific cue, time and place, such as 'After my morning coffee on weekdays, I do one 10-minute session at my desk'. Fire reminders at the chosen cue time. A weekly review asks whether the plan worked and lets the learner change it.

citations.ref: Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69-119.
Verification record quoting the Gollwitzer & Sheeran abstract (94 tests, d = .65)

findings.claim: New daily behaviours take weeks to months to become automatic, and missing a single occasion did not materially harm habit formation.
findings.population: 96 UK adult volunteers forming simple health habits, with self-reported automaticity; not a language-learning study.
findings.effect_notes: Lally et al. 2010: 12 weeks. Median of about 66 days to reach the automaticity plateau, range 18-254 days. Missing one opportunity did not materially affect the process. The figures come from multiple secondary records that agree with each other.
findings.design_implication: Tie sessions to a stable daily cue and time. Show 'sessions this week vs plan' instead of an unbroken streak, and never reset progress to zero after a missed day. Tell the learner that 2 or more months of regular practice is normal before it feels automatic.

citations.ref: Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W., & Wardle, J. (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998-1009.

findings.verified_url: https://github.com/eternity4719/HowToLiveBetter/blob/main/docs/核实记录/追加-戒烟戒酒学习与拖延的具体办法.md

findings.claim: Attrition from self-directed language apps is common. One survival analysis reportedly found about 43% of adult users dropped out within 3 months (from a secondary summary). Among Duolingo beginners, grit and age predicted attrition (n = 601). In one 9-learner case study, time on the app correlated with gains. Which session patterns cause persistence, and the best session length, are not established.
findings.population: Adult users of mobile language-learning apps (Duolingo and others); observational, not experimental.
findings.effect_notes: Hwang, Coss, Loewen & Tagarelli 2024 (SSLA 46(4), 969-995): survival analysis of adult, non-conventional mobile-app language learners. A secondary summary reports N = 3,319 and 43% dropout within 3 months. It says continued use was linked to sessions of 5+ minutes, 4+ sessions a week and 7+ active weeks, and that learners who paused and then resumed persisted more. These figures were not checked against the original. Sudina, Teimouri & Plonsky 2025: 601 Duolingo beginners over 6 months; grit (perseverance of effort) and age predicted attrition. Loewen et al. 2019: 9 learners; time on the app correlated moderately with gains. Evidence on the best session length for pronunciation is weak; 10-20-minute sessions 3-5 times a week are inferred defaults.
findings.design_implication: Default to short sessions (about 10 minutes, with an option to continue) at least 4 times a week, rather than long occasional ones. After a break, offer a 'welcome back' path: a short re-check session with a cap on the review backlog, instead of dumping every overdue item. Show a weekly summary of what changed in the learner's speech. Log adherence (sessions, gaps, returns) so reminders and targets can adapt.

citations.ref: Hwang, H.-B., Coss, M. D., Loewen, S., & Tagarelli, K. M. (2024). Acceptance and engagement patterns of mobile-assisted language learning among non-conventional adult L2 learners: A survival analysis. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 46(4), 969-995.
Secondary summary of Hwang et al. (2024) and Sudina et al. (2025) findings
Sudina, E., Teimouri, Y., & Plonsky, L. (2025). L2 grit and age as predictors of attrition in mobile-assisted language learning. Learning and Individual Differences.
Loewen, S., Crowther, D., Isbell, D. R., Kim, K. M., Maloney, J., Miller, Z. F., & Rawal, H. (2019). Mobile-assisted language learning: A Duolingo case study. ReCALL, 31(3), 293-311.

findings.claim: Self-efficacy correlates moderately with L2 achievement (r of about .46, correlational), and mastery experiences are its strongest source in academic samples. Growth language mindset correlates weakly-to-moderately with outcomes (r of about .26). Gamification shows small-to-medium average effects with high heterogeneity: effects on cognitive learning (g of about .49) held in rigorous studies, while effects on motivation and behaviour were less robust. Much of the benefit may come from the added goals and feedback.
findings.population: L2 learners in many settings (correlational). Self-efficacy sources: academic samples. Gamification: mixed education samples.
findings.effect_notes: SSLLT 2022 meta-analysis: 40 samples, N = 23,050, average r = .46 between self-efficacy and L2 achievement (correlational; direction unclear). Sources-of-self-efficacy meta-analysis (Journal of Counseling Psychology): k = 61, N of about 8,965; performance accomplishments had the strongest unique link. These two sets of figures come from a curated source list that marks them as checked. Language-mindset meta-analysis: 22 studies, 50 effect sizes, n = 17,622; growth mindset r = .26, fixed mindset r = -.19. Sailer & Homner 2020: gamification effects of g = 0.49 on cognitive outcomes (k = 19), g = 0.36 on motivation and g = 0.25 on behaviour, with high heterogeneity; these figures come from a Crossref-verified secondary record. One small study (n = 34) found that showing rank raised motivation, so the evidence is mixed.
findings.design_implication: Build motivation on visible mastery, not points. Once a month, record the same benchmark passage and a free-speech prompt, and play them side by side with earlier recordings. State plainly what is now reliable, for example 'you now produce /y/ vs /u/ correctly in 9 of 10 cold checks'. Frame skills as improvable. Keep v1's exclusion of streaks and leaderboards; if any counter is shown, make it forgiving and secondary.

citations.ref: Meta-analysis of self-efficacy and achievement in SLA ('Is learning really just believing?'), Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching 12(2), 2022
Unique effects and moderators of effects of sources on self-efficacy: A model-based meta-analysis. Journal of Counseling Psychology
Curated source list with check levels for the self-efficacy meta-analyses
'A Multilevel Meta-analysis of Language Mindsets and Language Learning Outcomes in SLA Research' (Scopus abstract export D3174)
Sailer, M., & Homner, L. (2020). The gamification of learning: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 77-112.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Repeating the same item many times in one sitting as a route to lasting gains; massed looks good immediately but loses on delayed tests; in speech it cut pauses but slowed articulation and increased verbatim repetition.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by Kim & Webb 2022, Cepeda 2006, Bird 2010 (delayed advantage for longer gaps) and Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022 (quasi-experimental, n = 79). Caveat: Suzuki 2021 found that BLOCKED within-day repetition of the same narrative gave better transfer (articulation rate, mid-clause pauses) than interleaving different tasks. Some within-session repetition is useful; the evidence is against relying on massing instead of spacing.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Treating in-session scores (especially retries right after hearing the model) as proof of mastery.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The principle is well supported by the learning-versus-performance literature (Soderstrom & Bjork 2015). The cited sources are weak support: Suzuki 2021 showed only a partial training-to-posttest dissociation (blocked also won at posttest), and David et al. 2024 found that learning judgments predict outcomes (β = .29), so it does not show that learners' sense of progress is misleading.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Letting the learner choose ordering and blocking by feel; learners prefer blocking even where mixing helps discrimination.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Abel & de Bruin 2024 (lab, N = 190/134) confirm the preference for blocking with confusable categories. Caveat: for new speech-sound contrasts, blocking may actually be better early on (Fuhrmeister & Myers 2020; Carpenter & Mueller 2013), so the learner's preference is not always wrong in this domain.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Relying on the learner's self-assessment of pronunciation to pick targets or declare mastery.
does_not_work_verified.notes: León et al. 2023 confirmed (overestimation g = 0.206; moderate agreement with experts). For L2 speech the bias depends on level: weaker speakers overestimate and stronger speakers underestimate (Trofimovich et al. 2016), so self-ratings mislead in both directions.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Asking for a self-rating on every single trial; required per-trial memory ratings reversed the benefit of retrieval practice.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Confirmed in the D3124 abstract: with a memory rating on all trials, restudy beat retrieval in Experiments 1-2, and retrieval won once ratings were removed. This is a single preregistered series on Swahili-English word pairs, not speech, so treat it as a caution rather than an established rule.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Assuming expanding-interval schedules beat equal intervals; a complex scheduling algorithm is not justified by learning outcomes.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by Nakata 2015, Kim & Webb 2022 and Latimier et al. 2021 (expanding vs uniform g = 0.034). Caveat: Latimier found expanding helped more as the number of retrievals rose, and adaptive algorithms can also save review time. 'Not justified' is fair for retention outcomes, but not proof that scheduling doesn't matter.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Interleaving hard, brand-new phonetic contrasts with high variability from the very first exposure.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by one study (Fuhrmeister & Myers 2020: naive listeners, one evening session, vowel-context variability, perception only) and indirectly by Carpenter & Mueller 2013. The evidence is weak, and it applies to naive learners; this user already has experience with English and French sounds. Brekelmans et al. 2022 found high variability was no better than low variability even in non-naive learners.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Punitive streak resets; missing a single occasion did not materially affect habit formation.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The Lally et al. 2010 quote was confirmed verbatim. It is a single study of health habits with self-reported automaticity; the author rightly labels it weak.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Promising outcomes from hours of practice; deliberate practice explained only about 4% of performance variance in education.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported. The corrected figure (2018 corrigendum) is 5% for education and about 14% overall. The meta-analysis is about practice amount, not quality.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Tongue-twister speed ladders as articulation training; no controlled L2 study found; controlled studies support repeated meaningful monologues or retellings under time pressure instead.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The absence-of-evidence framing is fair; tongue twisters appear in speech-error research, not in L2 training trials. But the '4/3/2' and retelling evidence covers temporal fluency (speech rate, pauses) and grammar, not segmental clarity or intelligibility. Boers 2014 cautioned that speed gains under shrinking time may partly reflect shortened content. So retell ladders are better supported for pacing than for articulation accuracy.

critique_of_v1: The weak-sound engine serves the '5 lowest rolling-average phonemes (min 3 attempts)'. That keeps pushing the same worst items in massed, blocked sessions. It never schedules spaced returns and never re-checks sounds that have passed 85, so forgetting is invisible. A rolling average over as few as 3 noisy Azure attempts is dominated by noise and by which exercises happened to be picked.

Mastery gates (advance a level at 85 or more; speed-ladder tier at 85 or more) are measured in the same session, usually right after hearing the TTS model and after unlimited 'Retry'. That measures imitation performance, not learning. Nothing requires a delayed, cold or transfer check before a target counts as mastered.

Model-first imitation is the default for every trial (listen to TTS, then record). The app never asks the learner to produce a target from memory, which removes the retrieval component that drives retention.

Progression goes isolate -> word -> sentence -> passage, blocked per sound. There is no planned shift to interleaved practice of confusable contrasts, no variation in voices or contexts, and no check on unseen material or spontaneous speech. Blocked-first is sensible early on, but blocked-only never tests discrimination or transfer.

Speed ladders drill tongue twisters at slow, normal and fast TTS tempo. That practises motor speed on memorised, unusual text, with no L2 evidence behind it. It rewards speed over clarity. The fluency literature shows massed repetition can cut pauses while slowing articulation or increasing verbatim repetition, and that meaningful retellings under time pressure with feedback transfer better.

There is no self-monitoring or calibration. The learner only reads Azure's green/amber/red colours, never predicts or rates their own attempt, and never practises hearing their own errors. That is the skill they will depend on outside the app, and self-assessment is known to be biased and to improve only with feedback.

Progress charts show the average overall score per day and a phoneme-by-week heatmap of averages. These mix up item difficulty, exercise choice and retries with learning, so the charts can rise while durable ability stays flat. The PRD's success metrics are engineering checks (engine serves 5 phonemes, latency), not learning outcomes (delayed retention, transfer, intelligibility).

There is no adherence design. The app has no goals, no if-then plans, no reminders tied to a cue, no planned session length or weekly target, no re-entry path after a break, and no weekly review; 'Next exercise' is an open-ended loop. Excluding streaks and gamification is right, but nothing evidence-based replaces them.
There is no mastery-experience display (for example, before-and-after recordings of the same benchmark passage). Self-efficacy is best built from visible past success, and v1 shows only scores.

Targets are chosen by 'lowest score', not by value. The engine does not weigh how much a sound matters for being understood, or the learner's still-unknown first language, so session time can go to low-priority sounds. The thresholds (85, 3 attempts, 5 phonemes) are arbitrary and not tied to how much Azure scores vary between attempts.
open_questions: No verified study tests spacing specifically for adult segmental pronunciation production in English or French. Li & DeKeyser (2019, Modern Language Journal 103(3), doi 10.1111/modl.12580) tested spacing for Mandarin tonal word production, but its abstract could not be opened here. The best intervals for articulatory targets are therefore inferred from vocabulary, grammar and fluency studies.
Is 'say it first, then hear the model' (retrieval) actually better than immediate imitation for L2 pronunciation? This needs an in-app A/B test or single-case design; no direct study was found.

The point at which to switch from blocked to interleaved practice for a new contrast, and how to measure the learner's perceptual aptitude to set it, are not established. Fuhrmeister & Myers used a single session; multi-week HVPT studies used mixed high-variability training successfully.

Does training self-assessment calibration improve pronunciation itself, or only calibration? And does listening back to one's own recording without targeted feedback help at all? Dlaska & Krekeler (2013, System 41(1), 25-37) compared individual corrective feedback with self-listening, but the abstract could not be verified here.

The learner's first language is unknown. Tolerance for interleaving and variability, and which contrasts are hard, depend on it and on aptitude. A short diagnostic (perception plus production) is needed before scheduling.

The best session length and weekly frequency for pronunciation are not established. 10-15 minutes, 3-5 times a week is a defensible default from engagement and shadowing studies, but it predicts adherence, not learning rate.

How noisy is a single Azure attempt score? Mastery thresholds and delayed-check rules should account for that measurement error, which is covered by the assessment-validity topic rather than this one.

Verification limits: publisher, DOI and index sites and web search were unavailable in this run. The figures for Kim & Webb (2022), Hwang et al. (2024), Macnamara et al. (2014), Sailer & Homner (2020), the self-efficacy meta-analyses and Lally et al. (2010) come from secondary GitHub-hosted verification records. They should be re-checked against the original papers before they are used in published documentation.

Lee, B., Plonsky, L., & Saito, K. (2020). The effects of perception- vs. production-based pronunciation instruction. System, 88, 102185. This directly supports the 'learners read effort as poor learning' claim that David et al. was cited for. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101237

They were missed as caveats to 'retell ladders'.

Contextual-interference meta-analysis in physical education and sport: 'The effects of contextual interference learning on the acquisition and relatively permanent gains in skilled performance: A critical systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis'. 36 studies; very limited support for random over blocked practice in the long term. Relevant because articulation is partly a motor skill, and it conflicts with other motor-learning syntheses. https://github.com/marcoweb/annif-experiments/blob/7b039e495c4618daae2c8600f3950084c15dfabe/education-en/raw-files/corpus-training/Corpus_entrenamiento_Education_6000_documentos/D3163.txt

Worth citing directly, not only through León et al.: its level-dependent pattern (weaker speakers overestimate, stronger speakers underestimate) matters for the calibration feature. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1366728914000832

general_review.summary:
The evidence points one way: the app should aim for intelligibility (the listener recovers the intended words) and comprehensibility (low listening effort), not for sounding native. Accent is only partly related to either. Which errors to fix should depend on three things: the contrast's functional load (FL), the learner's first language (L1), and whether the error happens in real speech.

ENGLISH. Only high-FL consonant substitutions (e.g., /l/→/r/, /v/→/b/) lowered comprehensibility in two samples of Japanese learners (Suzukida & Saito 2021). This matches Munro & Derwing (2006) and Kang & Moran (2014). Expert guidance based on the Lingua Franca Core (LFC; Walker, Low & Setter 2021) names these priorities: most consonant contrasts, aspiration of initial /p t k/, no deletion inside initial or medial consonant clusters, vowel length, word stress and nuclear stress. It rates /θ ð/ substitutes, exact vowel quality, weak forms, schwa and stress-timed rhythm as low priority when the goal is being understood internationally. The LFC is still disputed. Stress and prosody errors cost listeners more than many segmental errors: correct primary stress improved recall (Hahn 2004), prosody best predicted pronunciation ratings (Anderson-Hsieh et al. 1992), and speaking rate was the strongest correlate of comprehensibility (Kang 2010).

FRENCH-SPEAKING LEARNERS OF ENGLISH. The main bottleneck is hearing lexical stress. French listeners have trouble perceiving it (Dupoux et al. 1997; Michelas & Dufour 2020), but they can learn it (Schwab & Llisterri 2011). Smaller studies add English vowel categories, /h/ and question intonation.

L2 FRENCH. The evidence is much thinner. French marks prominence at the end of phrases (a final rise plus final lengthening on non-final accentual phrases), not on word stress. English and Japanese speakers have trouble with this. The front rounded vowels (/y/, /ɥi/) are hard for learners from many L1s. Contrasts that native speakers are merging, such as /a/–/ɑ/, are low priority. No functional-load ranking for French equivalent to Brown (1988) was found. Comprehensibility ratings of L2 French come out too high when the rater does not know what the learner meant to say (De Fino et al. 2024).

HOW SOURCES WERE CHECKED. The web-search budget was used up, and the network proxy blocked publisher, DOI and index sites. I read sources through GitHub-hosted mirrors instead: ACL Anthology XML (conference papers), Language Science Press book sources, researchers' BibTeX files that include abstracts, and a corpus of Scopus-derived abstracts. Some key works were checked only as bibliographic records, and I say so for each one: Munro & Derwing 2006, Kang & Moran 2014, Brown 1988, Jenkins 2000, Dauer 2005, Field 2005 (content) and Crowther et al. 2015. Their effect sizes should be re-checked before the design is final.

findings.claim: Accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility are separate dimensions. A strong foreign accent often still gives high intelligibility, so success should be measured by intelligibility and comprehensibility, not closeness to a native model. Comprehensibility ratings also come out too high when the rater does not know the intended message.
findings.population: Adult L2 English speakers of many L1s rated by native and non-native listeners (Kang et al. 2020; Munro & Derwing 1995). Adult German-L1 learners of French (9 speakers) rated by 80 native French listeners (De Fino et al. 2024). Expert consensus paper (Walker et al. 2021).
findings.effect_notes: Kang et al. 2020 (Applied Linguistics 41(4):453-480): accentedness only moderately correlated with comprehensibility and weakly with intelligibility (from the publisher abstract snippet; coefficients not seen). De Fino et al. 2024: 80 raters, 9 learners; comprehensibility significantly higher when rated without the intended meaning than with it, reported as a large effect. Munro & Derwing 1995: DOI checked; content as widely reported, full text not reopened in this session.
findings.design_implication: Make intelligibility the headline metric: the share of the intended words that an independent ASR recovers, run WITHOUT the reference text, compared with the intended text, on both read and spontaneous tasks. Add a comprehensibility proxy built from intelligibility, rate and pausing. Show Azure 'accuracy' (closeness to the native acoustic model) only as a secondary 'accent' metric that does not gate progress. Every spontaneous task must carry a known intended message (picture description with target words, retelling a story the learner has heard), so scoring checks the message and not only how fluent the speech sounds.

findings.claim: English errors differ in cost according to functional load. Substituting consonants in high-FL contrasts (e.g., /l/→/r/, /v/→/b/) lowers comprehensibility. Low-FL substitutions, and in Suzukida & Saito's data vowel substitutions too, had no significant effect. High-FL errors also track proficiency level on a speaking exam.
findings.population: Japanese adult EFL learners doing timed picture description: Exp. 1 n=40; Exp. 2 n=40 with a wide range of immersion (Suzukida & Saito 2021). Cantonese-L1 ESL speakers (Munro & Derwing 2006, exploratory). Cambridge ESOL speaking-test candidates (Kang & Moran 2014).
findings.effect_notes: Suzukida & Saito abstract (read in full): only high-FL consonant substitutions predicted native listeners' comprehensibility ratings, replicated across two experiments; no effect sizes in the abstract. Munro & Derwing 2006 (System 34:520-531) and Kang & Moran 2014 (TESOL Quarterly 48:176-187): bibliographic records checked in the Suzukida & Saito reference list; their samples and effect sizes were not reopened here and should be re-checked.
findings.design_implication: Store an FL-weighted contrast table for English as data, based on Brown's (1988) ranking. Rank drill targets by: this learner's substitution rate × FL weight × lexical frequency of the words involved, instead of by 'lowest rolling phoneme score'. Detect WHICH sound replaced the target (use Azure's phoneme-level results, or a phone recognizer), because FL belongs to the contrast (l→r), not to the phoneme alone. Mark low-FL deviations amber or 'optional', not red.

citations.ref: Suzukida, Y., & Saito, K. (2021). Which segmental features matter for successful L2 comprehensibility? Revisiting and generalizing the pedagogical value of the functional load principle. Language Teaching Research 25(3) (DOI not resolvable from this sandbox)
Abstract and reference list of Suzukida & Saito (2021) as read (Scopus-derived corpus copy)
Munro, M. J., & Derwing, T. M. (2006). The functional load principle in ESL pronunciation instruction: An exploratory study. System 34, 520-531 (record checked; text not opened)
Kang, O., & Moran, M. (2014). Functional loads of pronunciation features in nonnative speakers' oral assessment. TESOL Quarterly 48, 176-187 (record checked; text not opened)
Brown, A. (1988). Functional load and the teaching of pronunciation. TESOL Quarterly 22, 593-606 (record checked in the reference list above)

findings.claim: For international intelligibility, the LFC-based expert syllabus puts these first: consonant contrasts (with /θ ð/ substitutes and trilled or tapped r accepted), aspiration of initial /p t k/, no deletion in initial or medial clusters (an inserted vowel is tolerated better than a deleted consonant), long-short vowel contrasts and vowel shortening before voiceless consonants (fill/feel, back/bag), word stress and nuclear stress. It treats weak forms, schwa, assimilation and elision, stress-timed rhythm, pitch-movement types and exact vowel quality as low production priorities. The LFC remains contested.
findings.population: Jenkins's data came from English-as-a-lingua-franca interactions between non-native speakers. The position paper synthesizes later work in Europe and South-East Asia (Deterding 2013; Field 2005; others).
findings.effect_notes: Taken from Tables 1-2 of Walker et al. (2021), read in full. The paper itself says the LFC 'has given rise to a great deal of debate and controversy'. Critiques (e.g., Dauer 2005) were checked only as bibliographic records. Jenkins's original data were not quantitative intelligibility experiments.
findings.design_implication: Add a 'target listener' setting. 'International intelligibility' (default) runs the core list above. 'Native-like (General American)' also unlocks vowel reduction, weak forms, rhythm and pitch patterns. In either mode, teach weak forms and connected-speech processes as LISTENING drills, and do not score them in production in intelligibility mode. Never flag θ→t/f/s or a trilled r as red in intelligibility mode. Score deletions in initial or medial clusters above epenthesis.

citations.ref: Walker, R., Low, E.-L., & Setter, J. (2021). English pronunciation for a global world (OUP ELT position paper), Tables 1-2

Jenkins, J. (2000). The phonology of English as an international language (OUP); Dauer, R. (2005). The Lingua Franca Core: A new model for pronunciation instruction? TESOL Quarterly 39, 543-550 (records checked in the Suzukida & Saito reference list)

findings.claim: Suprasegmental features affect English listeners' judgements. Correct sentence-level primary (nuclear) stress improved recall and speaker evaluations for one international TA's lecture (Hahn 2004). Prosodic deviance was the strongest predictor of pronunciation ratings among 60 speakers from 11 L1s (Anderson-Hsieh et al. 1992). Prosody was 'important' for the comprehensibility of Mandarin-L1 utterances (Warren et al. 2009). Lexical and phrasal stress errors raised perceived accent for 2 Spanish-L1 speakers (Magen 1998). Evidence is mostly correlational or comes from small manipulated-speech studies with ratings or accent as the outcome. How large the effect is, compared with segmental, fluency and lexicogrammar factors, is not established and varies by study.
findings.population: Undergraduate native English listeners hearing an international TA's speech manipulated for primary stress (Hahn 2004). 60 speakers from 11 L1s rated by SPEAK-test raters (Anderson-Hsieh et al. 1992). Mandarin-L1 learners rated by naive and experienced native listeners (Warren et al. 2009). 2 Spanish-L1 speakers with acoustically edited phrases (Magen 1998). Field (2005) on lexical stress and intelligibility: DOI checked, content not reopened.
findings.effect_notes: Hahn 2004: recall and speaker evaluation significantly better with correct stress; faster processing was a non-significant trend; n not in the abstract. Anderson-Hsieh 1992: n=60 speakers, 11 L1s; prosody had the strongest effect. Warren 2009: naive and experienced raters did not differ. Magen 1998: listeners were sensitive to syllable structure, final /s/ deletion, consonant manner and lexical/phrasal stress, but NOT to voicing; the outcome was accent, not intelligibility.
findings.design_implication: Build a stress module rather than relying on Azure's single prosody number. Force-align syllables and compare relative duration, F0 and intensity of stressed against unstressed syllables to find misplaced word stress (BAlloon vs balLOON). Check nuclear stress in contrastive-focus dialogues ('I've rented a FLAT' vs 'I've RENTed a flat'). Weight stress errors above low-FL segmental errors in the priority queue. Start with frequent multisyllabic words.

citations.ref: Hahn, L. D. (2004). Primary stress and intelligibility: Research to motivate the teaching of suprasegmentals. TESOL Quarterly 38(2), 201-223

Anderson-Hsieh, J., Johnson, R., & Koehler, K. (1992). The relationship between native speaker judgments of nonnative pronunciation and deviance in segmentals, prosody, and syllable structure. Language Learning 42(4), 529-555

Warren, P., Elgort, I., & Crabbe, D. (2009). Comprehensibility and prosody ratings for pronunciation software development. Language Learning & Technology 13(3), 87-102 (abstract read in this BibTeX file)
Magen, H. S. (1998). The perception of foreign-accented speech. Journal of Phonetics 26(4), 381-400
Field, J. (2005). Intelligibility and the listener: The role of lexical stress. TESOL Quarterly 39(3), 399-423 (DOI checked; content not reopened)

findings.claim: Temporal features such as speaking rate and pausing are among the strongest correlates of comprehensibility in English. Temporal and rhythmic parameters, especially speech rate and voicing durations, separate learners from native speakers in French. Classic duration-based rhythm metrics were unreliable for French learners of English.
findings.population: 11 international teaching assistants (ITAs; 5-min lectures) rated by 58 US undergraduates (Kang 2010). French: Gaussian mixture model trained on 1,340 native speakers from the CEFC corpus, tested on 37 non-natives in the corpus and 29 Japanese A2 learners (Coulange & Rossato 2020). French learners of English at three university levels (Michardière et al. 2016). Utterance fluency measures in L2 French (Préfontaine et al. 2016): record only.
findings.effect_notes: Kang 2010: comprehensibility was 'mostly associated with speaking rates'; accent was best predicted by pitch range and word stress. Coulange & Rossato 2020: the non-natives in the corpus differed from natives only at trend level (p=0.067); Japanese A2 learners differed strongly (p<0.0001); speech rate and voicing durations were the key parameters. Michardière et al. 2016: classic rhythm measures were unreliable. Préfontaine et al. 2016 (Language Testing 33(1):53-73) checked only as a record.
findings.design_implication: Replace the 'speed ladder' with a 'pace and pausing' module scored on spontaneous speech. Measure articulation rate (syllables/s excluding pauses), pause rate, pauses inside a clause vs at phrase boundaries, and mean length of run. Target a normal-rate band rather than maximum speed. Give feedback when speech is too slow or pauses fall mid-phrase. In French, also score grouping into phrases and phrase-final lengthening. Do not show %V, ΔC or PVI-type rhythm scores to the learner.

citations.ref: Kang, O. (2010). Relative salience of suprasegmental features on judgments of L2 comprehensibility and accentedness. System 38, 301-315
Coulange & Rossato (2020). Proximité rythmique entre apprenants et natifs du français (JEP 2020)
Michardière, Guyot-Talbot, Ferragne & Pellegrino (2016). Étude transversale du rythme de l'anglais chez des apprenants francophones (JEP 2016)

Préfontaine, Y., Kormos, J., & Johnson, D. E. (2016). How do utterance measures predict raters' perceptions of fluency in French as a second language? Language Testing 33(1), 53-73 (record in the LangSci bibliography)

findings.claim: Error profiles differ by L1, and the features that predict comprehensibility differ by L1 group (Crowther et al. 2015). L1-based predictions still miss many individual difficulties (Munro 2018). The specific profiles listed come from small accent or error-frequency studies: Spanish n=2 (accent ratings); Arabic, Munro 1993 (isolated /bVt/-/bVd/ vowels rated for accent by 5 judges) and Lučić Rehman et al. 2020 (4 speakers, read L2-ARCTIC sentences); Cantonese n=40 (production problems); Japanese n=80 (high-FL consonants and comprehensibility). For Mandarin, prosody was shown to be 'important' for comprehensibility, not 'most important'.
findings.population: Adult L2 English learners: Japanese (n=80, Suzukida & Saito); Spanish (2 speakers, Magen 1998); Arabic (Munro 1993 vowel study; 4 advanced speakers and 599 read sentences from L2-ARCTIC in an exploratory FL study); Cantonese (40 university students, Chan 2010); Mandarin (Warren et al. 2009).
findings.effect_notes: Most of these studies measured accent or error frequency, not intelligibility. Linking them to comprehensibility depends on the FL evidence (priorities-2). Crowther et al. (2015, TESOL Quarterly 49:814-837) report that the linguistic predictors of comprehensibility differ by learner background: record checked, content not reopened.
findings.design_implication: Since the user's L1 is unknown, onboarding should include: an optional L1 question; a roughly 5-minute diagnostic made of a passage that covers every high-FL contrast plus stress items, a 1-minute picture description, and a short perception test (minimal pairs and stress ABX). Use L1 profiles only as starting estimates for the priority queue, and let measured error rates override them. Include an 'other L1' path that relies only on the diagnostic.

citations.ref: Magen, H. S. (1998). The perception of foreign-accented speech. Journal of Phonetics 26, 381-400
Munro, M. J. (1993). Productions of English vowels by native speakers of Arabic: Acoustic measurements and accentedness ratings. Language and Speech 36(1), 39-66

The English pronunciation of Arabic speakers: A data-driven approach to segmental error identification (exploratory FL-based error analysis using L2-ARCTIC; abstract read from a Scopus-derived corpus; authors and venue could not be retrieved in this session)
Chan, A. Y. W. (2010). Advanced Cantonese ESL learners' production of English speech sounds: Problems and strategies. System 38, 316-328
Suzukida & Saito (2021), Japanese EFL learners (see priorities-2)

findings.claim: French-L1 listeners show a robust, well-replicated difficulty in encoding and recalling non-native stress contrasts ('stress deafness'). Dupoux et al. 2008 reported that it persisted even in advanced French learners of Spanish. One short lab study (Schwab & Llisterri 2011) found French speakers could learn and retrieve, at least temporarily, stress-based pseudoword associations. Small French-university studies found that HVPT improved perception, and to a lesser degree production, of English vowel regions where English has several categories and French has one (with a confounding test-retest effect). Three sessions of F0-display training moved question contours closer to a model. No study measured intelligibility gains. That lexical stress is THE main priority for French learners is a reasonable hypothesis, not an established finding.
findings.population: Mostly native French listeners who were not trained learners (Dupoux et al. 1997; Michelas & Dufour 2020); French speakers trained on Spanish pseudowords (Schwab & Llisterri 2011); French-Canadian L2 learners of English (Tremblay 2009, record only); French university learners of English (Krzonowski et al. 2016: HVPT vs production training vs control; Guyot-Talbot et al. 2016: 3 sessions with F0 display); French speakers' ERP responses to English [h] (Mah et al. 2016, title only).
findings.effect_notes: Dupoux 1997: across 4 experiments, French listeners had more difficulty than Spanish listeners on stress-based ABX, but did respond to the acoustic correlates, which places the difficulty at the encoding and memory level. Schwab & Llisterri 2011: French speakers learned and retrieved stress information, which does not support absolute stress deafness. Krzonowski 2016: perception training improved both perception and production; production training had more limited effects; a test-retest effect in the control group complicates interpretation. Guyot-Talbot 2016: the distance to the model's F0 contours dropped significantly after training. None of these studies measured intelligibility gains directly.
findings.design_implication: If the learner's L1 is French, move the stress module to the front and start with perception: multi-talker stress-minimal pairs and ABX or sequence-recall tasks, then production with a display of the stressed syllable. Add vowel-length and quality drills (fill/feel type), /h/ presence (hair/air, heat/eat) as perception then production, and question-intonation practice with the learner's F0 contour overlaid on the model's. Deprioritize /θ ð/, which French speakers often miss but which has low FL.

citations.ref: Dupoux, E., Pallier, C., Sebastián-Gallés, N., & Mehler, J. (1997). A destressing 'deafness' in French? Journal of Memory and Language 36(3), 406-421
Michelas & Dufour (2020). Comment l'oreille de présentation affecte-t-elle la capacité des francophones à discriminer des contrastes accentuels natifs et non-natifs ? (JEP 2020)
Schwab, S., & Llisterri, J. (2011). Are French speakers able to learn to perceive lexical stress contrasts? Proceedings of ICPhS XVII, 1774-1777
Tremblay, A. (2009). Phonetic variability and the variable perception of L2 word stress by French Canadian listeners. International Journal of Bilingualism (record only)
Krzonowski, Ferragne & Pellegrino (2016). Perception et production de voyelles de l'anglais par des apprenants francophones : effet d'entraînements (JEP 2016)
Guyot-Talbot, Heidlmayr & Ferragne (2016). Entraînements à la prosodie des questions ouvertes et fermées de l'anglais chez des apprenants francophones (JEP 2016)

Mah, J., Goad, H., & Steinhauer, K. (2016). Using event-related brain potentials to assess perceptibility: The case of French speakers and English [h]. Frontiers in Psychology 7:1469 (title and DOI only)

findings.claim: French is a 'boundary language', not a 'stress language'. Prominence comes at the end of the accentual phrase: a final F0 rise with lengthening on non-final phrases and a fall at the end of the utterance. English speakers carry over word-level stress and falling accents and have trouble with phrase-final rises and phrase size. Japanese learners manage the F0 rises but do not reliably use final lengthening.
findings.population: Phonological description (Vaissière 1991). 12 Anglophone Canadian learners of French from immersion and core programs, with a literature background citing Lepetit 1989 and Colantoni et al. (Walton 2023). Japanese learners of French doing semi-spontaneous picture description (Albar 2020).
findings.effect_notes: Mostly descriptive or small-n studies. No study found that measures how much phrase-final prosody errors reduce comprehensibility of L2 French, which is a key gap. Walton 2023: group differences were not significant with n=12.
findings.design_implication: The French prosody track must NOT reuse English 'stress-timing' or word-stress drills. Build phrase-grouping drills instead: chunk sentences into 3-4 syllable accentual phrases; score (a) a rising F0 on the last full syllable of each non-final phrase, (b) lengthening of that syllable, and (c) a final fall on declaratives. Flag English-style prominence on the first syllable of a word. Use a visual F0 and duration overlay, since visual F0 feedback helped French learners of English in the reverse direction (priorities-7).

citations.ref: Vaissière, J. (1991). Rhythm, accentuation and final lengthening in French. In Sundberg, Nord & Carlson (eds.), Music, Language, Speech and Brain, 108-120
Walton, H. (2023). Does social identity play a role in the L2 acquisition of French intonation? In A half century of Romance linguistics (Language Science Press)
Albar (2020). Production de la continuation du français par des apprenants japonophones : gestion de la F0 et de la durée (JEP 2020)

findings.claim: The impact of segmental errors on L2 French intelligibility is under-researched. /y/-/u/ is a documented target of perceptual assessment for Spanish- and Japanese-L1 learners (IPFC; findings not checked). The /i/ in /ɥi/ tends toward /y/ in Mandarin-L1 learners. In one 4-week study of 30 learners comparing shadowing with delayed imitation, with no untrained control group, perception improved and production improved only in intermediate learners who shadowed. Word-final /a/-/ɑ/ has merged acoustically in broadcast/declamatory French over the 20th century, so it is a low-value target.
findings.population: Spanish- and Japanese-L1 learners in the IPFC corpus (Racine, Detey & Kawaguchi 2012: title only, no abstract). 30 Mandarin-L1 female learners, 4 weeks of self-directed shadowing vs delayed imitation (Fu et al. 2024). Native broadcast speech from 1925 to 2023 (Cęcelewski et al. 2024).
findings.effect_notes: Fu et al. 2024: F3-F2 separation of /i/ in /ɥi/ improved significantly for intermediate learners who shadowed; shadowing improved perception in beginners and intermediates but production only in intermediates. Cęcelewski et al. 2024: acoustic neutralization and merger of /a/-/ɑ/ across the 20th century. The weight of nasal vowels, /ʁ/, liaison and schwa could not be verified in this session.
findings.design_implication: Start the French segmental queue with high-contrast vowel sets: /y/-/u/ (tu/tout, dessus/dessous), /y/-/i/, and oral vs nasal vowels, taught through perception then shadowing. Deprioritize /a/-/ɑ/ and other contrasts that are variable in native speech. Until a French FL table exists, derive one from a frequency-weighted minimal-pair count over a French lexicon (e.g., Lexique) and label it provisional.

citations.ref: Racine, Detey & Kawaguchi (2012). Les voyelles /y-u/ dans IPFC : évaluation perceptive de productions natives, hispanophones et japonophones (JEP-TALN 2012)
Fu, Adda-Decker & Kühnert (2024). Effets du shadowing et de l'imitation en tant que méthodes d'entraînement à la prononciation du /ɥi/ en français (JEP 2024)
Cęcelewski, Gendrot, Adda-Decker & Boula de Mareüil (2024). Étude en temps réel de la fusion des /a/ ~ /ɑ/ en français depuis 1925 (JEP 2024)

findings.claim: In one 2-week study of 115 Japanese university EFL learners (pre/post/delayed tests), all four groups made major gains, and perception-based instruction 'may be' more effective than production-based instruction for both segmental and suprasegmental targets. Meta-analyses (not this study) show that perceptual HVPT transfers to production with smaller effects than on perception (Uchihara et al. 2024), and that instruction effects are larger on controlled than on spontaneous outcome measures (Lee, Jang & Plonsky 2015; Saito & Plonsky 2019).
findings.population: 115 Japanese university EFL learners; 2 weeks; 4 groups crossing segmental vs suprasegmental targets with perception- vs production-based methods; pre-, post- and delayed tests (Lee, Plonsky & Saito 2020).
findings.effect_notes: All four groups made large gains; perception-based training looked more effective across feature types; exact effect sizes are not in the abstract. This is a single study, so treat the ranking as provisional.
findings.design_implication: For each prioritized contrast or stress pattern, open the session with a multi-voice perception block (identification with immediate feedback), then production. Re-test the same targets in a spontaneous task before marking them 'mastered'.

citations.ref: Lee, B., Plonsky, L., & Saito, K. (2020). The effects of perception- vs. production-based pronunciation instruction. System 88, 102185

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using accent reduction or closeness to a native acoustic model as the goal or headline score.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by Munro & Derwing 1995 and 2020 ('redux'), Derwing & Munro 2005 (the abstract makes intelligibility the primary consideration), and Walker et al. 2021 ('working on what is damaging to intelligibility is far more productive than trying to eliminate accent'). The Kang et al. 2020 snippet repeats the moderate and weak correlations. Caveat: Azure 'accuracy' is not pure accent, and some features that reduce accent (e.g., high-FL segments, word stress) also help intelligibility. Demote the score; do not ignore it.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Treating every phoneme deviation as equally important (drilling the lowest-scoring phoneme).
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported by Suzukida & Saito 2021 (only high-FL consonant substitutions predicted comprehensibility, in 2 experiments with n=40 each) and Munro & Derwing 2006 (exploratory). Moderate strength, correlational, mostly with Japanese or Cantonese speakers. Bent, Bradlow & Smith 2007 found vowel accuracy mattered for Mandarin speakers' intelligibility, so do not zero-weight vowels.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Spending much practice time on /θ ð/ for intelligibility.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Walker et al. Table 1 lists /θ/, /ð/ and /r/ variants as 'acceptable and widely intelligible' ('tink', 'den'). Brown's FL ranking puts θ-f and ð-d low (based on the widely reported ranking; Brown 1988 not reopened). Caveats: the source is expert guidance, not a listener experiment. θ→s substitution may be riskier than θ→t/f. The advice does not apply when the learner chooses a native-like target.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Scoring production of weak forms, schwa, assimilation, elision and stress-timed rhythm when the goal is international intelligibility.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Walker et al. Table 2: vowel reduction, schwa and weak forms are 'unhelpful to intelligibility; only taught for receptive purposes'. Assimilation, elision and coalescence 'can be unhelpful'. Stress-timed rhythm is 'not important'. This is expert opinion based on ELF research. It is contested (e.g., Dauer 2005) and does not hold for native-listener or native-like goals, and the claim notes this.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using classic duration-based rhythm metrics as learner feedback.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Michardière et al. 2016 (JEP): 'manque de fiabilité des mesures classiques du rythme' across three levels of French university learners of English. Ballier, Martin & Amand 2016 (JEP, jep.82): a syllable typology based on positional, accentual and structural properties discriminated speaker level better than Ramus-type interval measures. Both are small conference papers, but the claim is modest.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Rating or auto-scoring comprehensibility without knowing the intended message.
does_not_work_verified.notes: De Fino et al. 2024: 80 native French raters and 9 German-L1 learners on a TRANSLATION task. Scores were significantly higher without the reference, 'avec une taille d'effet importante'. This is a single small L2 French study. Extending it to automatic scoring is an inference, but a reasonable one.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Transferring English word-stress or stress-timing drills to French.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Vaissière 1991 describes French as a boundary language. Walton 2023's background (Jun & Fougeron; Lepetit 1989) and data (under 50% target-like non-final AP rises among Anglophone learners) support it. Michelas & Dufour 2020 conclude that word-level accent variation 'est traitée par les auditeurs francophones natifs comme de la variation de surface'. The support is descriptive; no study compares the two drill types.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Fast tongue-twister speed ladders as a route to intelligibility.
does_not_work_verified.notes: This is correctly framed as absence of evidence. Kang 2010 links comprehensibility to speaking rate in normal lecture speech. Munro & Derwing 2001 (SSLA 23(4):451-468) report a curvilinear rate-rating relation, which argues for a target band, not maximum speed. The side claim that tongue twisters 'overload rare, low-FL sequences' is an unsupported assertion.

critique_of_v1: The v1 headline metric, Azure Pronunciation Assessment accuracy and green/amber/red colors, measures closeness to a native acoustic template, which is closer to accentedness than to intelligibility. v1 never checks whether a listener or independent ASR would recover the intended words, even though the evidence says that is what matters.

Choosing 'weak phoneme' drills by lowest rolling average ignores functional load and the learner's L1. It will over-drill low-FL targets that score badly but rarely cause misunderstanding (/θ ð/, fine vowel quality) and under-drill high-FL consonant contrasts, aspiration, cluster deletion and stress.

Scoring is phoneme-based, but FL belongs to the contrast (which sound replaced which). v1 records how badly a phoneme scored, not what it was replaced with, so it cannot tell a harmless /θ/→[t] from a harmful /l/→[r].

All practice is scripted read-aloud. The key comprehensibility studies used spontaneous tasks such as picture description, and gains on controlled tasks transfer only partly. v1 has no spontaneous task with a known intended message, so it cannot measure what matters.

There is no diagnosis of lexical or nuclear stress. Azure's single prosody score does not tell the learner which syllable was stressed, yet stress sits near the top of the English priorities and is the main bottleneck for French-L1 learners.

The shared 'prosody track (stress-timing)' is phonologically wrong for French. French prominence is phrase-final (final rise plus lengthening on non-final accentual phrases); English-style word-stress drills would reinforce the wrong pattern.

Speed ladders (move up at ≥85 accuracy on slow/normal/fast TTS tongue twisters) reward speed. The evidence links comprehensibility to normal-range rate and well-placed pauses, not to maximum speed. No study was found that shows tongue twisters improve intelligibility.

The color thresholds make every deviation equally 'red' and allow no accepted variants. The LFC treats θ→t/f and a trilled r as acceptable, and treats consistent L1-influenced vowel quality as acceptable when the goal is international intelligibility.

The French content (liaison, schwa, stress-timing) has no evidence-based priority order. The best-supported French targets (front rounded vowels, phrase-final prosody, skipping merging contrasts like /a/-/ɑ/) are not singled out.

There is no onboarding diagnostic, no L1 question, no perception test and no 'target listener' setting (international vs native-like). Priorities depend heavily on L1 and target, and the user's L1 is unknown.
Listening work on weak forms and connected speech is absent. The evidence treats these as receptive priorities, not production targets.
open_questions: What drives the comprehensibility of L2 French? The key studies could not be opened in this session and must be verified before the French syllabus is final: Bergeron & Trofimovich 2017 (Foreign Language Annals), Kennedy, Blanchet & Trofimovich 2014, IPFC corpus analyses by Detey and Racine, Préfontaine et al. 2016 (full text).

There is no published functional-load ranking for French equivalent to Brown (1988). Should the app compute one from a frequency-weighted lexicon (e.g., Lexique minimal pairs) and validate it against learner data?
How much do nasal vs oral vowels, /ʁ/ variants, liaison errors and schwa handling in L2 French affect intelligibility? Nothing verifiable was found this session.

Munro & Derwing 2006, Kang & Moran 2014, Field 2005, Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012, Derwing, Munro & Wiebe 1998, Crowther et al. 2015 and Munro, Derwing & Thomson 2015 were checked only as bibliographic records. Their samples and effect sizes should be re-read, especially whether vowel FL errors matter (Suzukida & Saito found they did not).

Who is the learner's target listener: international and lingua franca contexts, or native speakers in the US or France? The LFC priorities assume the former; native-listener contexts may justify vowel reduction and rhythm work.
The learner's L1 is unknown. Which diagnostic tasks, and how long, identify their high-FL error profile reliably in about 5 minutes?

How well do Azure Pronunciation Assessment scores (accuracy, prosody) correlate with human comprehensibility and intelligibility for L2 French and for non-read speech? This needs a validation check against a few human ratings.

Does the LFC's exclusion of vowel reduction and stress-timing from production targets hold for comprehensibility with native English listeners? Dauer (2005) and others disputed it; the content was not verified here.
missed_evidence_flagged: Munro, M. J., & Derwing, T. M. (2020). Foreign accent, comprehensibility and intelligibility, redux. Journal of Second Language Pronunciation 6(3), 283-309. Revisits the 25 years of evidence behind priorities-1. https://doi.org/10.1075/jslp.20038.mun

Dupoux, E., Sebastián-Gallés, N., Navarrete, E., & Peperkamp, S. (2008). Persistent stress 'deafness': The case of French learners of Spanish. Cognition 106(2), 682-706. Important contrary evidence for priorities-7 and the stress-deafness 'does not work' item. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010027707001102

Munro, M. J., & Derwing, T. M. (2001). Modeling perceptions of the accentedness and comprehensibility of L2 speech: The role of speaking rate. Studies in Second Language Acquisition 23(4), 451-468. Curvilinear rate effect, relevant to the pace module and speed ladders (record in LangSci bibliography: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/langsci/raw_texfiles/master/515/localbibliography.bib)

Lee, J., Jang, J., & Plonsky, L. (2015). The effectiveness of second language pronunciation instruction: A meta-analysis. Applied Linguistics 36(3), 345-366.
