Larger effects on controlled outcome measures; this is the correct source for the second sentence of priorities-10. https://doi.org/10.1093/applin/amu040

Saito, K., & Plonsky, L. (2019). Effects of second language pronunciation teaching revisited: A proposed measurement framework and meta-analysis. Language Learning 69(3), 652-708. Effects are clearest on controlled, feature-specific measures and much weaker on spontaneous speech. https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10068780/

Uchihara, T., Karas, M., & Thomson, R. I. (2024). Does perceptual high variability phonetic training improve L2 speech production? A meta-analysis of perception-production connection. Applied Psycholinguistics 45(4). Supports perception-first blocks, with smaller transfer to production. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716424000195

Bent, T., Bradlow, A. R., & Smith, B. L. (2007). Segmental errors in different word positions and their effects on intelligibility of non-native speech. In Bohn & Munro (eds.), Language Experience in Second Language Speech Learning (Benjamins). Vowel accuracy related to intelligibility for Mandarin speakers; qualifies the 'vowels don't matter' reading of Suzukida & Saito. Bibliographic record: https://github.com/cainesap/resources/blob/master/latex/bib.bib

Munro, M. J. (2018). How well can we predict second language learners' pronunciation difficulties? CATESOL Journal 30(1), 267-281. L1-based predictions are unreliable, which supports diagnostic-first onboarding (priorities-6). Cited in the Lučić Rehman et al. reference list: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marcoweb/annif-experiments/main/education-en/raw-files/corpus-training/Corpus_entrenamiento_Education_6000_documentos/D1420.txt

Munro, M. J., Derwing, T. M., & Thomson, R. I. (2015). Setting segmental priorities for English learners: Evidence from a longitudinal study. IRAL 53(1), 39-60. Some errors resolve without instruction, so persistence should enter the priority score (same reference list as above)

Lučić Rehman, I., Silpachai, A., Levis, J., Zhao, G., & Gutierrez-Osuna, R. (2020). The English pronunciation of Arabic speakers: A data-driven approach to segmental error identification. Language Teaching Research. These are the missing authors and venue for the priorities-6 Arabic citation (listed on co-author G. Zhao's publication page: https://guanlongzhao.github.io/)

Inceoglu, S., Chen, W.-H., & Lim, H. (2023). Assessment of L2 intelligibility: Comparing L1 listeners and automatic speech recognition. ReCALL 35(1), 89-104. Directly relevant to using reference-free ASR as the headline intelligibility metric (priorities-1). Citation seen in a reference list, not opened.

Saito, K., Macmillan, K., Kachlicka, M., Kunihara, T., & Minematsu, N. (2023). Automated assessment of second language comprehensibility: Review, training, validation, and generalization studies. Studies in Second Language Acquisition 45(1), 234-263. Relevant to the 'comprehensibility proxy' design. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263122000080

Isaacs, T., & Trofimovich, P. (2012). Deconstructing comprehensibility: Identifying the linguistic influences on listeners' L2 comprehensibility ratings. SSLA 34, 475-505. Comprehensibility depends on lexicogrammar and fluency as well as pronunciation (relevant to priorities-4 and 5; in the Suzukida & Saito reference list).

Oh, Y. M., Coupé, C., Marsico, E., & Pellegrino, F. (2015). Bridging phonological system and lexicon: Insights from a corpus study of functional load. Journal of Phonetics 53, 153-176. Corpus-based functional load across several languages; check whether French is included before building a French FL table (priorities-9). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wocn.2015.08.003

Bergeron, A., & Trofimovich, P. (2017). Linguistic dimensions of accentedness and comprehensibility: Exploring task and listener effects in second language French. Foreign Language Annals 50(3), 547-566. One of the few studies of what drives comprehensibility in L2 French (not verified in this session because web search was exhausted; confirm before citing).

general_review.topic: tech: Automatic pronunciation assessment technology, 2024-2026 (Azure per-locale features, machine-human agreement, failure modes, open-source and commercial alternatives, audio-LLM feedback) for en-US and fr-FR
general_review.summary:
How I checked: the WebSearch budget for this session ran out before I started, and the network proxy blocked publisher sites, arXiv, ISCA, learn.microsoft.com, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex. I therefore checked every claim below against GitHub-hosted primary material instead: the source files of Microsoft's own docs (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs, dated Nov 2025 to Sep 2026), the ACL Anthology's official metadata XML (titles, authors, DOIs, abstracts), tool and paper repositories (GOPT, speechocean762, MultiPA, Kaldi GOP, MFA models, Parselmouth, fairseq, Whisper model card, SpeechSuper, Speechace), and a few full texts or abstracts hosted on GitHub. I did not read full papers behind paywalls, and I note where a number comes only from an abstract or README.

Main conclusions:
(1) Azure does much less for fr-FR than for en-US. For fr-FR it returns per-phoneme scores with no phoneme labels, no syllables, no "what you actually said" phoneme candidates (spoken phonemes / NBest), and no prosody score. The v1 design assumed "phoneme-level scores for both locales" and prosody for both, so the French weak-sound engine and the French prosody track cannot work as specified.
(2) Machine scores agree with human raters only moderately, and agreement drops as the unit gets smaller. On the main open benchmark (Mandarin-L1 children and adults reading English), the best open models reach correlations with human scores of about 0.72-0.76 for the whole sentence, about 0.53-0.61 for words and 0.61-0.68 for single sounds. Word-stress correlation is only 0.15-0.33, and mispronunciation-detection F1 is about 0.64. Microsoft publishes only ">0.5 Pearson" overall, with no breakdown by locale or level, and it updated the en-US and fr-FR models without notice in August 2026.
(3) Scorers compare speech to one "canonical" dictionary pronunciation, so they can penalise valid variants and reduced forms (weak forms, schwa). Microsoft's own doc example treats [ə] in "hello" as an error. Scores also depend on recording quality, on speaking at normal rate and volume, and on accent. Speech recognisers, Whisper included, perform worse on non-native accents and can invent or "correct" words.
(4) French pronunciation-training technology has a thin evidence base: few annotated French L2 corpora, no public benchmark like speechocean762, and small studies on narrow targets (e.g., 72.6% binary accuracy for /R/ and /v/).
(5) Large audio-language models are not yet reliable judges of pronunciation. Off-the-shelf models are weak at mispronunciation detection and show position, verbosity and stereotyping biases. Their best-supported role is explaining errors that were measured by other means.

What can be measured reliably today in both languages: sentence-level pronunciation quality on read or repeated speech (as a trend, not a verdict); timing (speech and articulation rate, pauses, word and segment durations, completeness) from forced alignment of scripted speech; and pitch range and contour (F0 holds up across recording devices).

What cannot be measured reliably: single-attempt phoneme verdicts; lexical stress; Azure's prosody score for French (it does not exist); phoneme-level scoring of spontaneous speech; vowel-quality (formant) feedback from compressed browser audio; audio-LLM grading; and fairness across the user's unknown first language, because all benchmark numbers come from Mandarin-L1 learners of English.

findings.claim: Azure Pronunciation Assessment gives much less for fr-FR than for en-US. Only en-US gets phoneme names (IPA or SAPI), syllable groups and 'spoken phoneme' NBest candidates; zh-CN also gets SAPI names. For other locales, including fr-FR, 'you can only get the phoneme score'. The prosody score is 'only available in the en-US locale'. Content assessment was retired from Speech SDK 1.46.0 onward (Sept 2025), and Microsoft now points to Azure OpenAI chat models for it. Even in en-US, the prosody diagnostics are limited to Unexpected/Missing Break, whose confidence thresholds the app must tune (0.75 suggested), and a single utterance-level 'Monotone' flag. There is no lexical-stress error type.
findings.population: Not applicable: vendor documentation (docs dated 21 Nov 2025; release notes to Sept 2026)
findings.effect_notes: 33 locales are supported for basic scoring. The feature matrix covers phoneme alphabet, phoneme name, syllable group and spoken phoneme, each en-US only (SAPI phoneme names also zh-CN).
findings.design_implication: Give the app a per-locale capability map instead of one pipeline. French: do not key a 'weak phoneme' table on Azure phoneme labels, because there are none. Either derive phone identity from the app's own dictionary lookup (G2P) plus forced alignment (e.g., MFA french_mfa) and label the result 'experimental', or drive French sound work with minimal-pair forced-choice tasks. French rhythm and intonation must be measured by the app itself (see tech-10) or not scored at all. English: use NBest spoken phonemes only to show the most likely substitution, and only at high confidence. Do not build lexical-stress feedback on Azure.

citations.ref: Microsoft Learn: Use pronunciation assessment (supported features per locale; prosody en-US only; content assessment retired from SDK 1.46.0)
GitHub source of the same doc (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs, ms.date 11/21/2025)
Microsoft Learn: Language support, pronunciation assessment tab (33 locales incl. fr-FR, fr-CA, en-US, en-GB)
Microsoft Learn: Pronunciation assessment tool ('Content and prosody assessments are only available in the en-US locale'; prosody is an add-on price)

findings.claim: Microsoft's Responsible-AI note (ms.date 03/31/2026) gives only one aggregate figure: '>0.5 Pearson correlation with human judges'. It has no split by locale, granularity or task. It tells customers to 'conduct their own evaluations', 'select suitable thresholds', and have speakers repeat an item that scores below a threshold. Microsoft updates the scoring models per locale from time to time. These updates are announced in the STT release notes (Aug 2026: en-US, zh-CN, es-ES, es-MX, fr-FR, pt-BR 'improve the PCC'; also Apr 2025, Jun 2025, and a de-DE update), but they come without new agreement figures, and the docs describe no way to pin a scoring-model version. The docs also suggest trying several locale models and picking the one that 'scores higher', which implies scores are relative to the model.
findings.population: Not specified by vendor (internal evaluations)
findings.effect_notes: The only published figure is PCC >0.5, which Microsoft labels 'High' on its own scale (0.5-1.0). There are no per-locale, phoneme-level or unscripted figures.
findings.design_implication: Store the Azure API version and assessment date with every score, and draw a 'scorer changed' marker on progress charts. After an update, re-baseline on a fixed set of 10-20 anchor recordings kept on disk. Show trends as smoothed ranges, not single numbers. Build a small calibration step: occasional self-ratings, or a periodic check by a native speaker or tutor on about 20 items, to confirm whether Azure's fr-FR and en-US scores track real change for this learner.

citations.ref: Microsoft: Characteristics and limitations of Pronunciation Assessment (ms.date 03/31/2026)
GitHub source of the characteristics and limitations doc
Azure Speech-to-text release notes (Aug 2026: improved PA models for en-US, fr-FR and others)

findings.claim: On speechocean762 (5,000 read English sentences, Mandarin-L1 speakers, half of them children, 5 expert raters), agreement is highest at sentence level (GOPT utterance-total PCC 0.731-0.743). It is lower at phone level (0.616-0.679; the stronger private PAII acoustic models reach 0.664-0.679) and lowest at word level (word-total 0.552-0.606). So agreement is not a simple function of unit size: word is below phone. Word-stress PCC is 0.150-0.326 and completeness PCC is -0.044 to 0.122. These very low values probably also reflect how skewed those labels are, so they do not show that stress or omission cannot be detected at all. HMamba (Chao & Chen, NAACL 2025) reaches mispronunciation-detection F1 of 63.85% on the same benchmark. Parikh et al. (Interspeech 2025; Dutch- and Mandarin-L1 English) say softmax-posterior GOP 'may suffer from overconfidence'. Logit-based GOP classified errors better, but 'their effectiveness depends on dataset characteristics'.
findings.population: Mandarin-L1 children and adults reading English; one benchmark dominates the field
findings.effect_notes: GOPT (ICASSP 2022), 2,500 test utterances: phone PCC 0.612-0.679, word total 0.549-0.606, utterance total 0.731-0.743, word stress 0.150-0.326. HMamba (NAACL 2025) mispronunciation-detection F1 63.85%. Parikh et al. (Interspeech 2025) studied Dutch- and Mandarin-L1 English; no effect sizes in the abstract.
findings.design_implication: Never pick drills, or advance a level, from one attempt's phoneme score. Pool evidence per target sound over at least 15-20 tokens in different words and at least 2-3 sessions. Report a confidence band and flag a sound as 'weak' only when its interval sits clearly below the learner's own median. Make the sentence or utterance level the main score. Show phoneme colours only as tentative hints ('possible issue'). Remove automatic word-stress verdicts.

citations.ref: Gong, Chen, Chu, Chang & Glass (2022) GOPT, ICASSP. doi:10.1109/ICASSP43922.2022.9746743 (results table in repo README)
Zhang et al. (2021) speechocean762 corpus (5 experts; Mandarin L1; half children), arXiv:2104.01378
Chao & Chen (2025) HMamba, NAACL 2025. doi:10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.98
Parikh, Tejedor-Garcia, Cucchiarini & Strik (2025) Evaluating logit-based GOP scores for mispronunciation detection, Interspeech 2025 (abstract read via a GitHub-hosted arXiv digest)

findings.claim: Scoring works best on read speech. Moving to open responses, where the scorer sees an ASR transcript instead of a known reference, lowers agreement, most at the word level. Most APA research uses read-aloud tasks; 'assessing pronunciation quality in unscripted speech … remains relatively underexplored' (HiPPO, 2025). In MultiPA, switching speechocean762 from the true text to Whisper transcripts moved word-accuracy PCC from about 0.52 to 0.42, word-total from 0.53 to 0.44, and sentence accuracy from 0.73 to 0.70. Whisper output also varies between runs. Azure's unscripted mode uses a different speech-to-text model, and Microsoft recommends running STT first and then a scripted assessment when accuracy matters.
findings.population: Mandarin-L1 English learners (speechocean762); a small real open-response pilot set (MultiPA)
findings.effect_notes: MultiPA (Interspeech 2024), mean of 5 seeds. Closed vs open PCC: sentence accuracy 0.73 vs 0.70, fluency 0.79 vs 0.77, prosody 0.78 vs 0.76, word accuracy 0.52 vs 0.42, word stress 0.19 vs 0.24. The model was trained on clips under 20 s.
findings.design_implication: Limit sound-level scoring to elicited tasks with a known target: read, repeat after model, shadow, minimal pairs. For free speech (picture description, retelling), give only coarse, robust metrics: speech rate, pauses, run length, and whether ASR recognised the intended key words. Do not give phoneme verdicts on spontaneous speech. Split recordings longer than about 15-20 s before scoring.

citations.ref: Chen, Yu & Hirschberg (2024) MultiPA: open-response pronunciation assessment, Interspeech 2024 (PCC tables in repo)
Yan et al. (2025) HiPPO: hierarchical pronunciation assessment for unscripted speech, IJCNLP-AACL 2025. doi:10.18653/v1/2025.ijcnlp-long.45
Microsoft Learn: unscripted assessment uses a different STT model; recommends STT then scripted assessment

findings.claim: There is limited evidence that Azure en-US has penalised valid pronunciation variants. Issue #1530 (June 2022) reported [wʌt ər], [jʊ] and [həloʊ] flagged as wrong; the issue was labelled 'accepted', and SDK 1.31 (Aug 2023) lists a fix for correct pronunciations flagged 'where words could have multiple valid pronunciations'. In the current doc example, the expected /ɛ/ in 'hello' gets a phoneme AccuracyScore of 47 when [ə] is the most likely spoken phone. Yet the word scores 99 with ErrorType 'None' and the utterance scores 100. So the documented risk is at phoneme-level display, not word-level error flags. No systematic false-alarm rate on reduced forms, weak forms, liaison or schwa deletion has been published. Contrain et al. (JEP 2024) is a separate finding: on two common errors of Japanese learners of French, an alignment-based detector was 31.1 and 3.8 points (absolute) more precise than a transcription-based one.
findings.population: Native and L2 English speech (Azure issue and doc examples); Japanese learners of French (Contrain et al. 2024)
findings.effect_notes: This is a single issue report plus a documented example; I found no systematic false-alarm rate published for Azure. Contrain et al. give absolute precision gains of 31.1 and 3.8 for alignment-based over transcription-based detection.
findings.design_implication: Favour precision over recall: flag an error only when it is high-confidence and repeated. Keep a list of accepted variants per exercise: English weak forms (to, for, and, of, can), reduced vowels, and flapping; French optional liaisons, schwa deletion ('je n(e) le lui r(e)demanderai'), and regional variants. Do not score those positions, or score them against multiple references. Avoid Azure accuracy scores in English vowel-reduction and stress-timing drills and in French liaison/enchaînement drills. Use timing and duration measures (tech-10) or learner self-comparison with the model instead.

citations.ref: Azure-Samples/cognitive-services-speech-sdk issue #1530 (June 2022): valid pronunciations flagged as errors
Azure Speech SDK release notes (1.31, Aug 2023 fix for multiple valid pronunciations)
Microsoft Learn doc example: expected ɛ vs spoken ə in 'hello' (Assess spoken phonemes)
Contrain, Pinquier, Fontan & Ferrané (2024) Erreurs de prononciation en L2: comparaison de méthodes pour la détection et le diagnostic guidés par la didactique, JEP 2024

findings.claim: The evidence base for automatic French L2 pronunciation assessment is thin. There is no public French benchmark comparable to speechocean762; researchers cite 'la rareté des corpus dédiés incluant des annotations expertes' (the scarcity of dedicated corpora with expert annotation). Available resources are narrow: the IFCASL French-German corpus (about 100 speakers, read speech, phone-level segmentation, over 50% manually corrected) and a Korean-learner corpus with 100 h of French. Published French detectors cover narrow targets with modest accuracy: GOP vs CNN on /R/ and /v/ for 23 Japanese learners reached 72.6% binary accuracy, a 13.4% relative gain for the CNN. Open datasets on French accent variation are also scarce, which leads to performance gaps across speaker groups.
findings.population: Japanese learners of French; German learners of French; Korean learners; native French speakers of varied accents
findings.effect_notes: Pellegrini et al. 2016: n=23 learners, 72.6% accuracy on 2 target phonemes, thresholds tuned on native speech with artificial errors. IFCASL: about 100 speakers. Korean L2 corpus: 1,200 h total, of which 100 h is French. Fabre et al. 2026: perceptual study with 87 listeners.
findings.design_implication: Label French sound-level scores 'experimental' in the interface. For French segmentals (nasal vowels /ɑ̃ ɛ̃ ɔ̃/, /y/ vs /u/, /ʁ/), prefer tasks whose correctness can be checked with little ambiguity: minimal-pair forced choice (does a recogniser or scorer prefer 'vin' or 'vent'?), perception and discrimination drills, and listen-and-compare with a native model. Choose the target variety explicitly (fr-FR vs fr-CA) and never penalise other native varieties.

citations.ref: Contrain et al. (2024) JEP: scarcity of expert-annotated non-native corpora
Pellegrini, Fontan & Sahraoui (2016) CNN-based automatic pronunciation assessment of Japanese speakers learning French, JEP 2016
Trouvain et al. (2016) The IFCASL corpus of French and German non-native and native read speech, LREC 2016
Han, Kim & Chung (2024) Korean learners' L2 speech corpus of seven languages (incl. 100 h French), LREC-COLING 2024
Fabre, Avanzi & Portet (2026) Building a dataset for French accent classification evaluation, LREC 2026. doi:10.63317/5ayaxbnxjfen

findings.claim: General-purpose ASR, Whisper included, is biased against non-native and non-standard accents and can output words that were never said. That makes 'the ASR understood you' a biased and lenient proxy for pronunciation. Across several off-the-shelf English recognisers, WER for non-American accents was 2-12 percentage points higher than for General American (16-49% relative). OpenAI's model card reports 'disparate performance on different accents and dialects', hallucinated text, and repetition, which it expects to be worse in lower-resource conditions. French work reports 'une chute significative' (a significant drop) in ASR performance for non-native speakers.
findings.population: Native and non-native English speakers (dialogue-agent speech); French speakers of English; general Whisper evaluation
findings.effect_notes: Tadimeti et al. 2022: absolute WER gap about 2-12 points, relative 16-49%. The Whisper model card gives no per-accent numbers but documents the disparities and hallucination.
findings.design_implication: Do not use Whisper or Azure transcripts as a pronunciation score. If ASR serves as an intelligibility check, use low-predictability or semantically unpredictable sentences and minimal-pair word lists, so the language model cannot fill in the intended words (this last point is a design inference, not tested in these sources). Compare the transcript with the target word by word. Do not trust long free-form Whisper transcripts without checking for hallucination (e.g., text in silent stretches, repeated n-grams).

citations.ref: Tadimeti, Georgila & Traum (2022) Evaluation of off-the-shelf speech recognizers on different accents in a dialogue domain, LREC 2022
OpenAI Whisper model card (accent disparities, hallucination, repetition)
Bada, Fohr & Illina (2020) Génération des prononciations non natives pour l'enrichissement du lexique, JEP 2020
Imai, Chowdhury & Stent (2025) Evaluating open-source ASR systems across diverse audio conditions, COLING 2025

findings.claim: The recording chain and speaking style change the scores. Microsoft recommends 16 kHz or higher, a close microphone, no remote connection, little background noise, one speaker, and 'normal speaking speed and volume', avoiding shouting. In a JASA study comparing simultaneous recordings, F0 was 'tracked accurately by all devices'. Formants (F1-F3), however, differed by device and by extraction tool (Praat vs VoiceSauce), Zoom showed intensity drops, and the reviewed literature shows lossy compression distorting the F1-F2 vowel space unpredictably.
findings.population: Vendor guidance; a phonetics lab comparison of devices (cardinal vowels, small number of speakers)
findings.effect_notes: Zhang et al. 2021 (JASA 149(6)) is a device comparison, not a learner study. Lossless phone recordings came closest to the reference recorder.
findings.design_implication: Capture uncompressed PCM, e.g., AudioWorklet to 16-bit 16 kHz+ WAV. Do not record Opus/WebM with MediaRecorder and convert later: v1 does this, and the compression artifacts are already baked in. Add a pre-session mic check (clipping, noise floor or SNR, distance prompt), and reject or flag takes that fail it instead of scoring them. Use F0-based intonation displays freely. Show vowel-space (formant) plots only against the learner's own baseline on the same device, never as absolute targets. Keep 'over-articulation' and 'fast' tiers out of Azure scoring, since they break its 'normal speed and volume' assumption.

citations.ref: Microsoft: Characteristics and limitations of Pronunciation Assessment (audio quality, distance, noise, normal speed/volume)
Zhang, Jepson, Lohfink & Arvaniti (2021) Comparing acoustic analyses of speech data collected remotely, JASA 149(6)

findings.claim: A local open-source toolkit exists for both languages, but it is validated mainly on native read speech. The Montreal Forced Aligner (MFA) ships pretrained French and English acoustic models (v3.0.0, GMM-HMM, 2024). They were trained on read speech in low-noise conditions, and the only published metric is a 0%-WER sanity check on the training corpus; there is no held-out alignment accuracy. Parselmouth gives Python access to Praat for F0, intensity, formants and durations. fairseq offers XLSR-53 and LV-60 phoneme recognisers fine-tuned on 26 Common Voice languages with eSpeak IPA. Kaldi has a GOP recipe for speechocean762. The IFCASL team had to tune its forced-alignment models for CAPT on learner speech, and MultiPA shows alignment can find omitted words with an F1 of about 85%.
findings.population: Native read speech (training data); L2 English (speechocean762 for GOP and completeness)
findings.effect_notes: MultiPA forced-alignment completeness: a word-duration threshold of about 0.07 s gives F1 of about 85% for missing words (simulated insertions). No published MFA boundary accuracy for L2 French or English speech was found.
findings.design_implication: Run a small Python sidecar (MFA + Parselmouth + optionally a wav2vec2 phoneme model) next to, or instead of, Azure. Use it for (a) timing: segment and word durations, pauses, rate, French final lengthening, English stressed/unstressed vowel-duration ratios; (b) completeness and omission checks; (c) an in-house GOP-like score for French with explicit uncertainty. Validate the sidecar on 30-50 of the learner's own recordings, spot-checked by a human, before exposing its numbers.

citations.ref: MFA French acoustic model v3.0.0 model card (read speech, low noise; metrics caveat)
MFA English acoustic model v3.0.0 model card
Jadoul, Thompson & de Boer (2018) Introducing Parselmouth: A Python interface to Praat, Journal of Phonetics 71, 1-15
fairseq wav2vec 2.0 README: XLSR-53 zero-shot multilingual phoneme recognition (Xu et al. 2021, arXiv:2109.11680)
Kaldi GOP recipe for speechocean762
Chen et al. (2024) MultiPA forced-alignment completeness method (F1 ~85%)

findings.claim: Timing and pitch measures computed in the app are interpretable and work across languages, but the two cited validation studies are small and show group-level effects. Coulange & Rossato (LREC 2020): a GMM over 16 duration-based features (fully automatic, no ASR), trained on 1,340 native French speakers and applied to samples of at least 30 s, gave significantly lower native-likeness for 29 A2 Japanese learners from an independent corpus (p<.0001; different recording conditions may contribute). For 37 heterogeneous non-native speakers it gave only a trend (p=.067). These are group differences, not individual classification. The most informative parameters were intersyllabic mean duration and variation coefficient plus speech rate (non-native group), and speech rate and phonation ratio (Japanese group). Hincks & Edlund (2009; 14 Chinese learners of English, 7 per group, about 3 h of training): both the visual-feedback and the audio-feedback groups increased pitch variation (SD of F0 in semitones), and the effect held in a new presentation after training. The visual group increased significantly more.
findings.population: Native French speakers (n=1,340 train, 146 test), non-native French speakers (n=37), Japanese A2 learners of French (n=29); Chinese learners of English (n=14)
findings.effect_notes: Coulange & Rossato 2020: GMM log-likelihood; eta-squared used for feature ranking (values not in the abstract). Hincks & Edlund 2009: n=14, about 3 h of training, visual-feedback group improved significantly more than audio-feedback group; small sample.
findings.design_implication: Build the 'articulation' and 'prosody' panels from interpretable measures computed in the app for both languages: articulation rate, pause count and duration, mean length of run, pitch range in semitones, French phrase-final lengthening ratio, English stressed/unstressed vowel-duration ratio. Show each against a native model recording of the same text. Compute rhythm metrics only on passages of 30 s or more, and show them as trends across sessions, not per-sentence grades.

citations.ref: Coulange & Rossato (2020) Rhythmic proximity between natives and learners of French: evaluation of a metric based on the CEFC corpus, LREC 2020
Hincks & Edlund (2009) Promoting increased pitch variation in oral presentations with transient visual feedback, Language Learning & Technology 13(3), 32-50
Zhang et al. (2021) JASA: F0 robust across recording devices

findings.claim: Evidence that off-the-shelf audio-language models (ALMs) are unreliable pronunciation judges is emerging but thin. Liu et al. (Findings of EACL 2026; English, L2-Arctic-plus): existing ALMs and cascaded ASR+LLM pipelines were significantly outperformed by ALMs instruction-tuned on the task, for both mispronunciation detection and feedback generation (no absolute figures in the abstract). AudioJudge (EACL 2026): large-audio-model judges 'exhibit significant verbosity and positional biases'; prompting strategy (audio concatenation plus in-context examples) substantially changes performance; and with such prompting they can be useful. The system-level 0.91 Spearman is not per-utterance scoring. Kim et al. (Findings of ACL 2026) show multimodal LLMs hallucinating non-native accents for Asian speakers when identical native audio is paired with visual racial cues. This is a cross-modal bias that an audio-only app would not trigger. Wei et al. (Findings of EACL 2026) show sensitivity to language and option order on spoken multiple-choice QA, which is not pronunciation scoring. TextPA (EMNLP 2025), a single study, found that an LLM reasoning over text descriptions of speech was cost-efficient and competitive zero-shot, and significantly improved conventional models on out-of-domain data.
findings.population: Mostly L2 English (L2-ARCTIC-derived data, speechocean762); multilingual ALM bias benchmarks (English, Chinese, Korean)
findings.effect_notes: The effect sizes are not in the abstracts I could open. AudioJudge reports up to 0.91 Spearman for system-level ranking, which is not individual pronunciation scoring. Four 2025-2026 peer-reviewed papers agree on the reliability limits.
findings.design_implication: Do not send learner audio to a general audio LLM for scores or error verdicts. Measure first (Azure, MFA, Parselmouth), then pass only the structured results (target phones, detected deviations with confidence, durations, F0 stats) to a text LLM. Let it write a short, plain-language explanation and articulatory tip, restricted to the measured items. Tell it to say 'not sure' when confidence is low. Show pedagogical content from LLMs as advice, not assessment.

citations.ref: Liu, Cui, Gu & Wang (2026) Unlocking large audio-language models for interactive language learning, Findings of EACL 2026. doi:10.18653/v1/2026.findings-eacl.190
Manakul et al. (2026) AudioJudge: Understanding what works in large audio model based speech evaluation, EACL 2026. doi:10.18653/v1/2026.eacl-long.168
Kim et al. (2026) Visual interference in speech evaluation: cultural asymmetry and cross-modal bias in MLLMs, Findings of ACL 2026. doi:10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.1362
Wei et al. (2026) Bias in the ear of the listener: sensitivity in audio language models, Findings of EACL 2026. doi:10.18653/v1/2026.findings-eacl.80
Chen, Ma & Hirschberg (2025) Read to Hear: zero-shot pronunciation assessment using textual descriptions and LLMs (TextPA), EMNLP 2025. doi:10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.134

findings.claim: None of the commercial alternatives I could inspect publishes per-locale agreement with human raters, and none clearly solves French phoneme diagnosis. SpeechSuper's scripted API lists 8 spoken languages including French. Its 'highlight' features (syllable stress, liaison detection, sentence-final rise/fall, phoneme insertion/deletion/substitution) are described without saying which languages they cover, and its unscripted API is English-only. Speechace's public samples describe scores for 'how closely the speaker … matches a native English speaker' plus IELTS/PTE estimates. ELSA's APIs are English-only B2B services, documented only by a third-party catalogue. A 2025 Swedish system chose a hybrid of Azure plus open LLMs because low-resource languages lack assessment technology.
findings.population: Not applicable: vendor documentation; no independent validation found
findings.effect_notes: No accuracy or correlation figures appear in any vendor README I could access. The vendor documentation sites themselves were unreachable from this environment.
findings.design_implication: Switching vendors does not close the French gap by itself. Before adopting SpeechSuper or another vendor for French, run a 1-2 hour side-by-side pilot: 40-60 of the learner's French items, each scored by Azure, the vendor and a French native listener. Keep the vendor only if it agrees better with the human. Hide the scoring provider behind an interface so it can be swapped, and record which provider produced each score.

citations.ref: SpeechSuper API samples README (languages, scripted/unscripted features)
Speechace API samples README
API Evangelist catalog of ELSA APIs (third-party; English, B2B)
Geng & Alfter (2025) Real-time Swedish speech analyzer: hybrid Azure + LLM, BEA 2025. doi:10.18653/v1/2025.bea-1.14

does_not_work_verified.claim: Choosing 'weak phoneme' drills from a rolling average of a few (≥3) single-attempt phoneme scores.
does_not_work_verified.notes: This is a design inference, and a reasonable one. Phone-level PCC is 0.62-0.68 on GOPT, mispronunciation-detection F1 is 63.85% (HMamba), and GOP posteriors 'may suffer from overconfidence' (Parikh et al.). All of these come from speechocean762 (Mandarin-L1, half children) or similar English data. No study directly tests how reliable drill selection is from pooled tokens, so the '15-20 tokens' threshold is itself a heuristic.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using Azure phoneme labels (IPA) or 'spoken phoneme' substitutions for French.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Azure doc: phoneme names are en-US (and zh-CN SAPI) only; syllables and spoken phonemes are en-US only; 'For other locales, you can only get the phoneme score.'

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using Azure ProsodyScore for French, or as stress feedback in English.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Prosody is en-US only. The diagnostics are UnexpectedBreak and MissingBreak (thresholds set by the app) and utterance-level Monotone; there is no stress error type. Open-model word-stress PCC is 0.15-0.33 (GOPT) and about 0.19-0.24 (MultiPA). These low values partly reflect skewed stress labels in speechocean762.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Phoneme-level verdicts on spontaneous or unscripted speech.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported as an inference. HiPPO says unscripted assessment 'remains relatively underexplored'. MultiPA shows word-level PCC dropping from about 0.52 to 0.42 with Whisper transcripts, though part of that drop comes from label misalignment. No study directly measures phoneme-level accuracy on spontaneous L2 speech.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using an ASR transcript (Whisper or Azure STT) or its word error rate as the pronunciation score.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Accent WER gaps of 2-12 points absolute (Tadimeti 2022; pre-Whisper, General American vs non-American). The Whisper card documents accent disparities and hallucination. Some work compares ASR with L1-listener intelligibility (Inceoglu et al. 2023, see missed_evidence), so ASR may serve as a coarse intelligibility check but not as a pronunciation score.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using a general audio-LLM as the judge of pronunciation.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Moderately supported. Liu et al. 2026: off-the-shelf ALMs and ASR+LLM cascades were outperformed by task-tuned ALMs. AudioJudge 2026: verbosity and positional biases, strong dependence on prompting. The 'accent stereotyping' source (Kim et al. 2026) needs visual persona cues, so it is less relevant to audio-only use.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Scoring against a single canonical pronunciation in drills that target reduced vowels, weak forms, liaison or schwa deletion.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Only weakly supported. Issue #1530 (2022) was reported fixed in SDK 1.31 (2023). In the current doc example, [ə] in 'hello' gets phoneme accuracy 47, but the word scores 99 with no error. The risk is real at phoneme level; no systematic false-alarm data exists for weak forms or French liaison. Treat this as a precaution to test on the learner's own recordings.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Vowel (formant) feedback as absolute targets from browser-recorded, lossy-compressed audio.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Zhang et al. 2021: formants varied by device and extraction tool, and the literature they review reports lossy compression distorting F1-F2 unpredictably. 'F0 does not' is qualified: the study tested steady F0 on sustained vowels, and the authors say it is unclear whether this holds for dynamic F0. Small sample (n=7).

does_not_work_verified.claim: Treating score changes over months as learner progress without controlling for scorer updates.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The Aug 2026 release notes confirm updated scoring models for en-US and fr-FR (and zh-CN, es-ES, es-MX, pt-BR), with earlier updates in Apr and Jun 2025, and no new published PCC figures. The updates were announced, not silent.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Grading fast-tempo or over-articulated speech with a scorer calibrated on normal-rate, normal-volume speech.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The vendor guidance says it verbatim: 'compares the submitted audio to native speakers in general conditions. The speaker should maintain a normal speaking speed and volume.' There are no empirical data on how much scores shift at fast or exaggerated rates; the app should test this itself.

critique_of_v1: ADR decision 1 in docs/technical-design.md chose Azure for 'phoneme-level scores for both locales'. That premise is false for French. fr-FR gets unlabeled phoneme scores only, so phoneme_stats cannot be keyed by IPA for French, and the French weak-sound engine (nasals, /ʁ/, /y/ vs /u/) has no data. The pack's phonemes.json cannot be joined to Azure output without the app's own dictionary lookup (G2P) plus alignment.

PRD: 'Articulation → Azure fluency + prosody scores' and 'enableProsodyAssessment: true' for both locales. Prosody is en-US only, so French Track C (liaison, enchaînement, even-syllable rhythm, shadowing) is unscored. Even in English, Azure's prosody gives only break and monotone flags, not the stress feedback the F4 articulation panel promises.

Weak-sound engine (≥3 attempts, 5 lowest rolling averages) and level advancement at ≥85 average. At phone-level agreement of about PCC 0.6, three attempts cannot separate a real weak sound from scorer noise, word context, or a false alarm on a valid variant. Drills will chase artefacts.

Speed ladder: one attempt with accuracy ≥85 advances the tier, and TTS tempos of 0.75x/1.0x/1.25x (0.9/1.0/1.15 multipliers) feed an 'articulation index'. Azure is calibrated for normal-rate speech. Accuracy under speed mixes up the scorer's behaviour on fast speech with real articulation skill, and a single-attempt gate is noisy.

The green/amber/red phoneme colouring at 85/60 implies phoneme-level precision the technology does not have (mispronunciation-detection F1 about 0.64). Canonical-lexicon scoring can colour correct reduced forms red. That runs against the English stress-timing and vowel-reduction goals and against French optional liaison and schwa deletion.

Audio pipeline: MediaRecorder records WebM/Opus, which is then converted to WAV. The lossy compression is already baked in before the conversion, and formant-sensitive analysis suffers most. There is also no mic, noise, clipping or distance quality gate, although Microsoft says these factors lower scoring confidence.
No versioning of the scorer. Progress charts will mix Azure model generations (e.g., the Aug 2026 en-US and fr-FR updates) and could show 'improvement' or 'regression' that the vendor caused.

Azure's AccuracyScore is defined as closeness to 'a native speaker's pronunciation', and FluencyScore as closeness to native use of silent breaks. v1 treats these as the goal. Nothing in the pipeline measures intelligibility or comprehensibility, and scores for a speaker of another native variety may be unfairly low.

Unscripted or spontaneous practice is missing entirely. That is defensible for sound-level scoring, but the redesign should add free-speech tasks scored only on robust timing and intelligibility measures.
The v1 ADR rejected self-hosted and other vendors without piloting them. For French, an in-house timing and pitch layer (MFA + Parselmouth) is the only way to get rhythm and prosody signals at all.
open_questions: What is the learner's first language? All the main agreement benchmarks are Mandarin-L1 learners of English, so accuracy and false-alarm rates for this learner's L1 are unknown.
Which target varieties should the app use (fr-FR vs fr-CA; en-US vs en-GB)? Azure scores against the chosen locale model and advises trying several.
How well does Azure fr-FR (post-Aug-2026 model) agree with a human French listener on this learner's recordings? A 40-60-item pilot with one native rater would answer this cheaply.
Does the order of Azure's unlabeled fr-FR phoneme scores reliably match a G2P/MFA phone sequence, especially with liaison, schwa deletion and optional variants?
Is a Python sidecar (MFA, Parselmouth, wav2vec2) acceptable in the Node/React stack, or must analysis stay in-browser/Node (e.g., WASM pitch trackers)?
Would SpeechSuper's French scripted API agree better with human raters than Azure fr-FR? No independent validation was found.
Effect sizes for LLM/ALM pronunciation feedback (Liu et al. 2026; TextPA 2025) could not be extracted from abstracts. The full papers should be read before adopting any LLM explanation layer.

What are the published numbers for automatic utterance-fluency annotation validity (Matsuura et al. 2025, Research Methods in Applied Linguistics, doi:10.1016/j.rmal.2024.100177)? Only the tool's README was reachable.
missed_evidence_flagged: Arvaniti (2012) The usefulness of metrics in the quantification of speech rhythm, Journal of Phonetics 40(3):351-373. Rhythm metrics (ΔC, %V, PVIs, Varcos) showed large between-speaker variation and were very sensitive to elicitation method and syllable structure, 'making cross-linguistic comparisons and rhythmic classifications based on metrics unsafe at best'. This weakens rhythm-metric feedback (tech-10) and supports within-learner trends on fixed material only. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wocn.2012.02.003

Suzuki, Kormos & Uchihara (2021) The relationship between utterance and perceived fluency: A meta-analysis of correlational studies, Modern Language Journal 105(2):435-463. A meta-analysis supporting speed and pause measures (articulation rate, pause frequency and duration) as valid correlates of listener-perceived fluency. It strengthens the timing-panel part of tech-10 more than the cited sources do. https://doi.org/10.1111/modl.12706

Bosker, Pinget, Quené, Sanders & de Jong (2013) What makes speech sound fluent? The contributions of pauses, speed and repairs, Language Testing 30(2):159-175. Pause and speed measures predicted fluency ratings; relevant to which timing metrics to surface. https://doi.org/10.1177/0265532212455394

Rousso, Cohen, Keshet & Chodroff (2024) Tradition or Innovation: A Comparison of Modern ASR Methods for Forced Alignment, Interspeech 2024. MFA outperformed WhisperX and MMS on hand-aligned TIMIT and Buckeye. This supports MFA for timing measures (tech-9), but the validation is on native English only. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19363

Sanker et al. (2021) (Don't) try this at home! The effects of recording devices and software on phonetic analysis (Lingbuzz 005748; later published in Language 97(4)). A broader device and software comparison than Zhang et al. 2021, relevant to browser-recording choices and to whether F0 and formants are robust (tech-8). https://lingbuzz.net/lingbuzz/005748

Racine, Detey & Kawaguchi (2012) Les voyelles /y-u/ dans IPFC: évaluation perceptive de productions natives, hispanophones et japonophones, JEP-TALN 2012. IPFC (Interphonologie du Français Contemporain) is a multi-L1 French learner corpus that tech-6 omits; relevant to /y/-/u/ drills. https://aclanthology.org/F12-1049/

Inceoglu, Chen & Lim (2023) Assessment of L2 intelligibility: Comparing L1 listeners and automatic speech recognition, ReCALL 35(1):89-104. It directly compares ASR and L1-listener intelligibility of L2 English, which bears on whether 'ASR understood you' can serve even as a coarse intelligibility check (tech-7). I verified the citation via a GitHub reference list but did not open the article or check its DOI in this session.

Hincks & Edlund (2009) detail missing from tech-10: the audio-feedback control group also increased pitch variation; the visual group increased more. So the main effect comes from practice plus feedback of any kind, which matters for designing the prosody panel. http://llt.msu.edu/vol13num3/hincksedlund.pdf

Azure content already in the cited doc but not used: continuous mode (audio longer than 30 s) does not support EnableMiscue, so Omission and Insertion must be computed by the app against the reference text. This matters for passage-level reading tasks and the '≥30 s rhythm' recommendation. https://github.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/blob/main/articles/ai-services/speech-service/how-to-pronunciation-assessment.md

general_review.topic: gap-l1clarity: Evidence for improving speech clarity, articulation and intelligibility in healthy adult NATIVE speakers (English, French) and very advanced L2 speakers, outside clinical populations
general_review.summary:
WHAT I COULD ACCESS. This session had already used its whole web-search budget (200 of 200), and every academic domain was blocked (PubMed, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, ERIC, doi.org, publishers). I checked sources three ways: (a) GitHub-hosted bibliographies that carry full abstracts, such as the ACM Digital Library dumps in boudinfl/acm-cr and the HLP lab bibliography; (b) full texts mirrored on GitHub or in the shared scratchpad, including Hincks & Edlund 2009, Rodero et al. 2022, Tuttösí et al. 2026, the ACL Anthology XML for JEP 2016–2025 and the Cochrane abstract CD006372; and (c) a native-clarity evidence base left by an earlier run in this session, whose sources I re-used only where I could confirm them. Each finding says how its sources were checked. Take all numbers as abstract-level.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE DESIGN DECISION. If one of the two languages is the learner's native language, the v1 articulation track (tongue twisters, speed ladders, an articulation index that rewards speed) should be REPLACED, not kept.
- No study found that tongue twisters, speed ladders, over-articulation drills done for their own sake, cork/pen or bite-block work, or non-speech mouth exercises improve clarity or intelligibility in healthy adults. Tongue twisters and bite-blocks are research tools for causing speech errors or disturbing speech. The one systematic review of non-speech oral-motor work (in children) found no strong evidence it helps.
- What does exist:
  1. Healthy native adults produce clearer, more intelligible speech ('clear speech') at once when given a concrete instruction ('over-enunciate' works best, plain 'speak clearly' least). The size of the gain varies a lot from speaker to speaker.
  2. Speakers make targeted, lasting-within-session hyperarticulation when a listener, even a simulated one, occasionally misunderstands them. This works in controlled web experiments with native English speakers. Noise and a partner who struggles bring out the same effect in French speakers.
  3. Slowing down is not the lever. Clear speech at normal rate keeps most of the benefit. A 2026 English/French study found that listeners judged globally slowed speech clearer even though it increased their comprehension errors. How much vowels shrink as rate rises differs by speaker.
  4. Automated delivery coaches (pitch-variation meters, rate/volume feedback on Google Glass, virtual audiences, an automated interview coach) change the behaviour they target. In one small randomized study the gain carried over to a new presentation 48 h later. None showed a gain in listener-measured intelligibility, and the one that checked found no change in rated intelligibility.
  5. Habit-reversal training cuts filled pauses ('um') quickly and the effect lasted to follow-up at 2–5 weeks (single-case designs). Listener benefit was not measured.
  6. Voice-training trials for teachers and telemarketers (Cochrane: 6 RCTs, 262 people) show low-quality, non-significant effects on self-reported voice function. None measured intelligibility. In a randomized public-speaking course study, any rehearsal beat no rehearsal on instructor grades, and the practice medium made no difference.
- CARRYOVER is the weakest link. Clear speech fades within a conversation and restarts at each new task. The only training study with follow-up in healthy adults compared two spouses: 45 minutes of specific instruction versus 'speak clearly', held at 1 month. I found no controlled trial showing clear-speech practice changes habitual everyday speech.
- MEASUREMENT. Native speakers score near the ceiling on accuracy scores and in quiet, so outcomes need 'headroom': transcription in noise, low-predictability sentences, or pseudo-words. French teams have validated a pseudo-word transcription test (perceived phonological deviation score) that includes healthy speakers. Measures of listening effort or memory can show benefits that intelligibility scores miss. Listeners' own ratings of clarity can point the wrong way.

WHERE NO EVIDENCE EXISTS. I found none on: diction or actor training with intelligibility outcomes; Microsoft Presenter/Speaker Coach or Orai measured against a control; European-French clear-speech training; long-term carryover in healthy adults; and cork, pen or bite-block exercises as training.

findings.claim: Healthy adult native speakers can switch into a more intelligible 'clear speech' style immediately, without any training, when given an instruction. The wording matters. 'Overenunciate' produced the largest acoustic change and intelligibility gain, 'speak as if to someone with hearing loss' came second, and plain 'speak clearly' came last, though it still beat habitual speech. The benefit differs a lot between speakers: in one 41-talker database only about 23 talkers gave listeners a significant vowel benefit, and the talkers who benefited most lengthened their vowels and spread them apart more. Very advanced non-native talkers also produce a clear-speech benefit (Smiljanić & Bradlow 2011; the title and a secondary summary state this, and details were not verified).
findings.population: Typical adult American English talkers: 12 talkers reading 18 sentences, rated by 40 listeners transcribing in multitalker babble (Lam & Tjaden 2013; Lam, Tjaden & Wilding 2012); 41 talkers in the Ferguson database, with a 12-talker acoustic follow-up; high-proficiency L2 English talkers (Smiljanić & Bradlow 2011). Native speakers, not learners. Listeners had normal hearing and listened in noise.
findings.effect_notes: Rank order: habitual < clear < hearing-impaired < overenunciate, on both acoustic measures and intelligibility; 10 of the 12 talkers followed it (abstract-level, taken from the earlier run's verified summary). Dose: one instruction per condition, a single recording session, no training. Transfer and retention were not tested. I verified the DOIs for the Lam papers against a GitHub-hosted JSLHR bibliography; the 23/41 figure is secondary (reported in Ferguson 2012).
findings.design_implication: For the native language, make instructed clear speech the core target instead of 'articulation drills'. Each item is recorded twice: first habitual, then clear with a concrete cue ('overenunciate: open the jaw, finish every final consonant, give each vowel its full shape; your listener is hard of hearing'). The app scores only the user's own difference between the two takes on a feature panel (pauses, vowel length, pitch range, vowel spacing on carrier phrases, 1–3 kHz energy). It flags features the user does not change, because some speakers gain little. The same module serves a very advanced L2 speaker.

citations.ref: Lam J, Tjaden K (2013). Intelligibility of clear speech: Effect of instruction. JSLHR 56(5):1429-1440
Lam J, Tjaden K, Wilding G (2012). Acoustics of clear speech: Effect of instruction. JSLHR 55(6):1807-1821
Ferguson SH, Kewley-Port D (2007). Talker differences in clear and conversational speech: Acoustic characteristics of vowels. JSLHR 50:1241-1255
Smiljanić R, Bradlow AR (2011). Bidirectional clear speech perception benefit for native and high-proficiency non-native talkers and listeners: Intelligibility and accentedness. JASA 130(6):4020-4031

findings.claim: Carryover of clear speech into habitual speech is essentially untested in healthy adults, and the available evidence points to decay. In conversation, native speakers' clear speech became less intelligible in the later part of each conversation and reset at the start of the next one. The only training study with a follow-up in healthy adults (partners of people with hearing loss) compared one spouse, who got a single 45-minute session of specific instruction (slow down, pause, stress key words), with a spouse told only to 'speak clearly'. The instructed spouse used clear speech more consistently at 1 month. In a nearby domain, feedback-trained pitch variation carried over to a new presentation given within 48 h without feedback (Hincks & Edlund 2009), but that outcome was not clarity.
findings.population: Native English speakers in naturalistic conversations with partners (Lee & Baese-Berk 2020); 2 communication partners of adults with hearing loss, Canada (Caissie et al. 2005); 14 Chinese L1 intermediate-to-advanced English speakers (Hincks & Edlund 2009)
findings.effect_notes: Caissie et al.: n = 2 (one talker per condition), 1 session of 45 min, 1-month follow-up. Details come from a secondary clinical summary because the primary text was unreachable. Lee & Baese-Berk: the decline-and-reset pattern is quoted in a secondary thesis; I verified the DOI. No RCT of habitual-speech carryover was found for typical adults in English or French.
findings.design_implication: Do not claim that practice changes everyday speech unless the app measures it. Add an unprompted 'habitual probe' every 1–2 weeks: a 60–90 s picture description or retell given with no clarity cue, scored against the first baseline. Measure maintenance within a monologue (the slope of clarity features from start to end) and within conversation-like tasks. Use short, spaced sessions with 'reset' cues at task boundaries, and give one concrete strategy set (pausing, stressing key words, finishing consonants) rather than a vague 'be clear'.

citations.ref: Lee D-Y, Baese-Berk MM (2020). The maintenance of clear speech in naturalistic conversations. JASA 147(5):3702-3711

Caissie R, Campbell MM, Frenette WL, Scott L, Howell I, Roy A (2005). Clear speech for adults with a hearing loss: Does intervention with communication partners make a difference? J Am Acad Audiol 16(3):157-171
Secondary summary of Caissie et al. (EBSCO clinical review text mirrored on GitHub)
Hincks R, Edlund J (2009). Promoting increased pitch variation in oral presentations with transient visual feedback. Language Learning & Technology 13(3):32-50

findings.claim: Healthy native speakers adjust their clarity to how well the listener seems to understand them, and a SIMULATED listener is enough to trigger this. In a web-based task with a simulated partner, speakers hyperarticulated a target word (e.g., pill) when a confusable competitor (bill) was on screen. The effect nearly doubled when the partner occasionally misunderstood. It persisted across words and trials, came without any explicit request to clarify, and reduced confusable productions rather than shifting the whole target. Speakers also enhanced the specific length cues for coda voicing (dose/doze) only when the minimal pair was present in the context. French data agree: 6 Canadian French speakers in 85 dB babble hyperarticulated with lips and tongue, more so when interacting with a partner. British English pairs adapted when the partner heard degraded speech. Two Quebec French couples hypoarticulated to their spouse compared with an experimenter.
findings.population: Adult native English speakers in controlled web experiments (Buz et al. 2016; Seyfarth et al. 2016; n not given in the abstracts); 6 Canadian French speakers with articulography (Garnier et al. 2018); British English talker pairs (Hazan & Baker 2011); 2 Quebec French couples (Lancien 2020, preliminary)
findings.effect_notes: Buz et al.: the hyperarticulation effect was 'nearly doubled' with occasional partner misunderstanding (abstract verified via a GitHub-hosted bibliography). Garnier et al. measured articulation, not listener intelligibility. All effects are within one session; retention across days was not tested. These are controlled experiments, not training trials.
findings.design_implication: Replace score-driven twister drills with a 'listener simulation' game that works in EN and FR. The user instructs a partner to pick an item while a confusable competitor is on screen (minimal pairs such as pill/bill or poule/pull). ASR, run on the recording mixed with babble, plays the partner. When ASR mis-hears, the partner 'picks the wrong item', and this should happen only occasionally, as in Buz et al. Log the length, voice-onset time and vowel measures of the targeted contrast, so the app trains targeted clarity rather than global effort. Optional babble through earbuds at a capped level can elicit clear-Lombard speech; fade it over sessions.

citations.ref: Buz E, Tanenhaus MK, Jaeger TF (2016). Dynamically adapted context-specific hyper-articulation: Feedback from interlocutors affects speakers' subsequent pronunciations. Journal of Memory and Language 89:68-86

Hazan V, Baker R (2011). Acoustic-phonetic characteristics of speech produced with communicative intent to counter adverse listening conditions. JASA 130(4):2139-2152
Lancien M (2020). Variation stylistique en français québécois : l'effet de l'identité de l'interlocuteur. JEP 2020

findings.claim: The evidence suggests that slowing down on its own is not what makes clear speech intelligible, but it does not show that rate is a poor lever in general. A few extensively trained talkers kept most of the clear-speech benefit at normal rate (Krause & Braida 2002). In a TTS preprint whose key test (Study 3) used French-L1 listeners hearing English sentences, lengthening the tense-vowel target word and its nearby context cut errors by about half. Global slowing reduced errors on tense targets but increased them on lax targets. Listeners' clarity ratings favoured lengthened lax targets even though these raised errors, and Whisper ASR benefited most from global slowing. In French, the effect of speeding up on vowel reduction differs by speaker (Bourbon et al. 2020, a full JEP paper). A moderate rate of about 180 wpm was rated most effective and credible in a Barcelona perception study of actors on video; that study measured persuasion, not intelligibility. None of these studies trained real speakers' rate.
findings.population: A few trained American English talkers, with normal-hearing listeners in noise (Krause & Braida 2002); L1-English listeners plus L2-English listeners with French, Mandarin (n=25) and Japanese (n=19) L1s, English and French phrases, TTS-manipulated speech (Tuttösí et al. 2026); 29 French speakers (Bourbon et al. 2020); 120 university students in Barcelona (Rodero et al. 2022)
findings.effect_notes: Rodero et al. 2022: rate main effect on rated effectiveness F(2,118)=729.7, η²=.095; slow ≈150, moderate ≈180, fast ≈200+ wpm. Tuttösí et al. is a preprint, not peer-reviewed, and uses synthetic speech. Bourbon et al. is a conference abstract. The Tharumalingam 2025 figures are secondary. None of these trained speakers over time.
findings.design_implication: Drop tier multipliers (0.9/1.0/1.15) and any score that rewards speed or global slowness. The target is 'clear at your habitual rate'. Treat rate as a diagnostic band around the user's own habitual rate, plus pause placement at phrase boundaries, not as a goal to push. If a speed task stays, it passes only when the user's clarity features (vowel length and spacing, final-consonant release, ASR-in-noise accuracy) hold as rate rises. The French analysis must check reduction under speed for each speaker individually. For presentation delivery, recommend moderate rate and pitch variation, never 'as fast as possible'.

citations.ref: Krause JC, Braida LD (2002). Investigating alternative forms of clear speech: The effects of speaking rate and speaking mode on intelligibility. JASA 112(5):2165-2172
Tuttösí P, Lim A, Yeung HH, Wang Y, Aucouturier J-J (2026). Covertly improving intelligibility with data-driven adaptations of speech timing. arXiv:2603.30032 (preprint)
Bourbon A, D'Alessandro D, Fougeron C (2020). Débit et réduction vocalique : effets de la tâche de parole et du locuteur. JEP 2020

Rodero E, Larrea O, Rodríguez-de-Dios I, Lucas I (2022). The Expressive Balance Effect: Perception and physiological responses of prosody and gestures. Journal of Language and Social Psychology 41(6):659-684

findings.claim: Automated delivery coaches change what they target: pitch variation, fillers or unwanted words, speakers' satisfaction, and expert-rated interview or public-speaking performance. None of these studies measured listener intelligibility (transcription or speech-in-noise). The only intelligibility data are two raters on a 5-point scale (r=.41) in Hincks & Edlund, who saw little change. A preregistered randomized study (WSCoach vs the Orai app, n=24 fluent English speakers, 2025) found that both real-time and retrospective app feedback reduced unwanted words in conversation, real-time more so. The gains faded after feedback was withdrawn. Designs range from small randomized trials (n=14, n=24) to within-subject lab studies, so 'RCT' overstates the evidence base.
findings.population: Intermediate-to-advanced Chinese L1 speakers of English, engineering students in Sweden (Hincks & Edlund, n=14); native English speakers (Rhema, n=30); MIT undergraduates (MACH, n=90); participants in public-speaking lab studies (Chollet et al.; n not in abstract; AutoManner n=27)
findings.effect_notes: Hincks & Edlund (full text read): training ~181 vs 171 min; group effect F=6.74, p=.027; time effect F=8.36, p<.0005; reported effect sizes about .40–.45 (the symbol was lost in extraction, probably eta). There were only 2 raters, with r=.41 agreement. The paper cites Hahn (2004): monotone or misplaced focus reduced listeners' recall of lecture content. The ACM abstracts were verified via GitHub-hosted ACM DL bibliographies. None of these studies measured intelligibility in noise or listener transcription.
findings.design_implication: If the app adds a public-speaking or 'delivery' mode, follow what worked. Give sparse or transient feedback on ONE parameter at a time (pitch variation over a 10-s window, pause placement, fillers), not continuous streams. Train on utterances taken from the user's own recorded talk, then test transfer in a new unscripted talk with no feedback. Keep delivery metrics separate from the clarity score, and validate them against a listener-based outcome (see gap-l1clarity-9) before calling them 'clarity'.

citations.ref: Hincks R, Edlund J (2009). Promoting increased pitch variation in oral presentations with transient visual feedback. Language Learning & Technology 13(3):32-50 (full text also mirrored on GitHub)
Tanveer MI, Lin E, Hoque ME (2015). Rhema: A real-time in-situ intelligent interface to help people with public speaking. IUI '15, 286-295

findings.claim: Filled pauses ('um', 'uh') in public speaking drop quickly and stay down after brief habit-reversal training. The training has two parts: awareness training, then a competing response such as a silent pause. In 6 college students, fillers fell from a mean of 7.4 to 1.4 per minute right after training, and stayed stable at follow-up 2–5 weeks later. A 2022 review counted 7 such JABA studies (2016–2022). No study measured whether listeners understood or remembered more, so filler reduction is a delivery target, not an intelligibility target.
findings.population: Native English-speaking college students giving 3–5 minute speeches (single-case multiple-baseline designs)
findings.effect_notes: Mancuso & Miltenberger: n=6; a Bayesian re-analysis estimated a reduction of about 6.4 per minute (95% CrI 3.6–11.0). The details come from a GitHub re-analysis and the ERIC abstract. The strength rating applies to filler reduction only. Evidence on intelligibility or listener comprehension: none found.
findings.design_implication: Offer an optional 'filler awareness' module. ASR flags um/uh in English and euh/ben/du coup in French. The app then runs awareness training and a competing response ('pause silently instead'), and tracks fillers per minute in unscripted talks. Show it as a delivery metric only. Do not fold it into a clarity or pronunciation score, and do not treat low filler counts as proof of clearer speech.

citations.ref: Mancuso C, Miltenberger RG (2016). Using habit reversal to decrease filled pauses in public speaking. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis 49(1)
Public Speaking Disfluencies: A Review of Habit Reversal Training and Research (2022), ERIC record (authors not captured)
Kurz AS, re-analysis of Mancuso & Miltenberger (2016) data (GitHub)

findings.claim: There is no intelligibility evidence for voice, diction or public-speaking training. The Cochrane voice-disorder prevention review (6 small RCTs, 262 teachers, student teachers and telemarketers; searches to March 2010) found no significant effect even on self-reported vocal function (direct SMD 0.27, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.66; indirect SMD 0.44, -0.03 to 0.92; low-quality evidence), and no trial measured intelligibility. In Kryston et al., students randomly assigned to practise in VR, in front of a mirror or on video received similar instructor grades. Their advantage over students with no lab practice comes from a non-randomized comparison with self-selected non-attenders (mean grade ~50 vs ~95, which suggests missing or zero grades), so it is not causal evidence that rehearsal improves delivery.
findings.population: Teachers and telemarketers (Cochrane; 6 RCTs, 262 adults); US undergraduates in an introductory public-speaking course (Kryston et al.; Study 1 n=140 non-randomized, Study 2 n=234 randomized)
findings.effect_notes: Cochrane abstract read via a GitHub mirror; searches ran to March 2010. Outcomes were self-reported voice function, and there was no clarity outcome. Kryston et al. was read as full text on GitHub; I could not confirm the journal or DOI, and the course grades did not isolate delivery clarity. A 2022 teacher vocal-health meta-analysis (from the earlier run, not re-verified by me) also measured voice health.
findings.design_implication: Do not build voice-hygiene lessons or a 'diction course' into the core, and do not count them as clarity progress. The one supported element is rehearsing the user's real upcoming talk with a recording, and the medium does not matter. Add a 'rehearse my talk' mode that records, replays and applies the delivery checks in gap-l1clarity-5 and gap-l1clarity-6. If projection or loudness is a goal, train it together with a listener-in-noise check, because loud speech alone has no verified clarity outcome in healthy adults here.

citations.ref: Ruotsalainen JH, Sellman J, Lehto L, Isotalo LK, Verbeek JH. Interventions for preventing voice disorders in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev CD006372.pub2 (searches to March 2010)
Kryston K, Goble H, Eden A (2021). Incorporating virtual reality training in an introductory public speaking course (full text mirrored on GitHub; journal not confirmed)
The effectiveness of vocal health programs in the prevention of voice disorders in teachers: systematic review and meta-analysis (2022). Journal of Voice (from the earlier run, not re-verified)

findings.claim:
None of these exercises has evidence of improving clarity in native adults: tongue twisters, 'over-articulation' done as a stand-alone exercise without a listener or contrast, cork/pen-in-mouth, bite-block, or non-speech oral-motor exercises.
- Speech science uses tongue twisters to CAUSE speech errors (Wilshire 1999). The only training study (Ohkubo et al. 2025, unconfirmed) measured tongue movement distance and repetition speed, not intelligibility.
- Bite-blocks are a perturbation paradigm. In 5 French speakers they were used to study adaptation, not to train anyone (Didirková et al. 2020).
- A Cochrane review found no strong evidence that non-speech oral-motor treatments help even children with speech-sound disorders.
- I found no study of the 'cork technique' in healthy adults. The Brazilian speech-therapy literature, where the technique is common, was unreachable.
findings.population: Psycholinguistic lab participants (tongue-twister error paradigm); 5 French women (bite-block perturbation); children with developmental speech sound disorders (Cochrane); healthy Japanese women (Ohkubo, unconfirmed). None were healthy native adults trained for clarity.
findings.effect_notes: This is absence of evidence, not evidence of harm. The Lee & Gibbon conclusion is quoted via a secondary source: 'no strong evidence suggests that non-speech oral motor treatments are an effective treatment or an effective adjunctive treatment'. The Didirková et al. abstract was read in the JEP 2020 ACL Anthology XML.
findings.design_implication: Remove tongue-twister speed ladders and cork/bite-block style drills from the native-language core and from any progress index. If the user enjoys twisters, keep them as an unscored optional warm-up. Any 'over-articulation' belongs inside the habitual-versus-clear contrast with a listener goal (gap-l1clarity-1 and gap-l1clarity-3), not as an end in itself.

citations.ref: Wilshire CE (1999). The 'tongue twister' paradigm as a technique for studying phonological encoding. Language and Speech 42(1):57-82 (pre-2000, methodological)
Lee ASY, Gibbon FE (2015). Non-speech oral motor treatment for children with developmental speech sound disorders. Cochrane Database Syst Rev CD009383.pub2
Didirková I, Lancia L, Fougeron C (2020). Adaptations sur le F1 et le débit en réponse à diverses perturbations. JEP 2020
Ohkubo M et al. (2025). Evaluating effectiveness of articulation practice with tongue-twister movement distance using ultrasound. Bull Tokyo Dent Coll 66(3) (unconfirmed)

findings.claim:
Native-speaker clarity needs outcome measures with headroom, and some common proxies mislead.
- French pseudo-word test (Ghio, Rebourg et al., JEP 2020 and 2024): listeners transcribe pseudo-words. Scoring the difference between expected and heard features ('perceived phonological deviation') removes listeners' lexical guessing, gives stable scores for naive and expert listeners, and correlates with expert severity ratings. It was validated on 39 healthy speakers and 78 patients, with 52 pseudo-words per speaker and 40 listeners. Repeated items still show learning effects, so the item pool must be large.
- Listening effort: dual-task measures showed a benefit (better memory, faster reactions) where intelligibility scores showed none (Sarampalis et al. 2009).
- Benefits beyond noise: clear speech helped listeners segment words by statistical learning, but only in QUIET (Guo & Smiljanić 2021), so it can matter even when every word is heard.
- Listener ratings can point the wrong way: listeners judged globally slowed speech clearer even though it caused more errors (Tuttösí et al. 2026).
- Automated judges: an automatic French intelligibility predictor reached r up to 0.891 on clinical read speech (Quintas et al. 2024). LLM ratings of French public-speaking quality were weak; only the 'language level' criterion was predictable, with F1 0.56 (Barkar et al. 2025).
findings.population: French speakers, healthy and treated for head-and-neck cancer (Ghio 2020; Rebourg 2020, 2024; Quintas 2024); normal-hearing listeners (Sarampalis 2009); native listeners in quiet and noise (Guo & Smiljanić 2021); L1/L2 English and French listeners (Tuttösí 2026); French eloquence-contest speeches (Barkar 2025)
findings.effect_notes: PPD threshold of 0.6 features per phoneme for dysfunctional speech (Ghio 2020). The pseudo-word learning effect was similar in size to that for words when items repeat (Rebourg 2024). Sarampalis used noise-reduction processing, not clear speech, so it is an analogy for the method. No study validated any of these as a progress metric for training healthy native speakers.
findings.design_implication:
Build a periodic 'Clarity Check' kept separate from practice scores:
(1) Fresh, never-repeated low-predictability sentences, plus French and English pseudo-words drawn from a large pool.
(2) Mix the recording with babble at a fixed SNR and score it with ASR as a proxy, calibrated against a human transcriber (for example a friend) now and then.
(3) Score against the user's habitual baseline in both languages.
(4) Optionally add a listener-memory or effort check: the helper recalls key content after hearing it.
Do not use Azure accuracy, the user's self-rating, or an LLM's opinion as the native-clarity outcome.

citations.ref: Ghio A, Lalain M, Rebourg M, Fredouille C, Woisard V (2020). Evaluation de l'intelligibilité de patients avec traitement du cancer des cavités orales et pharyngales. JEP 2020
