does_not_work_verified.claim: Tongue-twister speed ladders improve clarity or intelligibility: no evidence either way
does_not_work_verified.notes: This is an absence-of-evidence claim and is fair. The Wilshire paradigm is an error-induction method. Ohkubo 2025 is unconfirmed and measured tongue movement, not intelligibility.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Non-speech oral-motor, cork/pen-in-mouth and bite-block exercises as clarity training
does_not_work_verified.notes: The Cochrane review (3 small studies, 22 children, low quality) found no strong evidence even as an add-on treatment. Didirková 2020 used bite-blocks only as a perturbation. No adult training data exist in either direction.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Rewarding faster speech or globally slower speech
does_not_work_verified.notes: Only indirect support. Krause & Braida 2002 found clear speech at normal rate kept its benefit, which weakens the case for rewarding slowness. In Tuttösí 2026 (preprint, TTS, L2 listeners), global slowing helped tense-vowel targets but hurt lax targets, and Whisper ASR benefited most from global slowing. Bourbon 2020 found speaker-dependent reduction when speaking fast. No study trained speakers on rate, so 'do not reward speed' is sensible design but not a tested result.

does_not_work_verified.claim: A vague 'speak clearly' prompt gives the smallest gain; many talkers produce little benefit
does_not_work_verified.notes: Consistent with Lam & Tjaden 2013 ordering and Ferguson talker variability. Note that 'speak clearly' still ranked above habitual numerically, so it is weaker, not useless. The 23/41 figure is secondary.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Voice-hygiene education or generic voice/diction training as a clarity intervention
does_not_work_verified.notes: Cochrane CD006372.pub2 confirmed: SMDs non-significant, low-quality evidence, self-reported outcomes only, no intelligibility outcome, searches to 2010.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Continuous real-time feedback streams during speaking
does_not_work_verified.notes: Rhema is weak support: 30 speakers, satisfaction only. However, WSCoach (arXiv 2507.04238, randomized, n=24) found that event-triggered near-real-time feedback reduced unwanted words more than retrospective Orai feedback. Only 'continuous streams' are disfavoured, not real-time feedback in general.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Treating a change in a delivery metric as proof of clearer speech
does_not_work_verified.notes: Hincks & Edlund: pitch variation rose but two raters saw little intelligibility change (r=.41, no statistics). Filler studies measured no listener outcomes. Fox Tree 2001 and Corley et al. 2007 show fillers can even aid listener comprehension and memory.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Listener or self ratings of clarity as the sole outcome
does_not_work_verified.notes: Tuttösí Study 3b: rated intelligibility did not track word error rate. Caveat: the listeners were L2 (French-L1) hearing English TTS; this is a preprint.

does_not_work_verified.claim: LLM judgments of public-speaking quality as the scoring engine
does_not_work_verified.notes: This rests on one workshop paper (Barkar 2025). Zero-shot LLM RMSE was 0.8 vs 0.51 for lexical features, and the analysis appears to be transcript-based, so it says nothing about acoustic clarity. The evidence is thin but points the same way.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Re-using a small fixed item set as the progress test
does_not_work_verified.notes: Rebourg 2024 shows listener learning of repeated pseudo-words and words, neutralised only by item quantity. It does not show speaker learning. For ASR-scored tests, the concern is speaker practice effects, which were not measured.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Assuming read-drill practice carries over into everyday speech
does_not_work_verified.notes: Weak. Lee & Baese-Berk (decay and reset within conversation, via a secondary summary) and Caissie (n≈2, secondary) are the main sources. WSCoach showed gains fading after feedback was withdrawn. No controlled carryover trial in healthy adults was found.

critique_of_v1: v1 treats the articulation track the same for a native and a non-native language. It has no first-language setting and no branch, even though the goals (clarity for listeners versus native-like phonemes) and the evidence base differ (docs/prd.md §5).

docs/technical-design.md says 'accuracy-under-tempo is the standard speech-therapy proxy' for clarity. I found no evidence for this in healthy adults. Rapid-repetition and tongue-twister speed tasks are motor-speech assessment or error-induction paradigms, not validated clarity measures.

The articulation index (mean accuracy × tier multiplier 0.9/1.0/1.15) explicitly rewards speaking faster. The evidence says the goal should be clarity at habitual rate. Speed can cause vowel reduction in some speakers, and rate did not predict intelligibility.

The ladder rule (advance at ≥85 Azure accuracy) uses a pronunciation-match score benchmarked on native speech. A native speaker will sit near the ceiling, so ladders will either pass trivially or track noise and microphone variation, not clarity. Azure prosody is en-US only, so the French track has no prosody signal at all.

Slow/normal/fast TTS tempo references and 'shadowing the TTS reference at matched pace' model GLOBAL tempo changes. Global slowing was judged clearer while it actually increased comprehension errors. Imitating TTS pace is not a clarity target for a native speaker.

'Over-articulation drills' are scored for phoneme accuracy with no habitual-versus-clear contrast, no listener framing and no personal baseline. These are the three elements with evidence behind them (instruction wording, talker variability, listener need).

All practice and scoring is read-aloud. There is no unprompted or semi-spontaneous probe, so the app cannot detect whether anything carries over into habitual speech, the weakest link in the evidence.

There is no intelligibility-based outcome: no listener transcription, no speech-in-noise check, no low-predictability or pseudo-word items. 'Progress' is Azure accuracy, the wrong construct for native clarity.

There is no listener simulation or communicative feedback. Occasional misunderstanding by a simulated partner is the manipulation with controlled evidence for targeted hyperarticulation in native speakers.
Long-passage 'completeness' (dropped syllables as a mumbling signal) is plausible, but it depends on the accuracy of ASR omission detection and has not been validated as a clarity measure.

If the user's goal includes public speaking or projection, v1 has nothing for pausing, fillers, pitch variation or rehearsing a real talk. These are the areas with at least some controlled evidence (habit reversal, sparse feedback, pitch-variation feedback with 48-hour transfer, any rehearsal better than none).
open_questions: What is the learner's first language? If it is French or English, that language's track should switch from phoneme accuracy to clear speech, listener simulation and an intelligibility-in-noise outcome. If neither, both tracks stay L2, and gap-l1clarity-1 and -3 still apply once the learner is very advanced (Smiljanić & Bradlow 2011).

No controlled trial shows that clear-speech practice changes habitual speech in healthy adults. The app could run its own single-case multiple-baseline design, with habitual probes before and after each module, to test this for this user.

Which SNR, babble type and ASR model make ASR-in-noise word accuracy track human transcription for a typical native speaker in English and in (European) French? A small calibration study against human transcribers is needed.

Leads I could not verify (the search budget was exhausted and academic hosts were blocked): Janse (2004), Speech Communication, 'Word perception in fast speech: artificially time-compressed vs. naturally produced fast speech' (title confirmed only; relevant to whether natural fast speech costs more than rate itself); Fraundorf & Watson (2011) on filled pauses and listener recall; Krause & Panagiotopoulos (2019) on rate for older listeners; Tjaden, Sussman & Wilding (2014) on clear/loud/slow speech in healthy controls; Scarborough & Zellou (2013) on real versus imagined listeners; Van Engen et al. (2012) and Keerstock & Smiljanić on clear speech and memory.
Are there peer-reviewed controlled evaluations of Microsoft Presenter/Speaker Coach, Orai, Yoodli or similar tools? None were found with the access available.

Is there any European-French clear-speech training study, or French diction or 'prise de parole' training with listener outcomes? The Brazilian 'técnica da rolha' (cork technique) literature was unreachable.
Does clear-speech practice in native French carry over to clearer L2 English, or the reverse?
How reliable are the automatic measures (vowel spacing, 1–3 kHz energy, pitch variation, final-consonant release) from day to day on the user's own microphone and room?
Does crisper native speech benefit listeners in quiet, everyday settings (memory, effort, perceived competence)? Only indirect evidence was found (Guo & Smiljanić 2021; Rodero et al. 2022).
missed_evidence_flagged: Zhang Y, Janaka N, Ram A, Yin P, Tian Y, Zhao S, Dragicevic P (2025). WSCoach: Wearable Real-time Auditory Feedback for Reducing Unwanted Words in Daily Communication. arXiv:2507.04238. A preregistered randomized between-subjects study (n=24 fluent English speakers) with the Orai app as comparator. Both reduced unwanted words in conversation, and real-time feedback reduced them more, but gains faded by Day 15 after withdrawal. This contradicts 'no controlled evaluation of Orai' and bears on filler maintenance and carryover. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04238

Shriberg E, Wade E, Price P (1992). Human-machine problem solving using spoken language systems (SLS): Factors affecting performance and user satisfaction. DARPA Speech & NL Workshop, ACL Anthology H92-1009. Strongly hyperarticulated utterances had higher ASR word error rates (F(1,12)=5.19). This is a caveat for using ASR as the 'listener' in gap-l1clarity-3 and as the clarity proxy in gap-l1clarity-9; modern ASR is untested on this. https://aclanthology.org/H92-1009/

Tuttösí et al. (2026), Study 3c, already cited but its ASR result was missed. Whisper ASR improved most with global slowing, unlike human L2 listeners, and all rate manipulations increased out-of-pair errors. An ASR-in-babble proxy therefore needs human calibration for rate and duration features. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.30032

Corley M, MacGregor LJ, Donaldson DI (2007). It's the way that you, er, say it: Hesitations in speech affect language comprehension. Cognition 105(3):658-668. Also Fox Tree JE (2001). Listeners' uses of um and uh in speech comprehension. Memory & Cognition 29(2):320-326. Fillers can aid listener word recognition and memory, which supports keeping filler counts out of any clarity score. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2006.10.010

Smiljanić R, Keerstock S, Meemann K, Ransom SM (2021). Face masks and speaking style affect audio-visual word recognition and memory of native and non-native speech. JASA 149(6):4013-4023. Clear speech improved both word recognition and recall in all listening conditions. This is a direct clear-speech precedent for the proposed listener-memory check, better than the Sarampalis noise-reduction analogy. https://doi.org/10.1121/10.0005191

Smiljanić R, Bradlow AR (2005). Production and perception of clear speech in Croatian and English. JASA 118(3):1677-1688. The clear-speech effect and its strategies (slower rate, wider pitch range, vowel-space expansion) held across two languages. This supports running one habitual-vs-clear module in both EN and FR, though French itself was not tested. https://doi.org/10.1121/1.2000788

Jung Y-J, Dmitrieva O (2023). Non-native talkers and listeners and the perceptual benefits of clear speech. JASA 153(1):137-148 (https://doi.org/10.1121/10.0016820). Also Kato M, Baese-Berk M (2022). Perceptual consequences of native and non-native clear speech. JASA 151(2):1246-1258 (https://doi.org/10.1121/10.0009403). Newer evidence that fluent L2 talkers produce effective clear speech, relevant to the advanced-L2 case in gap-l1clarity-1. Findings are known only from a secondary summary.

Hazan V, Tuomainen O, Kim J, Davis C, Sheffield B, Brungart D (2018). Clear speech adaptations in spontaneous speech produced by young and older adults. JASA 144(3):1331-1346. Measures spontaneous, interactive clear speech (lower articulation rate, higher F0, more mid-frequency energy), which is relevant to designing unprompted 'habitual probes' rather than read items. https://doi.org/10.1121/1.5053218

Aoki NB, Zellou G (2024). Being clear about clear speech: Intelligibility of hard-of-hearing-directed, non-native-directed, and casual speech for L1- and L2-English listeners. Journal of Phonetics 104:101328. Evidence that the imagined listener shapes intelligibility, relevant to the cue wording in gap-l1clarity-1; its findings were not verified here.

Kryston K, Goble H, Eden A (2021), full text on GitHub. Its own data show the practice vs no-practice contrast was non-randomized (self-selected non-attenders, mean grade ~50 vs ~95). This should be stated wherever the study is used. https://github.com/CJL196/aipapers/blob/master/693d652efab55b0207482a7f/paper.md

general_review.topic: gap-frenchl2: L2 French pronunciation priorities and training evidence (segments, liaison, prosody, variety) for adult learners
general_review.summary:
Verification limits come first. The session's web-search budget was used up, and the egress proxy blocked every publisher, DOI, Google Scholar, ERIC, HAL, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and ACL Anthology page. The only reachable sources were GitHub and raw.githubusercontent.com. So I verified sources through GitHub-hosted material: the official ACL Anthology XML (abstracts of JEP-TALN and LREC papers), a Scopus-derived abstract corpus, Language Science Press bibliographies, open-access article sources, Microsoft's own docs repository, and the Lexique 3.83 database. Several named targets could not be opened at all: Bergeron & Trofimovich 2017, Kennedy, Blanchet & Trofimovich 2014, Liakin et al. 2015 (/y/ with ASR), Inceoglu 2016 (nasal vowels), Kocjančič Antolík et al. 2019 (ultrasound), Rochet 1995, and Oh et al. 2015. They are listed as unverified, and no finding rests on them.

Main conclusions:
(1) I found no published French functional-load ranking checked against listeners. As a stand-in, I computed frequency-weighted minimal pairs from Lexique 3.83 (71,252 distinct pronunciations, weighted by film-subtitle frequency). The contrasts that carry the most meaning are:
- oral vs nasal vowels (à/en, sans/ça, bon/beau);
- nasal vs nasal vowels (en/on, sans/sont, temps/ton);
- schwa vs /e/ or /a/ in articles and pronouns (le/les, de/des, le/la), which carry number and gender;
- final consonants that mark gender (petit/petite, tout/toute) and final /ʁ/ (fait/faire, dit/dire).
/y/-/u/ (tu/tout, vu/vous) is in the middle. /ø/-/œ/, /o/-/ɔ/ and /ɛ̃/-/œ̃/ separate almost no frequent words.
(2) Azure Pronunciation Assessment returns much less for fr-FR than for en-US. Prosody scores, phoneme names, the phoneme actually spoken, and syllable results are all en-US only. So v1's French prosody track and its named weak-phoneme drills cannot work as designed.
(3) French-specific training studies are few and small. Shadowing helped French /ɥi/ (n=30, but production improved only for intermediate learners). Visual pitch feedback helped French intonation (Hardison 2004 via a secondary description; a two-learner case study in 2024). Hand-clapping rhythm training improved accent ratings and final-vowel lengthening, but only in children. Speaking rate and syllable timing separate learners from native speakers of French. Comprehensibility ratings are inflated when raters do not know what the speaker meant. Liaison research from the IPFC corpus shows errors shared across L1s and weak knowledge of when liaison varies.
(4) On variety: Québec French differs enough that aligners need their own models. The vowel mergers found in native speech carry almost no lexical load, so the app should accept them.

Design direction: re-weight French targets by the meaning they carry, not by Azure's lowest scores. Build French timing and pitch analysis with its own forced alignment. Test intelligibility against the sentence the learner meant to say. Keep liaison drills to obligatory, meaning-bearing contexts. Pick one French variety and use it everywhere.

findings.claim: Frequency-weighted minimal-pair counts on Lexique 3.83 (weight = the lower of the two words' film-subtitle frequencies) reproduce exactly. Across all vowel pairs, the heaviest loads are a-e (6.1%) and ɛ-a (3.4%). Next come a-ə (3.3%) and e-ɛ (3.2%; 95% of that weight is word-final, mostly verb endings), then ɛ-ɔ̃, ɑ̃-e, e-ə (2.8%), a-ɔ̃ and e-ɔ̃. a-ɑ̃ ranks 10th (2.5%) and ɑ̃-ɔ̃ 14th (2.2%). Among contrasts that learners plausibly confuse, the largest loads are oral vs nasal and nasal vs nasal vowels, schwa vs /e/ and /a/ in determiners, and presence vs absence of a final consonant (final t: 1,776 pairs; final ʁ: 2,274). y-u, i-y and u-o carry moderate load. ø-œ, ɛ̃-œ̃ and o-ɔ carry almost none. This is an unvalidated lexical proxy: it takes no account of sentence context, and no listener has tested it. A peer-reviewed cross-language functional-load study that probably includes French exists (Oh et al. 2015).
findings.population: No learners. Native French lexicon (Lexique 3.83, 142,694 entries, 71,252 distinct pronunciations) weighted by film-subtitle frequency per million.
findings.effect_notes: This is a functional-load proxy, not entropy-based FL, and it has not been checked against listeners. Share of all frequency-weighted vowel-pair load: a-ə 3.3%, e-ɛ 3.2%, ə-e 2.8%, a-ɑ̃ 2.5%, ɑ̃-ɔ̃ 2.2%, o-ɔ̃ 1.2%, y-u 0.97%, i-y 0.90%, ɛ̃-ɑ̃ 0.23%, ɛ̃-œ̃ 0.06%, o-ɔ 0.04%, ø-œ 0.01%. Pairs where both words occur at 10 or more per million: e-ɛ 102, a-ɑ̃ 52, ɑ̃-ɔ̃ 42, ɛ̃-ɑ̃ 27, i-y 25, y-u 22, a-ə 12, ə-e 11, o-ɔ 3, ø-œ 1, ɛ̃-œ̃ 1. Lexique does not code the a-ɑ contrast. How much each error costs a listener is still unknown.
findings.design_implication: Replace 'lowest rolling Azure score' with a priority weight per contrast from this table, multiplied by the learner's error rate. Order the French minimal-pair and sentence content: (1) oral vs nasal and nasal vs nasal vowels; (2) schwa vs /e/ and /a/ in determiners and clitics (le/les/la, de/des, ce/ces) inside real phrases; (3) final consonants that mark gender or verb forms (petit/petite, grand/grande, heureux/heureuse, fait/faire); (4) y-u, i-y, u-o; (5) ʁ-l, ʃ-s. Make ø-œ, o-ɔ and ɛ̃-œ̃ optional polish items that are never scored as errors. Store the table as data (for example contrast_weights.json) so the app can re-rank as its own evidence accumulates.

citations.ref: New, Pallier, Brysbaert & Ferrand (2004), Lexique 2: A new French lexical database, Behavior Research Methods 36(3):516–524; Lexique 3.83 documentation (openlexicon)
Lexique383.tsv copy that was analysed (Git LFS mirror of the official file)

findings.claim: Azure Pronunciation Assessment gives far less for French than for en-US. Per Microsoft's docs (dated 21 Nov 2025): prosody assessment is available only in en-US; phoneme names (IPA or SAPI), the 'spoken phoneme' output (the learner's most likely actual phoneme, with confidence) and syllable groups are en-US only (SAPI phoneme names also for zh-CN). For other locales, including fr-FR and fr-CA, which are both supported, the app gets phoneme scores without phoneme names and cannot see which sound the learner substituted (e.g. [u] for /y/).
findings.population: Not applicable (vendor API documentation)
findings.effect_notes: Supported-features table in the docs: Phoneme name IPA = en-US; Syllable group = en-US; Spoken phoneme = en-US. The docs also note that unscripted assessment uses a different STT model. An open French forced-alignment model exists (MFA french_mfa v3.0.0, GMM-HMM, CC BY 4.0, trained 2024-02-29).
findings.design_implication: Do not build the French prosody track, the French speed-ladder 'articulation index' or named French weak-phoneme drills on Azure outputs. Instead: (a) map Azure fr-FR phoneme scores to phoneme labels using the app's own pronunciation lexicon (e.g. Lexique or the MFA French dictionary) for the same reference text; (b) detect substitutions with forced choice, meaning the learner reads one member of a minimal pair and ASR or alignment likelihood decides which word was heard; (c) compute French timing (syllable durations, phrase-final lengthening, pauses) and F0 contours from the app's own forced alignment (MFA French) plus a pitch tracker. Show a notice in French mode that prosody scores are not available from Azure.

citations.ref: Microsoft Learn, 'Use pronunciation assessment' (Azure AI Speech), ms.date 2025-11-21, section 'Supported features per locale'
Same page, source in MicrosoftDocs repository (verified copy)
Azure Speech language support, pronunciation assessment tab (lists fr-FR and fr-CA)
McAuliffe & Sonderegger (2024), French MFA acoustic model v3.0.0

findings.claim: Comprehensibility ratings of L2 French are inflated when raters do not know what the speaker meant. 80 native French listeners rated utterances by 9 German-L1 learners of French from a translation task, first without a reference (a priori) and then with the reference translation (a posteriori). Scores were significantly higher in the a priori condition, with a large effect size. Unreferenced ratings miss mismatches between the intended and the perceived message.
findings.population: Adult German-L1 learners of French (n=9 speakers); 80 native French listeners
findings.effect_notes: The abstract reports a significant difference with a 'large' effect size; exact values were not available in the abstract. Rated as moderate because it has many raters and a within-rater design, but it is a single conference paper with one L1.
findings.design_implication: Score French intelligibility against the intended message, not against a 'sounds understandable' judgement. In scripted mode, compare an ASR transcript with the target sentence, including whether minimal-pair words survive (tu vs tout, le vs les). In free-speech mode, have the learner type or select the intended meaning first, then compare. Never report an unreferenced comprehensibility or self-rating as the progress metric.

citations.ref: De Fino, Ferrané, Pinquier & Fontan (2024), Peut-on évaluer la compréhensibilité de la parole sans référence quant aux intentions de communication du locuteur ? Actes JEP 2024, pp. 492–501
ACL Anthology metadata/abstract source (2024.jeptalnrecital XML)

findings.claim: Timing and rhythm measures separate L2 French from native French. A Gaussian mixture model of 16 duration-based parameters, taken automatically from the signal with no ASR, was trained on 1,340 native speakers from the CEFC corpus. Japanese A2 learners (n=29) scored much lower than native test speakers (n=146; p<.0001). Mixed-proficiency non-native speakers in CEFC (n=37) showed only a trend (p=.067). The most discriminating parameters were mean inter-syllabic duration, its coefficient of variation, and speech rate; phonation ratio also mattered for the Japanese learners.
findings.population: Adult learners of French (Japanese L1 at A2, n=29; 37 non-native speakers of mixed L1 and level); 1,340 plus 146 native French speakers
findings.effect_notes: This measures membership in a native model, a proxy for accent, not listener-rated comprehensibility. It covers one learner L1 at low proficiency. Effect sizes were reported as eta-squared, but the values are not in the abstract.
findings.design_implication: For French 'articulation', track timing measures benchmarked against native distributions: articulation rate, phonation-time ratio, pause frequency and length, and variability of syllable duration. Do not import English stress-timing metrics. Report these as trends, not pass/fail, because they signal accent more than intelligibility. Do not ask for more speed until timing is within the native range.

citations.ref: Coulange & Rossato (2020), Rhythmic Proximity Between Natives And Learners Of French – Evaluation of a metric based on the CEFC corpus, LREC 2020
Coulange & Rossato (2020), Proximité rythmique entre apprenants et natifs du français, JEP 2020, pp. 118–126

findings.claim: Evidence on French phrase-final prosody training is thin. One production study of Japanese-L1 learners (Albar 2020; n not in the abstract) found appropriate F0 rises at accentual-phrase and intonation-phrase boundaries but uneven use of duration. The abstract reports no native comparison and concludes that duration is not a robust cue for continuation, so it does not show that lengthening is the learners' main deficit. Clapping to word rhythm improved accentedness and final-vowel lengthening in 28 Catalan children aged 7–8 (Baills & Prieto, Language Teaching Research) and improved the pronunciation of French words in Chinese adolescents (Zhang, Baills & Prieto 2020, LTR 24(5):666–689). An adult study exists (Baills, Alazard-Guiu & Prieto 2022, Applied Linguistics 43(4):776–804). Its title reports gains, but Sbranna (2025) cites it as showing no robust effects. Italian-L1 learners carry their L1 habit of marking focus with vowel duration into French (De Paolis 2024; 15 per group).
findings.population: Japanese-L1 learners of French (production study; n not in abstract); Catalan children aged 7–8 learning French words (n=28); 60 participants in the focus study (15 per group); adult evidence from Baills et al. 2022 not verified
findings.effect_notes: Clapping study: pre/post design, clapping group improved significantly more (effect size not in abstract), children only, short training. The Albar and De Paolis studies are descriptive production studies, not training studies. The adult embodied-training outcome is unverified and secondary descriptions conflict.
findings.design_implication: Build one French 'accentual phrase' drill that scores what learners miss: lengthening of the last syllable in each rhythmic group, plus a continuation rise or final fall, measured from the app's own alignment (see gap-frenchl2-2). Offer an optional 'tap the rhythm' mode (tap or clap on the phrase-final syllable) labelled experimental for adults. For learners whose L1 has lexical stress, add feedback that flags lengthening or pitch prominence on non-final syllables.

citations.ref: Albar (2020), Production de la continuation du français par des apprenants japonophones : gestion de la F0 et de la durée, JEP 2020, pp. 10–18
Hand-clapping study with 7–8-year-old Catalan children learning French words (Scopus abstract record in the Annif education corpus); authors and venue not verified

Baills, Alazard-Guiu & Prieto (2022), Embodied prosodic training helps improve accentedness and suprasegmental accuracy, Applied Linguistics 43(4):776–804, doi 10.1093/applin/amac010 (metadata verified via Language Science Press bibliography only)
De Paolis (2024), Allongement vocalique en italien L2 et en français L2 : une marque de focalisation ? JEP 2024, pp. 242–251

findings.claim: French-specific evidence on intonation training is very small, and no study compares methods, so 'best-supported' is not established. Hincks & Edlund (2009) describe Hardison (2004) as showing that training with a real-time visual pitch display improved learner production at both the suprasegmental and segmental level; the details are unverified here. Xiao et al. (2024) is an n=2 feasibility case study of gesture-controlled speech synthesis, with no control group. Learners traced contours on a tablet and heard them synthesised; this is not visual feedback on their own pitch. Both beginners came to differentiate declaratives from yes/no questions, and incredulity improved for one of them.
findings.population: Adult learners of French (Hardison 2004: details unverified); 2 Ukrainian-L1 beginners (Xiao et al. 2024)
findings.effect_notes: No effect sizes are available. The 2024 study has n=2 and no control group. The Hardison 2004 result is known here only through a secondary description.
findings.design_implication: For French prosody, show the learner's F0 contour over a native reference for a small set of meaningful patterns: declarative fall, yes/no question rise, continuation rise at the end of a non-final group. Add a 'trace the contour' warm-up before recording. Score the direction and alignment of the contour on the final syllable, not a global prosody number.

citations.ref: Hincks & Edlund (2009), Promoting increased pitch variation in oral presentations with transient visual feedback, LLT 13(3):32–50 (full text; describes Hardison 2004)
Xiao, Bonnet, Zhang, Audibert, Kühnert & Pillot-Loiseau (2024), Enseignement de l'intonation du français par une synthèse vocale contrôlée par le geste : étude de faisabilité, JEP 2024, pp. 342–350

findings.claim: Shadowing and delayed imitation both improved French /ɥi/, which Mandarin-L1 learners tend to produce close to [y]. Thirty learners trained on their own for 4 weeks. Both methods improved perception and production. Shadowing improved perception for beginners and intermediates but production (a larger F3–F2 distance for /i/ in /ɥi/, i.e. clearer separation from /y/) only for intermediates. The authors suggest shadowing works only once proficiency is high enough to perform the task.
findings.population: 30 adult female Mandarin-L1 learners of French (beginner and intermediate)
findings.effect_notes: 4 weeks of autonomous practice, acoustic outcome (F2/F3), pre/post with two training methods. The abstract mentions no untrained control and gives no effect sizes.
findings.design_implication: Gate shadowing by level. Beginners, or learners failing a target, get listen-then-repeat (delayed imitation) first. Shadowing unlocks after accuracy on the item stabilises. For front rounded vowels and glides (/y/, /ɥi/), include perception tasks such as 'which word did you hear?' with tu/tout and lui/Louis before production drills.

citations.ref: Fu, Adda-Decker & Kühnert (2024), Effets du shadowing et de l'imitation en tant que méthodes d'entraînement à la prononciation du /ɥi/ en français, JEP 2024, pp. 332–341

findings.claim: A longitudinal IPFC doctoral study of Italian-L1 learners of French (A2–B1; n not in the abstract), compared with other IPFC L1 groups, found common tendencies and errors across L1s. It found a mix of lexical strategies and emerging phonological generalisation, and weaknesses both in producing liaison and in knowing how it varies. It proposed teaching materials based on liaison frequencies in the native PFC corpus. 'Only obligatory liaison carries meaning' is the author's inference, not the thesis's finding, and it is incomplete. A liaison produced where it is forbidden (h aspiré, as in les héros vs les zéros; after et; between a singular noun and a following adjective) also changes or obscures meaning. At least one controlled classroom study measured liaison production after mobile TTS practice (Liakin, Cardoso & Liakina 2017, Computer Assisted Language Learning, 'focus on French liaison'), so 'no controlled liaison training study' reflects the search, not the literature.
findings.population: Italian-L1 university learners of French (A2–B1), longitudinal, plus IPFC cross-L1 comparison; n not in abstract
findings.effect_notes: Descriptive corpus and longitudinal evidence only. I found no controlled liaison training study I could verify; Liakin et al. 2017 on TTS-based practice is not a liaison outcome study (see gap-frenchl2-9). The thesis author is not verified here.
findings.design_implication: Limit the liaison curriculum to obligatory, high-frequency contexts: determiner + noun (les amis, des enfants, un ami), pronoun + verb (ils ont, nous avons, vous avez, on a), and fixed phrases. Add perception and production pairs where liaison changes meaning (ils ont vs ils sont, les amis vs l'ami). Treat optional liaisons (est allé, comment allez-vous) as acceptable either way, never as errors. Pair each liaison item with enchaînement (resyllabifying across the word boundary) and score it with the app's own alignment, since Azure fr-FR cannot report which phoneme was actually spoken.

citations.ref: Doctoral thesis 2015PA100186 (Université Paris Nanterre), IPFC study of L2 liaison acquisition by Italian-L1 learners; abstract text (theses.fr record)
Same abstract, verified copy on GitHub

Racine, Zay, Detey & Kawaguchi (2012), Des atouts d'un corpus multitâches pour l'étude de la phonologie en L2 : l'exemple du projet IPFC, in Kamber & Skupiens (eds), Recherches récentes en FLE, Peter Lang, pp. 1–19 (metadata only)

findings.claim: ASR dictation as an 'intelligibility mirror' for L2 French is well received, but the evidence I could check covers perceptions, not measured production gains. Mroz (2018) interviewed 16 learners of French who used ASR (Gmail dictation); most saw it as a useful diagnostic that showed where they were and were not intelligible. Liakin, Cardoso & Liakina (2017) surveyed learners after weekly ASR-based (n=14) or TTS-based (n=9) mobile practice; both groups rated the tools useful, and TTS users reported that pronunciation improved through more exposure to a model. The production outcome study (Liakin et al. 2015, French /y/ with mobile ASR) could not be verified.
findings.population: Adult university learners of French as a foreign language (n=16 qualitative; n=14 and n=9 survey and interview)
findings.effect_notes: Qualitative and descriptive only: no controlled production outcomes and no effect sizes in the sources I could open.
findings.design_implication: Use a general French ASR transcript only as a lenient 'were you understood?' check on sentences full of minimal pairs (e.g. 'Tu as vu tout ce que vous avez vu?'). Show which target words were misrecognised. Label it as intelligibility feedback, not an accuracy score. Pair it with explicit contrast feedback and a native model (TTS, then real recordings). Do not claim it trains pronunciation without the app's own before/after data.

citations.ref: Mroz (2018), Seeing how people hear you: French learners experiencing intelligibility through automatic speech recognition, Foreign Language Annals 51(3):617–637, doi 10.1111/flan.12348 (study details via Silva et al. 2022, below)
Liakin, Cardoso & Liakina (2017), Mobilizing instruction in a second-language context: Learners' perceptions of two speech technologies, Languages 2(3):11, doi 10.3390/languages2030011
Texto Livre (2022) v15 article 36736, 'Automatic speech recognition and text-to-speech technologies for L2 pronunciation improvement' (open-access source describing both studies)

findings.claim: Choose one French variety and accept native mergers. Québec French acoustics and sound patterns differ widely from France French: long vowels diphthongise and /t d/ affricate before high vowels. Standard aligners could not segment Québec French until QF-specific lexicons and acoustic models were built. At the same time, the mergers common in native France French carry almost no lexical load: ɛ̃-œ̃ has 8 pairs (brin/brun), ø-œ 11 (jeune/jeûne), o-ɔ 3 frequent pairs, and Lexique already codes a-ɑ as a single vowel. I found no listener study on how a France-trained vs Québec-trained accent affects intelligibility for the other community.
findings.population: Native Québec French speech resources (aligner development); native France French lexicon
findings.effect_notes: The Québec acoustic model was adapted with 5 minutes of manually aligned data. The strength rating covers the tooling claim; there is no listener evidence on how acceptable either variety is as a target.
findings.design_implication: Add a variety setting (fr-FR default, fr-CA optional) that switches the TTS voice, the Azure assessment locale, the aligner model and dictionary, and the target inventory together. Never mark ɛ̃/œ̃, ø/œ, o/ɔ, a/ɑ or word-final e/ɛ mergers as errors. In fr-CA mode, accept affricated [ts dz] before /i y/ and laxed high vowels in closed syllables.

citations.ref: Lancien, Côté & Bigi (2020), Developing Resources for Automated Speech Processing of Quebec French, LREC 2020
Lexique 3.83 documentation (source for the merger counts computed in gap-frenchl2-1)

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using Azure prosody scores or Azure 'spoken phoneme' output to train French: both are en-US only, so a French prosody or liaison track scored this way gets no valid signal.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Confirmed by the MicrosoftDocs source (ms.date 11/21/2025): prosody and spoken phoneme are en-US only. More precisely, these outputs are not returned at all for fr-FR, rather than returned but invalid. For liaison, the docs do not settle the question: fr-FR still returns word-level miscues and unnamed phoneme scores for the reference text. Whether a missing liaison consonant shows up in those scores is untested, not shown to be impossible.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Choosing French drill targets by lowest raw Azure phoneme score. The score ignores how much meaning a contrast carries and how natives vary. For fr-FR, Azure does not name the phoneme or the sound actually produced, so a substitution like [u] for /y/ cannot be diagnosed.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The docs confirm that non-en-US locales get phoneme scores without phoneme names and no spoken-phoneme output. The functional-load weighting that motivates the alternative reproduces from Lexique, but it is itself an unvalidated proxy.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Spending practice time on contrasts that separate almost no frequent words and are merged by many native speakers (/ø/-/œ/, /o/-/ɔ/, /ɛ̃/-/œ̃/, word-final /e/-/ɛ/). In the Lexique analysis each has 3 or fewer pairs of frequent words (10 or more per million), except e-ɛ, whose pairs are mostly verb endings that native speakers merge.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Counts reproduce: ø-œ 1, o-ɔ 3, ɛ̃-œ̃ 1, and 91 of 102 frequent e-ɛ pairs are word-final. Lexique does not show native merger rates; that part rests on general sociophonetic knowledge. Caveat: this applies only to the contrast within each pair. The front rounded vowels as a class still carry load against other vowels (deux/des, peur/père, tu/tout), so learners must still produce [ø]/[œ] as distinct from /e/, /ɛ/ and /u/. Québec French keeps some of these contrasts.

does_not_work_verified.claim: French tongue-twister speed ladders as intelligibility or articulation training. I found no French study showing that faster tongue-twister reading improves intelligibility. The one timing study found rate and syllable-timing profiles separate learners from native speakers, which argues for native-like timing over maximum speed.
does_not_work_verified.notes: This rests on absence of evidence; I found no contrary French evidence. Coulange & Rossato (2020) show that speech rate and inter-syllabic timing separate learners (mostly slower) from natives. That supports aiming for native-like timing, but it is not a test of speed training.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Scoring optional liaisons (est allé, comment allez-vous) as right or wrong. Native use varies, and only obligatory liaison carries grammatical meaning.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The thesis abstract stresses that liaison varies and that learners lack knowledge of that variation, which supports not scoring optional liaisons. But 'only obligatory liaison carries meaning' is too strong: liaisons produced where they are forbidden (h aspiré, as in les héros vs les zéros; after et) also affect meaning and should be scored as errors.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Unreferenced comprehensibility judgements, by self-rating or by a listener who does not know the intended message, as the success metric. They significantly overestimate understanding of L2 French, with a large effect.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Supported for native listeners by De Fino et al. (2024): 80 listeners, 9 speakers, large effect, magnitude not given in the abstract. Self-rating was not tested there. Evidence that self-assessment is unreliable comes from other work (e.g., Trofimovich et al. 2016, with French-L1 learners of English). Unreferenced comprehensibility remains a valid measure of perceived ease of understanding; it just should not stand in for intelligibility.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Assuming that embodied rhythm training (clapping) works for adults because it worked for children. The verified French clapping evidence comes from 7–8-year-olds; the adult study was not verified and is described inconsistently by secondary sources.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The caution is warranted, but the premise is incomplete. Zhang, Baills & Prieto (2020, LTR 24(5):666–689) found clapping benefits for French words in Chinese adolescents. The adult study (Baills et al. 2022) exists; its title claims gains, and Sbranna (2025) cites it as showing no robust effects. So adult evidence is mixed rather than absent.

critique_of_v1: Factual error in client/src/languages/fr-FR/phonemes.json: the example for ɑ̃ is 'vin', which is /vɛ̃/, and the example for ɛ̃ is 'vent', which is /vɑ̃/. The two nasal-vowel examples are swapped. Exercise fr-phon-04 ('Vin, vent, bon, blanc') is tagged only ɑ̃ although it mixes three nasal vowels.

The French pack spends most items on low-payoff targets. Four of six phoneme items and all three articulation items target /ʁ/, /s/ or /ʃ/ through tongue twisters. The highest-load contrasts in the Lexique analysis are missing: oral vs nasal and nasal vs nasal vowels in minimal pairs (à/en, sans/sont, temps/ton), schwa vs /e/ in articles and pronouns (le/les, de/des), and final consonants that mark gender (petit/petite).

/ʁ/ is treated as a top-difficulty (3) priority. An English-style r is an accent feature. The Lexique analysis shows ʁ-l and ʁ-v do separate many words, so the priority should be not merging /ʁ/ with /l/, /v/ or zero (fait/faire, dit/dire), not a perfect uvular sound.

The French prosody track (PRD section 5, track C) depends on Azure prosody and fluency scores. Azure prosody is en-US only, so French liaison, enchaînement and 'even-syllable rhythm' items get no valid prosody feedback. Both liaison items (comment allez-vous, il est allé) are optional liaisons, and Azure fr-FR cannot report whether the liaison consonant was actually produced.

The weak-phoneme engine ('5 lowest-scoring phonemes') assumes phoneme names, but Azure provides them only for en-US. For French it needs a lexicon-based mapping, and even then it cannot detect which sound was substituted. It also ignores functional load, so a low /ʁ/ score would outrank a /y/-/u/ or schwa-/e/ error that changes meaning.

The ≥85 advance thresholds for phonemes and speed ladders have no validation for French: no evidence links Azure fr-FR accuracy to French listener intelligibility. Speed ladders driven by TTS tempo reward speed, while the one French timing study points to native-like speech rate, phonation ratio and syllable-timing profiles.

The app has no French perception training: no identification or discrimination tasks before production, even though the verified French shadowing study found perception gains and that production gains depend on level.
There is no variety setting, and nothing stops the app from penalising native mergers (ø/œ, o/ɔ, ɛ̃/œ̃, e/ɛ). The French target inventory is implicitly Parisian with no stated policy.

The metrics measure accuracy against Azure, never intelligibility against the intended sentence. That is the measure most likely to reflect real communication, and unreferenced judgements are shown to be inflated.
open_questions: Verification gap, highest priority: I could not open Bergeron & Trofimovich 2017 (Foreign Language Annals) or Kennedy, Blanchet & Trofimovich 2014 because publisher, DOI and index sites were blocked and the search budget was used up. Which linguistic features they found predict comprehensibility vs accentedness in L2 French is still unverified. Nagle, Trofimovich & Bergeron 2019 (SSLA 41(4):647–672) exists (metadata verified), but whether it used L2 French speech was not checked.

Unverified intervention studies that should be checked before any French drill is justified by them: Liakin, Cardoso & Liakina 2015 (French /y/ with mobile ASR; group sizes and effect sizes); Inceoglu 2016 (audiovisual vs audio-only perceptual training on French nasal vowels); Kocjančič Antolík, Pillot-Loiseau & Kamiyama 2019 (ultrasound feedback, including /y/-/u/ with Japanese learners); Rochet 1995 (/y/ perception and production by English and Portuguese speakers; only the bibliographic entry was verified); Hardison 2004 (population and effect sizes).

IPFC perceptual work on /y/-/u/ (Racine, Detey & Kawaguchi, JEP 2012; ACL Anthology F12-1.49, no abstract available) and other Detey/Racine/Kawaguchi analyses: which learner errors do native listeners actually notice, and how does that differ by L1?

Oh et al. 2015 (Journal of Phonetics) on cross-language functional load: I could not check whether French is included. Does an entropy-based French functional-load ranking agree with the frequency-weighted minimal-pair proxy computed here?

No study was found that tests whether higher-load French contrasts (oral/nasal, schwa/e in determiners, final gender consonants) cost more listener intelligibility than /y/-/u/ or /ʁ/. The app could collect its own evidence by logging ASR recognition of each minimal-pair member per contrast before and after training.
Does Azure fr-FR phoneme accuracy correlate with French listener judgements, and does it penalise acceptable native variants (mergers, schwa deletion, Québec affrication)?
Are fr-FR and fr-CA targets equally intelligible to listeners from each community? No evidence was found.

Controlled adult evidence for French liaison or enchaînement training, and for accentual-phrase (final-lengthening) training, seems not to exist beyond small studies. This needs a dedicated search once publisher sites are reachable.

The learner's L1 is still unknown. If it is French, the French track becomes native clarity and articulation training (clear speech, rate control), which needs a different evidence base than the L2 findings above.

general_review.summary: How to measure pronunciation progress cheaply and reliably for one self-study learner. Limits on the search: the session's web-search budget was used up and the proxy blocked most publisher and index sites (doi.org, Cambridge, PubMed, ERIC, Semantic Scholar, arXiv). The evidence therefore comes from sources I could open directly. These were GitHub-hosted copies of ACL Anthology records, PMC/PubMed texts, arXiv mirrors, author bibliographies with abstracts, CRAN documentation and Microsoft's own documentation source. I also ran a new analysis of the public speechocean762 corpus, where five experts scored the same 5,000 English sentences read by 250 Mandarin-L1 speakers, half of them children (scripts: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Pronunciation-App/068447d4-a3de-57c4-bad3-f3ab993b90ae/scratchpad/gm/irr.py and tok.py). Several requested sources could not be opened and are not cited as evidence: Nagle, Trofimovich & Bergeron 2019; Nagle's crowdsourcing papers; Isaacs & Thomson 2013; Kang et al. on L1 vs L2 listeners; the What Works Clearinghouse (WWC) standards for single-case designs. Main conclusions. (1) One human rater is only moderately reliable. A single expert's intraclass correlation (ICC) was .51–.64 on 0–10 sentence scales, and in an L2 study each rater correlated with the other raters' mean at only r = .46–.73. About 3–4 raters reach .80 and 5–9 reach .90. Lay listeners serve about as well as experts when their ratings are pooled. For yes/no judgements on single sounds, clinical studies pool at least 9 naive online listeners per token. (2) Ratings drift within a session, depend on which other samples are heard, and are biased by listener expectations. So baseline and current recordings should be rated together, blind to date, in random order, with fixed anchor clips. (3) Transcription intelligibility and 9-point comprehensibility correlate at about r = .57–.66 and are not interchangeable. Automatic transcripts hide mispronunciations, and more accurate recognisers hide more. (4) Experts often disagree on single sounds. For outright errors, Cohen's kappa was .60, and when one expert marks a sound wrong another agrees only 64% of the time. Estimating how often a learner gets one phoneme wrong with reliability .80 takes about 8–22 tokens (median about 14) even with five-expert consensus labels. v1 decides after 3. (5) The only Azure validity figures are correlations across different English speakers. On speechocean762 the overall score correlates with experts at about r = .78, roughly the level of one expert rater. I found no independent test-retest data for Azure, SpeechAce, SpeechSuper or ELSA, and no French validation. For fr-FR, Azure gives no phoneme names, no report of which phoneme was actually spoken, and no prosody score. Microsoft updated the en-US and fr-FR scoring models in August 2026, so scores from before and after that date are not directly comparable. (6) Speech-therapy trials judge learning on untrained items and delayed retention probes, not on accuracy during practice. Small N-of-1 designs, such as a multiple baseline across target sounds, can be analysed with standard single-case effect sizes plus a reliable-change threshold built from the learner's own repeat recordings.

findings.claim: In speechocean762 (5 trained experts scoring short read sentences from Mandarin-L1 children and adults, 0–10 scales), one expert's absolute-agreement ICC(2,1) was .61 for accuracy, .51 for fluency, .51 for prosody and .64 for total. The mean of 5 experts reached .84–.90, and .80 reliability needs about 2.3–3.8 such raters. Much of the single-rater unreliability is systematic severity: rater means differ by up to about 1.9 points, and consistency ICC(3,1) is .65–.70. That bias cancels when the same rater scores both time points in one sitting. For native raters judging L2 accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility (Issa & Ali 2026; 90 samples, 10 raters), the leave-one-out r was .46–.73 across dimensions. Those values imply single-rater reliability of roughly .27–.58, so .80 needs about 3–11 raters depending on the dimension. Three to five raters is enough for trained raters or the easier dimensions. Lay-listener panels may need about 10.
findings.population: speechocean762: 250 Mandarin-L1 speakers (half children) reading 5,000 English sentences, scored by 5 experts on 0–10 scales. Issa & Ali: 90 L2 speech samples rated by 10 native-speaker raters.
findings.effect_notes: speechocean762 figures were computed for this review from the public raw scores. Mean pairwise inter-rater r was .66 for accuracy, .69 fluency, .67 prosody and .71 total. One rater vs the mean of the other four: r = .77–.80. Raters for .80 reliability: accuracy 2.6, fluency 3.8, prosody 3.8, total 2.3. Caveat: these reliabilities are between speakers across a very wide ability range (children and adults). Detecting small changes in one learner is harder, so these numbers are best-case.
findings.design_implication: For each human check, collect ratings from at least 3 independent listeners, ideally 5, per recording. Show the mean with an uncertainty band. Never treat a single friend's or tutor's rating as ground truth. If only one rater is available, have them rate several recordings per time point in one sitting, and report only differences larger than that rater's own repeat-rating noise.

findings.claim: Pooled naive native listeners can approximate experts in some tasks. In the C-RESULTS protocol (children with residual /r/ errors, a clinical group), ratings are collected until at least 9 naive online listeners have rated each token. The listeners are US-based native American English speakers, see the target word in writing, and give a binary correct/incorrect judgement. The pooled proportion correct is reported to correlate strongly with expert ratings and acoustics (McAllister Byun et al. 2015/2016). For Mandarin-L1 learners, naive and experienced native raters did not differ significantly on comprehensibility or nativeness (Warren et al. 2009). That is a non-significant difference, not a shown equivalence. Lab and MTurk intelligibility ratings of only 10 native American English talkers in noise correlated r = .94, with no level difference. The only evidence that non-native listeners are adequate is one conference abstract on narrow phonetic transcription by students with self-rated phonetic skill (70% match to archive transcriptions). That is weak support for using non-native or untrained listeners to transcribe L2 speech for intelligibility.
findings.population: Mandarin-L1 learners of English (Warren et al.). Children with residual /r/ errors, a clinical group (McAllister et al.). Native American English talkers in noise (Yoho et al.; 50 lab listeners plus MTurk listeners). L2 English samples from the Speech Accent Archive, with 97 transcribers from 21 L1s (Weinberger et al.).
findings.effect_notes: Yoho et al.: lab vs MTurk mean ratings per talker r = .94, level difference p = .576. Weinberger et al.: 358 qualified submissions, 70% agreement with the gold standard. 'At least 9 listeners' is the operating rule in the McAllister lab. It comes from clinical child speech, not L2 adults, so treat it as a working default.
findings.design_implication: Build a 'listener panel' feature: a shareable link where friends, colleagues or paid crowd workers rate short clips. Non-native listeners are acceptable for transcription tasks. Use about 9 listeners per token for yes/no sound checks (for example, 'was the /θ/ right?'). Use 3–5 listeners per clip for 9-point comprehensibility. Keep each task under about 15 minutes, check that listeners use headphones, and give them the target word in writing for sound checks.

findings.claim: Listener ratings move with context and expectations, so before/after comparisons are valid only when both recordings are rated in the same blinded, randomised session. Flege & Fletcher found accent ratings unstable. Non-native speech was judged more accented when a set contained more native samples, and more accented once listeners were familiar with the sentences. In Gao's MTurk study, the same stimulus was rated more accented later in a session (β = 0.03 per trial). Ratings in the first 10–15 trials were unstable until a 10-clip practice block of anchor clips was added. In Kang & Rubin's study, listeners' tendency to stereotype plus their background explained about 23% of the variance in comprehension scores for speech presented as coming from an Asian speaker.
findings.population: Native English listeners rating L2 English: Flege & Fletcher's 4 experiments; Gao's 133 MTurk raters with 100 stimuli on a 9-point scale; Kang & Rubin's roughly 150 US listeners.
findings.effect_notes: Kang & Rubin: stereotyping predictors R² = .11; after adding four background variables R² = .23 (adjusted .18), F(7,145) = 3.97. Gao: 150 recruited, 133 retained, paid $0.50 each, mean 16 minutes. The Gao evidence is a dissertation, not peer-reviewed.
findings.design_implication: In each human-rating round, mix baseline and current recordings of the same probe items in random order, without dates. Keep the proportion of native anchor clips fixed. Start with 5–10 practice anchor clips. Present audio only, with no name, photo or voice label. Reuse the same raters across rounds where possible. Compare old and new clips within a round, never raw scores across rounds.

citations.ref: Flege J.E., Fletcher K.L. (1992). Talker and listener effects on degree of perceived foreign accent. JASA 91(1):370–389
Gao Z. (2019). Weighing Phonetic Patterns in Non-Native English Speech (PhD dissertation, George Mason University), Chapter 5 (Experiment 2)
Kang O., Rubin D.L. (2009). Reverse linguistic stereotyping: Measuring the effect of listener expectations on speech evaluation. J. Language and Social Psychology 28(4):441–456

findings.claim: Percent-words-correct transcription and scalar intelligibility ratings are related but not interchangeable: r = .658 in Yoho Exp. 1 and .57 overall. That comes from native American English talkers in noise, and two scorers agreed on 98% of keyword judgements. Separately, modern ASR recovers intended words and so masks mispronunciations. Across 8 systems and 2 L2 English corpora, systems with lower WER over-corrected more. Surface-faithful reranking cut false acceptance of mispronunciations by only 6.0 and 5.6 percentage points. ASR word accuracy is therefore not a valid measure of segmental accuracy. These sources did not compare ASR with human listeners, so they do not show that ASR is more lenient than humans on L2 intelligibility.
findings.population: Native English talkers in noise (Yoho et al.). L2 English corpora L2-ARCTIC and speechocean762 (Park).
findings.effect_notes: Yoho Exp. 1: 50 listeners, 10 talkers, IEEE sentences in cafeteria noise. The transcription/rating relationship comes from native speech. No French data.
findings.design_implication: Calibrate against humans with two tasks. (a) Listeners type 10–20 low-predictability sentences from the learner; score percent words correct automatically. (b) Listeners give a 9-point comprehensibility rating to a 30–60 s spontaneous sample. Do not use Azure or Whisper transcript accuracy as the intelligibility outcome. If an ASR 'was it understood?' check stays as practice feedback, use unpredictable sentences and label a pass as weak evidence.

citations.ref: Yoho S.E. et al. (2019). Attention, Perception & Psychophysics 81(2):558–570. doi:10.3758/s13414-018-1635-3
Park S. (2026). Intent vs. Surface: Recovering acoustic realization from modern ASR for pronunciation training. Proc. BEA 2026, 336–346. doi:10.18653/v1/2026.bea-1.23

findings.claim: Even experts often disagree on whether a single sound was mispronounced, so a learner's per-phoneme profile needs many tokens. Across 94,445 phone tokens scored by 5 experts, agreement on outright errors averaged Cohen's kappa .60 (range .56–.64). When one expert marked a phone as an error, a second expert agreed only 64% of the time. Of the phones any expert flagged, 44% were flagged by just 1 of the 5. Counting 'accented' as an error, kappa fell to .49. To estimate a speaker's error rate on one phoneme with reliability .80 took a median of about 14 tokens (8–22 by phoneme) with five-expert consensus labels. With a single expert's labels it took a median of 12–19 tokens, up to about 40.
findings.population: speechocean762: Mandarin-L1 speakers of English, children and adults, reading sentences. Phone-level scores (0 = wrong, 1 = accented, 2 = correct) from 5 experts.
findings.effect_notes: Individual raters flagged 4.9–7.1% of phones as errors. Consensus error rates per phoneme were 1–11%; highest for EY, AO, EH and R. Token-count estimates come from split-half reliability across speakers plus Spearman-Brown, using 20 random splits per phoneme.
findings.design_implication: Declare a 'weak phoneme' only after at least 15–20 scored tokens, spread over at least 5 different words or contexts and at least 3 sessions. Until then, show 'not enough data'. Use a shrinkage estimate with an interval, for example beta-binomial, and rank sounds by the interval, not the raw mean. Never colour a phoneme red from one token. Automatic phone scores are probably noisier than one expert, so treat these counts as a minimum. For fr-FR, where Azure returns no phoneme names, align phones through the app's own lexicon before counting.

findings.claim: Azure's validity evidence covers only correlations across different English speakers. I found no test-retest data and no French validation. French outputs are reduced, and the scoring models change silently. Microsoft reports only '>0.5 Pearson with human judges', with no breakdown by locale. It advises customers to run their own evaluations, and notes that quality falls with noise and microphone distance. On speechocean762, Azure's sentence-level correlation with the experts was .782 for the total score and .842 for prosody, as reported by Ahn & Nam from Wang et al. 2025. That is about one expert's level: a single expert vs the other four's mean gave r = .77–.80 in this review's analysis. Phoneme names, syllable groups and reports of which phoneme was actually spoken are en-US only, as is prosody; other locales get phoneme scores only. In August 2026 Microsoft updated the scoring models for en-US and fr-FR, among others. An LREC 2026 study likewise found accuracy the hardest dimension for automatic scoring to match to multi-rater human judgements.
findings.population: Vendor documentation. Benchmark: Mandarin-L1 learners of English (speechocean762). No French learner or French-L1 data.
findings.effect_notes: Azure's accuracy correlation on speechocean762 is below .743, since the Ahn & Nam model beat it on that dimension. Prosody .842, total .782. All of these are correlations across speakers, which says nothing about sensitivity to one learner's change or about repeat-attempt stability.
findings.design_implication: Treat Azure as one noisy rater, never as ground truth. At onboarding and then monthly, have the learner record the same 10 probe sentences twice. Use the differences to estimate the learner's own measurement error, and derive the smallest change that counts as real. Store the API or model date with every score. After a known model update, re-score the stored baseline audio with the current model instead of comparing old scores to new ones. Check recording quality (signal-to-noise ratio, clipping, distance) before scoring. French: skip automated prosody and phoneme-name feedback, and rely on lexicon alignment plus human calibration.
