findings.claim: Speech-therapy trials in clinical child groups (childhood apraxia of speech; residual /r/ errors) treat untreated-item probes and delayed retention probes as the key learning outcomes, on the principle that in-session performance is not learning. Direct evidence that practice gains fade is thin. It consists of one unreplicated RCT cited by McCabe et al. (NDP3: more effective during treatment, less retention) and one N = 8 adult L2 single-case study (Bu et al.; only 1 of 8 kept a functionally relevant /r/ change at follow-up). In McCabe et al.'s own pilot RCT (n = 14), gains on untreated words and sentences were retained at 1 month, and prosody improved by follow-up. C-RESULTS' primary outcome is in-treatment acoustics. Its listener-rated 50-word probe excludes in-treatment trials because they may be prolonged or unnatural, not because such gains fade.
findings.population: McCabe et al.: 14 children with childhood apraxia of speech, 12 sessions over 6 weeks, a clinical group. C-RESULTS: 110 children with residual /r/ errors, a clinical protocol. Bu et al.: 8 Korean-L1 adults learning English /r/.
findings.effect_notes: Bu et al. figures come from a verified secondary record (PMC8050114), not the article itself. Two of the three sources are clinical child populations. The probe-and-retention logic carries over to adult L2 learners, but the effect sizes do not.
findings.design_implication: Give each target a fixed probe bank: trained items, untrained words with the same sound, untrained sentences, and a short spontaneous task. Probe at least 3 times before training starts, at the end of each training block, and again 1–4 weeks later with no practice on that target in between. Mark a target 'mastered' only from untrained items plus the delayed probe, never from accuracy during practice.

citations.ref: McCabe P., Preston J.L., Evans P., Heard R. (2023). A pilot RCT of motor-based treatments for childhood apraxia of speech: ReST and ultrasound biofeedback. AJSLP 32(2):629–644. doi:10.1044/2022_AJSLP-22-00144
McAllister T. et al. (2020). C-RESULTS RCT protocol. BMC Pediatrics 20:66

Bu L., Nagano M., Harel D., McAllister T. (2021). Effects of practice variability on second-language speech production training. Folia Phoniatrica et Logopaedica (figures taken from a verified research record; the article itself was not opened in this session)

findings.claim: Standard single-case statistics can tell real change from noise in one learner, but each has constraints. Non-overlap of all pairs (NAP), Tau, baseline-corrected Tau and the log response ratio can all be computed for one case. Their standard errors assume independent observations, which repeated sessions for one learner may not satisfy. Tau-U has no known sampling distribution, so it has no standard error or confidence interval. The Jacobson–Truax reliable change index (RCI) needs a reliability estimate for the measure. A multiple-baseline design across target sounds, training one at a time with staggered starts, was used in the L2 /r/ study (Bu et al., finding 7). It separates training effects from general practice or time effects.
findings.population: Single-case methods, not specific to any population. Example application: 8 adult L2 English learners (Bu et al.).
findings.effect_notes: I could not verify the minimum points per phase (the commonly cited WWC 3/5 rule) from its source in this session; see open questions. 'At least 3 baseline probes' is a working default, not a verified standard.
findings.design_implication: Run a multiple baseline across 2–3 target sounds. Probe every target each session, start training on one target at a time, and claim an effect only when the trained target rises while the untrained ones stay flat. Report NAP with a confidence interval, or the log response ratio on probe accuracy. Set a reliable-change threshold from the learner's own repeat recordings (finding 6). Show 'no reliable change yet' instead of small score movements. Avoid Tau-U as the headline statistic.

citations.ref: Pustejovsky J.E. et al. SingleCaseES: effect size definitions vignette (NAP, Tau, Tau-U, Tau-BC, LRR)
Wilbert J., Lueke T. scan: Single-case data analyses for single and multiple baseline designs (CRAN)
Claus B. clinicalsignificance R package (Jacobson & Truax RCI); companion paper doi:10.18637/jss.v111.i01
Bu L. et al. (2021). Folia Phoniatrica et Logopaedica (multiple baseline across behaviours, adult L2)

findings.claim: Short general tests exist for onboarding, but they measure broad abilities and one session is only moderately reliable. Saito & Tierney gave an auditory-processing battery twice to 100 people. Test-retest reliability ranged from fair to excellent, ICC(2,2) = .4–.8, depending on the subtest. A meta-analysis of elicited imitation (46 reports, 60 effect sizes) found it correlates r = .66 with other proficiency measures, more strongly with longer stimuli. It indexes global proficiency, not a segmental error profile.
findings.population: Adult L2 learners from various L1s (elicited imitation meta-analysis). 100 adults tested twice (auditory processing).
findings.effect_notes: Both are abstract-level figures; per-subtest ICCs were not extracted. I found no reliability data for identification tests on specific contrasts (for example /i/-/ɪ/, /y/-/u/).
findings.design_implication: Use a short elicited-imitation block (about 20 sentences of increasing length, in each language) only to set content difficulty, not to find pronunciation weaknesses. If perception or auditory tests are included at onboarding, give them in two sessions and average the results. Do not make single-session decisions from subtests with ICC below .7.

citations.ref: Saito K., Tierney A. (2024). Domain-general auditory processing as a conceptual and measurement framework for L2 speech learning aptitude: a test-retest reliability study. SSLA 46(4):1206–1230
Kostromitina M., Plonsky L. (2021 online / 2022). Elicited imitation tasks as a measure of L2 proficiency: A meta-analysis. SSLA 44(3):886–911

findings.claim: For Japanese-L1 learners of English (2 experiments × 40, timed picture description), only high-functional-load consonant substitutions (e.g. /l/→/r/, /v/→/b/) lowered native listeners' comprehensibility ratings. Low-functional-load errors did not. This is consistent with Munro & Derwing 2006 and Kang & Moran 2014. It supports prioritising high-functional-load English consonant errors over raw error counts. No cited source validates a read passage plus free speech as a diagnostic of an individual's error profile when the L1 is unknown. The Speech Accent Archive figure is 70% agreement of crowdsourced narrow transcriptions with archive transcriptions, which is not diagnostic accuracy. Weighting by word frequency, and any French functional-load ranking, are untested.
findings.population: Japanese-L1 learners of English (Suzukida & Saito, 2 × 40). L2 English speakers from many L1s (Speech Accent Archive).
findings.effect_notes: Evidence is English-only and from a single L1 group for functional load. I could not open the Suzukida & Saito article's DOI page, so it is cited from its abstract record.
findings.design_implication: Onboarding: a standard read passage covering every phoneme in several contexts, plus a 60-second picture description, for each language. Treat errors found there as candidates only. Confirm each with a targeted probe of at least 15 tokens (finding 5) before it drives training. Rank confirmed errors by functional load × word frequency. For French, compute functional load from minimal-pair counts in a French lexicon such as Lexique; I found no French functional-load/comprehensibility study.

citations.ref: Suzukida Y., Saito K. (2021). Which segmental features matter for successful L2 comprehensibility? Revisiting and generalizing the pedagogical value of the functional load principle. Language Teaching Research (abstract record)
Weinberger S. et al. (2019). Crowdsourcing L2 Phonetics. 11th Pronunciation in Second Language Learning and Teaching conference (abstract record)

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using one listener (a friend or tutor) as the ground truth for progress.
does_not_work_verified.notes: speechocean762 single-expert ICC(2,1) = .51–.64 reproduced. Issa & Ali's leave-one-out r = .46–.73 is a range across dimensions and implies single-rater reliability of about .27–.58. Caveat: much of one rater's error is constant severity. A single rater scoring baseline and follow-up blind, in one session, is weak evidence, but not worthless.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using large audio language models in place of human raters.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Confirmed from the Issa & Ali abstract: 5 LALMs, 90 samples; only Gemini significant on comprehensibility (r = .28) and Qwen2-Audio on intelligibility (r = .32); biases −9.31 to +13.19. Scope: off-the-shelf models on global dimensions in one workshop paper, and the abstract does not name GPT-4o. Fine-tuned speech LLMs do much better on speechocean762 (Ahn & Nam 2025: accuracy PCC .743; Parikh et al. 2026), so the claim should read 'zero-shot LALMs'.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using ASR word error rate or transcripts as the learner's intelligibility score.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Park 2026 confirms intent bias: over-correction rises as WER falls. Yoho 2019 confirms that transcription and ratings are not interchangeable (r = .66/.57, native talkers). Whether ASR is more or less lenient than human listeners on L2 speech was not tested.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Declaring mastery from accuracy during practice or on a single attempt at a trained item.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The principle is supported: McCabe et al. state that primary outcomes should be untreated items, and they use a 1-month retention probe. But McCabe's own gains were retained, so it is not evidence of fading. The fading evidence is one unreplicated NDP3 RCT and Bu et al. (N = 8; figures from a secondary record). 'Often fail to last' is stronger than the cited evidence.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Calling a phoneme 'weak' after a handful of tokens.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Reproduced: kappa .605 (.56–.64). Tokens for .80 reliability: consensus medians 12–16; single-expert medians 15–23, with some phonemes needing 30–60. These are between-speaker reliabilities; precision for one learner requires more.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Comparing Azure scores across months as if the instrument were fixed.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The August 2026 release note confirms updated models for en-US, fr-FR and others. No version-pinning option appears in the release notes or the limitations doc.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Relying on Azure for French prosody or phoneme-identity feedback.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The docs confirm prosody is en-US only, syllable groups and spoken phonemes are en-US only, and other locales 'can only get the phoneme score'. Phoneme names are also available for zh-CN (SAPI), a minor inaccuracy that does not matter for French.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Rating baseline and follow-up recordings in separate sessions, or without anchor clips.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Flege & Fletcher (range and familiarity effects), Gao (within-session drift, β = 0.03 per trial) and Kang & Rubin (expectation effects from a photo cue) are all confirmed. The evidence for 'anchor clips' is indirect: Gao used a 10-trial familiarisation block, and that comparison is confounded with showing the script.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using Tau-U as the headline single-case statistic.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The SingleCaseES vignette states that Tau-U's sampling distribution has not been described, so no SE or CI is available.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Using elicited imitation as a pronunciation diagnostic.
does_not_work_verified.notes: The meta-analysis confirms r = .66 with general proficiency measures. The lack of evidence for segmental diagnosis is an absence claim, and I found nothing contrary.

critique_of_v1: Weak-phoneme threshold is far too low. getWeakPhonemes (server/src/db/index.ts) ranks phonemes by an all-time running mean once attempt_count >= 3 tokens. Even five-expert consensus labels need about 8–22 tokens (median about 14) for a .80-reliable per-phoneme estimate, and automatic scores are noisier than that. The running mean also never forgets, so it cannot show recent change, and it carries no uncertainty.

French phoneme tracking probably collects no data. The stats update in server/src/index.ts only records phonemes where ph.Phoneme is present, and Azure returns phoneme names only for en-US ('for other locales you can only get the phoneme score'). The fr-FR weak-phoneme engine and heatmap are therefore likely empty or mislabelled; this needs checking with a live fr-FR call. Azure's prosody score is also en-US only, so the French prosody track has no automatic measure.

Mastery and ladder progression use one noisy take on a trained item. applyLadderRule and levelGate (server/src/services/drills.ts) advance at a single accuracy >= 85. That measures practice performance, not retention or transfer, and a single automatic score is about as reliable as one rater.

The progress chart confounds learning with item choice and instrument changes. getDailyScores averages overall_score per day over whatever items were practised, not over a fixed probe set. Changes in difficulty or content, microphone conditions, and Azure's August 2026 model update all show up as 'progress'.

v1 has no baseline phase, no untrained-item probes, no delayed retention probes and no multiple-baseline structure. It cannot tell learning apart from practice effects, item familiarity or score noise.

v1 has no human calibration. The only criterion is Azure, whose published validity is '>0.5 Pearson', from between-speaker English data with no fr-FR figures. Nothing is ever checked against listener comprehensibility or transcription intelligibility on spontaneous speech.

Per-attempt green/amber/red phoneme colours overstate certainty. Even experts agree on single-phone errors at only kappa ≈ .60; when one flags an error, another agrees 64% of the time. A single red token is often disputable and should not drive drill selection.
v1 has no diagnostic onboarding. Weak phonemes are inferred only from items the app itself chose, a selection bias, and errors are not prioritised by functional load.
v1 has no audio-quality gate or repeat-recording reliability check, although Microsoft states that quality depends on noise and mic distance and advises customers to evaluate in their own conditions.

The speed ladder grades tongue twisters by Azure accuracy at TTS tempo tiers. No evidence reviewed here validates this as a measure of articulation or intelligibility, and its 85 cut-off has no reliability basis.
open_questions: Is Azure Pronunciation Assessment stable across repeated attempts of the same item by the same learner, in either locale? The same question applies to SpeechAce, SpeechSuper and ELSA. I found no independent test-retest study. The app should measure this itself (the same 10 probe sentences recorded twice per session at baseline) before setting thresholds.
How well does Azure fr-FR agree with human raters, before and after the August 2026 model update? Microsoft publishes no locale-specific figures.

Several key requested sources could not be opened: the web-search budget was exhausted and publisher and index domains were blocked. They are Nagle, Trofimovich & Bergeron 2019 (SSLA); Nagle's MTurk crowdsourcing paper and Nagle & Rehman 2021 (online ratings); Isaacs & Thomson 2013 (rater experience and scale length); Kang et al. on L1 vs L2 listeners; Inceoglu, Chen & Lim 2023 (ReCALL, ASR vs L1 listeners); and the WWC/Kratochwill single-case standards (minimum data points per phase). Verify them before fixing rater counts or phase lengths.

Are non-native (L2) listeners acceptable raters of this learner's English and French comprehensibility? One crowdsourced transcription study found the transcriber's L1 did not matter, but I found no evidence for 9-point ratings.
How many trials does a per-contrast perception identification test need to be reliable (for example /i/-/ɪ/, /y/-/u/, French nasal vowels)? I found no reliability data.
Do the between-speaker reliabilities (ICC, token counts) carry over to detecting one learner's small changes over weeks? A learner-specific reliable-change threshold from repeat recordings is needed.

How often should human ratings be collected? No study was found. A defensible default is at baseline and at the end of each 4–6 week training block, together with the delayed probe, with 3–5 listeners per round.
Functional-load rankings and their link to comprehensibility have not been validated for French as a target language.
missed_evidence_flagged: Rater severity in the author's own speechocean762 data: rater means differ by up to about 1.9 points on 0–10 fluency (6.6 vs 8.6). Consistency ICC(3,1) is .65–.70 against absolute ICC(2,1) of .51–.64. This supports reusing the same raters and comparing within a rating session. https://github.com/jimbozhang/speechocean762

Saito K., Plonsky L. (2019). Effects of second language pronunciation teaching revisited: A proposed measurement framework and meta-analysis. Language Learning 69(3):652–708. doi:10.1111/lang.12345. This is adult L2 meta-analytic evidence (77 studies) on how outcome type (controlled vs spontaneous tasks) and timing moderate pronunciation-instruction effects. It is directly relevant to gap-7 and a better anchor than child clinical trials. https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10068780/

Munro M.J., Derwing T.M. (1995). Foreign accent, comprehensibility, and intelligibility in the speech of second language learners. Language Learning 45(1):73–97. This is the origin of the 9-point comprehensibility scale and of transcription intelligibility as partly independent dimensions in L2 speech. It is a better L2 anchor for gap-4 than Yoho's native talkers (not opened in this session). https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-1770.1995.tb00963.x

Munro M.J., Derwing T.M. (2006). The functional load principle in ESL pronunciation instruction: An exploratory study. System 34:520–531; and Kang O., Moran M. (2014). Functional loads of pronunciation features in nonnative speakers' oral assessment. TESOL Quarterly 48:176–187. Both are corroborating functional-load evidence for gap-10, confirmed as references in Suzukida & Saito. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marcoweb/annif-experiments/main/education-en/raw-files/corpus-training/Corpus_entrenamiento_Education_6000_documentos/D1398.txt

Kratochwill T.R. et al. (2013). Single-case intervention research design standards. Remedial and Special Education 34(1):26–38 (the WWC standards). They require at least 3 demonstrations of effect (at least 3 tiers in a multiple baseline) and 3 (with reservations) or 5 data points per phase. So the '2–3 target sounds' plan should be at least 3. This is the verification the author could not complete (not opened in this session). https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932512452794

Randomization tests for single-case designs (e.g. Heyvaert M., Onghena P. 2014, J. Contextual Behavioral Science 3(1):51–64). Randomizing each target's training start point gives valid p-values without the independence assumption that NAP, Tau and LRR standard errors need. The scan package cited in gap-8 implements rand_test() (not opened in this session). https://github.com/cran/scan

Fine-tuned speech LLMs reach near-expert agreement on speechocean762: Ahn & Nam 2025 (accuracy PCC .743; Azure .842 prosody, .782 total), and Parikh et al. 2026 (uncertainty-calibrated Qwen2-Audio, multi-rater). This limits the 'LALMs don't work' claim to zero-shot use. https://github.com/will-rice/asr-papers/blob/main/papers/2025/2509.02915.md

Binomial precision for a single learner: with n = 15 tokens and a 20% error rate, the 95% interval is about 4–48%. Between-speaker reliability (gap-5) understates how many tokens are needed to detect change in one learner's error rate. Beta-binomial shrinkage, as the finding proposes, is the right response.

Isaacs T., Thomson R.I. (2013). Rater experience, rating scale length, and judgments of L2 pronunciation. Language Assessment Quarterly 10(2):135–159. It compares experienced and novice raters and 5- vs 9-point scales, and is relevant to gap-2's lay-vs-expert claim (not opened in this session). https://doi.org/10.1080/15434303.2013.769545

general_review.topic: gap-transfer: Self-directed, technology-mediated speaking and pronunciation practice for adult L2 learners. Covers transfer of practice to spontaneous speech, conversation partners (spoken dialogue systems, LLM voice chat), feedback given inside communicative tasks, task-repetition and proceduralisation designs, and adherence and dose in self-study tools (English and French).
general_review.summary:
HOW I VERIFIED. This session's web-search budget was used up before I started, and the network proxy blocked every publisher, DOI and index site (doi.org, Cambridge, Wiley, T&F, ERIC, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, arXiv, lltjournal.org). Only GitHub was reachable, so I checked sources in four GitHub-hosted places:
- Serge Bibauw's site repo: the full preprint of the Bibauw et al. (2022) dialogue-system meta-analysis, his 2022 thesis, and the abstract of a 2026 LLM-era meta-analysis.
- The ERCT papers repository: structured extractions that quote the full texts of about 20 trials (LLM chatbot, AI voice chat, ELSA, ASR, form-focused instruction, task repetition).
- The Texto Livre article sources, for McCrocklin & Edalatishams 2020 and Mroz 2018.
- Microsoft's azure-ai-docs repo.
Adherence figures (Hwang et al. 2024; Sudina & Plonsky; Loewen et al. 2020) come only from an audited secondary literature survey plus bibliographic records. The effect_notes say so, and these figures should be treated as approximate. I could confirm only the bibliographic record for McCrocklin 2019 (JSLP 5(1):98-118), so I cite no results from it.

BOTTOM LINE.
(1) Transfer to spontaneous speech. I found no controlled study showing that a self-study pronunciation app improves listener-rated comprehensibility of spontaneous speech.
- The closest are small, uncontrolled or course-embedded studies: mobile shadowing (comprehensibility and fluency up, accent unchanged), and ELSA or ASR used as part of a course.
- The clearest transfer evidence comes from short classroom form-focused instruction. A target sound was practised inside meaningful tasks with feedback on that sound only, and the gains reached timed spontaneous speech and held at delayed tests in spontaneous tasks. Decontextualised drill alone did not transfer, or did not last.
(2) Software conversation partners. They produce medium gains in general L2 proficiency (d about 0.6; LLM-era estimate g about 0.61).
- Gains are larger when practice and test are both spoken (spoken→spoken d=0.84 vs written→spoken d=0.29, n.s.), in guided or task-constrained dialogues, with corrective feedback, and at A1-B1.
- Fluency effects are uncertain, and no effect was found at B2.
- No included study measured pronunciation.
- Early LLM voice-chat trials show fluency and speaking-test gains and more voluntary practice time, but those two are confounded.
- One RCT of software feedback during conversation (typed text chat, grammar) found no learning difference between in-conversation and end-of-session feedback, though learners preferred immediate feedback.
(3) Task repetition at home. Repeating the same oral narrative across three days (a blocked schedule) improved fluency on new stories. Six back-to-back repetitions reduced pausing but slowed speech and increased verbatim repetition.
(4) Adherence. Voluntary app use decays: about 43% of adult MALL users dropped out within 3 months (secondary figure). Engagement tracked sessions of at least 5 min and at least 4 sessions a week. The about 94% compliance in the ELSA trial happened only because practice was set as part of a course.
(5) French. Direct evidence is nearly absent: one qualitative ASR study (n=16) and a vocabulary study with teenagers.

RECOMMENDATION.
- Add an unscripted spoken retell or role-play mode as the step that carries drilled targets into free speech, not as a separate chatbot toy.
- Limit its feedback to the 1-2 current targets.
- Use repeated retells within a session and new prompts across days.
- Use a periodic unscripted recording, rated for comprehensibility, as the main progress measure.
- Plan roughly 10-minute sessions, at least 4 times a week, in 8-12-week cycles, with a comeback path after gaps.

findings.claim: Dialogue-based CALL gives a medium, sustained overall effect (d = 0.59; delayed 0.56). Practice-test modality matching significantly moderates the effect (spoken to spoken 0.84 vs written to spoken 0.29, n.s.), and so does gamification. The advantages for system-guided and pre-set-meaning dialogues, and the A1-A2 vs B1-B2 gradient, are non-significant subgroup estimates based on few studies. One included child study (robots, Korean elementary pupils) measured holistic pronunciation. The analysis has no separate pronunciation outcome category.
findings.population: 17 experimental studies (419 screened), k = 100 effect sizes, N = 803. Mostly adult or university L2 learners across several target languages (English, French, German, Chinese, etc.). Settings: school, university, lab. No outcome category for pronunciation.
findings.effect_notes:
Three-level random-effects model: d = 0.59, 95% CI [0.35, 0.82]; I² = 68%. The funnel plot suggests possible publication bias.
Moderators:
- Corrective feedback: none d = 0.38; implicit 0.68; explicit 0.73 (moderator n.s., Q(2) = 2.08).
- Gamification: yes 0.99 vs no 0.45 (Q = 4.93, p = .026).
- Lab studies: d = 0.33 (weaker).
- Packed practice (1 week or less): 0.97 vs spaced 0.53 (n.s.).
- Sessions and time on task: b = 0.02, n.s.
- Outcomes: accuracy d = 0.60 and holistic proficiency d = 0.73 were significant; comprehension outcomes were not.
Verified from the authors' accepted-manuscript preprint.
findings.design_implication:
If a conversation mode is added, make it spoken end to end (voice in, voice out). Do not count typed chat as speaking practice.
Structure it as system-guided tasks with a goal and required content, not open chat. Examples: retell this story using these 5 words; order in a café; explain a route with an information gap.
Attach explicit feedback.
Calibrate expectations by level. At A2-B1 in a language, the mode can drive learning. At B2 or above (possible if the learner is advanced, or a native speaker of one of the two languages), use it mainly as a transfer probe and a carrier for targeted feedback, not as the main engine.
Never assume conversation alone will fix sounds. Pronunciation feedback has to be layered on explicitly (see gap-transfer-5).

citations.ref: Bibauw, Van den Noortgate, François & Desmet (2022). Dialogue systems for language learning: a meta-analysis. Language Learning & Technology 26(1):1-24 (author preprint)
Bibauw et al. (2022), journal page (LLT item 1035; handle 10125/73488)

findings.claim:
An updated LLM-era meta-analysis of dialogue systems and chatbots (67 studies, 2011-2025) again finds a medium effect: g = 0.61 overall, g = 0.54 for adults.
- Productive skills: g = 0.65; comprehension: n.s.
- Test-practice modality match: effects about 2.5 times larger.
- Delayed posttests: g = 0.92, vs 0.58 immediate.
- Technology generation was not a significant moderator, although LLM chatbots showed the largest estimate (g = 0.64). Design matters more than the model.
- Positive effects appeared both in and out of class.
This is a 2026 conference abstract of a paper under review. An audited 2026 survey found no independent, adequately powered controlled trial showing that an LLM conversation partner produces measurable proficiency gains.
findings.population: 67 studies, 237 effect sizes, 4,544 participants from 23 L1 backgrounds, including children, teenagers and adults. Outcomes are general L2 performance, not pronunciation.
findings.effect_notes:
g = 0.61, 95% CI [0.48, 0.74].
- Age: teenagers g = 1.05; adults 0.54; children 0.49.
- Outcomes: vocabulary 0.92; productive skills 0.65; language knowledge 0.60.
- Timing: delayed 0.92 vs immediate 0.58.
The typology of learner output freedom runs from repetition to free speech.
Not yet peer reviewed. Numbers are from the EUROCALL 2026 abstract on the second author's site.
findings.design_implication:
Choose the LLM for flexibility (varied prompts and scenarios, natural replies, generating retell stories in both languages), not because LLMs are known to teach better.
Spend the effort on task design and modality matching: spoken tasks tested by spoken probes.
Plan to measure the mode's value on this one learner with a monthly unscripted speaking probe (see gap-transfer-11), rather than trusting published averages.

citations.ref: Wang, Bibauw, Noreillie & Desmet (2026). Hype or hope? A meta-analysis of conversational chatbots on L2 learning. EUROCALL 2026 abstract (paper under review)
Bibauw & Dizon (2025). Conversational AI and chatbots (chapter abstract, doi 10.47908/38/1), bibliography record
Parle literature survey (2026), 06-existing-programmes-and-apps: LLM tutors section (secondary)

findings.claim:
Recent AI voice-conversation trials report speaking gains and more voluntary practice, but none measured pronunciation or comprehensibility with blind listeners, and practice time is a confound.
- Microsoft 365 Copilot voice chat vs peer speaking practice (8 weeks): greater gains in speech rate, mean length of run and pause reduction on a 2-minute monologue. 71% of learners voluntarily exceeded the required practice time.
- An ASR conversational bot vs listen-and-repeat (6 days): higher engagement and speaking-test gains, but bot users spent about 104 vs 45 minutes in the app.
- With children, 3 weeks of daily 45-minute GenAI chatbot talk beat regular class on speaking tests.
findings.population: Chinese university English majors (n = 56, randomized); Saudi university EFL (n = 52, two intact classes, quasi-experimental); Taiwanese elementary EFL children (n = 85, randomized). All English as L2. No French. No self-study outside a course.
findings.effect_notes:
Copilot study (Abdelrady et al. 2026): 5-10 min per session, 4 times a week, in supervised class time (about 160-320 min total). Autonomy gain d = 0.82. Researcher-made 2-minute speaking task, no delayed test.
Dai & Wu 2025: engagement M = 4.37 vs 3.87. Speaking gains p < .0001, rated on an IELTS-adapted rubric (including pronunciation) by the study's own tutors. Time on app 103.7 vs 45.1 min.
Tai & Chen 2024: individual and paired bot interaction did not differ; both beat no-bot.
All outcome measures were researcher-designed.
findings.design_implication:
Expect a voice conversation mode to raise voluntary practice. That may be its main mechanism, and it is useful for a busy adult.
Log minutes per mode and compare progress per minute against drills, rather than crediting the mode automatically.
Keep each conversation task to 5-10 minutes.
Check the audio budget. Each conversation minute also consumes ASR and assessment audio, and v1's Azure F0 tier caps it at 5 audio hours a month.
For the speaking scenario, Azure supports unscripted assessment (no reference text), but prosody is en-US only. Microsoft recommends running speech-to-text first and then a scripted assessment against that transcript when accurate recognized text matters.

citations.ref: Abdelrady et al. (2026). Speaking with AI: Microsoft 365 Copilot voice chat and EFL fluency. Frontiers in Education, doi 10.3389/feduc.2026.1851080 (ERCT extraction quoting full text)
Dai & Wu (2025). An AI-powered conversational system for college students learning English. Education and Information Technologies, doi 10.1007/s10639-025-13640-3 (ERCT extraction)
Tai & Chen (2024). Improving elementary EFL speaking skills with generative AI chatbots. Computers & Education, doi 10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105112 (ERCT extraction)
Microsoft Learn: Use pronunciation assessment (scripted vs unscripted; prosody en-US only)

findings.claim: In one small LLM text-chat RCT with grammar outcomes (no pre-test, no control, differential attrition), immediate vs end-of-session correction gave equivalent learning, and immediate correction was better liked. Some dialogue-based CALL systems have delivered pronunciation feedback inside dialogue, but no study has compared the timing of pronunciation feedback given by software during conversation.
findings.population: 66 Czech university learners of English (54 analysed), 12 text-chat sessions over 4 weeks. Grammar outcomes only. Classroom meta-analytic evidence covers human teachers.
findings.effect_notes:
Kamelabad et al. 2026:
- 3 sessions a week for 4 weeks; each session ended after 1,000 characters of learner text.
- 24 immediate vs 30 delayed learners analysed after differential attrition.
- Learning gains were measured from logged errors and a 25-sentence test built from each learner's own mistakes, with no pre-test.
Lyster & Saito 2010 (k = 15, N = 827): prompts > recasts on free constructed responses. Secondary summary; not opened.
findings.design_implication:
During a spoken task, do not interrupt for every error.
- Flag only the 1-2 target sounds of the current cycle, with a brief in-flow prompt such as "say 'think' again?" or a salient partial recast.
- End every task with a short report: 2-3 items with replay of the learner's own audio against the model, then an immediate re-say inside a new sentence.
- Make in-flow vs end-of-task feedback a user setting. Learning appears equivalent, and the learner may prefer one.

citations.ref: Kamelabad, Turano, Lundin & Skantze (2026). Personalized language learning with an LLM chatbot: immediate vs delayed corrective feedback. Frontiers in Education, doi 10.3389/feduc.2026.1703664 (ERCT extraction quoting full text)

findings.claim: In small, short classroom studies of adult Japanese learners (single target /r/, one lab's cohorts), communicative form-focused instruction with recasts produced /r/ gains that reached a timed picture description. Explicit articulatory information boosted gains and generalisation. For beginners, communicative FFI without feedback was sufficient. One small Iranian study found communicative practice outlasted drills in spontaneous tasks at a 2-week delay. Drill-only practice is not shown to be useless: perception training transfers modestly to production.
findings.population: Japanese university EFL learners (n = 65; n = 49; n = 49) and Iranian pre-intermediate EFL learners (n = 45). Classroom, teacher-delivered, 4-8 hours total. No self-study, no software delivery, no French.
findings.effect_notes:
Saito & Lyster 2012:
- Groups: form-focused instruction + feedback n = 29; instruction only n = 25; control n = 11.
- 2 one-hour lessons a week for 2 weeks; acoustic F3 measure; posttest 2 weeks later.
- Generalisation to novel words was unclear.
Saito 2013:
- Groups: with explicit explanation n = 17; without n = 18; control n = 14.
- With explanation: large effects plus generalisation; without: medium effects, familiar words only.
Tabandeh et al. 2018: 8-hour course, delayed posttest about 2 weeks later. The journal is a lower-tier venue.
Small samples, single target sounds, short delays.
findings.design_implication:
Rebuild the weak-sound path as a four-step proceduralisation sequence per target:
1. A 30-60 second explicit articulatory explanation with an exaggerated model.
2. Perception check plus controlled production (minimal pairs and phrases).
3. The same sound seeded into a meaningful spoken task (a retell or role-play whose required words contain the target), with feedback restricted to that sound.
4. A spontaneous probe with new words a few days later.
Graduate a sound only on step 4, not on read-aloud accuracy of 85 or more.
For absolute beginners in a language, weight steps 1-2 toward listening and keep correction light.

citations.ref: Saito & Lyster (2012). Effects of form-focused instruction and corrective feedback on L2 pronunciation development of /ɹ/. Language Learning 62(2), doi 10.1111/j.1467-9922.2011.00639.x (ERCT extraction)

findings.claim:
Repeating oral narratives improves fluency, and the schedule matters.
- Suzuki 2021: learners practising alone at home for 3 days repeated each story three times a day, one story per day. This blocked schedule gave faster articulation and shorter mid-clause pauses on new stories than rotating three stories each day.
- Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022: telling the same story six times in a row cut pausing most, but slowed articulation and increased verbatim repetition. Schedule effects mostly disappeared at the 1-week delayed test.
- Hunter 2023: same-task repetition raised fluency during the repetitions; parallel tasks did not.
- Duong et al. 2023: a single repetition two days later had no significant effect.
findings.population: Japanese university EFL learners (n = 50 randomized; n = 79 across 4 intact classes); ESL learners (n = 46); Vietnamese university EFL learners (n = 90). Fluency is measured acoustically: articulation rate, pauses, mean length of run. No pronunciation-accuracy or comprehensibility outcomes. English only.
findings.effect_notes:
Suzuki 2021:
- 24 blocked vs 26 interleaved learners; self-administered at home with a booklet and recorder.
- Posttest on new six-frame cartoons.
- Blocked practice also raised in-training mean length of run and phonation-time ratio, but these did not carry over to pre-post change.
Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022: quasi-experimental; massed n = 20, short-spaced n = 23, long-spaced n = 21, control n = 15.
findings.design_implication:
Build a retell or monologue mode with this default loop:
- Tell one prompt (a picture story, or a summary of a short text or TTS clip) 3 times in one sitting. Optionally shorten the time limit each round, as in 4/3/2 practice.
- Switch to a new prompt the next session.
- Measure fluency (articulation rate, mid-clause pauses) only on unseen prompts.
- Cap consecutive repeats at about 3. Flag rising verbatim repetition or a falling articulation rate as a sign of rote reciting.
This replaces tongue-twister speed ladders as the main articulation-under-load exercise.

citations.ref: Suzuki (2021). Optimizing fluency training for speaking skills transfer: blocked vs interleaved task repetition. Language Learning 71(2), doi 10.1111/lang.12433 (ERCT extraction quoting full text)
Suzuki & Hanzawa (2022). Massed task repetition is a double-edged sword for fluency development. SSLA 44(2), doi 10.1017/S0272263121000358 (ERCT extraction)
Hunter (2023). The poster carousel: L2 fluency during same and parallel task repetition. TESOL Quarterly, doi 10.1002/tesq.3257 (ERCT extraction)
Duong et al. (2023). Input, input repetition and task repetition on L2 lexical use and fluency. SSLLT, doi 10.14746/ssllt.29727 (ERCT extraction)

findings.claim:
Evidence that self-study pronunciation apps move spontaneous comprehensibility is thin, and I found no independent long-term field study of ELSA, Speakometer or similar apps.
- Foote & McDonough 2017 (mobile shadowing, no control): adults shadowed short dialogues on a phone at least 4 times a week for at least 10 minutes over 8 weeks. Listeners rated them more comprehensible and fluent; accentedness did not change.
- Abdelrady et al. 2026 (ELSA, quasi-experimental, 12 weeks): ELSA users gained more than a teacher-led group on a composite accuracy-intonation-fluency rating across read-aloud, picture description and free speaking. Practice was prescribed by the course (94% compliance, about 30 minutes a day).
- Sun 2023 (in class): ASR practice with peer correction beat teacher feedback on accentedness and comprehensibility (read-aloud) and on a short spontaneous conversation scored with the IELTS rubric.
- Ngo et al. 2024 (secondary): ASR programmes of 1-4 weeks showed almost no effect.
findings.population: Adult ESL in Canada (16 of 22 completed); Saudi university EFL (n = 60); Chinese B1 adults (n = 61, randomized, 14-week course). All English as L2. Only the shadowing study was outside class and self-paced.
findings.effect_notes:
Foote & McDonough: 27% attrition (6 of 22); 22 listener-raters. Details come from a secondary check of the author PDF; not opened.
Abdelrady ELSA: 2,174 cumulative minutes on average, no attrition. Three trained instructors rated the samples. The spontaneous tasks are not reported separately.
Sun 2023:
- 7 read-aloud sentences, rated by 2 instructors on 9-point scales.
- Spontaneous: 3-4 questions scored on the IELTS rubric by in-house raters, one of them the researcher.
Ngo et al. 2024: 1-4 weeks g = 0.07 vs 5-8 weeks g = 1.01 (secondary extraction).
findings.design_implication:
Plan in 8-12-week cycles of about 10 minutes, at least 4 times a week. Do not judge the programme after 2-3 weeks.
Keep shadowing of short, meaningful dialogues as a core activity, since it is the best-tested self-paced format.
Make comprehensibility and fluency of unscripted speech the headline outcome, and say plainly that accent may not change.
Start and end every cycle with the same unscripted probe: a 60-second picture story and a 60-second opinion answer, per language.

findings.claim: For read or dictated English sentences, general ASR recognition rates track human intelligibility and comprehensibility ratings (one study, 30 speakers). Small studies suggest modern ASR accepts some mispronounced words. French evidence is qualitative only. ASR transcripts are a plausible but unvalidated proxy for intelligibility of free speech, especially in French.
findings.population: 30 speakers (10 L1 English, 10 L1 Spanish, 10 L1 Mandarin) dictating 60 sentences; 16 US learners of French as a foreign language (interviews); a small 7-day browser-ASR self-study comparison in Japan.
findings.effect_notes:
McCrocklin & Edalatishams 2020 report that the recognition gap between native and non-native speech has narrowed from 18-20% to 3-5%.
Mroz 2018 is qualitative, with no outcome measure.
Both findings were verified through a 2022 Texto Livre review that quotes the originals. McCrocklin 2019 (JSLP 5(1), ASR dictation practice) exists, but I could not open its results.
findings.design_implication:
In the unscripted mode, show what a neutral listener heard. The learner retells known content or states the intended sentence, the app shows the ASR transcript, and mismatched words are highlighted and routed into the proceduralisation sequence (gap-transfer-5).
Label it "understood / not understood", never "correct".
Keep Azure phoneme scoring for diagnosis.
The signal works in both English and French. It is the most practical French comprehensibility proxy the app has, because Azure prosody scoring is en-US only.

citations.ref: Gottardi & Almeida (2022). ASR and TTS technologies for L2 pronunciation improvement. Texto Livre 15, doi 10.35699/1983-3652.2022.36736 (article source quoting McCrocklin & Edalatishams 2020 and Mroz 2018)
McCrocklin & Edalatishams (2020). Revisiting popular speech recognition software for ESL speech. TESOL Quarterly 54(4):1086-1097
Mroz (2018). Seeing how people hear you: French learners experiencing intelligibility through ASR. Foreign Language Annals 51(3):617-637
Umezawa et al. (2023). Utilizing ASR for English pronunciation practice (ERCT extraction; IEEE ICEED, doi 10.1109/ICEED59801.2023.10264049)

findings.claim: Secondary reports of one large survival analysis suggest high early attrition in voluntary app use (about 43% within 3 months). Session intensity (5+ min), frequency (4+ a week) and continuity (7+ weeks) all predicted persistence, and pausing did not mean permanent dropout. Evidence on whether frequency or total minutes better predicts learning is mixed and mostly secondary.
findings.population: 3,319 adult mobile-app users; 601-787 Duolingo beginners (sources give different Ns); 287 Duolingo users; 54 Babbel Spanish learners.
findings.effect_notes: All numbers come from an audited secondary survey. The primary papers could not be opened; the Hwang et al. bibliographic record was confirmed in Web of Science data. The Sudina & Plonsky attrition cohort is reported as 787 (34% completion) in one survey file and 601 over 6 months in another. The Babbel study had no control group.
findings.design_implication:
Assume dropout is the main threat to any benefit.
- Default session: 5-10 minutes (one drill block plus one short spoken task).
- Target: at least 4 sessions a week, tracked as sessions per week, not minutes.
- No backlog. After a gap of 7 days or more, open with a 3-minute comeback session.
- Keep weekly continuity visible, since at least 7 consecutive active weeks predicted persistence.
- Because no one sets the practice, the app should let the learner make a commitment: a chosen weekly target and a fixed cue time.

citations.ref: Hwang, Coss, Loewen & Tagarelli (2024). Acceptance and engagement patterns of MALL among non-conventional adult L2 learners: a survival analysis. SSLA 46(4):969-995
Parle survey 04-motivation-persistence-curriculum (secondary figures for Hwang et al., Sudina, Teimouri & Plonsky, and the n = 287 Duolingo usage study)

findings.claim:
What keeps a learner practising voluntarily is poorly studied. Several signals point toward interactive, meaningful tasks, light gamification tied to tasks, and immediate responsiveness:
- Interactive voice bots increased voluntary time: 104 vs 45 minutes against listen-and-repeat, and 71% of learners exceeded the required time with Copilot.
- Immediate in-conversation feedback improved user experience.
- Gamified dialogue systems produced larger learning effects (d = 0.99 vs 0.45).
- In a French study with teenagers, a truly interactive dialogue system produced more output and more fluency-focused behaviour than the same dialogues pre-scripted.
Against this, vendor data reportedly show that session accuracy correlates positively with proficiency while total time and session count correlate negatively. Forum studies describe streak and league mechanics driving easy-lesson grinding (secondary).
findings.population: University EFL learners (China, Saudi Arabia, Czech Republic); 215 Dutch-speaking teenage learners of French; Duolingo users (vendor and forum data). No adult self-study pronunciation cohort.
findings.effect_notes:
The gamification moderator is based on 17 effect sizes and concerns learning, not retention.
Bibauw thesis: 3 sessions, cluster-randomised; perceptions did not differ between versions, but engagement behaviour did.
The Duolingo accuracy-vs-time correlation (DRR-24-04) and the gamification-misuse findings are known only from secondary summaries.
Implementation-intention (d = .65) and habit-formation figures (median 66 days to automaticity; one missed day did not matter) are from general, non-language studies, also secondary.
findings.design_implication:
Make the meaningful spoken task the reason to open the app. Each session ends with one retell or role-play that uses the sounds just drilled.
Show progress as competence: can-do statements, before-and-after recordings of the monthly probe, and the share of words understood by ASR. Do not show XP or streaks.
If any game layer is added, reward completed tasks and quality re-tries, not time spent.
Keep feedback latency short (show local measures instantly).
At onboarding, ask for one if-then plan, for example "after my morning coffee, 10 minutes", and tell the learner that one missed day does not reset anything.

citations.ref: Bibauw et al. (2022) meta-analysis, gamification moderator
Bibauw (2022). Learning with conversational AI (PhD thesis, KU Leuven): LanguageHero experiment with learners of French
Dai & Wu (2025), time-on-app finding (ERCT extraction)
Kamelabad et al. (2026), user-experience finding (ERCT extraction)
Parle survey 06 (Duolingo DRR-24-04 accuracy vs time; gamification misuse, Hadi Mogavi et al. 2022), secondary

findings.claim: For French, a few small, classroom-embedded studies of mobile ASR or TTS pronunciation practice exist, with controlled or segmental outcomes. There is qualitative ASR-dictation work (Mroz 2018) and one typed dialogue-game RCT with teenagers (vocabulary only). No study found tests a French self-study tool, LLM partner or task-repetition method against spontaneous comprehensibility.
findings.population: US university learners of French (n = 16); Dutch-speaking teenage learners of French (N = 215); Duolingo French learners (vendor).
findings.effect_notes: This is an absence of evidence, not evidence of no effect. The French items above are weak or off-target for adults.
findings.design_implication:
Treat French versions of every feature as extrapolated from English research, and have the app evaluate itself on this learner. Once a month, per language:
- Record the same kind of unscripted probe.
- Store it.
- Score it with ASR word-recognition rate, speech rate and mid-clause pauses.
- Have the learner rate comprehensibility blind, on anonymised, shuffled recordings played back at least 2 weeks later, and optionally a native listener as well.
If French unscripted measures do not improve over 8-12 weeks while drill scores do, shift French time from drills to retell tasks.

citations.ref: Mroz (2018), Foreign Language Annals 51(3), as quoted in the Texto Livre 2022 article source
Bibauw (2022) PhD thesis: LanguageHero RCT with learners of French
Parle survey 06: Duolingo French speaking outcomes (vendor, secondary)

does_not_work_verified.claim: Typed chat as a substitute for speaking practice (written-to-spoken transfer d = 0.29, n.s., vs 0.84 spoken-to-spoken).
does_not_work_verified.notes: Exact figures from Bibauw et al. 2022: written to spoken 0.29 [-0.21, 0.79]; spoken to spoken 0.84 [0.42, 1.26]. The modality-matching moderator was significant (Q = 7.91, p = .005). The wide confidence interval means limited transfer, not zero transfer.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Listen-and-repeat or pre-scripted dialogue completion in place of interactive exchange (lower engagement, speaking gains, output, vocabulary).
does_not_work_verified.notes:
Descriptively accurate but weak:
- Dai & Wu ran only 6 days, the bot group spent more than twice the time on task, and the speaking ratings came from the study's own tutors.
- In the Bibauw thesis, the typed pre-scripted condition produced less output and only slightly less productive vocabulary, and perceptions did not differ.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Many back-to-back repetitions of the same text (six massed repetitions reduced pauses but slowed articulation, increased verbatim repetition, and faded by one week).
does_not_work_verified.notes: Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022 confirms the immediate-posttest pattern. It was a quasi-experiment with 4 intact classes. At 1 week the differences between schedules shrank; the study does not show that repetition's benefit itself vanished. Suzuki 2021 found 3 consecutive repetitions (blocked) beat interleaving, which supports a cap of about 3. Tongue-twister speed ladders are a different task from narrative retelling, so this is an extrapolation.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Treating general ASR recognition success as proof of correct pronunciation.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Umezawa et al. 2023 (IEEE conference paper, 28 participants, 7 days) reports that iOS recognition accepted mispronounced words. The evidence is weak but consistent with how language-model-based ASR works. McCrocklin & Edalatishams show recognition correlates with intelligibility, not with segmental accuracy.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Correcting every error immediately inside a conversation (no learning advantage over end-of-session feedback; no evidence for software pronunciation feedback mid-conversation).
does_not_work_verified.notes: The Kamelabad 2026 null result is confirmed: typed LLM chat, grammar outcomes, no pre-test, no control, 24 vs 30 learners analysed. Learners preferred immediate feedback. Correction: some dialogue-based CALL systems did give pronunciation feedback inside dialogue (Bibauw 2022 typology and thesis), though none compared its timing.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Expecting accent reduction from self-paced mobile practice (shadowing improved comprehensibility and fluency, not accentedness).
does_not_work_verified.notes: Consistent with the secondary check of Foote & McDonough 2017: 16 completers, no control, concurrent ESL classes. It is a single uncontrolled study, so it shows no accent change in that study, not a general impossibility.

does_not_work_verified.claim: Vendor or completer-only efficacy claims, and course-mandated compliance, as evidence about voluntary self-study.
does_not_work_verified.notes: Parle 06 documents single-group vendor studies with no control, self-selected subscribers and attrition. The ELSA trial's 94% compliance came under a course requirement. The trial's control group also had tracked out-of-class practice (92%).

does_not_work_verified.claim: Daily streaks and XP as the engagement engine (no study shows they improve learning; streak-driven grinding; one missed day did not impair habit formation).
does_not_work_verified.notes:
The evidence is secondary and non-language:
- Hadi Mogavi 2022 is qualitative forum and interview data.
- Lally 2010 is a general habit study.
- Parle cites Sailer & Homner's gamification meta-analysis (cognitive g = 0.49) and Hanus & Fox (negative).
'No study shows' is too absolute. It is fair to say there is no evidence that streaks specifically improve learning. The support for 'gamification tied to dialogue tasks' rests on a k = 17 subgroup.

critique_of_v1: All v1 practice is scripted reading or imitation (minimal pairs, loaded sentences, tongue twisters, passages, TTS shadowing). There is no unscripted speaking at all. The literature consistently shows controlled-practice gains shrinking or vanishing in spontaneous speech, and transfer depends on practising targets inside meaningful tasks (Saito & Lyster 2012; Tabandeh et al. 2018). v1 has no step that carries a drilled sound into free speech.

v1's success metrics (per-phoneme score trends; tier advance at 85 or more) measure accuracy on the same scripted items the learner practises. Test and practice are identical in task and content, which inflates apparent progress. Nothing in v1 measures comprehensibility or fluency of unscripted speech, the outcome the learner actually cares about.

Weak-sound drills advance through isolated sound, word, sentence and passage at 85 or more on read speech. The evidence-based sequence ends differently: explicit articulatory explanation, then controlled practice, then the target seeded into a meaningful spoken task with feedback on that sound, then a spontaneous probe with new words. v1 stops at read-aloud passages.

Speed ladders drill memorised tongue twisters at faster TTS tempos with massed repetition. No study I found shows that tongue-twister speed transfers to clarity or fluency in real speech. Massed repetition of one text can slow articulation and cause verbatim reciting (Suzuki & Hanzawa 2022). Fluency transfer is better supported by blocked retells of meaningful narratives, measured on new prompts (Suzuki 2021).

Feedback is a traffic-light score per word or phoneme with IPA. It gives no explicit articulatory cue, no prompt to self-repair, and no immediate re-say of the sound in a new context. It also never checks whether the sound holds up when the learner is not reading.

v1 has no dose or adherence design: no session-length target, no weekly frequency goal, no cue or reminder, and no comeback path after a gap. Voluntary app use decays sharply (secondary estimate: 43% dropout within 3 months), and persistence tracked at least 4 sessions a week of at least 5 minutes. v1 excluding streaks is consistent with the evidence, but nothing replaces them.

Articulation for French relies on Azure fluency and prosody, but Azure prosody scoring is en-US only. v1 therefore has no valid comprehensibility or articulation signal for French beyond phoneme accuracy on read text. ASR word-recognition rate on free speech, speech rate and pause location would give a language-neutral proxy.

The design never identifies the learner's L1 or level in each language. Conversation practice appears to help at A1-B1 but showed no gain at B2 in the meta-analysis, and native-speaker clarity is a different problem from L2 pronunciation. The app should record these at onboarding and route accordingly.

No retell, role-play or conversation mode means there is nothing meaningful to come back for. Interactive spoken tasks increased voluntary practice time in the available trials, which matters for one busy adult practising alone.

The v1 plan implies nothing about how long the programme must run before evaluation. Evidence suggests 8-12-week cycles with fixed pre and post unscripted probes; changes over 1-4 weeks are mostly noise.
open_questions: Does any software-delivered pronunciation feedback given during or after a spoken conversation (a prompt, a salient recast, or an end-of-task replay) improve target sounds in later spontaneous speech? I found no study; all pronunciation-in-communication evidence is teacher-delivered.

Do LLM voice conversation partners improve listener-rated comprehensibility, not only fluency or speaking-test scores? The published trials so far lack blind listener ratings, delayed tests and time-matched controls.
What real long-term usage do ELSA, Speakometer and similar apps see among voluntary adult users, and does it relate to comprehensibility gains? I found no independent field study.

Is the dialogue-system benefit absent at B2+ (Bibauw et al. 2022, small k) also true for LLM voice partners? This decides whether a conversation mode is worth building for an advanced or near-native learner in one of the two languages.

What is the learner's L1 and level in each language? If the learner is a native French or English speaker, that language needs a native-clarity design, not the L2 pronunciation evidence summarised here.

Primary-source checks still needed: McCrocklin 2019 (JSLP 5(1):98-118) results; Foote & McDonough 2017 outcome tasks and effect sizes; Hwang et al. 2024 and Sudina & Plonsky attrition figures (secondary numbers conflict: 601 vs 787 learners); Loewen et al. 2020 attrition; Wang, Cheung, Neitzel & Chai 2025 (Review of Educational Research) chatbot meta-analysis; Tyen, Caines & Buttery 2024 (NLP4CALL) LLM chatbot user study.
Is free-speech ASR word-recognition rate a valid within-learner proxy for French comprehensibility over time? Only one qualitative French study exists.
What is the best within-session balance between drill and meaningful task for transfer, for example 5 minutes drill plus 5 minutes retell? No study tested this ratio in self-study.

Lee, J., Jang, J., & Plonsky, L. (2015). The effectiveness of second language pronunciation instruction: A meta-analysis. Applied Linguistics 36(3):345-366. Saito, K., & Plonsky, L. (2019). Effects of second language pronunciation teaching revisited: A proposed measurement framework and meta-analysis. Language Learning 69(3). de Jong, N., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Fluency training in the ESL classroom: An experimental study of fluency development and proceduralization. Language Learning 61(2):533-568. 4/3/2 repetition on the same topic produced fluency gains that transferred to a new topic; supports gap-transfer-6 (from memory). https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9922.2010.00620.x
