Included in Bibauw et al. 2022 with holistic pronunciation outcomes (d = 1.62-1.75, Korean elementary children), which contradicts 'pronunciation was never measured'. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0958344010000273

Liakin, D., Cardoso, W., & Liakina, N. (2015). Learning L2 pronunciation with a mobile speech recognizer: French /y/. CALICO Journal 32(1):1-25. A controlled French mobile-ASR pronunciation study missing from gap-transfer-11; recalled from memory, publisher page blocked this session. https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.v32i1.25962

Liakin, D., Cardoso, W., & Liakina, N. (2017). Mobilizing instruction in a second-language context: Learners' perceptions of two speech technologies. Languages 2(3):11. Perceptions of mobile ASR and TTS pronunciation practice; bibliographic record verified via the Texto Livre bib. https://doi.org/10.3390/languages2030011

Su et al. (2015), a dialogue-based CAPT system for Chinese pronunciation, cited in Bibauw's 2022 thesis as producing large phoneme-level gains. It counters gap-transfer-4's statement that no software gave pronunciation feedback within dialogue. https://github.com/sbibauw/sbibauw.github.io/blob/main/assets/pdf/Bibauw_Thesis_2022.pdf

Thomson, R. I., & Derwing, T. M. (2015). The effectiveness of L2 pronunciation instruction: A narrative review. Applied Linguistics 36(3):326-344. Most of 75 studies used controlled tasks and few measured spontaneous speech, which supports the base-gap framing (from memory). https://doi.org/10.1093/applin/amu076

learner_profile_review.topic: French first-language speakers learning English: difficulties and priorities (key: frl1-english)
learner_profile_review.summary:
How this was checked: web search gave abstract-level or index-level summaries for about 30 sources, each linked below. Direct page fetching was blocked for every academic domain I tried (Cambridge, PubMed, ERIC, HAL, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, publisher PDFs). The session's shared web-search budget ran out partway through. So effect sizes are reported only where an abstract or index summary gave them, and several requested sub-topics could not be checked (see open_questions).

Ranking for this learner (adult, French first language, wants to be easily understood in English):

1. Lexical (word) stress, including how it is signalled. The consistent finding in Montreal studies of French speakers (Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012; Saito, Trofimovich & Isaacs 2017; Crowther et al. 2015) is that misplaced word stress hurts comprehensibility at every proficiency level. The signals include duration, pitch and reduced unstressed vowels (schwa). "Stress deafness" is real and lasting (Dupoux et al. 1997, 2008), but it can be reduced by a few hours of perceptual training (Schwab & Llisterri; Schwab et al. 2022; Carpenter 2015).
2. Vowel contrasts that French lacks: /iː-ɪ/, /uː-ʊ/, /æ-ʌ-ɑː/. French speakers recognise English vowels less well than German or Norwegian speakers (Iverson & Evans 2007). Vowel and consonant errors are linked to comprehensibility (Saito et al. 2017). High-variability phonetic training (HVPT: identification practice with many different voices) helps whether or not the learner lives in an English-speaking country (Iverson, Pinet & Evans 2012).
3. /h/, both dropped and wrongly added. This causes confusion at the word level (Melnik & Peperkamp 2019). Eight online HVPT sessions improved it, and the gain held four months later (Melnik & Peperkamp 2021).
4. Fluency and pausing in spontaneous speech. This matters most at lower levels and depends on the speaking task.
5. Intonation: French learners tend to put a rise on every phrase end, which hides where the word stress is (Herment et al. 2014; Horgues 2013). Pitch range itself did not predict comprehensibility.
6. /θ ð/ and word-final consonant clusters. I found no French-specific comprehensibility evidence for these, so they are ranked lowest pending checking.

Methods that worked for French speakers:
- Perceptual training with many voices, including exaggerated stress cues that fade back to natural speech.
- Implicit matching tasks, which worked as well as explicit rule teaching.
- Online HVPT for vowels and /h/.
- Production practice alongside perception training, because perception training alone carried over to production only partly (Krzonowski et al. 2016).
- Visual feedback has only pilot support (6 learners, no control group).

Main caveats:
- Most comprehensibility evidence is correlational and comes from one Montreal research group, often reusing the same 40-speaker French-L1 dataset.
- Several stress-training studies used Spanish or nonwords, not English.
- Almost all training studies are small, with short follow-up.

kept.claim: In one cross-sectional sample of 40 Quebec French speakers telling picture stories, word-stress error was the only pronunciation measure that told comprehensibility levels apart at every level. Lexical richness and fluency separated low-level speakers, and grammar and discourse separated high-level speakers. Across other studies, word stress is one of several correlates of comprehensibility, alongside segmentals, rhythm and speech rate, and grammar, lexis and discourse also matter in demanding tasks. That makes word stress a strong candidate priority, but it has not been shown to be the single most important feature, and nothing here shows causation.
kept.population: 40 adult French-L1 speakers of English in Montreal, rated by 60 native listeners (Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012). 40 French-L1 speakers, 20 raters (Saito et al. 2017). 60 speakers from 4 L1 groups including a Romance group of 15 (Crowther et al. 2015).
kept.design_implication: Make lexical stress the top English module. Score stress placement on every word of 2 or more syllables (was the stressed syllable the most prominent one?) and report it separately from phoneme accuracy. Choose practice words by frequency, word length (3 or more syllables) and suffix patterns that move stress (-tion, -ic, -ity, photograph/photography). Also include English words that look like French cognates, where French phrase-final prominence pulls stress to the end.
kept.effect_notes: Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012: 19 speech measures. Index summaries report strong correlations with comprehensibility (|r| > .70) for word-stress error ratio and vowel-reduction ratio, moderate ones (r > .40) for most other measures, and no relationship for pitch range. Saito et al. 2017: comprehensibility was linked to vowel/consonant errors, word stress, fluency, lexis and grammar; accentedness mainly to pronunciation. Crowther et al. 2015: on the IELTS long-turn task, comprehensibility was linked only to segmentals, word stress, rhythm and speech rate for all L1 groups except Farsi. All studies are cross-sectional, so causation is not shown.

citations.ref: Isaacs & Trofimovich (2012). Deconstructing comprehensibility. SSLA 34, 475-505
Saito, Trofimovich & Isaacs (2017). Using listener judgments to investigate linguistic influences on L2 comprehensibility and accentedness. Applied Linguistics 38(4), 439-462
Crowther, Trofimovich, Isaacs & Saito (2015). Does a speaking task affect second language comprehensibility? Modern Language Journal 99, 80-95

kept.claim: Native French listeners reliably have trouble encoding stress-only contrasts in memory-demanding tasks. The ABX difficulty of Dupoux et al. 1997 was placed at the level of short-term memory, and the multi-talker sequence-recall method comes from Dupoux et al. 2001. In French late learners of Spanish tested on nonwords, this did not improve with proficiency (Dupoux et al. 2008), and it also appears in French-dominant simultaneous bilinguals (2010). For French learners of English with real words the evidence is weaker and mixed: some French Canadian learners do use stress in word recognition (Tremblay 2008), and short training improves stress identification (Schwab et al. 2022).
kept.population: Native French adults compared with Spanish adults (Dupoux et al. 1997). 39 French late learners of Spanish (Dupoux et al. 2008). Canadian French learners of English at several proficiency levels (Tremblay 2008).
kept.design_implication: (a) Diagnose stress perception with hard tasks: many voices, recall of sequences, or lexical decision on stress-only minimal pairs, not a single-voice 'same or different?' check. (b) Store the stress pattern as part of each practised word (show it, e.g. ●○○, and quiz it). Tremblay found that only learners who know where the stress falls can use it to recognise words. (c) Expect slow progress and track stress perception as its own trend line.
kept.effect_notes: Dupoux et al. 1997: French listeners had trouble with stress-only contrasts only under high phonetic variability and memory load. Dupoux et al. 2008: all late learners had significant trouble encoding and using stress contrasts in sequence recall and speeded lexical decision, whatever their level of practice. The authors call it a lasting encoding problem. Tremblay 2008: some learners could use primary stress in cross-modal word identification, but only those who knew the target stress placement. A 2023 HAL study and others suggest proficiency and musical ability lessen the deafness.

citations.ref: Dupoux, Pallier, Sebastián & Mehler (1997). A destressing 'deafness' in French? J. Memory and Language 36, 406-421
Dupoux, Sebastián-Gallés, Navarrete & Peperkamp (2008). Persistent stress 'deafness': the case of French learners of Spanish. Cognition 106(2), 682-706
Tremblay (2008). Is second language lexical access prosodically constrained? Applied Psycholinguistics 29(4), 553-584
Revisiting 'stress-deafness' amongst upper intermediate learners of English in words containing stress-imposing endings (HAL, 2023)

kept.claim: In ab initio French-speaking listeners, two 4-hour perceptual trainings on Spanish stress, one explicit and one a non-explicit shape/word matching task, were each followed by better stress identification and discrimination, with no difference between the methods. The abstract reports no untrained control group, so test-retest gains cannot be ruled out. Training also had no effect on stress processing under different phonetic-variability conditions. Evidence on English words, on production, and on the benefit of exaggerated-then-faded cues is lacking or unverified.
kept.population: French adults: some with no Spanish (Schwab et al. 2022), French learners of Spanish (Schwab & Llisterri 2011), and French and English adults on an English-style stress task (Carpenter 2015). Most studies are not on English words.
kept.design_implication: Build a 'Which syllable is stressed?' perception game. The learner hears a word and taps the stressed syllable or matches it to a shape (●○ / ○●). Use several TTS or recorded voices. Start with lengthened and pitch-boosted stressed syllables (via SSML prosody or signal processing) and fade back to natural speech as accuracy rises. Budget about 4 hours in total, for example 4-5 minutes per session over 6-8 weeks. Keep rule explanations short. Test transfer on new words and new voices.
kept.effect_notes: Schwab & Llisterri 2011: brief training raised identification accuracy, but it stayed below native level; pitch (F0) was the most useful cue for French listeners. Schwab et al. 2022: two 4-hour perceptual trainings (explicit vs. a non-explicit shape/word matching task) both improved identification and discrimination, with no difference between them. Carpenter 2015: the trained French group made fewer errors and responded faster in an ABX stress task than untrained French groups. Sample sizes and effect sizes were not in the abstracts I could access. Transfer to English production has not been shown.

citations.ref: Schwab, Giroud, Meyer & Dellwo (2022). Explicit versus non-explicit prosodic training in the learning of Spanish L2 stress contrasts by French listeners. J. Second Language Studies
Schwab & Llisterri (2011). Are French speakers able to learn to perceive lexical stress contrasts? ICPhS XVII
Llisterri & Schwab (2019). Perception of lexical stress in Spanish L2 (overview of the French-listener series)
Carpenter (2015). Phonetic training significantly mitigates the stress 'deafness' of French speakers. Int. J. Linguistics 7(3), 94-108

kept.claim: French and English listeners weight stress cues differently (Frost 2011). On the same 40 Montreal speakers, the vowel-reduction ratio was reported to correlate with comprehensibility, while rhythm was tied more to accent than to comprehensibility. French learners' English timing differs from native timing, but classic duration-based rhythm metrics (%V, varco, nPVI) have proved unreliable for tracking French learners across proficiency levels. Syllable-based measures appear more informative. The evidence is mixed, and rhythm metrics should not be used as a progress indicator without validation.
kept.population: English and French listeners, perception experiment (Frost 2011). French learners of English reading aloud: ANGLISH corpus (Tortel & Hirst 2010). 40 Montreal French-L1 speakers (Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012; Trofimovich & Isaacs 2012).
kept.design_implication: Break stress feedback into the cues the learner can control: (1) is the stressed syllable longer? (2) does the pitch move on it? (3) are the unstressed vowels reduced to schwa or shortened? Add short 'weak forms' drills for function words (to, for, can, of, and, that) and schwa-heavy phrases. Measure rhythm with tempo-normalised metrics (e.g. varco-V / nPVI of vowel durations) and show them as a secondary indicator, not a pass/fail score.
kept.effect_notes: Tortel & Hirst 2010: normalised rhythm metrics classified natives, advanced learners and beginners with about 70% accuracy. Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012: vowel-reduction ratio was among the strongest correlates of comprehensibility (reported |r| > .70). Trofimovich & Isaacs 2012 (same speakers): accent was uniquely tied to rhythm and segmental/syllable-structure accuracy, while comprehensibility was mainly tied to grammar and lexis.

citations.ref: Frost (2011). Stress and cues to relative prominence in English and French: a perceptual study. JIPA 41(1), 67-84
Tortel & Hirst (2010). Rhythm metrics and the production of English L1/L2. Speech Prosody 2010
Trofimovich & Isaacs (2012). Disentangling accent from comprehensibility. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition
Isaacs & Trofimovich (2012). Deconstructing comprehensibility. SSLA

kept.claim: French speakers have a smaller native vowel system and recognise English vowels less accurately than German or Norwegian speakers. They still learn new cues (formant movement, duration) instead of simply mapping English vowels onto French ones, so the gap is trainable.
kept.population: Adult Spanish, French, German and Norwegian learners of English, cross-sectional perception study (Iverson & Evans 2007). 40 French-L1 speakers for the link between vowel errors and comprehensibility (Saito et al. 2017).
kept.design_implication: Set the vowel targets to the contrasts French does not have: /iː-ɪ/ (sheep/ship, leave/live), /uː-ʊ/ (fool/full, pool/pull), /æ-ʌ-ɑː/ (cat/cut/cart, hat/hut/heart). Train both vowel quality and length/glide cues. In feedback, report which vowel was heard instead (e.g. 'your /ɪ/ sounded like /iː/'), not just a low score, because the confusions are predictable.
kept.effect_notes: Iverson & Evans 2007: the larger-inventory groups (German, Norwegian) were more accurate than the smaller-inventory groups (Spanish, French). All groups used formant movement and duration. Saito et al. 2017: rater-judged vowel/consonant errors were linked to both comprehensibility and accentedness.

citations.ref: Iverson & Evans (2007). Learning English vowels with different first-language vowel systems. JASA 122(5), 2842-2854
Saito, Trofimovich & Isaacs (2017). Applied Linguistics 38(4)

kept.claim: HVPT on English vowels improved French speakers' vowel identification whether they were experienced (living in England) or inexperienced (in France), so training adds something beyond exposure (Iverson et al. 2012; session count not verified). The small French study of perception vs production training (Krzonowski et al. 2016) reported that perception (HVPT) training affected both perception and production, while production training had a more restricted effect. Its authors say interpretation is difficult because the untrained control group also improved between tests. Meta-analyses show perception HVPT transfers to production, with smaller effects than on perception.
kept.population: French speakers who learned English at school, experienced (tested in England) and inexperienced (tested in France), 8 HVPT sessions (Iverson, Pinet & Evans 2012). 48 French first-year university students, 5 sessions of perception training vs. production training vs. none (Krzonowski, Ferragne & Pellegrino 2016). Supporting evidence from Greek learners, a different population (Lengeris 2018).
kept.design_implication: Pair each vowel contrast with two short activities per session: (1) HVPT identification with many voices and immediate right/wrong feedback, and (2) production of the same words with per-vowel feedback (formant-based or assessment-API phoneme scores). Package each contrast as roughly an 8-session unit that fits the phone-based 5-15 minute format. Check transfer with spontaneous speech (describe a picture) as well as read words.
kept.effect_notes: Iverson et al. 2012: both groups improved to a similar degree after 8 sessions. Krzonowski et al. 2016: vowels were judged by a discriminant classifier trained on native speech; the control group did not improve. Lengeris 2018 (Greek L1): auditory training improved vowel production in read sentences and, to a lesser extent, in spontaneous speech. Standardised effect sizes were not in the accessible abstracts.

citations.ref: Iverson, Pinet & Evans (2012). Auditory training for experienced and inexperienced second-language learners: Native French speakers learning English vowels. Applied Psycholinguistics 33(1), 145-160

Krzonowski, Ferragne & Pellegrino (2016). Perception et production de voyelles de l'anglais par des apprenants francophones: effet d'entraînements en perception et en production. JEP-TALN-RECITAL 2016
Lengeris (2018). Computer-based auditory training improves second-language vowel production in spontaneous speech. JASA 144(3), EL165

kept.claim: French learners of English mainly drop /h/ and show perceptual 'deletion' of it, which affects word recognition (misses on /h/-words, false alarms on h-less nonwords). Hypercorrect /h/ insertion occurs in production but appears far rarer; the finding's own background figures are about 45-55% deletion vs under 2% insertion. One online HVPT study reported gains in /h/ identification and lexical decision that lasted at follow-up. /h/ is a promising, low-cost target, but it rests on a single training study.
kept.population: Late French learners of English in France, lexical decision and online HVPT (Melnik & Peperkamp 2019, 2021). French-speaking learners in Montreal, EEG mismatch-negativity study (Mah, Goad & Steinhauer 2016). Sociolinguistic data on /h/ hypercorrection (Janda & Auger 1992).
kept.design_implication: Add an /h/ module with online HVPT identification (heat/eat, hair/air, hold/old, hand/and) across many voices, including word-level decisions ('is "usband" a word?'). In production, track dropped /h/ and wrongly added /h/ as separate error types. A drill that only rewards adding /h/ can increase the wrong insertions. /h/ is a clear, cheap, well-supported win for this learner.
kept.effect_notes: Melnik & Peperkamp 2019: more misses on /h/-initial words (holiday) and more false alarms on vowel-initial nonwords (usband), matching the pattern seen in production. Melnik & Peperkamp 2021: 8 online sessions improved accuracy on both the identification and lexical decision tasks, and the gains were still there 4 months later; this is the first evidence that short training improves word recognition, not only sound perception. Mah et al. 2016: French learners showed a mismatch-negativity response only for non-linguistic stimuli, which points to a missing sound category. Background figures summarised with that paper (about 45-55% /h/ dropping, under 2% insertion) come from secondary summary and were not checked against the primary source.

citations.ref: Melnik & Peperkamp (2021). High-Variability Phonetic Training enhances second language lexical processing: evidence from online training of French learners of English. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition
Melnik & Peperkamp (2019). Perceptual deletion and asymmetric lexical access in second language learners. JASA 145(1), EL13-EL18
Mah, Goad & Steinhauer (2016). Using event-related brain potentials to assess perceptibility: the case of French speakers and English [h]. Frontiers in Psychology 7, 1469
Janda & Auger (1992). Quantitative evidence, qualitative hypercorrection, sociolinguistic variables - and French speakers' 'eadhaches with English h/Ø. Language & Communication 12(3-4)

kept.claim: Being easy to understand (comprehensibility) and sounding native (accent) come apart for French-L1 speakers. Accent follows rhythm and segmental/syllable accuracy, while comprehensibility also depends on fluency, vocabulary, grammar and discourse. Which features matter also changes with the speaking task: read or simple monologue tasks favour pronunciation and fluency, and demanding integrated tasks add grammar, lexis and discourse.
kept.population: 40 Montreal French-L1 speakers of English (Trofimovich & Isaacs 2012; Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012). 60 speakers from 4 L1s including Romance (Crowther et al. 2015, 2018). 120 Japanese learners, a different population (Saito et al. 2016). Mandarin speakers, a different population (Kennedy & Trofimovich 2008).
kept.design_implication: Make comprehensibility the app's main outcome, not nativeness. Include spontaneous speaking tasks (60-second picture description or opinion) alongside read-aloud, because read-aloud hides the fluency and vocabulary parts of comprehensibility. Track speech rate and pause placement, i.e. pauses inside phrases vs. at phrase boundaries. Kennedy & Trofimovich found that listener experience and meaningful context inflate how much is understood, so an ASR 'was it understood?' check should use unpredictable sentences as a stricter intelligibility test.
kept.effect_notes: Trofimovich & Isaacs 2012: 19 measures, 60 novice raters and 3 teachers. Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012: lexical richness and fluency separated low-level learners, grammar and discourse separated high-level learners, and word stress separated all levels. Crowther et al. 2015: on the TOEFL integrated task, comprehensibility was also linked to grammar, lexis and discourse for all groups. Saito et al. 2016 (Japanese): comprehensibility was related to all linguistic domains.

citations.ref: Trofimovich & Isaacs (2012). Disentangling accent from comprehensibility. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition
Crowther, Trofimovich, Saito & Isaacs (2018). Linguistic dimensions of L2 accentedness and comprehensibility vary across speaking tasks. SSLA 40, 443-457

Saito, Trofimovich & Isaacs (2016). Second language speech production: linguistic correlates of comprehensibility and accentedness for learners at different ability levels. Applied Psycholinguistics 37(2)
Kennedy & Trofimovich (2008). Intelligibility, comprehensibility, and accentedness of L2 speech: the role of listener experience and semantic context. Canadian Modern Language Review 64(3)

does_not_work_supported.claim: Aiming for a native accent (accent reduction) rather than comprehensibility
does_not_work_supported.notes: Supported by Trofimovich & Isaacs 2012 (phonology categories, including rhythm, uniquely distinguished accent) and Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012. The evidence is correlational, from 40 Quebec French speakers, so it justifies making comprehensibility the priority, not a claim that accent work is useless.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Relying on exposure or immersion to fix stress and vowels
does_not_work_supported.notes: Dupoux et al. 2008 found no effect of experience, but for French learners of Spanish on nonwords. Iverson et al. 2012 found that experienced French learners living in England still gained from HVPT. Caveat: Tremblay 2008 shows some French Canadian learners of English do use stress in word recognition, so exposure is not useless.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Long explicit rule lessons as the main method
does_not_work_supported.notes: Schwab et al. 2022 (abstract confirmed) found explicit instruction no better than non-explicit shape/word matching, in ab initio learners of Spanish with no untrained control. Capliez is unverifiable. Reasonable as a design stance, but weakly evidenced.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Judging progress only on read-aloud sentences
does_not_work_supported.notes: The Crowther et al. 2015 abstract (read in full) shows that the features linked to comprehensibility change with the task. No cited study compared read-aloud directly, but including spontaneous tasks is well justified.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Tongue-twister speed ladders (v1 feature)
does_not_work_supported.notes: I found no evidence either way within the accessible sources. The 'untested, not disproven' wording is appropriate.

open_questions: /θ ð/ substitutions and word-final consonant clusters: I found no French-specific evidence on how much they cost in comprehensibility or intelligibility, because the web-search budget ran out before these could be searched. Their low ranking here is provisional and should be checked (e.g. functional-load research, Munro & Derwing).
Shadowing: I retrieved no controlled evidence for French-L1 learners of English. Whether shadowing beats listen-and-repeat for stress and rhythm in this population is unknown.

Most stress-training evidence for French listeners uses Spanish or nonwords (Schwab; Carpenter). Controlled studies showing that English stress perception training carries over to production and comprehensibility in spontaneous speech are still missing.
Outcomes of the Frost & Picavet / Innovalangues 'putting prosody first' work and Frost & O'Donnell 2018 could not be retrieved.
Quebec vs. European French: the comprehensibility studies are from Montreal, while the /h/ and vowel training studies are from France. Priorities are probably shared but this has not been tested.

Can Azure Pronunciation Assessment's prosody/stress output reliably detect misplaced lexical stress and missing vowel reduction in French-accented English? This needs a small validation against human judgments before stress scores are shown as feedback.

How much training is needed for an intermediate-advanced adult in 5-15 minute phone sessions: the studies used 4 hours (stress) or 8 sessions (vowels, /h/), and the best spacing and upkeep schedule are unknown.

Effect sizes: the index summaries I could access mostly gave direction and significance only. The primary full texts (blocked in this environment) should be read to get d or r values for Iverson et al. 2012, Melnik & Peperkamp 2021, Schwab et al. 2022 and Carpenter 2015.
missed_evidence: Field, J. (2005). Intelligibility and the listener: The role of lexical stress. TESOL Quarterly 39(3):399-423. Stress shifts hurt intelligibility, reportedly rightward shifts more than leftward, which is directly relevant to French final prominence. https://doi.org/10.2307/3588487

Lepage, A. & Busà, M. G. (2014). Intelligibility of English L2: The effects of incorrect word stress placement and incorrect vowel reduction in the speech of French and Italian learners of English. Concordia Working Papers in Applied Linguistics 5:387-400. Tests stress placement and vowel reduction in French learners; not read live, reference confirmed.

Dupoux, Peperkamp & Sebastián-Gallés (2001). A robust method to study stress 'deafness'. JASA 110(3):1606-1618. The actual source of the variability plus memory-load (sequence recall) method. https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1380437

Dupoux, Peperkamp & Sebastián-Gallés (2010). Limits on bilingualism revisited: Stress 'deafness' in simultaneous French-Spanish bilinguals. Cognition 114:266-275. Deafness persists even in French-dominant simultaneous bilinguals.

Qin, Chien & Tremblay (2017). Processing of word-level stress by Mandarin-speaking second language learners of English. Applied Psycholinguistics 38(3). Notes that Canadian French speakers may use stress cues more than European French speakers; a generalisation caveat for Montreal-based evidence.

Ortin & Simonet (2022). Phonological processing of stress by native English speakers learning Spanish as a second language. SSLA 44:460-482. Stress processing is graded across languages, with a modest proficiency effect in a different L1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263121000309

Uchihara, Karas & Thomson (2024). Does perceptual HVPT improve L2 speech production? A meta-analysis of perception-production connection. Applied Psycholinguistics 45:591-623. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716424000195
Uchihara, Karas & Thomson (2025). High Variability Phonetic Training: A meta-analysis of L2 perceptual training studies (79 studies). SSLA 47:794-827. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263125100879

Brekelmans, Lavan, Saito, Clayards & Wonnacott (2022). Does high variability training improve the learning of non-native phoneme contrasts over low variability training? A replication. JML 126:104352. No high-variability advantage found. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jml.2022.104352
Sadakata & McQueen (2014). Frontiers in Psychology 5:1318. Interaction of variability and aptitude: high variability helped high-aptitude learners and hindered low-aptitude ones (tones, Dutch L1).

Guyot-Talbot, Heidlmayr & Ferragne (2016). Entraînements à la prosodie des questions ouvertes et fermées de l'anglais chez des apprenants francophones (prosody training on English wh- and yes/no questions for French learners). JEP 2016:265-273. Three sessions of repetition with F0-contour visual feedback reduced the distance to the model contour. https://aclanthology.org/2016.jeptalnrecital-jep.30/

Michardière, Guyot-Talbot, Ferragne & Pellegrino (2016). Étude transversale du rythme de l'anglais chez des apprenants francophones (a cross-sectional study of English rhythm in French learners). JEP 2016:328-336. Classic rhythm metrics were unreliable across learner levels. https://aclanthology.org/2016.jeptalnrecital-jep.37/

Ballier, Martin & Amand (2016). Variabilité des syllabes réalisées par des apprenants de l'anglais (syllable variability in French learners of English; ANGLISH corpus). JEP 2016:732-740. Syllable-based measures separated learner levels better than Ramus-style intervals. https://aclanthology.org/2016.jeptalnrecital-jep.82/

Korzekwa et al. (2021). Detection of lexical stress errors in non-native (L2) English with data augmentation and attention. arXiv 2012.14788 / Interspeech 2021. 94.8% precision and 49.2% recall: automatic per-word stress scoring is still unreliable. https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.14788

Azure Pronunciation Assessment documentation: no lexical-stress error type; ProsodyScore is en-US only and full-text level only; syllable-level accuracy is en-US only. The stress, intonation and weak-form feedback in these design implications therefore needs custom F0, duration and intensity analysis. https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/ai-services/speech-service/how-to-pronunciation-assessment

Saito & Plonsky (2019). Effects of second language pronunciation teaching revisited: A proposed measurement framework and meta-analysis. Language Learning 69(3):652-708. Gains are larger on controlled than spontaneous measures, which supports testing transfer with spontaneous speech.

learner_profile_review.topic: native-clarity: Clearer speech for native speakers (training and measurement), with a focus on French
learner_profile_review.summary: Research on "clear speech" shows that ordinary adult native speakers can switch into a clearer speaking style on request. The style has consistent acoustic features: a slower rate built from more pauses and longer sounds, a wider pitch (F0) range, an expanded and tighter vowel space, released stop bursts and word-final consonants, more energy in the 1-3 kHz band, and deeper low-frequency modulation of the loudness envelope. For listeners with normal hearing in noise, it raises keyword intelligibility by roughly 14-18 percentage points. The effect is found across languages, including Croatian and Canadian (Quebec) French: French clear speech shows longer vowels, greater vowel contrast, less spread within each vowel category, and larger lip and tongue movements. The wording of the instruction matters: "over-enunciate" gives the largest gain and a vague "speak clearly" the smallest. The benefit also varies a great deal between talkers (only 23 of 41 talkers in one study produced a significant vowel benefit), so the app has to measure each user's own change from habitual to clear speech. Slowing down is not required: trained talkers produced clear speech at normal rate that kept about 78% of the benefit, and across normal talkers speaking rate did not predict intelligibility. Evidence on keeping the style is thin. Minimal instruction works right away, and the difference between styles grows with practice over trials. In conversation, however, clear speech fades and then resets at each new task. No controlled long-term carry-over trial in typical adults was found. For automatic measurement: word error rate from speech recognition (ASR) tracks human intelligibility in moderate-to-severe dysarthria, but it is unreliable for mild speakers and for individual second-language (L2) speakers, and Whisper tends to fill gaps with fluent but wrong words. On clean audio, a typical native speaker will score at the ceiling. Clarity metrics should therefore be compared with the user's own baseline and combined: articulation rate and pauses, band energy, vowel contrast on controlled carrier phrases, and ASR scored on noise-degraded, low-predictability sentences. One study found that feedback from ASR alone made healthy speakers clearer. No evidence was found that tongue twisters or speed drills improve clarity or intelligibility: in research they are used to cause speech errors, and the only training study measured oral-motor repetition rate. Recommendation for the native-French module: train "clear speech at a natural rate" through habitual-versus-clear contrast recordings, concrete over-enunciation instructions, simulated-listener and noise conditions, and semi-spontaneous speech tasks. Score everything relative to the user's own baseline. Method note: fetching full texts was blocked in this environment, so all details come from abstracts and index summaries returned by search. The search budget ran out before French speaking-rate and vowel-reduction norms could be checked.

kept.claim: Averaged across talkers, instructed clear speech reliably makes speech more intelligible: about 17 percentage points for listeners with hearing loss (Picheny et al. 1985), with similar gains for listeners with normal hearing in noise or reverberation (Payton et al. 1994). The benefit varies a lot between talkers, and some produce little or none. Typical acoustic correlates are: slower rate (pauses plus lengthening), wider F0 range, less vowel reduction and an expanded vowel space, released stop bursts and final consonants, more obstruent energy, and more 1-3 kHz energy. Clear-speech intelligibility benefits and vowel-space expansion have been found in Croatian as well as English.
kept.population: Typical adult native talkers of English and Croatian; listeners with normal hearing (in noise), with hearing loss, older, or non-native
kept.effect_notes: Keywords in clearly spoken nonsense sentences were about 15 percentage points more intelligible than conversational ones, both for listeners with hearing loss in quiet and for listeners with normal hearing in noise (Picheny et al. series). Later reviews report 14-18 point gains for listeners with normal hearing in noise. Smiljanic and Bradlow (2005) found vowel space expansion in both Croatian (5 vowels) and English (10+ vowels).
kept.design_implication: Make 'clear speech' the explicit training target for the native-French module instead of generic 'diction'. Show a feature panel for each recording (pauses, articulation rate, F0 range, vowel contrast, final-consonant release, 1-3 kHz energy) so the user can see which clear-speech features they already use and which they do not.

citations.ref: Smiljanić R, Bradlow AR (2009). Speaking and hearing clearly: Talker and listener factors in speaking style changes. Language and Linguistics Compass 3(1):236-264
Picheny MA, Durlach NI, Braida LD (1986). Speaking clearly for the hard of hearing II: Acoustic characteristics of clear and conversational speech. JSHR 29:434-446
Uchanski RM (1996). Speaking clearly for the hard of hearing IV: Further studies of the role of speaking rate. JSHR 39(3):494-509
Smiljanić R, Bradlow AR (2005). Production and perception of clear speech in Croatian and English. JASA 118(3):1677-1688
Uchanski RM (2005). Clear speech. In Pisoni & Remez (Eds.), Handbook of Speech Perception, pp. 207-235

kept.claim: Small studies of Canadian French show that clear speech has longer and more intense vowels, greater contrast between vowel categories and less spread within each category, produced with larger articulator movements. The clear-speech benefit appeared in audio-only, visual-only and audiovisual conditions, but varied between talkers. In 85 dB babble, 6 French speakers changed both lip and tongue movements, more so when interacting with someone. Only some speakers specifically enhanced visible lip cues when the listener could see them. No verified European French clear-speech studies are cited. Garnier, Henrich & Dubois 2010 on Parisian French Lombard speech is the nearest candidate.
kept.population: Adult native speakers of Canadian French: Gagné et al. 6 female talkers and 12 listeners; Ménard et al. sighted and congenitally blind adults; Garnier et al. 6 speakers recorded with articulography. Stimuli were syllables, vowels in carrier phrases, and short utterances, not connected discourse. No studies of European French clear speech were verified here.
kept.effect_notes: Gagné et al. (2002): 1,728 video items (CV/VCV syllables with /b d g v z ʒ/ in /a i y/ contexts). Clear speech was more intelligible than conversational speech in all three modalities. Ménard et al. (2016): 10 repetitions of /i y u e ø o ɛ œ a/ in the carrier sentence 'Le mot /pVp/ me plaît'. Sighted speakers exaggerated lip movements for sighted listeners only. Garnier et al. (2018): 85 dB babble; interaction increased the adaptation.
kept.design_implication: For French clarity, measure (a) contrast between neighbouring vowels, especially the crowded front rounded/unrounded series /i y e ø ɛ œ/ and /u o ɔ/; (b) consistency of each vowel, meaning low spread across repetitions; and (c) vowel duration. Measure these on short carrier-phrase probes such as 'Le mot __ me plaît'. Because French clarity is partly visible, an optional front-camera mode that gives feedback on lip opening could be tested, but it would be a later-stage feature, not part of the core.

citations.ref: Gagné J-P, Rochette A-J, Charest M (2002). Auditory, visual and audiovisual clear speech. Speech Communication 37(3):213-230

Ménard L, Trudeau-Fisette P, Côté D, Turgeon C (2016). Speaking clearly for the blind: Acoustic and articulatory correlates of speaking conditions in sighted and congenitally blind speakers. PLOS ONE 11(9):e0160088
Garnier M, Ménard L, Alexandre B (2018). Hyper-articulation in Lombard speech: An active communicative strategy to enhance visible speech cues? JASA 144(2):1059

kept.claim: The exact instruction changes how much speakers change. 'Over-enunciate' produced the largest changes in vowel spectra and timing and the largest gain in intelligibility. 'Speak as if to a listener with hearing impairment' came second, and plain 'speak clearly' came last.
kept.population: 12 typical adult American English speakers reading 18 sentences in 4 conditions; 40 listeners transcribing in multitalker babble
kept.effect_notes: Ranking: habitual < clear < hearing-impaired < overenunciate, for both acoustic change and intelligibility. 10 of the 12 speakers followed this ranking. The size of the benefit differed between male and female speakers.
kept.design_implication: Replace vague prompts ('be clearer') with concrete over-enunciation cues such as 'open the jaw more, finish every final consonant, give each vowel its full shape'. Add listener framing ('your listener is hard of hearing'). A/B test the instruction wording inside the app against the user's measured change.

citations.ref: Lam J, Tjaden K, Wilding G (2012). Acoustics of clear speech: Effect of instruction. JSLHR 55(6):1807-1821
Lam J, Tjaden K (2013). Intelligibility of clear speech: Effect of instruction. JSLHR 56(5):1429-1440

kept.claim: In one 41-talker database, the clear-speech benefit for identifying vowels in /bVd/ words in noise varied widely between talkers, and a sizeable minority showed no significant individual benefit. In a 12-talker acoustic follow-up, talkers with a large benefit lengthened vowels and expanded vowel space more than talkers with no benefit. Individual improvement should therefore be measured, not assumed.
kept.population: 41 adult talkers of American English (Ferguson 2004 database); acoustic follow-up on 6 'big-benefit' and 6 'no-benefit' talkers; young listeners with normal hearing identifying vowels in noise
kept.effect_notes: Only 23 of 41 talkers (56%) showed a significant clear-speech benefit for vowel intelligibility. Big-benefit talkers increased vowel duration and vowel-space measures significantly more than no-benefit talkers.
kept.design_implication: Do not assume that trying harder produces clearer speech. Every session should include a paired habitual recording and a clear recording of the same material, and the app should report the user's own difference. The app then finds which features this user does not change (for example, vowel space stays flat while only the rate drops) and targets those.

citations.ref: Ferguson SH, Kewley-Port D (2007). Talker differences in clear and conversational speech: Acoustic characteristics of vowels. JSLHR 50:1241-1255

Ferguson SH (2012). Talker differences in clear and conversational speech: Vowel intelligibility for older adults with hearing loss. JSLHR (reports the 23/41 result from Ferguson 2004, JASA 116:2365-2373)

kept.claim: A few trained talkers learned to produce clear speech at their normal rate, and this kept a substantial part (reported as about 78%) of the clear/slow benefit for listeners with normal hearing in noise. These talkers showed more 1-3 kHz energy and deeper low-frequency envelope modulation. But when these properties were imposed on conversational speech, they recovered only a small part of the benefit, so they are correlates rather than proven carriers. Older listeners may still need a slower rate.
kept.population: A small number of trained American English talkers (the 2004 acoustic analysis used 5 talkers); listeners with normal hearing in noise; older adults with hearing loss
kept.effect_notes: Clear/normal speech gave listeners with normal hearing in noise about 78% of the benefit of slow clear speech, as reported in follow-up work.
kept.design_implication: For a native speaker who wants crisper but natural-sounding speech, the end goal is 'clear at your habitual rate'. Progress in two stages: first slow and clear, then keep the clarity features while bringing the rate back up. Track 1-3 kHz band energy relative to overall level, and envelope modulation depth, as 'crispness' indices. Do not reward slowness by itself.

citations.ref: Krause JC, Braida LD (2002). Investigating alternative forms of clear speech: The effects of speaking rate and speaking mode on intelligibility. JASA 112(5):2165-2172
Krause JC, Braida LD (2004). Acoustic properties of naturally produced clear speech at normal speaking rates. JASA 115(1):362-378
Krause JC, Braida LD (2009). Evaluating the role of spectral and envelope characteristics in the intelligibility advantage of clear speech. JASA 125(5):3346-3357

kept.claim: Among typical native talkers, F0 range (Bradlow et al. 1996), and 1-3 kHz energy plus word duration (Hazan & Markham 2004), are associated with intelligibility, while speaking rate and mean F0 are not. The relation between vowel-space size and intelligibility is inconsistent across studies: some find a positive association, others none. No single acoustic measure should serve as a stand-alone clarity score.
kept.population: Typical native English adults: 20 talkers reading 100 Harvard sentences (Bradlow et al.); 45 talkers (adults and children) and 135 listeners (Hazan & Markham)
kept.effect_notes: Hazan and Markham: energy in a specific frequency region plus word duration explained about half of the variance in word intelligibility between talkers. Bradlow et al.: F0 range correlated positively; speaking rate and mean F0 did not; the vowel-space correlation was moderate (r = +0.34) only in the extreme-talker subset.
kept.design_implication: Use several features together, not a single 'clarity score'. Present vowel-space area only relative to the user's own baseline, measured on controlled probes with speaker normalization, and never as a comparison with other speakers or norms. Put more weight on F0 range, band energy, and segment or word duration, and treat articulation rate as a diagnostic, not a goal.

citations.ref: Bradlow AR, Torretta GM, Pisoni DB (1996). Intelligibility of normal speech I: Global and fine-grained acoustic-phonetic talker characteristics. Speech Communication 20:255-272
Hazan V, Markham D (2004). Acoustic-phonetic correlates of talker intelligibility for adults and children. JASA 116(5):3108-3118
The effect of hyperarticulation on speech comprehension under adverse listening conditions (review statement that the vowel-space/intelligibility link is associative, not causal)

kept.claim: Clear speech can be produced immediately with minimal instruction by young and older talkers. In interaction it declines over time and resets at task boundaries, and read, instructed clear speech is more extreme than interactive clear speech. One study suggests clear-Lombard adaptations can increase over the first trials. Evidence that training produces lasting carry-over in typical adults is essentially absent: only small partner-training studies with the hearing-impaired exist.
kept.population: Schum: young and older American talkers; Shen et al.: 78 young Dutch-speaking adults; Lee & Baese-Berk: native English speakers talking with non-native partners; Hazan & Baker: British English (LUCID); Caissie et al.: 2 spouses of adults with hearing loss
kept.effect_notes: No randomized controlled trial of long-term carry-over of clarity training in typical adults was found. Caissie et al. is effectively a two-talker case comparison.
kept.design_implication: Start each short session with a few clear-speech warm-up trials, because the gain grows over trials. Include semi-spontaneous tasks (picture description, 60-90 s retell) alongside read sentences, and measure the decline in clarity within the monologue as a 'maintenance' metric. Add periodic 'reset' cues. Use spaced, repeated short sessions. Treat long-term retention as unproven and track it with monthly probes of unprompted habitual speech.

citations.ref: Schum DJ (1996). Intelligibility of clear and conversational speech of young and elderly talkers. J Am Acad Audiol 7:212-218
Shen C, Cooke M, Janse E (2023). Speaking in the presence of noise: Consistency of acoustic properties in clear-Lombard speech over time. JASA 153(4):2165
Lee D-Y, Baese-Berk MM (2020). The maintenance of clear speech in naturalistic conversations. JASA 147(5):3702-3711
Hazan V, Baker R (2011). Acoustic-phonetic characteristics of speech produced with communicative intent to counter adverse listening conditions. JASA 130(4):2139-2152
Caissie R et al. (2005). Clear speech for adults with a hearing loss: Does intervention with communication partners make a difference? J Am Acad Audiol 16:157-171

kept.claim: Background noise and a listener in difficulty elicit clearer articulation without explicit instruction, and interaction strengthens this: in 6 Canadian French speakers in 85 dB babble, and in British English pairs whose partner heard degraded speech. Explicit instruction on read material produces larger acoustic changes. Whether noise-elicited clarity persists after the noise is removed has not been tested.
kept.population: 6 Canadian French speakers (Garnier et al., with articulography); British English talker pairs (Hazan & Baker, LUCID/Diapix tasks)
kept.effect_notes: The adaptation was larger in interactive conditions than when reading. The effects were measured acoustically and articulatorily; this work did not measure intelligibility gains in French.
kept.design_implication: Add a 'listener simulation' mode. It frames each prompt around a specific listener (for example, a colleague on a bad phone line or someone in a noisy café). Optionally it plays moderate-level babble through earbuds to trigger clear-Lombard speech, with volume capped for safety. Then fade the noise so the user learns to produce the same articulation without it.

citations.ref: Garnier M, Ménard L, Alexandre B (2018). Hyper-articulation in Lombard speech: An active communicative strategy to enhance visible speech cues? JASA 144(2):1059
Hazan V, Baker R (2011). Acoustic-phonetic characteristics of speech produced with communicative intent to counter adverse listening conditions. JASA 130(4):2139-2152

kept.claim: ASR word error rate is a partial, population-dependent proxy for human intelligibility. It tracks human transcription in dysarthria recorded in noise and in children with dysarthria. It is inaccurate and unstable for mildly impaired speakers. For L2 speakers, average ASR and human scores can match while failing to correlate for individual speakers. In noise, Whisper matched or beat human listeners on L2 speech but 'filled in' with fluent, wrong content.
kept.population: Speakers with dysarthria (20 people with Parkinson disease and 20 controls recorded on phones; people with ALS; children with dysarthria); 4 Taiwanese L2 English learners with 12 native listeners; L1-Mandarin L2 English speech at 8 signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). No validation in typical native French speakers was found.
kept.effect_notes: Parkinson study: probability 0.8 (95% CI 0.65-0.91) that ASR performs as well as or better than the average human listener. ALS: Google ASR word error rate was insufficient for grading severity, and especially poor in mild cases. L2: ASR matched L1 listener judgments for only 1 of 4 speakers (plus 1 more per task). Mean word scores: ASR 40.8% vs humans 38.6%; sentences: 75.5% vs 83.9%.
kept.design_implication: A typical native speaker will score close to 0% word error rate on clean audio, a ceiling effect, so raw ASR is useless there as a clarity meter. Instead, mix the recording with babble at a fixed SNR before transcription to create headroom. Use low-predictability or semantically unpredictable sentences so the ASR language model cannot guess the words. Score word accuracy against the user's own habitual baseline, and show it next to the acoustic measures, never alone.

citations.ref: Moya-Galé G, Walsh SJ, Goudarzi A (2022). Automatic assessment of intelligibility in noise in Parkinson disease: Validation study. JMIR 24(10):e40567
Gutz SE, Stipancic KL, Yunusova Y, Berry JD, Green JR (2022). Validity of off-the-shelf ASR for assessing speech intelligibility and speech severity in speakers with ALS. JSLHR 65(6):2128-2143
Automatic Speech Recognition for Intelligibility Assessment in Children With Dysarthria (2025). JSLHR
Inceoglu S, Chen W-H, Lim H (2023). Assessment of L2 intelligibility: Comparing L1 listeners and automatic speech recognition. ReCALL 35(1):89-104
Automatic recognition of second language speech-in-noise (2024). JASA Express Letters 4(2):025204

kept.claim: No evidence shows that tongue-twister practice improves clarity or intelligibility in typical native speakers. In speech science tongue twisters are used to induce errors. The single training study found (unconfirmed) measured only oral-motor outcomes: repetition rate and tongue movement distance. It did not measure intelligibility, so it neither supports nor refutes a clarity benefit.
kept.population: Healthy Japanese-speaking women (Ohkubo et al. 2025; sample size not verified); psycholinguistic lab participants (Wilshire 1999)
kept.effect_notes: Outcomes were diadochokinetic (rapid syllable repetition) rate and ultrasound tongue-movement distance, not intelligibility, listener ratings, or clear-speech acoustics. No control group was reported in the summary.
kept.design_implication: Drop tongue-twister speed ladders as a core clarity trainer for the native-French module. If kept at all, use them as a short optional warm-up where accuracy must pass a gate before speed increases. Reframe the ladder as 'keep the clarity features while the rate returns to normal' (see native-clarity-5), not 'go as fast as possible'.

citations.ref: Wilshire CE (1999). The 'tongue twister' paradigm as a technique for studying phonological encoding. Language and Speech 42(1):57-82
Ohkubo M, Kuriyama S, Nakata H, Sugiyama T (2025). Evaluating effectiveness of articulation practice with tongue-twister movement distance using ultrasound. Bull Tokyo Dent Coll 66(3):107-115

kept.claim: Trials of professional voice training (mostly in teachers) target vocal health, not articulation or intelligibility. The low-quality evidence available favours direct voice practice over hygiene education alone, such as tips or booklets. No controlled evidence was identified that diction or public-speaking courses improve measured intelligibility in typical adults.
kept.population: Teachers and other professional voice users; 26 studies in the teacher meta-analysis; one controlled study of preschool teachers
kept.effect_notes: Preschool-teacher study: direct voice training gave small-to-medium effects (r = 0.25-0.38), versus limited gains (r < 0.3) from a booklet alone. Measured outcomes were jitter, shimmer, maximum phonation time, and perceptual voice quality, not articulation.
kept.design_implication: Do not market voice-hygiene content as clarity training, and do not substitute text tips for practice. Build the app around doing and measuring (direct practice with acoustic feedback). Voice-care advice can be a small optional side panel for users who talk a lot, but it should not count toward clarity progress.

citations.ref: The effectiveness of vocal health programs in the prevention of voice disorders in teachers: A systematic review and meta-analysis (2022). Journal of Voice
The effect of vocal hygiene education programs on voice quality in professional voice users: A systematic review (2022). JSLHR
The effectiveness of voice hygiene and practical training for preschool teachers in Bosnia and Herzegovina (2025). Logopedics Phoniatrics Vocology 51(1)

does_not_work_supported.claim: Tongue-twister speed ladders as a clarity/intelligibility trainer for native speakers
does_not_work_supported.notes: Supported as absence of evidence. Wilshire 1999 frames tongue twisters as an error-inducing paradigm. The one training study (Ohkubo 2025) could not be confirmed, and it measured only oral-motor outcomes. Saying it found 'reduced tongue movement, not clearer speech' implies a negative clarity result that was never measured. Not live-verified.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Vague instructions such as 'speak clearly' give the smallest gains; concrete over-enunciation instructions give the largest
does_not_work_supported.notes: Consistent with Lam et al. 2012 and Lam & Tjaden 2013. However, 'speak clearly' still gave significant gains over habitual speech, and the 'overenunciate' condition was a short verbal cue, not concrete articulatory cues. The wording should say 'smallest of the instructed conditions', not imply the instruction fails. Not live-verified.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Rewarding slowness by itself
does_not_work_supported.notes: Bradlow et al. 1996 found no correlation between speaking rate and intelligibility across talkers. Krause & Braida 2002 found clear/normal speech kept much of the benefit. Picheny et al. 1989 and Uchanski et al. 1996 found that artificially slowing conversational speech did not reproduce the clear-speech benefit. Caveat: older listeners may still need a slower rate (Krause & Panagiotopoulos 2019). Not live-verified.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Raw word error rate on clean audio as the clarity metric for a typical native speaker
does_not_work_supported.notes: Supported by inference. Gutz et al. 2022 (insensitive for mild ALS), Inceoglu et al. 2023 (poor agreement for individual L2 speakers) and Kim et al. 2024 (Whisper fills in fluent content) all concern clinical or L2 speakers. No study validated ASR word error rate as a clarity metric in typical native French speakers. The ceiling-effect argument is reasoned, not directly tested. Not live-verified.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Assuming that effort equals improvement (about 44% of talkers showed no significant vowel benefit)
does_not_work_supported.notes: The direction is supported by Ferguson 2004 and Ferguson & Kewley-Port 2007 (wide variation between talkers). The exact 18 of 41 figure is unconfirmed. The outcome was vowel identification in /bVd/ words, and individual non-significance partly reflects limited power. Not live-verified.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Voice-hygiene tips or booklets as training
does_not_work_supported.notes: Consistent with Ruotsalainen et al. 2007 (Cochrane): hygiene education alone shows no clear effect, and direct training shows low-quality evidence of benefit. The cited 2022 and 2025 papers are unconfirmed. The outcomes concern voice health, not articulation. Not live-verified.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Read-aloud-only practice as proof of lasting clarity
does_not_work_supported.notes: Hazan & Baker 2011 found read, instructed clear speech more extreme than interactive clear speech. Lee & Baese-Berk 2020 found clear speech declines during conversation. Carry-over from drills to everyday speech is untested in typical adults. Not live-verified.

open_questions: Norms for European French articulation rate, pauses, and vowel reduction were not checked because the search budget ran out. Meunier & Espesser (2011), 'Vowel reduction in conversational speech in French: The role of lexical factors' (J. Phonetics, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0095447010000951), was located by title only and should be reviewed before choosing French baselines.

No validation was found of ASR-in-noise word accuracy as an intelligibility proxy for typical native French speakers. The best signal-to-noise ratio, babble type, and French ASR model (Whisper, Azure fr-FR, others) need a small in-app calibration study that compares against human transcription.
Long-term retention: no controlled trial was found showing that clarity training in typical adults carries over into unprompted everyday speech weeks or months later.

Does clear-speech training in L1 French transfer to clearer L2 English (or the reverse)? This is plausible given that clear-speech features are shared across languages, but it was not tested in the sources reviewed.

Reliability of formant tracking (vowel space, within-category dispersion) and of 1-3 kHz band-energy measures on phone microphones in uncontrolled rooms is unknown for this app. It needs test-retest checks before these are shown as progress metrics.
Detecting final-consonant and stop-burst release automatically, a key clear-speech feature, lacks a validated method in the sources gathered and may need forced-alignment heuristics.

Most clear-speech evidence uses listeners with hearing loss or in noise. The benefit of 'crisper' native speech for everyday listeners in quiet, and its effect on perceived competence or professionalism, was not examined here.

Method limitation: full-text fetching was blocked in this environment. Numbers come from abstracts and index summaries found by search. Sample sizes marked 'not verified' should be checked against the full texts.
