Lee ASY, Gibbon FE (2015). Non-speech oral motor treatment for children with developmental speech sound disorders. Cochrane Database Syst Rev CD009383. No evidence that non-speech oral-motor drills improve speech; supports dropping twister or oral-motor drills as clarity training. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD009383.pub2

Ruotsalainen JH, Sellman J, Lehto L, Isotalo LK, Verbeek JH (2007). Interventions for preventing voice disorders in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev CD006372. A better-established anchor than the unconfirmed 2022/2025 citations in native-clarity-12. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD006372.pub2

Smiljanic R (2021). Clear speech perception: Linguistic and cognitive benefits. In Pardo, Nygaard, Remez & Pisoni (Eds.), The Handbook of Speech Perception, 2nd ed., Wiley. A more recent review than the 2005 and 2009 sources in native-clarity-1.

learner_profile_review.topic: mobile: Short phone-based practice (5-15 min): evidence on mobile-assisted pronunciation training, session distribution and adherence, plus technical constraints (mobile browser audio capture, phone mics and noise, on-device vs cloud models, latency)
learner_profile_review.summary:
How I verified: this session had used up its web-search budget before I started, and the network proxy blocked every publisher and index site (doi.org, Wiley, Cambridge, T&F, arXiv, ERIC, HAL, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, learn.microsoft.com, webkit.org). Only GitHub and npm could be reached. So I checked the technical claims against the official sources that live on GitHub: WebKit and Chromium source code, MDN browser-compat-data and MDN content, MicrosoftDocs azure-ai-docs, and the Whisper, whisper.cpp, transformers.js and fairseq repos. I checked the literature through full texts, abstracts and bibliographic records hosted on GitHub: the arXiv full text of Zhang et al. 2021, Scopus/WoS records, ERCT study extractions quoting full texts, and published bib files. Wherever effect sizes come only from secondary extractions, the effect_notes say so. Treat those as approximate until someone checks the primary papers.

Bottom line for a French-L1 adult practising on a phone in 5-15 min sessions:
(1) Automated pronunciation training works moderately well, but only with explicit, localized corrective feedback and only over roughly 5-8+ weeks. One meta-analysis found 1-4-week programs gave almost no effect (g=0.07). Machine feedback on prosody is weaker than on individual sounds.
(2) Controlled mobile studies show gains in comprehensibility and fluency, but not in accent. They used about 10-30 min sessions, several times a week, for 8-12 weeks; shadowing on a phone is one of the best-tested formats.
(3) Spread practice across days, and favour how often the learner practises over how long each session lasts. Within a session, clustered repetition of one target is still fine for fluency.
(4) Dropout is the main risk: about 43% of adult app users quit within 3 months. Persistence tracks at least 5 min per session and at least 4 sessions per week. Use forgiving weekly goals, a fixed daily cue and a short comeback session, not fragile daily streaks.

Technically, a reliable phone session needs:
- HTTPS hosting, because browsers only allow the microphone on secure pages.
- AudioWorklet PCM capture producing 16 kHz mono WAV. Azure's REST API accepts neither iOS's audio/mp4 nor Chrome's audio/webm, and v1's hard-coded audio/webm fails wherever WebM recording is missing.
- One microphone stream kept for the whole session, and short foreground takes of 30 s or less. iOS interrupts capture when the page is hidden.
- Instant on-device feedback (level, pitch, speaking rate, pauses) while the cloud score loads, aiming for 2-3 s or less to first feedback.

Azure's own documentation reports only moderate agreement with human raters (Pearson above 0.5) and says quality falls with noise and mic distance. Microsoft also updates the models silently: the en-US and fr-FR scoring models changed in August 2026. The app should therefore check audio quality before each take, show trends rather than single scores, and keep anchor recordings to catch drift. Prosody, syllable and spoken-phoneme feedback is en-US only, so the French 'polish' track needs its own measures computed by the app.

On-device models: small ASR models (Whisper tiny/base, 75-142 MiB) are feasible via WebGPU or WASM. They are built to be robust to accents, though, so they hide mispronunciations and should not be used as the scorer.

kept.claim: ASR/CAPT pronunciation training shows a medium average effect (g about 0.69 across 15 ASR studies; d about 0.68 across 31 CAPT studies), mostly in Asian university EFL samples. Secondary extractions suggest larger effects with explicit corrective feedback, 5-8-week programs rather than 1-4 weeks, and segmental rather than suprasegmental targets (g about 0.82 vs 0.37). These moderator results come from small subgroups, I could not verify them against the primary paper, and they say nothing about programs longer than 8 weeks.
kept.population: Mostly university EFL learners in Asian classroom-linked settings: 15 ASR studies (Ngo et al.) and 31 CAPT studies (Mahdi & Al Khateeb). No French-L1 adult subgroup; small k.
kept.effect_notes: Ngo, Chen & Lai 2024 (ReCALL 36(1)), k=15: overall g=0.69; explicit corrective feedback g=0.86 vs indirect g=0.50; 5-8-week programs g=1.01 vs 1-4 weeks g=0.07; segmental g=0.82 vs suprasegmental g=0.37. Mahdi & Al Khateeb 2019 (Review of Education 7(3):733-753): 31 CAPT studies, d=0.68. Effect sizes come from secondary extractions; I checked DOIs and bibliographic data but could not open the publisher pages.
kept.design_implication: End every take with explicit, localized feedback: the word, the sound, what went wrong, one articulatory cue, and an immediate retry. A bare 0-100 score is not enough. Run the program in 6-8-week cycles with a pre-test and post-test, and do not judge it after 2-3 weeks. Treat automated prosody scores as weaker guidance than phoneme feedback.

citations.ref: Ngo, Chen & Lai (2024) ReCALL 36(1) - ASR in ESL/EFL pronunciation meta-analysis
Mahdi & Al Khateeb (2019) The effectiveness of computer-assisted pronunciation training: A meta-analysis, Review of Education 7(3)
Secondary extraction of Ngo/Mahdi effect sizes (GitHub research dossier)

kept.claim: Small studies of phone or app practice (n = 16-61; roughly 10-30 min a session, 8-14 weeks), most of them uncontrolled or quasi-experimental, report gains in comprehensibility, fluency or general oral proficiency. In the one mobile-shadowing study (no control, n = 16), comprehensibility and fluency improved but accentedness did not change significantly. Two classroom-embedded ASR studies did report gains on accentedness.
kept.population: Adult or university L2 learners (ESL in Canada; EFL in Saudi Arabia and China; Spanish learners in the US). Small samples (16-61), several without true controls. None are French-L1.
kept.effect_notes: Foote & McDonough 2017 (JSLP 3(1):34-56): 22 recruited, 16 finished 8 weeks of mobile shadowing of short dialogues, at least 4 times a week for at least 10 min. 22 listeners rated comprehensibility and fluency as improved; accentedness did not change significantly (details from secondary notes that checked the author PDF). Loewen, Isbell & Sporn 2020 (FLA 53(2)): Babbel, n=54, 12 weeks, about 10 min/day, gains in oral communicative ability; study time was the strongest predictor (secondary). Abdelrady et al. 2026 (WJEL 16(4)): ELSA Speak, n=60 (30/30), 12 weeks, 30 min/day outside class; 94% compliance under a course requirement; greater gains on all CAFIS dimensions. Sun 2023 (Front. Psychol.): randomized, n=61, 14 weeks; ASR plus peer correction beat teacher-led feedback on accentedness and comprehensibility.
kept.design_implication: Make a 10-minute core session the default, with a 5-minute minimum and an optional extension to 15. Aim for at least 4 sessions a week. Make shadowing of short, meaningful dialogues (native audio, then imitate, then compare) a core phone activity alongside targeted drills. Use comprehensibility and fluency as the main progress outcomes (intelligibility check, speaking rate, pause placement), not 'accent'.

citations.ref: Foote & McDonough (2017) Using shadowing with mobile technology to improve L2 pronunciation, JSLP 3(1)
Secondary check of Foote & McDonough methods (n, schedule, outcomes)
Loewen, Isbell & Sporn (2020) App-based instruction and oral communicative ability, Foreign Language Annals 53(2)
Abdelrady et al. (2026) ELSA Speak and EFL oral proficiency, World Journal of English Language
ERCT extraction of Abdelrady et al. (quotes on schedule and compliance)
Sun (2023) ASR and L2 pronunciation/speaking, Frontiers in Psychology

kept.claim: Spacing practice across days beats massing it, most clearly on delayed tests, and equal and expanding intervals perform about the same (Kim & Webb 2022; mostly vocabulary and grammar, moderate evidence). The evidence that clustered repetition within a session helps fluency, and that frequency beats total minutes, is indirect and correlational (weak).
kept.population: L2 learners across 48 experiments, mostly vocabulary and grammar outcomes; little direct pronunciation data. Duolingo users (n=287) for the dose study.
kept.effect_notes: Kim & Webb 2022 (Language Learning 72(1):269-319): 48 experiments, 98 effect sizes, N=3,411. Spaced beats massed with a medium-to-large effect; the benefit of longer spacing shows on delayed, not immediate, tests; equal and expanding schedules were statistically equivalent (secondary extraction; DOI checked). Suzuki & DeKeyser 2017 (LTR): massed practice produced faster utterances, pointing to a proceduralization benefit (secondary). Sudina & Plonsky 2023 (JSLS 6(2), n=287): frequency was the more dependable correlate; total minutes correlated with written but not oral gains (secondary).
kept.design_implication: Bring weak phonemes and phrases back across days with a simple fixed or ladder interval (about 1-3-7-14 days); do not build a complex expanding algorithm. Within a session, do 3-5 back-to-back repetitions of one target phrase (speed ladder or shadowing) for fluency, then move on. Put daily frequency ahead of long sessions.

citations.ref: Kim & Webb (2022) The effects of spaced practice on second language learning: A meta-analysis, Language Learning
Sudina & Plonsky (2023) Frequency, duration, and intensity of L2 learning through Duolingo, JSLS 6(2)
Secondary summaries of Kim & Webb, Suzuki & DeKeyser, and Sudina & Plonsky

kept.claim: Many adult mobile-language-app users stop within about 3 months, and many pause and later resume (single survival analysis, figures from a secondary summary). In a non-language habit study, missing one opportunity did not materially slow habit formation. Together these suggest strict unbroken daily streaks are not required. No cited study directly compares weekly-frequency goals against streaks for retention or learning.
kept.population: 3,319 adult users of a mobile language app (survival analysis); 601 Duolingo beginners over 6 months; 96 adults forming everyday habits (not language-specific).
kept.effect_notes: Hwang, Coss, Loewen & Tagarelli 2024 (SSLA 46(4):969-995): 43% dropped out within 3 months, with about 3 months of dormancy before resumption or permanent dropout. Engagement was predicted by at least 5 min per session, at least 4 sessions per week, and at least 7 consecutive active weeks; learners who paused and resumed persisted more (numbers from a secondary summary; bibliographic record checked in WoS data). Sudina, Teimouri & Plonsky 2025: grit and age were the only robust predictors of attrition (secondary). Lally et al. 2010: median 66 days to automaticity (range 18-254); missing one opportunity did not materially affect habit formation (secondary summary).
kept.design_implication: Replace daily streaks with a weekly goal (for example 4 of 7 days, at least 5 minutes each). Let the user pick a fixed daily cue and time, and send one reminder then. Make a complete, useful session possible in 5 minutes. After a gap, offer a 3-minute comeback session with no backlog. Do not penalize missed days.

citations.ref: Hwang, Coss, Loewen & Tagarelli (2024) Acceptance and engagement patterns of MALL among non-conventional adult L2 learners: A survival analysis, SSLA 46(4)
WoS record for Hwang et al. 2024 (WOS:001229053200001)
Sudina, Teimouri & Plonsky (2025) L2 grit and age as predictors of attrition in MALL, Learning and Individual Differences
Lally et al. (2010) How are habits formed, European Journal of Social Psychology 40(6)

kept.claim: Lossless phone recordings match a lab recorder for pitch (F0) and mostly for vowel formants. Lossy compression, call-app processing and background noise distort vowel-space and intensity measures unpredictably.
kept.population: Device-comparison phonetics studies with few adult speakers (Zhang et al.: 7 speakers, 504 tokens). The outcomes are acoustic measures, not ASR scores.
kept.effect_notes: Zhang, Jepson, Lohfink & Arvaniti 2021 (JASA 149(6)) compared a Zoom H6 reference, lossless phone apps (.wav/.ogg), and Zoom meetings (lossy .m4a). F0 had no device effect. Phone F1/F2 were close to the reference in Praat. Zoom showed lower F1 and random, extreme intensity drops. Their literature review adds that lossy formats distort F1-F2 inconsistently across speakers and that noise distorts vowel space (De Decker 2016). Sanker et al. 2021 (Language 97(4)) likewise report effects of device and software.
kept.design_implication: Capture uncompressed PCM and send 16 kHz mono PCM WAV, with no AAC or Opus step before scoring. Test getUserMedia with noiseSuppression and autoGainControl off against on. For any metric the app computes itself (vowel formants for French diction, pitch range), compare takes only within the same device, and store the device and browser with each take.

citations.ref: Zhang et al. (2021) Comparing acoustic analyses of speech data collected remotely, JASA 149(6)
Full text (arXiv 2103.01059) via GitHub mirror
Sanker et al. (2021) (Don't) try this at home! Effects of recording devices and software on phonetic analysis, Language 97(4)
De Decker (2016) Noise and LPC-based vowel formant estimates, Linguistics Vanguard

kept.claim: Microsoft reports a Pearson correlation above 0.5 with human judges and itself calls this 'high' agreement. For single-take feedback to one learner, that still leaves a lot of disagreement. Microsoft documents that quality drops with low sample rates, mic distance or remote connections, noise and multiple speakers. It updates PA models server-side and announces the updates in release notes (for example August 2026 for en-US and fr-FR); I found no documented way to pin a version. Prosody, syllable-group and spoken-phoneme outputs are en-US only.
kept.population: Azure Speech Pronunciation Assessment (en-US, fr-FR and 31 other locales), as documented in 2026.
kept.effect_notes: The transparency note (ms.date 2026-03-31) reports Pearson above 0.5 with human judges. It recommends 16 kHz or higher, the speaker close to the mic and not over a remote connection, little background noise, one speaker, and normal volume. It suggests asking for a repeat when a take scores below a threshold, and tells customers to evaluate the service in their own scenario. The how-to page says prosody, syllable groups and spoken-phoneme NBest are en-US only, and that REST audio for pronunciation assessment is limited to 30 s. Content assessment was retired in July 2025. The August 2026 speech-to-text release updated the en-US and fr-FR pronunciation assessment models.
kept.design_implication: Before sending a take, check audio locally (clipping, loudness, noise floor, single voice) and ask for a re-take if it fails. Show rolling averages and trends, not single-take scores. Save the scoring date or model version with each result, and re-score a fixed set of anchor recordings monthly to catch drift. Do not rely on Azure for French prosody or articulation: build the French 'polish' track on measures the app computes itself (speech rate, pause location, pitch range, elision and liaison checks) plus self or peer rating.

citations.ref: Microsoft: Characteristics and limitations of Pronunciation Assessment (docs source)
Microsoft: Use pronunciation assessment (prosody en-US only; 30 s limit)
Microsoft: Speech to text release notes (Aug 2026 en-US/fr-FR pronunciation assessment model update)

kept.claim: MediaRecorder output formats differ between iOS Safari and Android Chrome, and Azure's REST API accepts neither container directly. AudioWorklet PCM capture is the portable path, and the microphone only works on HTTPS pages.
kept.population: iOS Safari (WebKit) and Android Chrome (Chromium) in 2024-2026.
kept.effect_notes: WebKit always accepts audio/mp4 (AAC by default; Opus, PCM and ALAC optional) and uses it as the default type. WebM recording sits behind the MediaRecorderEnabledWebM preference, which current WebKit main turns on for Cocoa, so older iOS releases lack it. Chromium supports audio/webm (Opus or PCM) and audio/mp4 (AAC or Opus). Azure REST short audio accepts only WAV/PCM 16 kHz mono or OGG/Opus. Support per browser-compat-data: AudioWorklet in Chrome 66 and Safari 14.1; the AudioContext sampleRate option in Chrome 74 and Safari 14.1; MediaRecorder on iOS 14; Permissions.query for the microphone in Chrome 64 and Safari 16. MDN: getUserMedia is available only in secure contexts (HTTPS or localhost).
kept.design_implication: Replace v1's recorder (/home/user/Pronunciation-App/client/src/hooks/useRecorder.ts). It hard-codes audio/webm and decodes it in the browser, which breaks wherever WebM recording is missing. Use AudioWorklet PCM capture instead, downsample to 16 kHz, and encode WAV on the client. Keep MediaRecorder only as a fallback, chosen by isTypeSupported (audio/mp4 first on iOS). Serve over HTTPS, because a plain-http LAN address will not get the phone microphone. Check the permission state before prompting and explain the prompt up front.

citations.ref: WebKit MediaRecorderPrivateAVFImpl.cpp (supported MIME/codecs)
WebKit UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml (MediaRecorderEnabledWebM default)
Chromium media_recorder_handler.cc (audio/webm and audio/mp4 codecs)
Azure Speech to text REST API for short audio (accepted formats, 30 s PA limit, chunked transfer)
MDN browser-compat-data: AudioWorklet
MDN browser-compat-data: AudioContext (sampleRate option)
MDN: MediaDevices.getUserMedia (secure context requirement)

kept.claim: iOS interrupts microphone capture and audio when the page is hidden, and WebKit has a separate 'interrupted' AudioContext state. Developers report repeated permission prompts in installed PWAs when getUserMedia is called again.
kept.population: iOS Safari and iOS home-screen web apps (WebKit).
kept.effect_notes: In WebKit's UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml, InterruptAudioOnPageVisibilityChangeEnabled defaults to true on PLATFORM(IOS_FAMILY) (under MEDIA_STREAM). WebKit's AudioContextState.idl lists suspended, running, interrupted and closed. The re-prompting comes only from developer code comments citing WebKit bug 215884; I could not reach bugs.webkit.org, so treat it as weak evidence.
kept.design_implication: Keep takes as short foreground actions (15-30 s or less) and add no background or lock-screen practice mode. On visibilitychange to hidden, stop the take and discard the partial audio; on return, resume an interrupted or suspended AudioContext. Request the microphone once per session after a tap and reuse that stream across takes. v1 stops the tracks after every take, which invites repeated prompts. Upload each take right away through a retry queue.

citations.ref: WebKit UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml (InterruptAudioOnPageVisibilityChangeEnabled)
WebKit AudioContextState.idl ('interrupted' state)
Developer code note citing WebKit bug 215884 (standalone PWA re-prompts; unverified)

kept.claim: Small ASR models can run in a mobile browser today (WebGPU on Chrome Android 121+ and Safari/iOS 26; WASM elsewhere). General ASR is built to be robust to accents, though, so it hides mispronunciations and is not a validated pronunciation scorer. Phoneme-level recognizers are much larger.
kept.population: Browser inference stacks (transformers.js 4.3.0, ONNX Runtime Web) and the Whisper and wav2vec2 model families. One small study (Umezawa et al.) of browser ASR in self-study.
kept.effect_notes: Whisper tiny has 39M parameters and base 74M. In ggml form they take 75 MiB and 142 MiB on disk and about 273 MB and 388 MB of memory. The Whisper model card claims improved robustness to accents and noise, warns of hallucinations driven by language-model priors, and reports uneven accuracy across accents. transformers.js defaults to q8 on WASM and fp32 on WebGPU, with q4 and fp16 options. Browser-compat-data: WebGPU in Chrome Android 121 and Safari 26. Umezawa et al. 2023: in a 7-day comparison, iOS 15 speech recognition understood words even when mispronounced, and the authors judged it unsuitable for self-study pronunciation practice. The wav2vec2 phoneme recognizers (XLSR-53/LV-60 espeak fine-tunes) are Large-class models.
kept.design_implication: Keep Azure in the cloud for phoneme-level scoring. Use on-device processing only for cheap, instant signals: voice detection and auto-stop, a level meter, a pitch contour, speaking rate, and pause detection. These cover much of articulation (pacing, pausing, pitch range) in both English and French with zero latency. If a local 'was I understood?' ASR check is added, label it as lenient. Download models only on Wi-Fi, lazily, and cache them.

citations.ref: OpenAI Whisper README (model sizes)
OpenAI Whisper model card (accent robustness, hallucination)
whisper.cpp README (disk and memory per model)
transformers.js README (WebGPU/WASM, dtypes)
MDN browser-compat-data: GPU (WebGPU) support
Umezawa et al. (2023) Utilizing ASR for English pronunciation practice (ICEED)
fairseq wav2vec 2.0 README (phoneme recognition models)

kept.claim: Feedback within about 1-5 s keeps users engaged; beyond about 10 s they tend to abandon the task. Azure's short-audio REST API returns only final results, but chunked upload during recording cuts latency.
kept.population: General interactive-app users (HCI guidance); Azure Speech REST and SDK clients.
kept.effect_notes: Microsoft Power Platform guidance, citing Nielsen Norman Group: 0-100 ms feels instantaneous, 1-5 s is acceptable, 5-10 s lets attention wander, and 10 s or more leads to frustration or abandonment. Azure REST short audio gives no partial or interim results, and chunked transfer 'can significantly reduce the latency'. One developer dossier reports Azure adding about 3 s per assessment (anecdotal, unverified). There is no controlled study of feedback latency in pronunciation apps.
kept.design_implication: Aim for 2-3 s or less from stop-tap to first feedback. Show local feedback at once (waveform, duration, pitch and rate) while the cloud score loads. Stream audio during the take, either by chunked HTTP upload through the server or with the Speech SDK over WebSocket using a short-lived server-issued token, so AZURE_SPEECH_KEY never reaches the client. Keep items to 10-15 s or less. Avoid hosting that sleeps and cold-starts; v1's render.yaml uses a free tier with ephemeral storage.

citations.ref: Microsoft Power Platform: UX strategies for performance (response-time perception table)
Azure REST API for short audio (chunked transfer, no partial results)

does_not_work_supported.claim: General dictation ASR (Web Speech API, iOS dictation, Whisper transcripts) as the pronunciation judge
does_not_work_supported.notes: Supported by Umezawa et al. 2023 (n=28, 7 days: iOS 15 recognized words even when they were mispronounced) and by the Whisper model card's claim of accent robustness. The evidence is small and indirect for Whisper, but the logic holds: a correct transcript does not validate phonemes.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Expecting results from very short (1-4 week) ASR programs (g=0.07 vs 1.01)
does_not_work_supported.notes: This matches the secondary extraction of Ngo et al. 2024, but it is a subgroup contrast inside a k=15 meta-analysis that I could not verify at the primary level. Treat it as tentative. It shows little measurable gain in the studies included, not proof that short programs never work.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Accent reduction as the progress metric for short mobile practice
does_not_work_supported.notes: Foote & McDonough 2017 (uncontrolled, n=16) found no significant change in accentedness. However, Sun 2023 and Abdelrady et al. 2026 reported accent-related gains. The recommendation (use comprehensibility and fluency as primary outcomes) is still sound because accentedness is only partly related to comprehensibility (Munro & Derwing 1995). Saying accent never moves would be overstated.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Expanding-interval schedules as a special advantage
does_not_work_supported.notes: Kim & Webb 2022 found equal and expanding spacing statistically equivalent (confirmed by several independent summaries of the abstract). Its outcomes are mainly vocabulary and grammar.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Relying on Azure for French prosody, syllable or spoken-phoneme feedback
does_not_work_supported.notes: The how-to doc says prosody is en-US only, and syllable groups, spoken phonemes and phoneme names are en-US only (phoneme name also zh-CN with SAPI). The fr-FR model did receive an accuracy update in August 2026, but the feature set did not change.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Hard-coding audio/webm MediaRecorder, or sending MediaRecorder output straight to Azure REST
does_not_work_supported.notes: WebKit defaults to audio/mp4, and WebM depends on a preference that is enabled on Cocoa only in current WebKit, so older iOS lacks it. Azure REST accepts only WAV/PCM 16 kHz mono or OGG/Opus. Note that v1 decodes and re-encodes in the browser, so it does not send WebM to Azure. Its actual risk is constructing MediaRecorder with an unsupported WebM type.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Background, lock-screen or hands-free recording on iOS
does_not_work_supported.notes: InterruptAudioOnPageVisibilityChangeEnabled defaults to true on iOS (an embedder-level preference). WebKit also exposes an 'interrupted' AudioContext state.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Lossy or conferencing-processed audio for acoustic measures
does_not_work_supported.notes: Zhang et al. 2021: Zoom (lossy .m4a plus default noise suppression) had random intensity drops and formant differences, while lossless phone apps did not in Praat (VoiceSauce showed some Phone F2 differences). Compression and processing are confounded.

does_not_work_supported.claim: Comparing single-take Azure scores across sessions as proof of progress
does_not_work_supported.notes: The conclusion is supported: sensitivity to noise and mic distance is documented, and models change server-side (the August 2026 en-US/fr-FR update). Two supporting statements are inaccurate, though. Microsoft labels >0.5 Pearson as 'High', not moderate, and updates are announced in release notes rather than made silently.

open_questions: Verification gap: the web-search budget was used up and the proxy blocked all publisher and index domains. Effect sizes for Ngo et al. 2024, Mahdi & Al Khateeb 2019, Kim & Webb 2022, Hwang et al. 2024, Sudina & Plonsky 2023, Loewen et al. 2020 and Foote & McDonough 2017 come from secondary extractions and should be checked against the primary papers before they appear in project docs.

I found no accessible study measuring how much Azure Pronunciation Assessment scores shift between phone mics and studio mics, or across realistic noise levels (SNR). A personal calibration is needed: record the same items in quiet and noisy settings on the user's phone, then check score variance and test-retest reliability.

There is no MAPT evidence for French-L1 adults learning English, and practically none on app-based diction or articulation training for native speakers (the French 'polish' goal). This track would rest on transfer from speech-science measures (rate, pauses, pitch range) rather than tested interventions.
Optimal session length for pronunciation (5 vs 10 vs 15 minutes) has not been tested directly. The 5-min, 4-sessions-a-week thresholds predict engagement, not learning rate.
Li & DeKeyser 2019 (MLJ 103(3):607-628, doi:10.1111/modl.12580) is a pronunciation-specific spacing study (L2 Mandarin tonal words), but I could not access its results.
iOS 26 behaviour of microphone permission persistence in installed PWAs (the reported WebKit bug 215884) and WebGPU memory limits for 75-150 MB models on iPhones need testing on a real device.
Does disabling browser noiseSuppression and autoGainControl improve or hurt Azure scores on phones? This needs a small A/B test on the user's device.

Hosting: v1's render.yaml uses a free tier with ephemeral storage; free-tier cold-start behaviour is not verified here but is a likely source of slow first feedback. Phone use needs HTTPS hosting that stays warm and storage that persists.
missed_evidence: Saito & Plonsky (2019), Language Learning 69(3):652-708, DOI 10.1111/lang.12345 (77 studies): pronunciation instruction works best on specific targets measured in controlled tasks, and effects on globally rated spontaneous speech are much less clear. The app should include a spontaneous-speech transfer check, not only read-aloud scores. https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10068780/

Lee, Jang & Plonsky (2015), Applied Linguistics 36(3):345-366 (86 reports): d about 0.80-0.89, with larger effects for longer interventions, feedback, and controlled outcome measures. This is the base meta-analysis behind the ASR/CAPT findings. https://doi.org/10.1093/applin/amu040 (DOI from memory; not opened)

Uchihara, Karas & Thomson (2024), Applied Psycholinguistics, meta-analysis of HVPT effects on production (31 studies; per secondary summary: g about 0.49 within-group, low perception-production link at the participant level, explicit phonetic information roughly doubles production gains, about 20-30 min sessions). Also Uchihara et al. (2025) SSLA on perception (79 studies, g about 0.92). High-variability perceptual training is a strong candidate for short phone sessions and is missing from the findings. https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/applied-psycholinguistics/article/does-perceptual-high-variability-phonetic-training-improve-l2-speech-production-a-metaanalysis-of-perceptionproduction-connection/E38D8F5CE65DC708137B0E95F97C6BC7

Systematic review of shadowing for L2 pronunciation (2025; 44 studies per secondary summary): gains in comprehensibility, fluency and prosody, inconclusive for segmental accuracy, generally weak study quality. It updates and tempers mobile-2's reliance on one shadowing study. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/29984475.2025.2546827

Sun (2023), Front. Psychol., DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1210187: contrary evidence for 'accentedness does not change'. The ASR plus peer-correction group beat teacher-led feedback on accentedness and comprehensibility. It was a class-level assignment of 2 intact classes over 14 weeks. https://github.com/vassiliphilippov/erct-papers/blob/main/_papers/244-sun-impact-automatic-speech-recognition-technology.md

Silverman & Barasch (2023), Journal of Consumer Research, 'On or Off Track: How (Broken) Streaks Affect Consumer Decisions' (per secondary summary): intact streaks raise engagement, broken streaks demotivate, and flexible streak definitions preserve motivation. This refines mobile-4 toward forgiving streaks or weekly goals rather than removing streaks entirely. Secondary summary: https://github.com/Selftend/selftend/blob/main/docs/research/2026-07-14-habit-stacking-behavioral-activation.md

Lally et al. (2010) details the findings omit: only 62 of 82 analysed participants fitted the model (39 well), and about half never reached habit status in 12 weeks. So 66 days is a median among successful formers, not a planning guarantee. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.674

Microsoft's own interpretation table in the PA transparency note calls a 0.5-1.0 Pearson correlation 'High'. It should be quoted accurately if the app explains score reliability. https://github.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/blob/main/articles/foundry/responsible-ai/speech-service/pronunciation-assessment/characteristics-and-limitations-pronunciation-assessment.md

Munro & Derwing (1995), Language Learning 45(1):73-97: accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility are partly independent. This is the primary justification for choosing comprehensibility and fluency, rather than accent, as outcomes in mobile-2 and the does-not-work list.

Kessler, Loewen & Gonulal (2023), Computer Assisted Language Learning, DOI 10.1080/09588221.2023.2215294: a head-to-head Babbel vs Duolingo comparison of learning gains and user experience, relevant to app-dose and engagement claims (not verified beyond bibliographic record). https://doi.org/10.1080/09588221.2023.2215294

profile.claim: French learners carry French phrase-final prominence into English. They tend to put a pitch rise at the end of every prosodic word or phrase and misplace pitch accents before phrase boundaries and in final rises, which blurs where the word stress is. Pitch range itself did not predict comprehensibility.
profile.notes: I could not open Horgues 2013 (Research in Language 11(1)) or Herment et al. 2014 (Speech Prosody). Horgues does publish in Research in Language, and the AixOx corpus exists (Herment, Loukina, Tortel, Hirst & Bigi 2012), but the specific claims could not be checked. The 'pitch range was the only one of 19 measures unrelated to comprehensibility' detail from Isaacs & Trofimovich 2012 was not confirmed. The 'weak' label and 'descriptive only' caveat are appropriate. The note 'no training studies' is wrong for French learners: Guyot-Talbot, Heidlmayr & Ferragne 2016 (JEP; https://aclanthology.org/2016.jeptalnrecital-jep.30/) trained French students of English on yes/no and wh-question intonation. Three sessions of repetition with an on-screen display of the learner's and the model's F0 contours significantly reduced the learner-to-model contour distance. The design implication (compare contours with a model, focus on nuclear-accent placement) is reasonable.

profile.claim: For French university learners, teaching focused on prosody and teaching focused on individual sounds both improved English perception and production compared with no teaching, and neither beat the other. Together with Schwab et al. 2022, this suggests the amount of targeted practice matters more than the style of explanation.
profile.notes: I could not open the freelang.com Capliez thesis, so the group sizes, CEFR levels, ten 40-minute sessions and results are all unverified. Capliez also has a peer-reviewed article on French learners' segmental vs suprasegmental errors (Cahiers de l'APLIUT, 2011) that could be cited instead; not verified live. Schwab et al. 2022 is confirmed (see frl1-english-3). The design implication (short tips, a listen-and-repeat core loop, and both a prosody and a sounds track) is sensible and does not depend on this source.

profile.claim: Real-time visual feedback on word stress (a 3D spectrogram) gave French learners only a small gain in a tiny pilot with no control group, so for this population it is unproven.
profile.notes: Metadata confirmed through the author's GitHub-hosted publication list: Ivanova, M. (2024), 'Training English word stress perception and production with technology', The EuroCALL Review 31(2):45-56, doi 10.4995/eurocall.2024.20400. I could not read the abstract. The author (TU Chemnitz) mainly works with German and Slavic learners, so the claim that the 6 participants were French learners is unconfirmed and may be wrong. The figures (65% to 72.8%, 10 weeks, no control group) are unverified. The cautious conclusion stands on general grounds. But the idea that visual feedback is unproven for French learners overlooks Guyot-Talbot et al. 2016 (JEP), which found F0-contour display training improved French learners' English question intonation in 3 sessions. That study covered intonation, not word stress, was small and had no control reported in the abstract.

profile.claim: Feedback from ASR alone can elicit clear speech in healthy speakers. When shown an ASR transcription-accuracy value, speakers became clearer and more intelligible than in habitual speech, and they converged on the same acoustic changes as instructed over-enunciation: more distinct vowels and a slower rate.
profile.notes: Not live-verified (all hosts blocked; search budget exhausted). The citation gives no authors. A 2023 AJSLP paper with this title is plausible, and the PMID/PMCID look well-formed, but I could not confirm authors, sample (23 adults aged 23-40), ASR engine (Mozilla DeepSpeech), or the finding that acoustic changes converged with instructed over-enunciation. Even if accurate, this is one small within-subject study: immediate effect only, no retention, English only. 'Moderate' is too strong, and weak is the right level. The design proposal to fade feedback frequency draws on motor-learning principles (Maas et al. 2008), not on this study.
